whyNots.D: Savings Plans have no dependency on Auto Scaling being enabled.

hints: Savings Plans = discount on usage. Capacity reservation is a separate concept.
If guaranteed capacity in a specific AZ matters, that's what a (zonal) Reserved Instance or a dedicated Capacity Reservation is for.

questions.stem: A team commits to a modest hourly amount under a Compute Savings Plan. During a traffic spike, actual usage grows well past that committed amount. What happens to the usage beyond the commitment?

options.text: It's billed at regular On-Demand rates
It's throttled or blocked until the next billing cycle
It's billed at Spot pricing automatically
It's free, since the commitment already covers the account

questions.explanation: Any usage beyond a Savings Plans commitment is simply charged at standard On-Demand rates — the discount only covers usage up to the committed amount, and nothing is blocked or throttled because of it.

whyNots.B: Savings Plans don't throttle or block usage — extra usage is just billed differently, at On-Demand rates.
whyNots.C: There's no automatic fallback to Spot pricing; Spot is a separate, distinct purchasing option.
whyNots.D: Usage above the commitment is not free — it's billed at full On-Demand rates.

hints: The commitment sets a floor for the discount, not a ceiling on usage.
Go over it, and the extra is simply On-Demand — no penalty, no interruption.

questions.stem: A company runs workloads across EC2 (EBS volumes), RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS. Today each team schedules and manages its own snapshots independently, and nobody has a single view of backup compliance across the account. Which service lets them define one backup policy and apply it centrally across all of these resource types?
questions.explanation: AWS Backup is a fully managed service that centralizes and automates data protection across many AWS services in one place -- including EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, and more -- replacing the need for separate per-service backup tooling and giving one place to see backup compliance.

whyNots.A: Data Lifecycle Manager automates only EBS snapshots (and EBS-backed AMIs) -- it doesn't reach RDS, DynamoDB, or EFS.
whyNots.C: AWS Config records and evaluates resource configuration over time; it doesn't take or manage backups itself.
whyNots.D: Systems Manager Automation could be scripted to trigger backups, but that's building your own tool, not using a managed, centralized backup service.

hints: One service, one policy, applied across many AWS resource types at once -- that's the whole pitch here.
Its name is literally what it does.

questions.stem: A healthcare company keeps its production backups in the same AWS Region as its production workload. A new compliance requirement says a copy of every backup must also exist in a different Region, in case the primary Region becomes unavailable. Which AWS Backup capability satisfies this without building a separate replication pipeline?

options.text: Enabling S3 Cross-Region Replication on the backup vault
Taking a second manual snapshot by hand in the other Region on a schedule
Setting the backup vault's storage tier to Glacier Deep Archive
Configuring a cross-Region copy rule in the backup plan

questions.explanation: AWS Backup plans support copy rules that automatically copy completed backups to a backup vault in a different AWS Region (or even a different account), satisfying disaster-recovery and compliance requirements without any custom replication pipeline.

whyNots.A: Cross-Region Replication is an S3 bucket feature; AWS Backup vaults aren't S3 buckets, so this doesn't apply.
whyNots.B: That works, but it's manual, error-prone toil -- AWS Backup's whole purpose is to automate exactly this instead.
whyNots.C: A storage tier controls cost and retrieval speed, not which Region the data lives in.

hints: The feature is a rule you add inside the backup plan itself -- "copy to another Region."
No custom pipeline needed, and it can target another account too, not just another Region.

questions.stem: A team deletes a CloudFormation stack that includes an AWS::RDS::DBInstance resource with no DeletionPolicy specified. To their surprise, the database itself is gone, but a final DB snapshot of it still exists afterward. Why?

options.text: For AWS::RDS::DBCluster, and for DBInstance resources not part of a cluster, CloudFormation's default DeletionPolicy is Snapshot, not Delete
CloudFormation always takes a snapshot before deleting any resource, regardless of type
RDS automated backups are retained by default even without any DeletionPolicy setting
Someone must have manually added DeletionPolicy: Snapshot to the template before the delete

questions.explanation: Most CloudFormation resource types default to DeletionPolicy: Delete when none is specified. RDS is a documented exception: AWS::RDS::DBCluster resources, and AWS::RDS::DBInstance resources that don't specify a DBClusterIdentifier, default to DeletionPolicy: Snapshot instead -- so a final snapshot is created automatically even though the template never mentions a DeletionPolicy at all.

whyNots.B: The Delete default applies to most resource types -- a plain EC2 instance or S3 bucket, for example, is just deleted, with no automatic snapshot.
whyNots.C: Automated backups are deleted along with the instance unless a final snapshot is taken at deletion time -- this question is about a separate, CloudFormation-level default behavior, not the RDS automated-backup setting.
whyNots.D: The scenario states no DeletionPolicy was specified in the template -- the snapshot happened without anyone adding one.

hints: Most resources default to Delete. RDS is the documented exception.
It applies specifically to DBCluster, and to DBInstance resources that aren't part of a cluster.

questions.stem: Someone opened the console and manually changed a security group rule that a CloudFormation stack originally created, bypassing the template entirely. Weeks later, the team needs to know exactly which resources in the stack no longer match what the template defines. What should they use?

options.text: Re-run create-stack with the same template to reset everything
AWS Config's configuration history for that one security group
CloudFormation drift detection on the stack
Delete and recreate the stack from the template

questions.explanation: CloudFormation drift detection compares a stack's actual resource configuration against the configuration defined in the template, and reports exactly which resources have drifted and what changed -- precisely what's needed to find out-of-band manual changes across a whole stack.

whyNots.A: You can't "re-run create-stack" on an existing stack, and even an update wouldn't by itself reveal what had silently changed first.
whyNots.B: Config's history could show that one resource changed, but it won't tell you across the whole stack which resources still match the template and which don't -- that's what drift detection is for.
whyNots.D: That's destructive and throws away the running resources -- drift detection answers the question without touching anything.

hints: The feature is named for exactly this situation: template says one thing, live resource says another.
It reports per-resource, and per-property, what changed.

questions.stem: An architect keeps mixing up two AWS resilience concepts. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?

options.text: Multi-AZ protects against the loss of an entire AWS Region; Multi-Region protects against the loss of a single Availability Zone
Multi-AZ protects against the failure of a single Availability Zone; Multi-Region protects against the loss of an entire Region
Both Multi-AZ and Multi-Region only protect against the failure of one specific EC2 instance
Multi-AZ and Multi-Region are the same mechanism, just marketed under different names

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ deploys redundant resources across two or more Availability Zones within one Region, so the workload survives the loss of a single AZ. Multi-Region goes further, running (or standing ready to run) the workload in a second, geographically separate Region, so the workload can survive the loss of an entire Region -- something Multi-AZ alone cannot do.

whyNots.A: This has the two backwards -- Multi-AZ is the AZ-level protection, Multi-Region is the Region-level protection.
whyNots.C: Neither is about a single instance -- Multi-AZ and Multi-Region are both about surviving the loss of a whole facility (an AZ or a Region), not one server.
whyNots.D: They operate at different scopes (one Region's AZs vs. multiple Regions entirely) and typically involve very different architecture and cost trade-offs.

hints: Match the scope of the word to the scope of the protection: "AZ" protects at the AZ level, "Region" protects at the Region level.
Only one of these can survive an entire Region going dark.

questions.stem: A company wants disaster recovery for a fleet of on-premises servers: continuous replication so almost no data is lost, recovery in minutes if disaster strikes, and -- critically -- they don't want to pay for a full-size standby environment sitting idle in AWS the whole time. Which approach fits best?

options.text: A hand-built warm standby: a permanently running, scaled-down copy of the whole environment in a second Region
Daily EBS snapshots copied to a second Region, restored manually if disaster strikes
A hand-built pilot light: core data stores kept live in a second Region, application servers built from AMIs only after disaster strikes

questions.explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery uses continuous, block-level replication into a low-cost staging area (minimal compute, inexpensive storage) instead of running full-sized standby servers around the clock. AWS states it delivers RPOs of seconds and RTOs of minutes, and lets you pay for the full-size recovery environment only when you actually launch it -- for a drill or a real failover -- matching both the "almost no data lost" and "don't pay for idle standby" requirements at once.

whyNots.A: A hand-built warm standby runs a scaled-down copy continuously, which is exactly the ongoing idle cost this company wants to avoid.
whyNots.B: Daily snapshots mean up to a day of potential data loss and a slower, manual recovery -- not "almost no data lost" or minutes-level RTO.
whyNots.C: Pilot light is closer, but it's still a manually built and maintained architecture; DRS achieves comparable or better RPO/RTO with less operational effort and a cheaper staging footprint.

hints: The service name literally starts with "Elastic Disaster Recovery."
The trick is the staging area: cheap storage and minimal compute while idle, full-size only when you actually need it.

questions.stem: A team deletes an RDS DB instance without taking a final snapshot first, assuming the automated backups AWS had been taking every day would still let them restore it afterward. A week later, they try to restore from those automated backups and can't. What happened?

options.text: RDS automated backups (and the point-in-time recovery window they support) are deleted along with the DB instance unless a final snapshot is explicitly taken at deletion time
Automated backups are retained for exactly 35 days regardless of what happens to the source instance
Automated backups convert automatically into manual snapshots when the instance is deleted
RDS never deletes automated backups; the team must have deleted them separately by mistake

questions.explanation: Automated backups -- which power point-in-time recovery -- are tied to the life of the DB instance. When the instance is deleted, its automated backups are deleted with it, unless you choose to create a final snapshot at deletion time. Manual snapshots, by contrast, are independent objects that persist until explicitly deleted, whether or not the source instance still exists.

whyNots.B: 35 days is only the maximum allowed retention setting (0-35 days, 7 by default) -- it doesn't mean backups outlive the instance they came from.
whyNots.C: Automated backups don't automatically convert into anything at deletion time -- the only way to keep a restorable point is to explicitly create a final snapshot.
whyNots.D: This is RDS's documented default behavior, not an accident -- automated backups are deleted with the instance by design unless a final snapshot is taken.

hints: Automated backups are tied to the DB instance's lifecycle; manual snapshots are independent, standalone objects.
There's exactly one way to keep a restorable point when deleting an instance: take a final snapshot at deletion time.

questions.stem: A company wants their bare root domain -- example.com, with no subdomain prefix -- to point at an Application Load Balancer. A CNAME record isn't allowed at the zone apex per the DNS spec. What should they use instead?

options.text: An MX record pointing at the ALB's DNS name
A TXT record containing the ALB's DNS name
A Route 53 Alias record pointing at the ALB
A PTR record pointing at the ALB's DNS name

questions.explanation: Route 53 Alias records are a Route 53-specific extension that behaves like a CNAME for AWS resources (ALB, CloudFront, S3 website endpoints, and more) but -- unlike CNAME -- is allowed at the zone apex. Queries to an Alias record that targets an AWS resource are also free of charge.

whyNots.A: MX records route email for a domain -- they don't point a hostname at a load balancer.
whyNots.B: TXT records hold arbitrary text (often used for domain verification or SPF/DKIM) -- they don't resolve traffic to a target.
whyNots.D: PTR records map an IP address back to a hostname (reverse DNS) -- the opposite direction from what's needed here.

hints: This record type is a Route 53-specific feature, not a standard DNS record type.
It behaves like a CNAME for AWS resources, but the DNS spec's apex restriction doesn't apply to it -- and it's free to query.

questions.stem: A company runs a private hosted zone in Route 53 for internal.example.com, resolvable only from inside their VPCs. Now their on-premises servers, connected over Direct Connect, also need to resolve those same internal names. What should they set up?

options.text: A public hosted zone duplicating the private zone's records
A Route 53 health check pointed at the on-premises DNS server

questions.explanation: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint accepts DNS queries arriving from outside the VPC -- such as from an on-premises network over Direct Connect or VPN -- and resolves them using the VPC's Resolver, including records in private hosted zones. That's exactly the direction of traffic (on-premises asking AWS) this scenario needs.

whyNots.A: Duplicating records into a public zone would expose internal names to the internet and create a second copy to keep in sync -- the private zone should stay the single source of truth.
whyNots.C: An outbound endpoint does the opposite: it lets the VPC forward queries out to an on-premises DNS server, not the other way around.
whyNots.D: A health check monitors endpoint health for DNS failover routing -- it has nothing to do with resolving names across a hybrid network.

hints: The traffic direction here is on-premises asking AWS to resolve a name -- match the endpoint to that direction.
"Inbound" and "outbound" are named from the VPC's point of view: inbound means queries coming in from outside.

questions.stem: A news site's CloudFront distribution keeps serving a stale, hours-old version of an article that was just updated at the origin. The team wants CloudFront to check back with the origin for a fresh copy much sooner after each edit. What should they adjust?

options.text: The viewer protocol policy (HTTP vs. HTTPS)
The cache behavior's TTL (minimum/default/maximum TTL) settings

questions.explanation: CloudFront keeps an object at the edge for as long as its TTL allows before re-checking the origin (or honoring the origin's own Cache-Control/Expires headers, if the cache behavior is set to respect them). Lowering the relevant TTL in the cache behavior makes CloudFront revalidate with the origin more often, so fresh content reaches viewers sooner.

whyNots.A: Price class controls which edge locations serve the distribution, to manage cost -- it has no effect on how long objects stay cached.
whyNots.B: S3 versioning tracks object versions in the bucket itself; it doesn't change how long CloudFront caches a response at the edge.
whyNots.C: The viewer protocol policy controls HTTP vs. HTTPS for viewer connections -- unrelated to cache freshness.

hints: This is purely about how long an object is allowed to sit at the edge before CloudFront asks the origin again.
TTL settings live on the cache behavior, not as a single distribution-wide switch.

questions.stem: A CloudFront-fronted site needs a very cheap, very fast bit of logic that runs on every single viewer request: normalize the cache key, add a security header, and rewrite one query-string parameter. It must scale to millions of requests per second with virtually no added latency. What's the best-fit tool?

options.text: A plain AWS Lambda function (not deployed to the edge), invoked per request
An Application Load Balancer rule engine placed in front of CloudFront

questions.explanation: CloudFront Functions runs lightweight JavaScript directly at every CloudFront edge location, with sub-millisecond startup and enough throughput for millions of requests per second -- purpose-built for exactly this kind of simple, high-volume request/response manipulation (cache-key normalization, header edits, URL rewrites).

whyNots.B: Lambda@Edge can do this too, but it's built for heavier logic (network calls, larger runtimes, more compute) -- for this simple, ultra-high-scale case, CloudFront Functions is the lighter, cheaper, faster-starting fit.
whyNots.C: A plain Lambda function isn't deployed to edge locations at all -- every request would add real network round-trip latency back to a single Region.
whyNots.D: An ALB sits behind CloudFront in a typical architecture and isn't a substitute for edge request/response manipulation in front of the cache.

hints: "Millions of requests per second" and "sub-millisecond" both point at the lightest-weight edge-compute option.
This one runs JavaScript only, and only does simple request/response manipulation -- no external network calls.

questions.stem: On top of the usual header rewriting, one CloudFront behavior now also needs to call an external authentication API over the network before deciding whether to let a request through, using a small third-party SDK. Which edge-compute option actually supports this?

options.text: CloudFront Functions, since it already handles header manipulation
CloudFront's default cache behavior settings alone

questions.explanation: Lambda@Edge runs Node.js or Python functions, with up to 30 seconds of execution time depending on the trigger point, and supports network access, third-party libraries, and the AWS SDK -- capabilities CloudFront Functions deliberately doesn't offer in exchange for its sub-millisecond, JavaScript-only simplicity. Whenever the logic needs to reach out over the network or pull in a larger runtime or library, Lambda@Edge is the fit.

whyNots.A: CloudFront Functions is JavaScript-only, sub-millisecond, and explicitly doesn't support outbound network calls or external libraries -- exactly what this requirement needs.
whyNots.B: Route 53 Resolver is a DNS service; it has no role in per-request CloudFront logic.
whyNots.D: Default cache behavior settings configure caching rules, not custom application logic like calling an external API.

hints: The requirement list -- network calls, a third-party SDK -- is the textbook trigger for choosing the heavier of the two edge-compute options.
This one supports Node.js or Python, not just JavaScript.

questions.stem: A request flows through API Gateway, into a Lambda function, which then reads from DynamoDB before responding. Customers report the whole chain feels slow, but the team can't tell which of the three hops is actually the bottleneck. What should they add to find out?

options.text: A single CloudWatch alarm on the Lambda function's Duration metric
AWS X-Ray tracing across the request path
VPC Flow Logs on the Lambda function's subnet
A CloudTrail trail capturing API Gateway management events

questions.explanation: AWS X-Ray traces individual requests as they travel through each component of a distributed application, breaking the total time down into per-segment latency -- API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and any other hop -- and visualizes it as a service map. That's exactly what's needed to see which specific hop is slow, instead of just knowing the whole chain feels slow.

whyNots.A: A Duration alarm on Lambda alone only tells you about that one hop -- it can't show whether the real bottleneck is actually API Gateway or DynamoDB.
whyNots.C: VPC Flow Logs capture network-level IP traffic metadata, not per-request application latency broken down by component.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail records management and API calls, for auditing who did what -- not per-request end-to-end latency.

hints: The goal is a per-hop breakdown of one request's total time, not an aggregate metric on any single service.
The output is often described as a "service map" showing latency at each node.

questions.stem: A team is deciding, case by case, whether to write their new edge logic as a CloudFront Function or as a Lambda@Edge function. Which pairing correctly matches each tool to a scenario it's actually built for?

options.text: CloudFront Functions for logic that needs the AWS SDK to look up a value in DynamoDB before responding
Lambda@Edge for validating a JWT's format with sub-millisecond overhead at millions of requests per second
Either tool is equally suited to any of these scenarios, since both run "at the edge"
CloudFront Functions for lightweight header/URL rewriting at massive scale; Lambda@Edge for logic that needs network calls, larger runtimes, or more compute

questions.explanation: The two tools are deliberately built for different weight classes. CloudFront Functions is JavaScript-only, sub-millisecond, and scoped to simple request/response manipulation at enormous scale (millions of requests per second) -- no network access or external libraries. Lambda@Edge supports Node.js or Python, longer execution (up to 30 seconds depending on trigger point), the AWS SDK, third-party libraries, and outbound network calls, at a lower request-rate ceiling. Matching the tool to the workload means choosing based on exactly those constraints.

whyNots.A: A DynamoDB lookup via the AWS SDK needs network access and SDK support -- that's Lambda@Edge territory, not CloudFront Functions.
whyNots.B: Sub-millisecond overhead at millions of requests per second is CloudFront Functions' specialty, not Lambda@Edge's -- this pairing is backwards.
whyNots.C: They have different runtimes, different execution-time limits, and very different request-rate ceilings -- the choice genuinely matters.

hints: Match "needs network access, an SDK, or heavier compute" to one tool, and "simple, ultra-high-scale, JavaScript-only" to the other.
Two of the four options here describe a real capability but assign it to the wrong tool -- read carefully.

questions.stem: A company has 40 AWS accounts organized under AWS Organizations. Security wants the same CloudFormation template -- a baseline set of IAM roles and a security group -- deployed consistently into every one of those accounts, across 3 Regions, as one operation, and automatically applied to any new account added to the organizational unit later. What should they use?

options.text: AWS CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions
A single CloudFormation stack deployed once in the management account
A shell script that assumes a role into each account and runs a CloudFormation deploy in a loop

questions.explanation: CloudFormation StackSets extends a single template into "stack instances" across many accounts and Regions with one operation. With service-managed permissions -- integrated with AWS Organizations -- StackSets can also auto-deploy to new accounts as they join the target organizational unit, matching every part of this requirement in one managed feature.

whyNots.B: A single stack deploys to one account and Region at a time -- it can't reach 40 accounts times 3 Regions as one operation.
whyNots.C: A Config conformance pack checks and reports on compliance; it doesn't provision IAM roles or security groups for you.
whyNots.D: A hand-rolled loop script could eventually reach every account, but it wouldn't automatically extend to new accounts joining the OU, and it's exactly the kind of undifferentiated operational work StackSets is built to replace.

hints: "Same template, many accounts and Regions, one operation" is the StackSets tagline.
"Service-managed permissions" is the specific StackSets option that ties into AWS Organizations for auto-deployment to new accounts.

questions.stem:
You want bread. You can: buy flour and an oven and make everything; buy ready-made dough and just bake it; or buy bread already made at the bakery.

Using Gmail is like buying bread already made at the bakery. What model is this?

options.text: PaaS — you just deploy your code

questions.explanation: Gmail is SaaS — you just use it; you don't manage servers or code.

whyNots.B: PaaS is when you still manage your code. With Gmail you don't even do that — you just use it.
whyNots.C: IaaS is building everything (server, OS). With Gmail you don't do any of that.

hints: Think of cloud as bread — IaaS = flour + oven (you do almost everything); PaaS = ready-made dough (you just handle code); SaaS = bakery bread (comes ready).

questions.stem:
You need to ensure the company system does NOT go down if a data center catches fire or loses power.

What is the right way to avoid going down if a data center fails?

options.text: Store everything in an Edge Location
Distribute across multiple AZs in the same Region
One very large instance in a single AZ

questions.explanation: Multiple AZs = if one falls, the others hold. It's the foundation of High Availability.

whyNots.A: Edge Location is content delivery cache, not data center redundancy.
whyNots.C: A big machine in one AZ goes down with the AZ. Size doesn't give availability.

hints: A Region is like a city; AZs are different neighborhoods, each with independent power and network. If one neighborhood goes dark, the other keeps running.

questions.stem:
Your website runs on a server in Virginia (US). Users in another country complain that images and videos are SLOW to load.

What fixes the slowness for remote users?

options.text: Keep switching Regions all the time
Replace the server with a bigger one in Virginia
Use CloudFront with Edge Locations near the users

questions.explanation: CloudFront serves from the nearest Edge — performance goes up and users are happy.

whyNots.A: Constantly switching Regions doesn't bring content closer to users — CloudFront does.
whyNots.B: A bigger server in Virginia is still far away; distance is the problem, not size.

hints: An Edge Location is like a corner store — instead of fetching bread from a distant factory, you grab it nearby. Content is cached close to the user.

questions.stem:
A new learner is afraid of creating the account and getting a surprise bill at the end of the month.

What is the safest way for a learner to start practicing without a surprise?

options.text: Use the Free Tier with small resources like t3.micro
Create the biggest instance to learn fast, without worrying about consumption
Don't create an account and just read, since the exam doesn't require practice

questions.explanation: New AWS accounts enter the Free Tier, which includes a 12-month free tier and always-free limits for many services. There is no automatic upgrade to paid — you only pay if you explicitly upgrade. Using small resources like t3.micro keeps usage within free limits and lets you practice longer.

whyNots.B: A large instance burns through free-tier limits much faster — practice time ends sooner.
whyNots.C: Reading alone doesn't stick; practice is what passes the exam. And you can practice for free within the Free Tier.

hints: Every new AWS account enters the Free Tier — use small resources so the free allowance lasts longer.

questions.stem:
A regulation requires that customer data never leave a specific country.

How do you meet the data residency requirement?

options.text: Use the AWS Region located in that country (for example, sa-east-1 in São Paulo)

questions.explanation: The Region defines where data physically resides. Choose the AWS Region located in the required country — for example, sa-east-1 in São Paulo for Brazil. (In the exam, Route 53 Geolocation may appear alongside.)

whyNots.A: Edge Location is just content delivery cache, not where data lives.
whyNots.C: You decide where data lives by choosing the Region — it's not up to AWS.

hints: Choosing a Region is choosing the city where your data physically lives.
There is a Region in São Paulo — sa-east-1. Data stays there.

questions.stem:
A developer joins the call with a problem: 'I need a machine to run API tests. Variable load all day, no monster processing spikes. What instance type should I request?'

For an API server with variable load and no extreme CPU or memory spikes, which EC2 instance family is most suitable?

options.text: General Purpose (e.g., t3, m6i) — balanced CPU, memory, and networking
Accelerated Computing (e.g., p3, g4dn) — with dedicated GPU
Storage Optimized (e.g., i3) — many fast disks
Memory Optimized (e.g., r6i) — lots of RAM for in-memory data

questions.explanation: General Purpose balances CPU, memory, and networking — the right choice when the workload is varied and doesn't stress any specific resource. It's the family of t3.micro, the same as the Free Tier.

whyNots.B: GPU (Accelerated Computing) is for machine learning or rendering — expensive and unnecessary for a common API.
whyNots.C: Storage Optimized is for heavy disk read/write. A test API doesn't need that.
whyNots.D: Memory Optimized is for holding lots of data in RAM, like a large Redis. This isn't the case.

hints: Choosing an instance is like choosing a vehicle for a trip. You don't ride a motorcycle to move apartments, and you don't rent a truck to go to the grocery store. For an API that doesn't demand much, a balanced daily-use car is enough.

questions.stem:
'And when the team really migrates?' the manager asked. 'We will have three production servers running 24 hours a day, every day, for about 2 years. How do we pay for that without burning money?'

Three production servers that will stay on 24/7 for about 2 years. Which EC2 purchase model is the most economical?

options.text: Dedicated Hosts (an entire physical server just for you)
Spot Instances (spare capacity, can be interrupted)

questions.explanation: Reserved Instances offer up to 72% discount in exchange for a 1- or 3-year commitment. With 2 years of guaranteed continuous use, the discount pays for itself quickly (break-even usually comes in about 7-8 months). Predictable use calls for commitment.

whyNots.A: Dedicated Hosts only make sense for compliance or software licensing tied to hardware. Here it's just extra cost.
whyNots.C: Spot can be interrupted with 2 minutes' notice — you don't want that for a production server that must stay up.
whyNots.D: On-Demand is flexible but has the highest hourly price. For something always on, you'd be paying full price for no reason.

hints: It's like a transit pass. If you ride every day, the monthly pass is much cheaper than paying per ride. Steady, certain use? A commitment pays off.

questions.stem:
'There is also a job that runs every weekend, processing historical data,' said the developer. 'If it crashes in the middle, it's fine: just restart from scratch, nothing is lost.'

A batch processing job that runs on weekends and can be restarted without loss if interrupted. Which purchase model saves the most?

options.text: Spot Instances (up to 90% discount, can be interrupted)

questions.explanation: Spot uses AWS spare capacity with up to 90% discount. The trade-off is being interruptible with 2 minutes' notice — which is no problem for a job that tolerates restart. Interruptible workload + Spot is a classic cost-saving pair on the exam.

whyNots.A: Reserved is for long-term continuous use. A weekend job doesn't run enough to justify the commitment.
whyNots.B: Dedicated Hosts have nothing to do with this case — it's hardware isolation, not batch savings.
whyNots.D: On-Demand would work, but you'd throw away the huge Spot savings on a job that accepts interruption.

hints: It's like buying day-old bakery bread at a discount. Extremely cheap — but it can run out anytime. If you're not in a hurry and can come back tomorrow, it's worth it.

questions.stem:
The question left open at the start of the chapter: an unpredictable load with sudden, short spikes that must serve the user exactly when the spike happens.

An unpredictable workload with sudden, short spikes that must be available EXACTLY when the spike happens. Which purchase model makes the most sense — and why doesn't Spot work here?

options.text: Dedicated Hosts — only with dedicated physical hardware can you handle sudden spikes
Reserved — the long-term commitment solves any case, even unpredictable loads
Spot — it's always the cheapest, so it's always the best choice, even in this spike
On-Demand — available immediately, no commitment, and Spot could disappear right in the middle of the spike

questions.explanation: Unpredictable eliminates Reserved (commitment only pays off with certain, continuous use). Short and immediate eliminates Spot: it can be interrupted with 2 minutes' notice, and you can't risk the instance disappearing with a user waiting at the peak. On-Demand gives the flexibility to scale up immediately, paying only for what you use.

whyNots.A: Dedicated Hosts is about physical isolation (compliance/licensing), not handling spikes.
whyNots.B: Reserved requires predictable, continuous use to justify the discount. Unpredictable load doesn't match a 1-3 year commitment.
whyNots.C: 'Spot is always the cheapest, so always the best' is the trap. Cheap doesn't help if the instance is interrupted exactly when you need it.

hints: For this case, On-Demand is like a taxi. You pay more per ride, but it's there when you need it, with no advance arrangement. Spot would be a ride share that can cancel last minute — great when you're not in a hurry, terrible when a customer is already waiting at the peak.

questions.stem:
A developer ran a port scan on the environment and wants to understand what is blocking connections to the instance.

What is an EC2 Security Group?

options.text: A virtual firewall at the instance level that controls inbound and outbound traffic
A fixed IP address for the instance that identifies and allows permitted connections
An automatic daily backup of the instance disk, taken whenever a connection is blocked
A script that runs when the instance first boots and closes open ports

questions.explanation: Security Group is a virtual firewall that acts at the EC2 instance level, controlling inbound and outbound traffic. By default it blocks all inbound and allows all outbound — you open only what you need.

whyNots.B: Fixed IP is the Elastic IP.
whyNots.C: Disk backup is snapshots/EBS territory, not Security Group.
whyNots.D: Script on first boot is User Data.

hints: Think of a Security Group as the instance's doorman: it decides who can knock on the door (inbound) and where the instance can call (outbound).

questions.stem:
A developer needs a web instance: it serves HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443) to the internet, is managed by SSH only from the office (fixed IP 203.0.113.50), and the application talks to an RDS database on 3306.

What INBOUND rules must the web instance's Security Group have?

options.text: 80, 443, and 22 all from 0.0.0.0/0, plus 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0 — everything open to guarantee nothing is blocked
80 and 443 from 0.0.0.0/0; and 22 only from 203.0.113.50/32 — the RDS connection is outbound, not inbound
80, 443, and 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0; SSH doesn't need an inbound rule because its response is stateful
Only port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0; AWS automatically opens the web and database ports when it detects traffic

questions.explanation: Inbound: 80 and 443 open to the internet (0.0.0.0/0), and 22 restricted to the office IP (principle of least privilege). The connection to RDS originates from the instance — it's outbound traffic, automatically allowed. The inbound rule for port 3306 would go in the RDS Security Group, not the web instance's.

whyNots.A: Opening SSH (22) and the database (3306) to the whole world is a serious security hole.
whyNots.C: SSH restriction is missing, and 3306 is not inbound to the web instance — it's outbound from it.
whyNots.D: Security Group doesn't open anything by itself — by default it blocks all inbound.

hints: Separate inbound from outbound. HTTP/HTTPS is the public knocking on the door (inbound, from any IP). SSH is you logging in — restrict it to the office IP.

The instance CALLS the database; the database doesn't call it. A connection that LEAVES the instance is an outbound rule, and outbound is allowed by default. So no inbound rule for 3306 is needed here.

questions.stem:
A developer no longer wants to log in via SSH, install everything by hand, and close the instance every time a new one is created. They want the machine to come up with the environment ready.

Which EC2 feature runs a script automatically when the instance first boots, to configure the environment without anyone logging in?
questions.explanation: User Data is a script passed at instance creation that runs automatically on first boot — updates packages, installs dependencies, starts the application. It runs once by default, before any access.

whyNots.A: Elastic IP is a fixed address, not configuration automation.
whyNots.B: Key Pair is the SSH access key, not initialization.
whyNots.D: Security Group is a firewall, it doesn't run scripts.

hints: It's like leaving a note on the new apartment's refrigerator door: 'when you turn on, do X, Y, and Z.' The instance reads the note by itself on first boot.

questions.stem:
Layered architecture: a load balancer in front and application instances behind. The developer wants only the load balancer to talk to the instances on port 8080 — and this must keep working even if the load balancer's IP changes.

How do you configure the application instances' Security Group to open port 8080 ONLY to the load balancer, in a way that survives IP changes?

options.text: Pin the load balancer's current IP in the inbound rule for port 8080 — the ELB IP never changes after creation
Open port 8080 to 0.0.0.0/0 and trust that only the load balancer will use it — outsiders don't know the port
Create an outbound rule on port 8080 on the application instances — outbound controls who can enter
In the inbound rule, use the load balancer's Security Group as the source (group reference), not an IP

questions.explanation: Referencing the load balancer's Security Group as the source of the inbound rule opens the port only to instances in that group, without depending on IP. It's the layered architecture pattern: the application only accepts traffic coming from the load balancer's group.

whyNots.A: Pinning an IP breaks when the load balancer changes address (and it does change).
whyNots.B: Opening to the whole world is the opposite of least privilege — anyone on the internet could try 8080.
whyNots.C: Controlling who ENTERS port 8080 is an inbound rule, not outbound.

hints: A load balancer's IP can change. There is a way to say 'allow from whoever belongs to this group' instead of 'allow from this address'.
Security Groups can use another Security Group as the source. Then IP doesn't matter — what matters is which group the connection comes from.

questions.stem:
A developer drew the network blueprint: some resources need to be accessed from outside, others must stay hidden.

What is the difference between a public subnet and a private subnet in a VPC?

options.text: The public one has a route to the Internet Gateway; the private one does not — so resources in it are not directly reachable from the internet
The private subnet has all traffic encrypted by default; the public one transmits everything unencrypted
The public subnet has a higher hourly cost; the private one is free, which is why it's used for databases
The public subnet is always in a different region from the private one, to guarantee geographic isolation between them

questions.explanation: The difference is in the Route Table: the public subnet has a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing to the Internet Gateway; the private one doesn't. That's why resources in a private subnet (databases, internal servers) are invisible to the internet.

whyNots.B: Public vs private is about internet routing, not encryption.
whyNots.C: The difference is not price — it's routing to the internet.
whyNots.D: Subnets live inside a VPC and an AZ; it's not about different regions.

hints: Think of a building. The lobby is the public subnet — any visitor can enter. The archive in the basement is the private subnet — only insiders can access it. What decides this is the path (route) to the street.

questions.stem:
A database is in a private subnet and must never be accessed from outside. But it needs to download package updates from the internet occasionally.

What do you add to the VPC so an instance in a private subnet can REACH the internet (download updates) without becoming reachable from outside — and where must this component live?

options.text: An Elastic IP on the database instance itself
A NAT Gateway, placed in a public subnet
An Internet Gateway attached directly to the private subnet
A VPC Peering with the internet

questions.explanation: The NAT Gateway allows outbound internet access (updates, external APIs) without allowing inbound. It lives in a public subnet (has Elastic IP and route to the IGW), and the private subnet's Route Table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the NAT Gateway.

whyNots.A: An Elastic IP on a private instance would make it reachable from outside.
whyNots.C: Giving the IGW directly to the private subnet would make it public — the database would be exposed, the opposite of the requirement.
whyNots.D: VPC Peering connects two VPCs, it doesn't provide internet access.

hints: You want a one-way path — the instance goes out, but no one comes back in.
This outbound intermediary needs a public IP and access to the Internet Gateway, so it lives in the public subnet. The private subnet points its outbound route to it in the Route Table.

questions.stem:
Time to decide where each piece lives: the API that receives users, the PostgreSQL database, and the NAT Gateway.

In the architecture (API + database + NAT Gateway), which subnet should each resource live in?

options.text: Database in public (easier access), API in private (protected), NAT Gateway in private
Everything in the private subnet for security — users reach the API through the NAT Gateway
API in public (receives users), database in private (not exposed), NAT Gateway in public
Everything in the public subnet for simplicity — the Security Group already protects the database

questions.explanation: API in the public subnet (receives requests from the internet), database in private (never exposed — exposing a database is a serious risk), and NAT Gateway in public (needs Elastic IP and route to the IGW to forward outbound traffic from private subnets).

whyNots.A: Database in public is exactly what you want to avoid; NAT in private doesn't work (it needs public outbound).
whyNots.B: Everything private prevents users from reaching the API.
whyNots.D: Everything public exposes the database to the internet — unacceptable risk.

hints: The rule is simple — does it need to be reached from outside? Public. Only from inside? Private. And the NAT needs a public IP to do its outbound job, so it also belongs to the public team.

questions.stem:
Three VPCs: A (production), B (staging), and C (monitoring). There is peering between A↔B and B↔C. An instance in A needs to send metrics to C.

Can A talk to C automatically because of the existing peerings?

options.text: No — and the only possible solution is to redo everything in a single VPC, migrating A, B, and C to the same network
Yes — peering is always transitive in AWS: any chain of connections propagates routes by itself
Yes — since B talks to both, traffic from A passes through B to C, which acts as an intermediate router
No — VPC Peering is not transitive; you need a direct peering A↔C (or a Transit Gateway as a hub)

questions.explanation: VPC Peering is not transitive: A↔B and B↔C do not create A↔C. For A to reach C, create a direct peering A↔C. When there are many VPCs (or connection with on-premises), Transit Gateway acts as a central hub and avoids the tangle of point-to-point peerings.

whyNots.A: There are direct solutions (peering A↔C or Transit Gateway) without redoing everything in one VPC.
whyNots.B: Peering is never transitive in AWS.
whyNots.C: Exactly what peering does NOT do — traffic does not 'hop' through B.

hints: VPC Peering is a bridge between two neighborhoods. Having a bridge from A to B and from B to C doesn't give you free passage from A to C.
The keyword is 'transitive.' Peering is NOT. For many VPCs talking, there is a central hub that avoids building a bridge to each one.

questions.stem:
A developer wants defense in depth and asks about the difference between the two network controls that appeared.

What is the fundamental difference between Security Group and NACL?

options.text: Security Group acts at the instance level and is stateful; NACL acts at the subnet level and is stateless
Security Group acts at the subnet level and is stateless; NACL acts at the instance level and is stateful
Security Group is paid per rule; NACL is free — the difference is only price
They are the same thing with different names — both stateful at the same network level

questions.explanation: Security Group acts at the instance level and is stateful (the response of an allowed connection is automatically allowed). NACL acts at the subnet level and is stateless (requires separate inbound AND outbound rules; evaluates in numeric order and allows explicit Deny).

whyNots.B: It's reversed: SG = instance, NACL = subnet.
whyNots.C: The difference is not price.
whyNots.D: They are different layers (instance vs subnet) with different behaviors (stateful vs stateless).

hints: A Security Group is like an employee badge — once you pass the entrance gate, the exit is automatic (stateful). A NACL is like customs — you need separate authorization to enter and to leave (stateless).

questions.stem:
A malicious IP keeps showing up. The developer wants to BLOCK that specific IP at the entry of the entire subnet, before it reaches any instance.

Which resource allows you to explicitly DENY a specific IP at the subnet level?

options.text: Security Group (just create a Deny inbound rule)
NACL (has explicit Deny rule, at the subnet level)
Internet Gateway (has an IP blocklist at the edge)
Route Table (Deny route drops the IP at the subnet)

questions.explanation: Security Group only has Allow rules — everything not allowed is denied, but you can't deny a specific IP if the rest is open. NACL has explicit Deny and acts at the subnet: you create a rule denying the malicious IP (e.g., number 100, DENY) and another allowing the rest.

whyNots.A: Security Group does NOT have Deny rules — only Allow. That's the classic trap.
whyNots.C: Internet Gateway connects the VPC to the internet; it doesn't filter IPs.
whyNots.D: Route Table defines where traffic goes, it doesn't block IPs for security.

hints: Security Groups can only say 'you may enter.' They have no way to say 'this one may NOT.'
The one with explicit Deny rule, acting at the subnet level (before reaching the instance), is the NACL.

questions.stem:
An instance in a private subnet needs to read and write to Amazon S3 without traffic going over the public internet (and without paying NAT Gateway transfer charges).

Which type of VPC Endpoint is used to access S3 privately?

options.text: Interface Endpoint — the only one that works for S3, and it's free
It's not possible: S3 always requires the public internet, because it's a global service
Gateway Endpoint — available specifically for S3 and DynamoDB, and free
An additional NAT Gateway just for S3, which doesn't charge transfer

questions.explanation: S3 and DynamoDB support the Gateway Endpoint: free, configured via a Route Table route, keeping traffic inside the AWS network. For other services (Secrets Manager, SQS, SNS, EC2 API...), use the Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink), which creates an ENI with a private IP.

whyNots.A: For S3 the correct and economical type is the Gateway Endpoint; Interface Endpoint is for other services.
whyNots.B: Yes it is — the VPC Endpoint exists exactly to access S3 without the public internet.
whyNots.D: NAT Gateway makes traffic go out over the internet and charges per GB — the opposite of what's requested.

hints: Instead of ordering pizza over the public network, it's like having an internal extension straight to the pizzeria in the same building.
Only TWO services have the free Route Table type — S3 and DynamoDB. For the others (Secrets Manager, SQS...), use the Interface Endpoint.

questions.stem:
An instance receives HTTPS (443) requests. In the subnet's NACL, inbound 443 is allowed. But responses don't get back to the client. The Security Group is correct.

Why doesn't the client receive the response, even with inbound 443 allowed in the NACL?

options.text: An Internet Gateway is missing in the account: without it the NACL drops any response leaving the subnet
The Security Group blocked the response automatically — it is stateless and requires an outbound rule
Port 443 needs to be closed on the inbound for the response to leave through ephemeral ports
NACL is stateless: the OUTBOUND rule for ephemeral ports (1024–65535) is missing for response traffic

questions.explanation: NACL is stateless: unlike Security Group, it does not automatically allow the response. Response traffic leaves through an ephemeral port (1024–65535), and without an outbound rule allowing that range, the default `* DENY` rule blocks the response. Security Group would handle this automatically — NACL requires the explicit rule.

whyNots.A: The symptom (response getting stuck) is from a stateless NACL, not a missing Internet Gateway.
whyNots.B: Security Group is stateful — it would NOT block the response of an allowed connection.
whyNots.C: Closing 443 has nothing to do with it; the problem is the outbound ephemeral port range.

hints: Remember badge vs customs? One lets the return pass automatically, the other doesn't.
NACL is stateless — inbound and outbound are evaluated separately. Response traffic leaves through a temporary high port (ephemeral).
If inbound 443 is fine but the response gets stuck, it's because the OUTBOUND ephemeral ports 1024–65535 are not allowed in the NACL.

questions.stem:
The developer warned: if the only server crashes, everything goes offline. Traffic needs to be distributed among several instances.

What does a load balancer (ELB) do?

options.text: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple instances so one failing doesn't take everything down
Stores files uploaded by application users, acting as object storage
Creates a daily automatic backup of instances, ensuring recovery if one fails
Increases the RAM of a single instance on demand, preventing it from overloading

questions.explanation: The load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple instances. Instead of one server receiving everything (single point of failure), the load is split — and if one instance fails, the others absorb the traffic.

whyNots.B: Storing files is the job of S3/EFS, not the load balancer.
whyNots.C: Backup is another topic (snapshots/AWS Backup).
whyNots.D: Increasing RAM is vertically scaling one instance, not balancing load.

hints: Imagine a bank with ten teller windows and a greeter at the entrance sending each customer to the shortest line. The load balancer is that greeter — no one gets overloaded, and if one teller closes, the others absorb the customers.

questions.stem:
An e-commerce application needs to route by URL path: /api goes to the back-end, /static goes to the image service.

Which type of load balancer does path-based routing?

options.text: CLB (Classic Load Balancer) — the old generation, which routes by path and header
ALB (Application Load Balancer) — layer 7, understands HTTP and routes by path/host/header
GWLB (Gateway Load Balancer) — built to inspect HTTP and route by path
NLB (Network Load Balancer) — layer 4, understands HTTP and routes by path/host

questions.explanation: Routing by path/host/header is a layer 7 (HTTP) feature, and the load balancer that operates at this layer is the ALB. It reads the request and sends /api and /static to different Target Groups.

whyNots.A: CLB is legacy and lacks the content-based routing of the ALB; avoid in new projects.
whyNots.C: GWLB is for network security appliances, not for web application routing.
whyNots.D: NLB is layer 4 (TCP/UDP) — it doesn't read HTTP content, so it can't route by path.

hints: Routing by /api vs /static means reading the HTTP request content. That's layer 7 stuff.
The load balancer that understands HTTP and decides by path, header, or host is the Application Load Balancer — ALB.

questions.stem:
An online game server uses UDP for real-time communication and needs latency below 1 millisecond.

Which type of load balancer is most suitable?

options.text: GWLB (Gateway Load Balancer) — optimized for game UDP traffic
CLB (Classic Load Balancer) — the veteran, with the fastest UDP on AWS
NLB (Network Load Balancer) — layer 4, ultra-low latency, supports UDP
ALB (Application Load Balancer) — layer 7, with native UDP support

questions.explanation: UDP and sub-1ms latency are layer 4 territory. The NLB just forwards packets (without inspecting content), with minimal latency, and supports TCP/UDP — plus it can have a static IP.

whyNots.A: GWLB is for inspecting traffic with security appliances, not for a UDP game.
whyNots.B: CLB is legacy, without the performance and features of the NLB.
whyNots.D: ALB is layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and doesn't support UDP or layer 4 latency.

hints: UDP and minimum latency call for the load balancer that DOESN'T waste time reading content — it just forwards packets. That's the network load balancer, layer 4: the NLB.

questions.stem:
A reservation application has a predictable peak (9 AM to 6 PM on weekdays, low at night and weekends) AND unpredictable spikes when surprise promotions launch.

Which combination of Auto Scaling policies is most efficient for both patterns at the same time?

options.text: No policy — leaving the number of instances fixed at the maximum all the time is cheaper
Only Simple Scaling with a CPU alarm — it already covers both the predictable and surprise patterns
Only Scheduled Scaling — just schedule everything, even surprise promotions fit the schedule
Scheduled Scaling (for the predictable daily pattern) + Target Tracking (reacts to surprise spikes)

questions.explanation: Scheduled Scaling provisions before the predictable peak (e.g., scale up at 8:45 AM, down at 6:15 PM) — proactive and economical. Target Tracking maintains a target (e.g., 60% CPU) and reacts to unpredictable promotion spikes, scaling beyond the schedule. Together, they guarantee capacity at the right time and absorb surprises — a classic cost + availability pattern.

whyNots.A: Staying at maximum all the time wastes money at night and on weekends — the opposite of cost optimization.
whyNots.B: Simple Scaling reacts, but it's crude (oscillates) and doesn't take advantage of the predictable daily pattern.
whyNots.C: Scheduling alone doesn't cover surprise promotions — you don't know when they come.

hints: There are two different patterns. One you know the time for (every day 9 AM to 6 PM). The other you DON'T know when it comes (surprise promotion).
For the predictable one, schedule. For the unpredictable one, you need something reactive that watches CPU/load and scales by itself. You can use both together.

questions.stem:
A developer was saving user files inside the instance. When Auto Scaling terminated the instance, the files disappeared. A central place outside the instance is needed.

What is Amazon S3?

options.text: Object storage (files), accessed by key — not a database or file system
A managed network firewall that filters inbound and outbound bucket traffic
The block-based virtual disk that attaches to an EC2 instance to store the system
A managed relational database with tables and SQL, for storing files as records

questions.explanation: S3 is OBJECT storage: any file (image, video, backup, log), stored in a bucket and retrieved by key. Eleven nines durability. Not a file system or database.

whyNots.B: Firewall is Security Group / NACL.
whyNots.C: Instance disk is EBS.
whyNots.D: Managed relational database is RDS.

hints: Think of S3 as a warehouse with numbered shelves. You store a box (object) and note the number (the key). To retrieve it, you ask by number. It's not a real folder — it's a label.

questions.stem:
Audit logs must be kept for 7 years at the lowest possible cost. They are almost never accessed — and when they are, waiting up to 12 hours to retrieve is acceptable.

Which S3 storage class is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest for storage, with retrieval in 12–48 hours — perfect for long-term compliance retention that is almost never read. The wait cost is acceptable per the statement.

whyNots.A: Standard-IA is cheaper than Standard, but still much more expensive than Glacier for 7-year archive.
whyNots.C: Standard is for frequent access — very expensive for storing 7 years of idle logs.
whyNots.D: Glacier Instant delivers in milliseconds (and costs more) — you're paying for speed the statement doesn't require.

hints: The rule is — the less you access, the cheaper to store (and slower/more expensive to retrieve). Here access is extremely rare and urgency is zero.
A 12-hour wait is the green light for the cheapest level of all, made for dead compliance archives.

questions.stem:
A dataset has UNPREDICTABLE access patterns — sometimes heavily accessed, sometimes forgotten for months. The developer doesn't want to keep guessing the class manually.

Which S3 class automatically moves objects between cost tiers based on access?
questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering monitors access and moves objects between tiers (frequent, infrequent...) automatically, with no retrieval charge — only a small monitoring fee. It's the choice when the pattern is unpredictable.

whyNots.A: Glacier Flexible is archive with hour-scale retrieval — bad for data that is sometimes heavily accessed.
whyNots.B: One Zone-IA is cheap but stores in one AZ only (loss risk) and doesn't move automatically.
whyNots.D: Standard is fixed at the most expensive tier — it doesn't optimize itself.

hints: When you DON'T know the access pattern, let AWS observe and move objects by itself. There's a class that does exactly that, for a small monitoring fee.

questions.stem:
Nightly database backups: rarely used, but if restoration is needed, the team must be able to access them within 5 minutes.

Which class balances low storage cost AND near-instant availability (minutes)?

options.text: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (retrieval in milliseconds, minimum cost)
S3 Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest class, near-instant access)
S3 Standard (lowest storage cost among all classes)
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (access in milliseconds, cheap storage)

questions.explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval stores cheap (rarely accessed archive) and retrieves in milliseconds — meeting the 'within 5 minutes' requirement. Standard-IA would also work, but Glacier Instant has lower storage cost for rarely accessed data.

whyNots.A: Glacier Flexible takes minutes to hours (standard 3–5 hours) — risks exceeding the 5 minutes.
whyNots.B: Deep Archive takes 12–48 hours — far beyond the requirement.
whyNots.C: Standard meets the speed but is the most expensive for storing something almost never accessed.

hints: The trap is retrieval time. 'Within 5 minutes' eliminates any class that takes HOURS.
You want cheap archive BUT fast access. There's a Glacier that delivers in milliseconds — that's the one.

questions.stem:
A Lambda function needs to write files to an S3 bucket. The developer thought about putting a fixed access key in the code.

What is the CORRECT way to give the Lambda permission to S3 without exposing credentials in code?

options.text: Assign an IAM Role to the Lambda with s3:PutObject permission
Share the instance .pem file with the Lambda
Make the bucket public so anyone can write
Put the Access Key and Secret Key hardcoded in the Lambda code

questions.explanation: The Lambda assumes an IAM Role at execution, and that Role carries the permission (e.g., s3:PutObject). No fixed key in code — the credential is temporary and managed by AWS.

whyNots.B: .pem is an EC2 instance SSH key, unrelated to Lambda permission on S3.
whyNots.C: A public bucket opens content to the world — the opposite of secure.
whyNots.D: Hardcoded keys leak easily (repository, logs) and are a bad practice.

hints: Credentials in code are a classic security hole. The right way is for the Lambda to 'wear a temporary badge' at runtime — an IAM Role — that says what it can do.

questions.stem:
A regulation requires that certain objects in S3 cannot be deleted or altered by ANYONE — not even the account root user — for 5 years.

Which feature guarantees this total immutability?

options.text: S3 Object Lock in Governance mode
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode
A bucket policy with Deny on DeleteObject

questions.explanation: Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents deletion or alteration by any entity — including the root account — until the retention period ends. That is true immutability for compliance.

whyNots.A: In Governance mode, a user with a special permission CAN bypass the lock — it does not meet the 'not even root' requirement.
whyNots.C: A bucket policy can be changed by whoever administers the account; it does not guarantee immutability.
whyNots.D: Versioning keeps versions, but it does not prevent permanent deletion the way Object Lock Compliance does.

hints: Think about which Object Lock mode allows no exceptions for anyone.
Remember that Object Lock has two modes. One can be bypassed by authorized users; the other is true, exception-free immutability — Compliance.

questions.stem:
A healthcare company stores medical records in S3. It needs: encryption at rest, a log of who used the key and when, and the ability to revoke access to the key WITHOUT deleting the data.

Which encryption option meets all of these requirements?

options.text: None — S3 does not encrypt at rest, only in transit via HTTPS
SSE-C (you provide the key in each request), audited directly in CloudTrail
SSE-KMS (key managed in KMS, with CloudTrail audit and revocation)
SSE-S3 (AWS manages everything automatically), with per-key logging and revocation

questions.explanation: SSE-KMS uses KMS: every key use is logged in CloudTrail (audit), and you can disable the key to revoke access without deleting the objects (they remain in S3 but become inaccessible).

whyNots.A: S3 does encrypt at rest — SSE-S3 has been the default since 2023.
whyNots.B: SSE-C leaves the key with you and provides no AWS-managed audit of key use.
whyNots.D: SSE-S3 encrypts, but it does not provide per-key audit logging or controlled revocation.

hints: Think about which key service records every use and lets you turn off the key.
Remember that SSE-S3 is automatic but does not audit per key; SSE-C gives you the key without AWS audit. KMS records use in CloudTrail and allows revocation.

questions.stem:
A user wants to download their own document stored in S3. The bucket is PRIVATE and must stay private, and the user has no AWS credentials.

How do you allow that file download without making the bucket public?

options.text: Disable Block Public Access and make the bucket public for a few minutes, then lock it down again
Move the file to Glacier Deep Archive, which generates a public download link on demand
Give the end user an AWS access key with a read policy — the recommended pattern
The backend generates a temporary presigned URL (e.g., 15 minutes) and delivers it to the authenticated user

questions.explanation: Presigned URL: the backend, authenticated by its IAM role, generates a temporary URL for that specific object. The user downloads directly from S3 until the URL expires, and the bucket stays private. This is the standard pattern for one-time access without exposing the bucket.

whyNots.A: Making the bucket public violates the requirement and exposes everyone's files.
whyNots.B: Changing the storage class has nothing to do with securely enabling a download.
whyNots.C: Giving AWS credentials to an end user is a serious security risk.

hints: Think about opening a door for just one file, for a limited time, without unlocking the whole bucket.
Remember that the backend, using its IAM role, can sign a short-lived URL. The recipient can access only that object until it expires — no AWS credentials required.

questions.stem:
A developer noticed that every EC2 instance already comes with a disk. They want to understand how that disk differs from S3.

What is Amazon EBS?

options.text: Block storage — a virtual disk (HDD/SSD) attached to an EC2 instance
A shared file system used by several instances at the same time via NFS
A managed database with backups and replicas handled by AWS
Object storage accessed over HTTP, with public URLs for each file

questions.explanation: EBS (Elastic Block Store) is block storage: a virtual disk attached to an EC2 instance that the instance sees as a local HDD/SSD. It lives in a single AZ and persists after the instance stops.

whyNots.B: A shared file system across instances is EFS.
whyNots.C: A managed database is RDS.
whyNots.D: Objects over HTTP are S3.

hints: Think of the difference like a thumb drive versus an internal hard drive. S3 is a warehouse you reach by key over HTTP. EBS is the instance's disk — it looks like a normal drive and holds the operating system.

questions.stem:
Two EC2 instances in DIFFERENT Availability Zones need to read from and write to the SAME file system at the same time.

Which storage service supports this cross-AZ sharing?

options.text: Amazon S3 with a local File Gateway
Amazon EFS (shared NFS file system, multi-AZ)
Amazon EBS (one volume per instance, tied to one AZ)

questions.explanation: EFS is a managed NFS file system accessible from any AZ in the region: multiple instances can mount it and share the same files simultaneously. EBS is per instance and tied to one AZ (Multi-Attach io1/io2 still stay within the same AZ).

whyNots.A: File Gateway is for extending on-premises storage, not for sharing between EC2 instances in the cloud.
whyNots.C: EBS is tied to one AZ and generally to one instance — it is not the multi-AZ sharing requested.
whyNots.D: Instance Store is ephemeral disk — it disappears when the instance stops and is not shared.

hints: Remember that EBS is like a laptop's hard drive — only you use it. Here you need a company file server that everyone mounts at the same time.
Think about what works across different AZs. EBS is locked to one AZ. The managed, multi-AZ NFS file system is EFS.

questions.stem:
A bank needs to migrate 2 PB of historical data from its data center to S3. The company's internet link is 1 Gbps, so uploading everything would take more than a year.

What is the fastest and most practical way to migrate this data?

options.text: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration, which solves any volume problem even over a slow, unstable link
Upload everything over the internet with parallel multipart upload, which compensates for limited bandwidth
AWS Snow Family (e.g., Snowball Edge) — a physical device AWS ships, you copy data, and return it
Buy a larger EC2 instance, since the upload bottleneck is the source machine

questions.explanation: For huge volumes with limited bandwidth, the Snow Family is the way to go: physical devices (each Snowball Edge holds 80 TB; for 2 PB, use several in parallel) that AWS ships, you copy data, return them, and AWS loads the data into your S3 bucket. It is faster and cheaper than the internet in this case.

whyNots.A: Transfer Acceleration helps with long-distance uploads, but it cannot solve the magnitude of 2 PB over 1 Gbps.
whyNots.B: 2 PB at 1 Gbps would still take more than a year, even parallelized — not feasible.
whyNots.D: A larger instance does not speed up transfer over the internet.

hints: Remember that if uploading over the internet would take more than a week, it is time to calculate Snow. AWS ships one or more physical devices, you copy the data, return them, and the data appears in S3.

questions.stem:
An EC2 instance runs SQL Server and needs 50,000 consistent IOPS without fluctuation.

Which EBS volume type meets this high, consistent IOPS requirement?

options.text: st1 — throughput-optimized HDD with high, consistent IOPS
sc1 — cold HDD, the cheapest, sufficient for any transactional database
gp3 — general-purpose SSD, up to 16,000 IOPS, the only type with provisioned IOPS
io2 (or io1) — SSD with provisioned IOPS, up to 64,000 (256,000 with io2 Block Express)

questions.explanation: io2/io1 are SSD volumes with provisioned, consistent IOPS — io2 reaches 64,000 IOPS (256,000 with Block Express), covering the 50,000 required by a critical database. gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS, which is insufficient.

whyNots.A: st1 is a throughput HDD for sequential access, not for the high random IOPS of a database.
whyNots.B: sc1 is a cold, cheap, slow HDD — the opposite of what is needed.
whyNots.C: gp3 is cost-effective, but its ceiling of 16,000 IOPS falls below the 50,000 requested.

hints: Think about which EBS family is built for critical databases with provisioned IOPS.
Remember that gp3 stops at 16,000 IOPS — not enough for 50,000. The io family delivers guaranteed high IOPS.

questions.stem:
A database administrator managed MySQL by hand inside an EC2 instance: backups, patching, failover — everything was their responsibility. One failure caused 60 minutes of downtime.

When using Amazon RDS, what does AWS manage for you?

options.text: Automatic backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover — you handle only the schema, queries, and data
Your queries and data model, but not the infrastructure — patching and backup stay with you
Only the daily automatic backup; patching, failover, and monitoring remain manual
Nothing — RDS is just an EC2 instance with a different name, and you still manage everything via SSH

questions.explanation: RDS is a managed relational database: AWS handles automatic backups (PITR), patching, monitoring, and Multi-AZ failover. You remain responsible for the schema, queries, and data.

whyNots.B: This is reversed — AWS manages the infrastructure; the schema and queries stay with you.
whyNots.C: AWS handles far more than backups: patching, failover, and monitoring too.
whyNots.D: RDS abstracts exactly the infrastructure management that a raw EC2 instance would require.

hints: Remember that RDS takes infrastructure weight off your shoulders. AWS handles backup, patching, and failover; you keep what is truly yours — the schema, queries, and data.

questions.stem:
An RDS MySQL application becomes SLOW on READ queries during traffic spikes (heavy dashboards). Writes remain normal.

What do you add to scale reads without affecting the primary instance?

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ (the standby starts serving reads and splits the dashboards)
Read Replicas and point heavy queries to them
Switch to a faster EBS volume, which separates reads from writes
Increase the primary instance's storage — more space means more reads

questions.explanation: Read Replicas are asynchronously replicated copies that accept reads. You point heavy queries (reports/dashboards) to the replica endpoint, offloading the primary. Multi-AZ does NOT help here — the standby exists only for failover, not for reads.

whyNots.A: The Multi-AZ standby does not accept reads — it only takes over on failure. Multi-AZ is availability, not read scaling.
whyNots.C: A faster disk helps I/O but does not separate read load from write load the way a replica does.
whyNots.D: More storage does not resolve a concurrent read bottleneck.

hints: The problem is only READS. You want to remove that load from the instance that also handles writes.
Remember there is a feature that creates read-only copies of the database. Move the dashboards to them and the primary can breathe.

questions.stem:
Requirement: the database must not be down more than 2 minutes if the instance suffers a hardware failure. Failover must be automatic.

Which RDS feature guarantees high availability with automatic failover?

options.text: Hourly manual snapshots — instant restore if the instance fails
Read Replica — a synchronous replica that takes over automatically on failure
Multi-AZ — synchronous replica in another AZ, automatic failover in ~1–2 minutes
Increase backup retention to 35 days, covering hardware failure

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ; if the primary fails, RDS automatically points the endpoint to the standby in ~1–2 minutes. A Read Replica is asynchronous and requires MANUAL promotion — it does not guarantee automatic failover.

whyNots.A: Snapshots are backups, not failover — restoring takes time and creates a new instance.
whyNots.B: A Read Replica does not fail over automatically — you must promote it manually, and replication is asynchronous.
whyNots.D: Backup retention is data recovery, not continuous availability.

hints: Here the topic is availability (staying up), not read speed.
Remember the mode that keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and switches the endpoint automatically on failure. A Read Replica would require manual promotion.

questions.stem:
A serverless Lambda application triggers thousands of parallel executions, each opening a connection to RDS. The database is exhausting its connection limit.

What do you place between Lambda and RDS to solve the connection exhaustion?

options.text: A Read Replica for each Lambda function to spread the connections
Increase Lambda memory — with more RAM it reuses the same connection
An Application Load Balancer in front of RDS, balancing SQL
RDS Proxy — maintains a persistent connection pool and reuses them

questions.explanation: RDS Proxy sits between the application and the database, maintaining a persistent connection pool that is reused — preventing each Lambda invocation from creating a new connection and exhausting the database. It also speeds up failover and supports IAM authentication.

whyNots.A: A Read Replica scales reads, it does not solve an excess of CONNECTIONS (each replica would have the same problem).
whyNots.B: More Lambda memory does not change the number of open database connections.
whyNots.C: An ALB balances HTTP/web traffic, it does not manage a database connection pool.

hints: The problem is not reads or hardware — it is each Lambda invocation opening and closing a connection, and the database cannot handle the volume.
Remember there is a managed intermediary that holds a connection pool and reuses it instead of opening a new one every time. It is built specifically for Lambda + RDS.

questions.stem:
The application stores session keys, preferences, and shopping cart data — dictionary-shaped data read by a key that needs millisecond response at any scale.

Which AWS service is built for this key-value, fast, unlimited-scale access?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB (key-value NoSQL, serverless, millisecond latency)
Amazon RDS (relational database) — primary index delivers ms at any scale
Amazon S3 (object storage) — key-based access, ideal for sessions
Amazon Redshift (data warehouse) — columnar, responds by key in ms

questions.explanation: DynamoDB is a key-value/document NoSQL database, serverless and fully managed, with single-digit millisecond latency — the same with 10 or 10 billion items. It is perfect for sessions, preferences, and shopping carts.

whyNots.B: RDS is relational (SQL, JOINs); great for transactions, but it does not deliver key-value ms scale like DynamoDB.
whyNots.C: S3 stores files by key, but it is not an operational database for application items.
whyNots.D: Redshift is analytical (OLAP), for large historical volumes.

hints: Think of a contacts list — you open it by name (the key) and see the data instantly. No one runs complex queries on a contacts list. That is key-value, fast, at any scale — DynamoDB.

questions.stem:
An orders table uses orderId as its key. Now a developer needs to frequently search by STATUS (for example, all PENDING items) — an attribute that is not the primary key.

What do you create to efficiently query by an attribute other than the primary key?

options.text: A Scan with a status filter on every query, fast and cheap
A GSI (Global Secondary Index) with status as the partition key
A DynamoDB Read Replica dedicated to status queries
Change the primary key to status, without affecting orderId

questions.explanation: A GSI creates a view of the table with a different partition key (for example, status), maintained automatically, allowing efficient Query by that attribute. A Scan would read the entire table — expensive and slow in production.

whyNots.A: Scan reads the entire table and filters — inefficient and costly; the index exists precisely to avoid this.
whyNots.C: DynamoDB does not use 'Read Replicas' for this — scale is native; the alternative-query solution is the index.
whyNots.D: Changing the primary key would break lookups by orderId, which are still needed.

hints: Think about querying by a field that is not the key without scanning the whole table — it requires an 'alternate view' of the table with a different key.
Remember that alternate view, with a different partition key and creatable at any time, is the GSI. Scan reads everything — costly and slow.

questions.stem:
A food delivery app will run on Black Friday: traffic is completely unpredictable — it could be 5x or 50x normal at any moment. Throttling means a lost order.

Which DynamoDB capacity mode is most appropriate?

options.text: Provisioned without Auto Scaling, which absorbs any spike on its own
Do not use DynamoDB for this — it cannot handle 50x spikes
On-Demand (instant scaling, no throttling, pay per request)
Provisioned with low fixed RCU/WCU that AWS raises during the spike

questions.explanation: On-Demand scales instantly to any volume without throttling — you pay per request. For unpredictable spikes like Black Friday, where throttling equals a lost sale, it is the right trade-off (even though it costs more per request).

whyNots.A: Without Auto Scaling, Provisioned cannot follow unpredictable spikes.
whyNots.B: DynamoDB is exactly strong for this key-value pattern at high scale; the adjustment is the capacity mode.
