whyNots.D: Low fixed capacity would throttle during spikes — lost orders.

hints: Remember that when traffic is unpredictable and every lost order hurts, you do not want to bet on a fixed capacity number. The mode that scales instantly on demand without throttling is On-Demand.

questions.stem:
You need an alternate sort order for the SAME items under a partition key, and this need is known BEFORE the table is created.

What is the difference between LSI and GSI, and which fits this case?

options.text: GSI — because LSI was discontinued and no longer exists in DynamoDB for new tables
Neither — in DynamoDB you can only sort results by doing a full table Scan
Either one: LSI and GSI are identical in keys, cost, and creation time; just nicknames
LSI — same partition key, different sort key, created WITH the table; that is what fits here

questions.explanation: An LSI keeps the SAME partition key as the table with a different sort key, but it can only be created at table creation time. A GSI uses a DIFFERENT partition key and can be created at any time. Because here the partition key is the same, only the sort order differs, and the need is known in advance, an LSI fits.

whyNots.A: LSI does exist — it simply has the restriction of being created together with the table.
whyNots.B: Indexes exist precisely to avoid Scanning for alternate ordering.
whyNots.C: They differ: LSI = same partition key / different sort key (at creation); GSI = different partition key (any time).

hints: The clues are 'same partition key' + 'different sort order' + 'known before table creation'.
Remember: LSI = same partition key, different sort key, only creatable at table creation. GSI = different partition key, creatable anytime.
Because the partition key stays the same, you only want another order, and you know this in advance — an LSI fits perfectly.

questions.stem:
An application runs the SAME RDS query thousands of times per second. The data changes very rarely. The team wants to relieve the database — and needs rich data structures such as sorted sets (leaderboards/rankings).

Which service and engine do you add to solve this?

options.text: ElastiCache for Redis (in-memory cache with rich structures such as sorted sets)
ElastiCache for Memcached, which also has rich structures such as sorted sets
An RDS Read Replica, which delivers the same latency as an in-memory cache
Amazon Redshift, which works as an ideal in-memory database for live rankings

questions.explanation: ElastiCache puts an in-memory cache in front of RDS: frequently accessed, stable data is served in microseconds, relieving the database. Among the engines, Redis has rich structures (sorted sets, lists, hashes, pub/sub), while Memcached only handles strings — so for sorted sets, choose Redis.

whyNots.B: Memcached is a pure string cache, multi-threaded, but it does NOT have sorted sets or persistence.
whyNots.C: A Read Replica helps with reads, but it does not deliver the microsecond latency of an in-memory cache for the same repeated query.
whyNots.D: Redshift is an analytical data warehouse — not relevant for operational query caching.

hints: Remember that data read heavily and rarely changed lives well in memory — a cache in front of the database returns results in microseconds.
Among the two engines, only one has rich structures (sorted sets, lists, pub/sub). Memcached is strings only. Sorted set means Redis.

questions.stem:
A marketplace wants to recommend products based on 'users who bought X also bought Y' — the central query traverses RELATIONSHIPS between users and products.

Which database is most appropriate?

options.text: Amazon RDS with lots of JOINs

questions.explanation: When the central data is the RELATIONSHIP between entities (recommendations, 'friends of friends', fraud detection), a graph database is ideal. Neptune traverses nodes and edges natively — far more efficient than simulating a graph with relational JOINs.

whyNots.A: DynamoDB is excellent for key-value access, not for traversing complex relationships.
whyNots.C: RDS could store the data, but graph traversals would become expensive, slow JOINs at scale.
whyNots.D: Redshift is for OLAP analysis of large volumes, not for real-time graph traversal.

hints: The value here lies in CONNECTIONS between things (who bought what, who knows whom), not in the things alone.
Remember there is a database type built to traverse relationships (nodes and edges) natively — the graph database.

questions.stem:
The company needs to analyze YEARS of historical sales data — BI reports that scan many rows but few columns, in large volumes. These are not real-time transactions.

Which service is indicated for this analytical (OLAP) workload?

options.text: Amazon RDS (row-oriented relational database, optimized for real-time transactions)
Amazon DynamoDB (serverless key-value, made for OLAP analytical queries)
Amazon Redshift (data warehouse, columnar storage, parallel processing)
Amazon ElastiCache (in-memory cache, ideal for heavy analytical aggregations)

questions.explanation: Redshift is the AWS data warehouse, with columnar storage and MPP (massively parallel processing) — ideal for scanning a few columns across many rows in large volumes (OLAP). RDS/Aurora are for OLTP (real-time transactions), not this kind of analysis.

whyNots.A: RDS is OLTP — individual real-time transactions, not analytical scanning of years of data.
whyNots.B: DynamoDB is operational key-value, not OLAP analysis.
whyNots.D: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not an analytics tool.

hints: The keyword is analysis of large historical volumes — OLAP, not OLTP (real-time transaction).
Remember the AWS data warehouse, columnar and with massive parallel processing, is Redshift.

questions.stem:
A developer logged into the console with a developer account and noticed they had access to everything — S3, EC2, RDS, billing. Something seemed wrong.

What is IAM in AWS?

options.text: A network firewall for EC2 instances, filtering inbound and outbound ports and IPs
An automatic backup service that protects users and permissions from deletion
A managed database for storing your web application's end users
The service that controls authentication and authorization — who can do what to each resource

questions.explanation: IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the global service that controls authentication (proving who you are) and authorization (what you can do) over AWS resources.

whyNots.A: An instance firewall is a Security Group.
whyNots.B: Backup is a different topic (snapshots/AWS Backup).
whyNots.C: End-user identity for applications is Cognito; IAM is for access to AWS itself.

hints: Think of IAM as the building's front desk. It authenticates (who are you?) and authorizes (can you enter the fifth floor?). Without it, anyone could enter any room.

questions.stem:
A team of 50 developers needs read-only access to S3. Soon this permission may change for everyone at once.

What is the most efficient way to manage this permission in IAM?

options.text: Create an IAM Group, attach the read policy to the group, and put all 50 users in it
Attach the policy individually to each of the 50 users — this is what IAM recommends
Create 50 policies, one for each user, so each change stays isolated and traceable
Share the root account with the 50 devs, since it always has the needed permission

questions.explanation: IAM Groups aggregate users: you attach the policy to the group and everyone inherits. Did the rule change? Edit the group once and it applies to all 50. Attaching policies directly to each user is unsustainable at scale.

whyNots.B: Editing 50 users every time a rule changes is unsustainable — the group exists for this.
whyNots.C: 50 identical policies is pure duplication; one policy on a group solves it.
whyNots.D: The root account is never for daily use and must never be shared with the team.

hints: If you attach permissions to each user, changing the rule later means editing 50 times. Put everyone in a group and manage it in one place — they inherit the permission together.

questions.stem:
A user has a policy that allows s3:* on a bucket. At the same time, another policy applied to them has an explicit Deny for s3:DeleteObject on the same bucket.

Can the user delete objects in this bucket?

options.text: Yes — the Allow for s3:* includes delete and prevails
No — an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow
It depends on the order in which the policies were created
Yes — Deny only works in SCPs, not in IAM policies

questions.explanation: IAM evaluation rule: an explicit Deny always wins over any Allow, from any policy, regardless of order. By default everything is denied; only what is explicitly allowed (and not denied) passes.

whyNots.A: The Allow s3:* is overridden by the explicit Deny on DeleteObject.
whyNots.C: Order does not matter — an explicit Deny always wins.
whyNots.D: An explicit Deny works in IAM policies too, not only in SCPs.

hints: In AWS permission evaluation there is a golden rule that decides ties.
Remember that an explicit Deny beats any Allow, no matter where it comes from or in what order. And the default, with nothing, is already deny.

questions.stem:
An identity in account A needs to access an S3 bucket located in account B (cross-account access).

What is normally required for cross-account access to work?

options.text: Create the account A IAM user inside account B, since IAM cannot see external identities
Only a policy on the account A user — the caller is the one that needs to authorize
An identity-based policy in account A AND a resource-based policy (Bucket Policy) in account B
Make the bucket public so any account can access it — the standard way to share

questions.explanation: For cross-account access, both sides normally need to agree: the identity-based policy in the source account (allows the identity to act) and the resource-based policy on the destination resource — the Bucket Policy in account B stating it accepts that identity. Both must align.

whyNots.A: The whole point of cross-account is to NOT need to create account A users in account B (use Bucket Policy or AssumeRole).
whyNots.B: Only the source-account policy is not enough — the bucket in account B must also authorize.
whyNots.D: Making the bucket public is a security hole and is not the correct cross-account approach.

hints: There are two sides to the story — the identity in account A that requests, and the resource in account B that accepts. Both must agree.
Remember that an identity-based policy says 'I may ask'; the resource-based policy (Bucket Policy) says 'I accept from whom'. Cross-account usually requires both.

questions.stem:
A Lambda function needs to write to DynamoDB. The temptation was to put a fixed access key in the code.

What is the secure way to grant this permission without fixed keys in the code?

options.text: Save the key in a Lambda environment variable — outside the code it is no longer a risk
Put Access Key and Secret Key in the Lambda function code — function code is already private
Use the root account for the Lambda, guaranteeing it never lacks permission for DynamoDB
An IAM Role (execution role) that the Lambda assumes at runtime, with permission on DynamoDB

questions.explanation: The Lambda assumes an IAM Role (execution role) at runtime and receives temporary credentials from STS — no static key in the code. The Trust Policy allows lambda.amazonaws.com to assume the role; the Permissions Policy grants access to DynamoDB.

whyNots.A: An environment variable is better than code, but it is still a static key to rotate and can leak.
whyNots.B: A fixed key in code leaks easily (git, logs) and does not expire — exactly the practice to eliminate.
whyNots.C: The root account is never used — it grants unrestricted access and must never be given to services.

hints: Think of a role as a visitor badge — AWS issues TEMPORARY credentials that expire on their own, with no fixed key in the code. The Lambda 'wears' the role when it runs.

questions.stem:
An engineer found a config.env with AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in an EC2 instance's code. They need to give the instance access to S3 with no key stored on disk.

How should the EC2 instance access S3 securely?

options.text: Attach an IAM Role to the instance (Instance Profile); the SDK picks up temporary credentials automatically
Keep the permanent Access Key, but move it to an environment variable — that way it stops being a risk
Copy the .pem file into the instance, which then authenticates S3 calls automatically
Leave the bucket public only during usage hours, so the instance accesses it without any credential

questions.explanation: Attaching an IAM Role to EC2 (via Instance Profile) lets the SDK/CLI obtain temporary credentials automatically through the Instance Metadata Service — no key on disk or in code, and automatic rotation. If the instance is compromised, the credentials expire within hours.

whyNots.B: An environment variable is still a static key — leakable and without automatic expiration.
whyNots.C: .pem is an SSH key to access the instance, not a credential for accessing S3.
whyNots.D: A public bucket is a serious risk and is not instance access control.

hints: The goal is zero static keys on disk or in code.
Remember that you attach a role to the instance (Instance Profile). The SDK fetches temporary credentials automatically through instance metadata, and they renew on their own.

questions.stem:
Leadership wants to ensure that NO account in the Production OU can create resources outside the sa-east-1 region — not even an account administrator.

Which resource imposes this permission ceiling at the OU level?

options.text: An IAM Policy attached to every user in the account
Service Control Policy (SCP) applied to the Production OU
A Security Group restricting the region

questions.explanation: SCP (Service Control Policy) defines the permission ceiling for an OU/account in Organizations: even a user with AdministratorAccess cannot exceed what the SCP allows. An SCP denying actions outside sa-east-1 blocks all accounts in the OU, including admins.

whyNots.A: An IAM Policy controls one identity; an admin could grant themselves more. An SCP is the upper limit of the entire account.
whyNots.C: A Security Group is an instance firewall; it does not control regions or permissions.
whyNots.D: A Bucket Policy controls access to one bucket, not resource creation by region.

hints: The clue 'not even an account administrator can' means you need something ABOVE the account's IAM policies.
Remember that in AWS Organizations there is a policy that sets the permission CEILING for an entire OU/account. It does not grant anything — it only limits the maximum. That is the SCP.

questions.stem:
A member account has an SCP that DENIES use of the Redshift service. A user in that account has an IAM Policy with Allow for redshift:*.

Can the user use Redshift?

options.text: Yes — the IAM Policy grants the permission and always prevails over the SCP
It depends: the SCP grants the permission if the IAM also grants Allow
No — the SCP is the maximum ceiling; if it denies, the IAM Allow does not help
Yes — SCPs only apply to the root account; regular IAM users bypass it

questions.explanation: The SCP defines the maximum permissions of the account and does NOT grant anything — it only restricts. If the SCP denies Redshift, no user or role in the account can use Redshift, no matter what the IAM Policy allows. Effective permission is the intersection of what IAM allows AND the SCP does not deny.

whyNots.A: An IAM Allow does not bypass an SCP Deny — the SCP is the upper limit.
whyNots.B: An SCP never grants permission; it only limits. IAM policy grants permission within the SCP ceiling.
whyNots.D: SCPs apply to all identities in the member account, not only the root.

hints: SCPs and IAM policies do not add permissions — one sets the ceiling, the other grants within the ceiling.
Remember that an SCP does NOT grant anything; it only restricts the maximum. If the SCP denies Redshift, no one in the account uses Redshift, regardless of IAM Allows.

questions.stem:
An auditor asked: 'I want to see who deleted the production bucket, from which IP, and at what time.'

Which service records all API calls in the account (who, what, from where, when)?
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records all API calls in the account (console, CLI, SDK): identity, action, resource, source IP, time, and result. It is the audit trail — it answers 'who did what and when'.

whyNots.A: CloudWatch is for metrics and operational logs, not the per-identity API call trail.
whyNots.B: GuardDuty detects threats; it is not the audit log of every action.
whyNots.C: Config records the STATE/configuration of resources over time, not every API call.

hints: When someone asks for PROOF, they do not want opinion — they want a trail. Every AWS API call leaves a trace: who, what, from where, when. That trail is CloudTrail.

questions.stem:
The company needs to PROVE to external auditors that no security configuration (public buckets, unencrypted volumes, missing MFA) fell out of compliance over the last 90 days.

Which service continuously monitors the CONFIGURATION compliance of resources over time?
questions.explanation: AWS Config records the configuration state of resources over time and evaluates compliance Config Rules (for example, s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, encrypted-volumes, mfa-enabled-for-iam-console-access). It answers 'is the resource in compliance, and did it stay in compliance?'. CloudTrail records actions; Config records state/configuration.

whyNots.B: CloudTrail shows actions (who did what), not the historical compliance of configuration.
whyNots.C: WAF filters application traffic; it has nothing to do with compliance reporting.
whyNots.D: Inspector finds vulnerabilities (CVEs) in EC2/containers, not general configuration compliance.

hints: This question is not 'who did it' (that is CloudTrail) — it is 'is the resource configured in compliance, and did it remain so?'.
Remember there is a service that records configuration STATE over time and checks rules (public bucket? unencrypted volume? MFA?). That is AWS Config.

questions.stem:
The team wants to be alerted IN REAL TIME if an EC2 instance starts communicating with known malicious IPs or shows anomalous behavior (sign of compromise).

Which service detects active threats by analyzing AWS logs with machine learning?
questions.explanation: GuardDuty uses machine learning on VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail to detect threats: malicious IPs, command-and-control communication, credential exfiltration. It alerts (but does not block) — the response is up to you (manual or via EventBridge + Lambda).

whyNots.A: CloudTrail is the API call log; GuardDuty is what analyzes and detects threats from that data.
whyNots.C: Config checks configuration compliance, not active real-time threats.
whyNots.D: Macie finds sensitive data (PII) in S3, not malicious instance communication.

hints: Here it is not 'configuration' or 'raw logs' — it is detecting SUSPICIOUS behavior in real time.
Remember there is a service that uses ML on VPC Flow Logs, DNS, and CloudTrail to detect threats and alert — though it does not block. That is GuardDuty.

questions.stem:
There is a suspicion that a spreadsheet with customer government ID numbers was accidentally uploaded to an S3 bucket. The team wants to automatically discover where sensitive data (PII) is stored in S3.

Which service specializes in discovering and classifying sensitive data in S3?
questions.explanation: Macie uses ML to discover and classify sensitive data (PII such as government IDs, credit card numbers, credentials) stored in S3 and alert about exposure. GuardDuty is for real-time threats; Inspector is for vulnerabilities (CVEs) in EC2/containers — neither discovers PII.

whyNots.A: Inspector looks for CVEs in instances and containers, not sensitive data in S3.
whyNots.B: GuardDuty detects behavior-based threats (network/API), it does not scan buckets for PII.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail records actions, it does not classify object contents.

hints: Be careful not to confuse the 'detectives'. Here the target is SENSITIVE DATA (government IDs, cards) sitting in S3 — not a network threat, not a CVE.
GuardDuty = real-time threat; Inspector = vulnerability (CVE) in EC2/containers; Macie = sensitive data (PII) in S3. The case is PII in S3 → Macie.

questions.stem:
A web application is receiving SQL injection and XSS (malicious script) attempts from varied IP addresses, embedded in HTTP request fields.

Which service filters this malicious traffic at the application layer (layer 7)?
questions.explanation: AWS WAF protects at layer 7 (HTTP): you create Web ACLs with rules (including managed rule groups such as AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet) that detect SQL injection, XSS, bots, and rate limiting, blocking the request before it reaches the application. It integrates with CloudFront, ALB, and API Gateway.

whyNots.A: Shield protects against volumetric DDoS (layers 3/4); it does not inspect HTTP payload.
whyNots.B: GuardDuty detects threats in logs; it does not filter HTTP requests at the edge.
whyNots.C: Security Groups filter by port and IP; they do not understand SQL injection in request content.

hints: SQL injection and XSS are malicious payloads INSIDE the HTTP request. The service that inspects request content at layer 7 and blocks with a 403 is WAF.

questions.stem:
An attack is trying to take down a website by flooding the infrastructure with a huge volume of network traffic (volumetric DDoS, layers 3/4).

Which service protects against this type of attack and is already active for free for everyone?

options.text: AWS Shield Standard (DDoS L3/L4, automatic and no cost)
AWS Secrets Manager, active by default against floods
AWS Config, which detects and mitigates traffic spikes on its own
AWS WAF, which is active for free and handles volumetric attacks

questions.explanation: Shield Standard protects against layer 3/4 DDoS (volumetric: UDP/SYN flood, amplification) automatically and at no cost for CloudFront, Route 53, ALB, and Elastic IP. WAF is complementary but acts at layer 7 (HTTP payload). Shield Advanced (paid) adds L7 protection, DDoS Response Team, and cost protection.

whyNots.B: Secrets Manager stores credentials — it has nothing to do with DDoS.
whyNots.C: Config is configuration compliance, not DDoS protection.
whyNots.D: WAF filters application attacks such as SQL injection and XSS, not volumetric network floods.

hints: A flood of network traffic meant to take a site down is a volumetric DDoS. WAF is for application payloads, not network volume.
AWS already protects everyone against L3/L4 DDoS by default and at no cost — that is Shield Standard. (Shield Advanced is the paid add-on for L7, response team, and cost protection.)

questions.stem:
The production RDS database password must be rotated automatically every 30 days, with no downtime and no manual intervention.

Which service stores that password with native automatic rotation?

options.text: A .env file encrypted on the instance

questions.explanation: Secrets Manager stores secrets encrypted with KMS and provides native automatic rotation integrated with RDS, Redshift, and DocumentDB — it changes the database password and updates the secret without downtime. The application retrieves the password at runtime via API using its IAM role.

whyNots.A: SSM Parameter Store does not have native automatic rotation (it would require a custom Lambda).
whyNots.C: KMS manages encryption KEYS; it does not store or rotate database passwords.
whyNots.D: A file on the instance is a static credential — exactly the problem you want to eliminate.

hints: The key phrase is 'automatic database password rotation.' There is a service that integrates with RDS and swaps the password on its own, with no downtime — Secrets Manager.

questions.stem:
You need to store a NON-sensitive feature flag: HABILITAR_NOVO_CHECKOUT=true. You want the simplest, most economical option.

Where should you store this non-sensitive configuration parameter?

options.text: Hardcoded in the application code — the boolean flag rarely changes, so it is free
AWS Secrets Manager (with automatic rotation) — the free option for every config
SSM Parameter Store (Standard) — free and simple for non-sensitive config
In a public S3 bucket — the flag is not sensitive, so it can be open, and S3 is very cheap

questions.explanation: For NON-sensitive configuration (feature flags, public URLs), SSM Parameter Store Standard is free and sufficient. Secrets Manager (~$0.40 per secret per month plus rotation) is for sensitive credentials that need rotation — using it here is wasted cost.

whyNots.A: Hardcoding forces a deployment every time the flag changes and mixes config with code.
whyNots.B: Secrets Manager is paid and aimed at secrets with rotation — overkill for a non-sensitive flag.
whyNots.D: A public bucket unnecessarily exposes configuration — a security bad practice.

hints: It is not a secret and does not need rotation. Paying for Secrets Manager here would be a waste.
For simple, non-sensitive configuration, use the free SSM Parameter Store (Standard tier).

questions.stem:
A report job used to run for 10 minutes a day, but the EC2 instance stayed on the other 23 hours and 50 minutes doing nothing — paying for the whole month.

Which service runs code on demand, scales automatically, and charges only for execution time?

options.text: Amazon RDS running the job in SQL
A larger and cheaper EC2 instance

questions.explanation: Lambda is serverless, event-driven compute: you upload the function, an event (trigger) fires, AWS runs it in an ephemeral environment, and you pay only for duration plus memory. No idle server left running.

whyNots.A: RDS is a database, not on-demand code execution.
whyNots.B: S3 stores files; it does not execute code.
whyNots.C: A larger EC2 instance still stays on (and charging) 24 hours for a 10-minute job.

hints: Lambda is like a microwave: you put in the plate (code), press the button (event), it cooks for as long as needed, and turns off by itself. You do not keep the oven on waiting for the next plate.

questions.stem:
A file processing job can take up to 20 minutes to complete. The team wants to run this on Lambda.

What prevents using Lambda here, and what is the alternative?

options.text: Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes; for 20 minutes use Fargate (or EC2)
You must create a Security Group for the function — without it the job cannot run for 20 minutes
Nothing prevents it — Lambda runs for any amount of time with no duration limit
Lambda does not accept files, only text — a 2 GB binary would never reach the function

questions.explanation: Lambda has a maximum timeout of 15 minutes per execution. A ~20 minute job exceeds that limit, so the alternative is a container on Fargate (or an EC2 instance), which do not have that ceiling.

whyNots.B: Security Groups have no relation to a function's duration limit.
whyNots.C: Lambda does NOT run for any length of time — it stops at 15 minutes.
whyNots.D: Lambda can process files (it has up to 10 GB of /tmp); the issue here is time.

hints: Lambda has a ceiling on execution time. 20 minutes exceeds that ceiling.
The limit is 15 minutes. For longer processes, a managed container (Fargate) or EC2 solves it.

questions.stem:
A payment API on Lambda has a strict latency SLA. The cold start (initialization time on first invocation) is exceeding the SLA.

What eliminates the cold start by keeping environments pre-warmed?

options.text: Replace the function with a Lambda Layer

questions.explanation: Provisioned Concurrency keeps execution environments pre-initialized (warmed), eliminating cold starts — ideal for critical endpoints with latency SLAs. Reserved Concurrency guarantees/limits the number of concurrent executions but does not eliminate cold starts.

whyNots.A: A longer timeout does not reduce initialization time.
whyNots.C: Reserved Concurrency reserves/limits the number of concurrent executions but does not warm environments — cold starts continue.
whyNots.D: A Layer shares dependencies across functions; it does not address cold starts.

hints: A cold start is the time to start the environment. To eliminate it, you need environments already running and waiting.
There is a feature that keeps pre-initialized (warmed) executions ready. Be careful not to confuse it with the one that only guarantees/limits the number of executions.

questions.stem:
A real-time chat app needs the server to SEND messages to the client while the window is open — without the client repeatedly asking (polling).

Which API Gateway type is appropriate?

options.text: REST API (the server sends via response)
None — API Gateway is not for live chat

questions.explanation: WebSocket API maintains a persistent bidirectional connection: the client connects once and the server can send messages at any time (postToConnection) — exactly what real-time chat needs. REST/HTTP APIs are request-response, so the server only responds when asked.

whyNots.A: HTTP API is also stateless request-response, with no server push.
whyNots.B: REST API is request-response; real-time push would require polling, which is inefficient.
whyNots.D: API Gateway does work for chat — using the WebSocket type.

hints: REST and HTTP APIs are request-response (stateless): the server only speaks when the client asks. Here the server needs to PUSH messages.
For the server to send data to the client at any time, with an open connection in both directions, the right type is WebSocket.

questions.stem:
During signup, the application tried to send the welcome email in the SAME request. If the email service went down, signup failed too.

Which pattern/service decouples the two processes so signup does not depend on email?

options.text: Put the email service in a separate Security Group, which decouples the two processes
Increase the signup request timeout until the email goes out, avoiding any 500 error
Run signup and email on a larger EC2 instance that processes both without blocking the response
An Amazon SQS queue — record the message, respond 200, and a consumer sends the email later

questions.explanation: SQS decouples producer and consumer: the application puts the message in the queue and responds 200 immediately; a separate consumer processes and sends the email later. If the email service fails, messages stay in the queue waiting — signup does not fail with it.

whyNots.A: Security Groups are firewalls — they have nothing to do with decoupling processes.
whyNots.B: A longer timeout only makes the user wait longer; the coupling remains.
whyNots.C: A larger instance does not decouple the processes.

hints: SQS is like an inbox: the sender does not wait for you to read. Signup drops the message in the queue and responds immediately, and another process sends the email at its own pace. If email fails, the message waits in the queue.

questions.stem:
A stock exchange processes buy/sell orders where the ORDER of arrival determines the price, and duplicates are unacceptable.

Which SQS queue type meets this requirement?

options.text: SNS Topic, which queues orders in order
EventBridge bus with FIFO ordering in rules

questions.explanation: FIFO (First In, First Out) guarantees exact arrival order and exactly-once delivery — essential when sequence defines the result (execution price) and duplicates are unacceptable. Standard has higher throughput but only best-effort ordering and may duplicate.

whyNots.B: SNS is pub/sub (broadcast), not an ordered processing queue.
whyNots.C: Standard may deliver out of order and duplicate — unacceptable for stock orders.
whyNots.D: EventBridge routes events by rule; it does not guarantee FIFO processing order.

hints: The two keywords are 'order matters' and 'no duplicates'.
Standard is fast but may deliver out of order and duplicate. The queue that guarantees order (First In, First Out) and exactly-once delivery is FIFO.

questions.stem:
When an order is confirmed, THREE things must happen in parallel: send email, update inventory, and record analytics — each independent of the others.

Which pattern delivers the same event to multiple consumers in parallel, with buffering and retry per consumer?

options.text: Call the three services in sequence within the same request
Fan-out: SNS Topic → one SQS queue for each consumer
A single SQS queue read by all three processes
A Security Group for each service

questions.explanation: The fan-out pattern uses SNS (pub/sub) to deliver a copy of the event to multiple SQS queues — one per consumer. Each SQS provides independent buffering and retry, so if inventory fails, email and analytics continue. SNS directly to Lambda would lose the event if the Lambda failed.

whyNots.A: Calling them in sequence in the same request returns to tight coupling (slow and fragile).
whyNots.C: In a single queue, each message is consumed by only one consumer — it would not reach all three.
whyNots.D: Security Groups are firewalls; they are irrelevant to event distribution.

hints: You want one event to become COPIES for several destinations, and one destination failing must not bring down the others.
SNS publishes to many subscribers (pub/sub). Putting an SQS queue in front of each gives every consumer its own buffer and retry. That is fan-out.

questions.stem:
In an SQS queue, one specific message always fails processing and returns to the queue, being reprocessed over and over, affecting the rest.

What isolates these repeatedly failing messages without blocking the queue?

options.text: Delete the queue and create a new one from scratch, without the bad message
Replace the Standard queue with FIFO, which discards failures on its own
A Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) with maxReceiveCount configured
Increase the Visibility Timeout to 12 hours, which already isolates it

questions.explanation: A DLQ automatically receives messages that failed more than maxReceiveCount times (e.g., 3). The poison message is isolated for analysis without reprocessing forever and without blocking the rest of the queue. It is a production best practice.

whyNots.A: Recreating the queue would lose everything and does not fix the cause (the failing message).
whyNots.B: Switching to FIFO changes ordering/duplication behavior, not isolation of failing messages.
whyNots.D: A longer Visibility Timeout only delays reprocessing; the message remains stuck in the queue.

hints: You do not want a poison message spinning forever. You want to move it aside and analyze later.
By configuring a maximum number of attempts, SQS automatically moves the message to a separate queue — the Dead Letter Queue.

questions.stem:
The website loads fast in one city, but customers in other regions complain that images take 2-3 seconds. The content is in an S3 bucket in the first city.

Which service brings content closer to users by serving it from a global cache?

options.text: Amazon SQS, which queues images close to users
An Amazon RDS Read Replica in Europe serving the website images
A larger EC2 server in the first city to compensate for distance
Amazon CloudFront (CDN, with Edge Locations near users)

questions.explanation: CloudFront is the AWS CDN: it distributes content across 400+ Edge Locations and serves from the point closest to the user (cache hit), reducing latency. It only goes to the origin (S3) when the content is not cached.

whyNots.A: SQS is a message queue; it has nothing to do with content delivery.
whyNots.B: A Read Replica scales database reads, not global static content delivery.
whyNots.C: A larger server in the first city is still far from other regions — distance is the problem.

hints: Think of a central library and branch copies. Instead of everyone traveling to the central city to fetch a book, content is cached at the branch (Edge Location) closest to whoever is accessing it. That network of branches is CloudFront.

questions.stem:
You want to serve an S3 bucket through CloudFront, but the bucket must stay PRIVATE — no one can access it directly over the internet, only through CloudFront.

Which feature gives CloudFront access to the private bucket without making it public?

options.text: Disable Block Public Access and open the bucket
A NAT Gateway in front of the bucket
A Presigned URL for each object

questions.explanation: With OAC (Origin Access Control), CloudFront signs requests to S3, and the bucket policy accepts only CloudFront — the bucket remains private and no one can access it directly. OAC is the modern successor to OAI (it supports SSE-KMS and newer regions).

whyNots.B: Opening the bucket violates the requirement to keep it private.
whyNots.C: A NAT Gateway is for outbound internet from a private subnet — it has nothing to do with serving a bucket.
whyNots.D: Presigned URLs grant temporary access to objects; they are not how CloudFront integrates with a private bucket.

hints: The bucket stays private, but it must accept requests from one specific client: CloudFront.
There is a feature that makes CloudFront sign requests to S3, and the bucket policy accepts only CloudFront. It is OAC (successor to OAI).

questions.stem:
The application has a primary environment in sa-east-1 and a disaster recovery environment in us-east-1. If the primary fails, DNS must point to DR automatically.

Which Route 53 routing policy performs this automatic failover?

options.text: Simple, which detects failure on its own
Failover (with Health Check on the primary)

questions.explanation: The Failover policy defines the primary (sa-east-1) and secondary (us-east-1). With a Health Check on the primary, if it fails Route 53 automatically starts responding with the DR. It is the active/passive DR policy.

whyNots.A: Simple returns a single destination, with no health check or failover.
whyNots.C: Geolocation routes by country/continent, not by resource failure.
whyNots.D: Weighted splits traffic by weight (A/B testing), not by health failover.

hints: This is a classic DR scenario — one active resource (primary) and one standby, with automatic swap on failure.
There is a policy that marks one destination as Primary and another as Secondary, and switches via Health Check when the primary fails.

questions.stem:
For data residency compliance, Brazilian users MUST be served by a server in Brazil and European users by a server in Europe — deterministically by country, not by latency.

Which Route 53 routing policy guarantees this geographic-location-based routing?
questions.explanation: Geolocation routes by the geographic origin of the query (country/continent), deterministically — ideal for data residency compliance (Brazilian user → Brazil, European user → Europe). Latency-based would route to the fastest endpoint, which usually coincides but does not guarantee the country rule.

whyNots.A: Weighted splits by percentage, unrelated to geography.
whyNots.B: Multi-Value returns several healthy IPs; it does not route by country.
whyNots.D: Latency-based optimizes latency; it does not guarantee the country residency required by compliance.

hints: Watch the trap — Latency-based would route to the fastest endpoint, but the requirement is by COUNTRY, deterministically (compliance).
The policy that decides based on the geographic location of the querier (country/continent) is Geolocation.

questions.stem:
A developer has a Docker image ready and wants to run it in production on AWS WITHOUT managing any servers.

Which combination runs containers without you managing instances?

options.text: An EC2 instance where you install Docker manually
Amazon ECS with launch type Fargate

questions.explanation: ECS with Fargate runs containers without you managing servers: define the task CPU and memory, and AWS allocates the infrastructure, charging per vCPU/memory per second. It is the simplest path for most use cases.

whyNots.A: A Layer shares Lambda dependencies; it does not run long-lived containers.
whyNots.B: EC2 with Docker manually returns all the server management you want to avoid.
whyNots.C: S3 stores objects; it does not run containers.

hints: You want to just say 'run this container with this much CPU and memory' and not manage any server. In ECS, the launch type that does this (AWS allocates the infrastructure invisibly) is Fargate.

questions.stem:
An on-premises Windows server with IIS and a .NET application must move to EC2. The application CANNOT be rewritten (lift-and-shift).

Which service replicates the entire server to EC2 without rewriting the application?
questions.explanation: MGN (Application Migration Service) does lift-and-shift: an agent continuously replicates the source server disk to AWS; when ready, cutover launches an EC2 running the application exactly as before — no rewrite. DMS migrates databases; DataSync migrates files.

whyNots.B: ECR is a container image repository, not server migration.
whyNots.C: DMS migrates DATABASE data, not the whole server with the application.
whyNots.D: DataSync transfers FILES between storages; it does not stand up the server as EC2.

hints: This is not just the database or just files — it is the WHOLE server, as-is, becoming an EC2 instance.
There is a lift-and-shift service that installs an agent, continuously replicates the server disk, and launches an identical EC2. It is MGN.

questions.stem:
An on-premises Oracle database (800 GB) must migrate to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, with schema conversion and MINIMUM downtime.

Which service (and auxiliary tool) performs this database migration?

options.text: AWS MGN (Application Migration Service), which converts schema and migrates data
AWS DMS (Full Load + CDC) with the Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) for the schema
AWS DataSync, which replicates databases with CDC and converts schema together
AWS Snowmobile, the migration truck indicated for small databases

questions.explanation: DMS migrates databases with Full Load (initial copy) + CDC (real-time change capture), allowing cutover with minimal downtime. Because it is a heterogeneous migration (Oracle → PostgreSQL), the Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) converts the schema first.

whyNots.A: MGN migrates whole servers to EC2; it does not convert/migrate databases between engines.
whyNots.C: DataSync transfers files, not relational databases with CDC.
whyNots.D: Snowmobile is physical transport for exabytes — overkill and out of context for 800 GB of database with CDC.

hints: It is a DATABASE migration, and it also changes engine (Oracle → PostgreSQL = heterogeneous).
DMS does the initial copy (Full Load) + ongoing replication (CDC) with minimal downtime; and because the engine changes, SCT converts the schema first.

questions.stem:
An on-premises NAS with 50 TB of files must be transferred to Amazon S3, and the company network has sufficient capacity.

Which service is indicated for this FILE transfer over the network?
questions.explanation: DataSync is specialized in transferring FILES between storages (on-premises NFS/SMB → S3/EFS/FSx) over the network, with scheduling, verification, and encryption. Since the network can handle the 50 TB, DataSync is the path (if the network were insufficient, then Snowball Edge would be appropriate).

whyNots.A: DMS migrates relational databases, not files from a NAS.
whyNots.B: MGN migrates whole servers to EC2, not files.
whyNots.D: Snowmobile/Snow is physical transport — only when the network cannot handle it; here the network can.

hints: Be careful not to confuse migration tools: here it is FILES (NAS), not database and not server.
DMS = database; MGN = server; Snow = physical hardware when the network cannot handle it. Files over the network (NFS/SMB → S3/EFS/FSx) = DataSync.

questions.stem:
Leadership wants to understand where the money is going on AWS: chart of spending by service, by month, and a forecast for the coming months.

Which tool is used to visualize, analyze, and predict account costs visually?
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer is the visual tool for analyzing actual costs and usage: charts by service/account/tag, up to 13 months of history, forward forecast, and RI/Savings Plans recommendations.

whyNots.A: CloudWatch is for operational metrics/logs, not bill analysis.
whyNots.B: Pricing Calculator ESTIMATES the cost of something that has not been created yet; it does not analyze actual spend.
whyNots.C: CUR is raw data, line by line, in S3 — not a ready-made visual view.

hints: Think of Cost Explorer as the car dashboard — it shows, in charts, how much you spent, on what, and estimates how much you will spend. It is visual analysis of what ALREADY happened.

questions.stem:
A developer wants to be NOTIFIED as soon as monthly spending passes $1,000 (or when forecast indicates it will pass), to avoid a bill shock.

Which service triggers alerts when cost crosses a defined threshold?
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets defines cost/usage budgets and triggers alerts (email/SNS) when actual OR forecasted spend crosses the threshold. It is the proactive ALERT mechanism.

whyNots.B: Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of a future project; it does not monitor spend.
whyNots.C: CUR is raw data export, not an alert.
whyNots.D: Cost Explorer analyzes and forecasts visually, but it is not the threshold alert mechanism.

hints: Budgets is the bill alarm — you set the ceiling, and it goes off (alerts) when actual or forecasted spend approaches it.

questions.stem:
The finance team wants the MOST detailed billing data possible — line by line, by resource, by hour, with cost-center tags — to load into their BI tools.

Which resource delivers this granular data into an S3 bucket for self-service analysis?

options.text: The default Cost Explorer dashboard, which exports the aggregated view as PDF
Cost and Usage Report (CUR), delivered to S3 (and queried with Athena/QuickSight)
AWS Pricing Calculator, which estimates and details actual usage by resource
AWS Budgets, which automatically writes granular usage into an S3 bucket

questions.explanation: The CUR is the most complete billing dataset — line by line, by hour, by resource, and by tags — delivered to an S3 bucket (CSV/Parquet) to load into Athena/QuickSight/BI. Cost Explorer is visual; CUR is the raw data for your own tools.

whyNots.A: Cost Explorer is great for visualization, but it is not the raw export for your own tools.
whyNots.C: Pricing Calculator estimates costs that have not yet occurred.
whyNots.D: Budgets is a threshold alert, not a granular data source.

hints: The word is GRANULAR — line by line, to load into their own tools. It is not a ready-made chart; it is raw data.
The most detailed AWS report drops into your own S3 bucket, for you to query with Athena/QuickSight. It is the CUR.

questions.stem:
Before migrating to AWS, the architect needs to present leadership the estimated monthly cost of the proposed architecture (EC2, EBS, RDS). Nothing has been created yet.

Which tool produces this estimate for an architecture that does not yet exist?
questions.explanation: Since nothing has been deployed, there is no real cost to analyze — you need an upfront estimate of the proposed architecture, which is exactly what AWS Pricing Calculator provides (planning, ROI, migration).

whyNots.A: Budgets alerts on actual/forecasted spend; it does not estimate a new project from scratch.
whyNots.B: Cost Explorer analyzes costs ALREADY incurred — there are none here.
whyNots.D: CUR reports actual usage — there is no usage yet.

hints: 'Nothing has been created yet' rules out any tool that looks at REAL spend. To estimate before anything exists, use Pricing Calculator.

questions.stem:
The company will have stable COMPUTATION load for 1-3 years, but wants flexibility to change instance type, region, and even use Fargate/Lambda, without losing the discount.

Which usage commitment model gives a high discount with this flexibility?

options.text: Dedicated Hosts (dedicated physical host, with flexible discount across services)
On-Demand (no commitment, full price — but with automatic volume discount)
Spot Instances (spare capacity, can be interrupted at any time)
Compute Savings Plans (spend-per-hour commitment, flexible across EC2/Fargate/Lambda)

questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans provide up to ~66% discount for a per-hour spend commitment (1 or 3 years), and — unlike Reserved Instances — the flexibility applies across EC2 (any family/region/OS), Fargate, and Lambda. (EC2 Instance Savings Plans reach ~72% but lock instance family and region — less flexible.) Perfect for stable usage that may still change shape.

whyNots.A: Dedicated Hosts are about isolation/licensing, not flexible commitment discount.
whyNots.B: On-Demand has no commitment but is the most expensive for continuous usage.
whyNots.C: Spot is very cheap but can be interrupted — not suitable for stable load that must stay up.

hints: Stable long-term usage calls for a commitment (discount). But you want to be able to swap instance/region/service without losing the discount.
Reserved Instances lock to a family/region. Compute Savings Plans commit a dollar-per-hour amount and apply to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda — much more flexible.

questions.stem:
A developer suspects several EC2 instances are over-provisioned and wasting money. She wants automatic right-sizing recommendations.

Which service analyzes usage and recommends the ideal size/type of resources (right-sizing)?
questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer uses usage metrics (and ML) to recommend right-sizing for EC2, Auto Scaling Groups, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate, and RDS/Aurora databases (plus license and idle-resource recommendations) — pointing out over-provisioned resources and the ideal size to save money.

whyNots.B: Budgets alerts on spend thresholds, it does not recommend resizing.
whyNots.C: Pricing Calculator estimates costs for new projects; it does not analyze current usage.
whyNots.D: CUR is raw billing data, not right-sizing recommendations.

hints: There is a service that looks at usage metrics and says 'this instance is too large, switch to this smaller one and save.' It is Compute Optimizer.

questions.stem:
Leadership wants a general account check-up: cost-saving opportunities, security gaps, service limits near the ceiling, and fault-tolerance points.

Which service performs these automatic checks across categories (cost, security, performance, fault tolerance/resiliency, operational excellence, and service limits)?
questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor runs automated checks across 6 categories — cost optimization, performance, resiliency (fault tolerance), security, operational excellence, and service limits — and recommends actions. It is the general account check-up.

whyNots.A: GuardDuty detects threats, not cost opportunities or limits.
whyNots.C: Config monitors configuration compliance over time, not the summary of opportunities across Trusted Advisor's 6 categories.
whyNots.D: Inspector scans for CVE vulnerabilities in EC2/containers, not this multi-category check-up.

hints: Think of Trusted Advisor as an account health check-up — it runs a fine-tooth comb and points out savings, security risks, limits near the ceiling, and weak spots across categories.

questions.stem:
The company wants to know HOW MUCH each team (marketing, data, platform) spends on AWS, to allocate costs. Each team's resources must be identifiable on the bill.

Which feature lets you track and separate costs by team/project in the account?

options.text: One VPC per team — the bill is separated by VPC
Reserved Instances allocated by team on the bill
Security Groups per team, which group cost

questions.explanation: Cost Allocation Tags mark resources (e.g., Team, Project, Environment); once activated in billing, Cost Explorer and CUR can group and allocate costs by those tags — that is how you separate spend by team or project.

whyNots.A: One VPC per team isolates networking, but it is not the cost-allocation mechanism on the bill.
whyNots.B: Reserved Instances are a commitment discount, not cost tracking by team.
whyNots.D: Security Groups are firewalls; they do not track cost.

hints: For the bill to know 'this belongs to the data team,' each resource needs a standardized label.
You tag resources (e.g., Team=data) and enable Cost Allocation Tags — then Cost Explorer/CUR can split spend by tag.

questions.stem:
The company has 12 AWS accounts (prod, dev, data, etc.). Finance wants a SINGLE bill and wants to benefit from volume discounts by aggregating usage across all accounts.

Which AWS Organizations feature delivers a single bill and aggregated volume discount?

options.text: AWS Config Rules summing the 12 bills

questions.explanation: Consolidated Billing (in AWS Organizations) brings all member accounts under a single payer account: one bill, per-account visibility, and volume discounts (e.g., for S3, data transfer) are calculated on the AGGREGATED usage across all accounts.

whyNots.A: SCPs set the permission ceiling for accounts — governance, not billing/discounts.
whyNots.B: Config Rules check compliance; they do not consolidate bills.
whyNots.C: VPC Peering connects networks; it has nothing to do with billing.

hints: Putting all accounts under a single payer account gives one bill — and the combined usage across all accounts helps reach volume discount tiers. That is Consolidated Billing in AWS Organizations.

questions.stem:
Four requests on the same day: (1) estimate the cost of an architecture that does not yet exist; (2) understand and forecast last quarter's spending in a chart; (3) be alerted if the month exceeds a limit; (4) export all billing line by line to analyze in Athena.

What is the correct tool → task mapping?

options.text: 1 Pricing Calculator · 2 Cost Explorer · 3 Budgets · 4 CUR
1 CUR · 2 Budgets · 3 Cost Explorer · 4 Pricing Calculator
1 Pricing Calculator · 2 Budgets · 3 Cost Explorer · 4 CUR
1 Cost Explorer · 2 Pricing Calculator · 3 Budgets · 4 CUR

questions.explanation: Each cost tool has a purpose: Pricing Calculator ESTIMATES the future (not-yet-built); Cost Explorer ANALYZES/forecasts actual spend (visual); Budgets ALERTS when a threshold is crossed; CUR EXPORTS raw data line by line to S3. Knowing which tool does what is what the exam tests.

whyNots.B: Everything is mixed up — CUR does not estimate, Budgets does not analyze quarters.
whyNots.C: Analyze and alert are swapped (Budgets alerts, Cost Explorer analyzes).
whyNots.D: Estimate and analyze are swapped: Cost Explorer does not estimate a new project; Pricing Calculator does not analyze the past.

hints: Four different purposes — ESTIMATE (future), ANALYZE (past), ALERT (threshold), EXPORT (raw data).
estimate=Pricing Calculator; analyze/forecast=Cost Explorer; alert=Budgets; export line by line=CUR.

questions.stem:
Two colleagues debate: one advocates Reserved Instances, the other Savings Plans, for a stable EC2 fleet that MAY change instance family over time.

What difference makes Savings Plans (Compute) the more flexible choice here?

options.text: Reserved Instances always give the biggest discount in any scenario, so they are better even when the workload changes family or region
Savings Plans commit an hourly amount and apply across families/regions and even Fargate/Lambda; Reserved tends to lock a specific configuration
Savings Plans and Reserved Instances are identical in flexibility and discount; AWS merely renamed the old product
Savings Plans only apply to Spot instances, so it never covers On-Demand EC2, Fargate, or Lambda in any region

questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans offer a discount similar to Reserved Instances, but the commitment is an hourly spend amount — the discount follows you even if you switch instance family, region, or migrate to Fargate/Lambda. Reserved Instances (Standard) tend to bind a specific configuration. For a stable fleet that may still change shape, Savings Plans is more flexible.

whyNots.A: Standard Reserved can offer a slightly bigger discount in exchange for LESS flexibility — and here flexibility is the requirement.
whyNots.C: They are not identical; the flexibility axis is exactly the difference.
whyNots.D: Savings Plans is about a usage commitment (discounted On-Demand), not Spot.

hints: The clue is 'MAY change instance family'. Which model does not lock you into one configuration?
Reserved usually locks type and region; Compute Savings Plans commits hourly spend and the discount follows you across families, regions, and even to Fargate/Lambda.

questions.stem:
The team builds the same environment (VPC, EC2, database) manually every time a new account is opened. They always forget a detail and production breaks.

Which service lets you describe the entire infrastructure in a text file and recreate it identically as many times as you want?
questions.explanation: CloudFormation is infrastructure as code (IaC): you describe resources in a declarative template (JSON/YAML), and it creates a stack with everything — repeatable, versionable, and without missing details. CloudFormation itself is free; you pay only for the resources it creates.

whyNots.A: Config audits and records resource configuration changes — it does not create infrastructure.
whyNots.B: CloudWatch is metrics, logs, and alarms — it observes, not provisions.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail audits API calls (who did what) — it does not build environments.

hints: Think of a written recipe. Instead of assembling everything by eye, you write the steps (JSON or YAML) and AWS executes them identically every time. This is 'infrastructure as code'.
The name contains 'Formation' — it FORMS (creates) your resources from a template. The other three only observe what already exists.

questions.stem:
You need to deploy the SAME security baseline template across 40 accounts and 3 regions in a single operation. You also want new organization accounts to receive the baseline automatically.

Which CloudFormation feature solves this?
questions.explanation: StackSets deploys and maintains a template across multiple accounts AND regions in a single operation. With service-managed permissions through Organizations, accounts added later receive the stacks automatically — great for governance/security baselines.

whyNots.A: Drift detection compares live resources with the template — it is diagnostic, not deployment.
whyNots.B: Nested stacks split a large template into reusable pieces WITHIN one stack — they do not spread across accounts.
whyNots.C: Change sets only preview what will change before you apply — they do not perform multi-account deployment.

hints: The 'Set' in the name is the clue — it is a SET of stacks spread across multiple accounts and regions at once.
Combined with AWS Organizations and service-managed permissions, new accounts are onboarded with the stacks already applied.

questions.stem:
Your CloudFormation stack includes a production RDS database with real data. You fear that deleting the stack will delete the database and you will lose everything.

Which attribute on a stack resource protects the database from being destroyed when the stack is deleted?
questions.explanation: DeletionPolicy is the resource attribute that controls what happens when the stack is removed. `Retain` keeps the resource, `Snapshot` takes a final snapshot (supported by RDS, EBS, etc.), and `Delete` (default) removes it. For production stateful data, use `Retain` or `Snapshot`.

whyNots.B: Termination protection is an EC2 instance safeguard, not CloudFormation's mechanism for an RDS in a stack.
whyNots.C: UpdateReplacePolicy handles replacement during an UPDATE; and `Delete` would remove the resource, the opposite of what is wanted.
whyNots.D: DependsOn only controls the ORDER of resource creation, not what happens on deletion.

hints: There is an attribute whose name literally means 'deletion policy'. That is where you say: when deleting the stack, do NOT delete this resource.
`Retain` keeps the resource alive; `Snapshot` takes a final snapshot before releasing it (valid for RDS, EBS). The default is `Delete`.

questions.stem:
Someone logged into the console and manually changed a security group rule outside the template. You want to know WHICH stack resources no longer match what CloudFormation expects.

Which CloudFormation feature points out those differences?
questions.explanation: Drift detection compares the live configuration of each resource with what the template expects and reports what has drifted (changes made outside CloudFormation). It does not cascade into nested stacks — run it directly on the nested stack.

whyNots.A: Change sets show what WILL change before you apply an update — they do not detect manual changes already made.
whyNots.C: Automatic rollback undoes a failed deployment — it does not compare manual state versus template.
whyNots.D: Stack policy protects resources from accidental updates — it does not detect drift.

hints: 'Drift' means deviation — when reality has deviated from the plan. The feature compares the LIVE resource with what the template mandates.
Be careful — drift detection does not automatically cascade into nested stacks; for those, run it directly on the nested stack.

questions.stem:
A developer wrote a Python web app and just wants to deploy it quickly. They do not want to configure EC2, load balancer, and auto scaling manually — but they also do not want to lose all access to the infrastructure.

Which service deploys the application by provisioning the underlying infrastructure while still letting you see and adjust the resources?
questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk is PaaS: you upload the code (Python, Java, Node.js, .NET, Docker...) and it provisions and manages EC2, ELB, auto scaling, and monitoring — with no extra charge for Beanstalk itself (you pay only for the underlying resources). You retain visibility and can customize the infrastructure.

whyNots.A: S3 static website only serves static files — it cannot run Python server code.
whyNots.B: Lambda is event/function serverless; it is not the way to host a traditional 'always-on' web app with visible infrastructure.
whyNots.D: Plain EC2 gives maximum control, but it is exactly the manual work the developer wants to avoid.

hints: You just provide the code; AWS builds EC2, load balancer, auto scaling, and monitoring for you. It is the middle ground between assembling everything manually and giving up all control.
There is no additional service cost — you pay only for the AWS resources it creates underneath.

questions.stem:
Four teams debate where to run workloads. One wants full machine control; another wants to just upload web app code with managed infrastructure; another wants event-driven serverless functions.

Which association is CORRECT?

options.text: All three do exactly the same thing; it is just a naming preference
Full control = Lambda; managed web app = EC2; event function = Beanstalk
Full control = Beanstalk; managed web app = Lambda; event function = EC2
Full control = EC2; managed web app = Elastic Beanstalk; event function = Lambda

questions.explanation: EC2 delivers maximum control and flexibility (you manage the server). Elastic Beanstalk sits in the middle: you upload code and it manages the infrastructure for a web app. Lambda is serverless: you upload the function and do not think about servers, paying per execution.

whyNots.A: They are very different responsibility models; the exam point is knowing which to choose.
whyNots.B: Reverses everything — Lambda is not 'full control' and Beanstalk is not event-driven functions.
whyNots.C: Also swaps roles; Beanstalk does not give full control and EC2 is not event-driven functions.

hints: Order by how much AWS does for you. EC2 = you do everything. Beanstalk = you give the code, it builds the house. Lambda = you give the function, it even manages the server.

questions.stem:
A request passes through API Gateway, then Lambda, then DynamoDB. The customer complains it is slow, but nobody knows WHICH step is consuming the time.

Which service shows the path of the request across components and where the bottleneck is?
questions.explanation: X-Ray performs distributed tracing: it follows each request through components, groups the segments into a trace, and builds a visual service map (nodes = services, with latency and failure rate). It is how you find the bottleneck step by step in a microservices/serverless architecture.

whyNots.B: CloudTrail audits API calls (who did what), not per-step request latency.
whyNots.C: CloudWatch Alarms trigger on aggregated metrics — it warns that something is slow but does not show WHERE along the path.
whyNots.D: Config records/evaluates resource configuration — nothing to do with tracing a request.

hints: Think of an X-ray of the request — it shows every 'bone' along the path (each service) and how much time the request spent in each one.
It builds a visual service map, with average latency and failure rate per node. Distributed tracing.

questions.stem:
The exam presents the triad. You need to separate: aggregated metrics/logs/alarms; API call audit; and the path of a single request across services.

Which mapping is correct?

options.text: CloudWatch = API audit; CloudTrail = per-request path; X-Ray = metrics and alarms
CloudWatch = metrics/logs/alarms; CloudTrail = API audit; X-Ray = per-request path
CloudWatch = per-request path; CloudTrail = metrics and logs; X-Ray = API audit
All three are interchangeable for any of these goals — they collect the same data

questions.explanation: CloudWatch handles metrics, logs, and aggregated alarms; CloudTrail records API calls for audit (who did what, when); X-Ray traces the path of each request across services. On the exam, this separation resolves most observability trick questions.

whyNots.A: Swaps roles — CloudWatch does not audit APIs and CloudTrail does not trace per-request paths.
whyNots.C: Also scrambles all three; none of those pairs are correct.
whyNots.D: They are not interchangeable — each answers a different question.

hints: 'Trail' suggests an audit trail (who called which API). 'Watch' suggests watching numbers (metrics/alarms). X-Ray is the X-ray of the path.

questions.stem:
An online game uses UDP and players complain about lag depending on their country. You want traffic to enter the AWS network at the edge closest to the player and travel over the AWS backbone to the region.

Which service delivers this, with static entry IPs?
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator provides static anycast entry IPs and moves traffic onto the AWS global network at the closest edge, traversing the backbone to the regional endpoint. It works over TCP/UDP, ideal for non-HTTP (UDP games, IoT MQTT, VoIP) and HTTP that requires fixed IPs or fast regional failover.

whyNots.A: Route 53 resolves DNS by latency, but it depends on DNS caching and does not provide a static entry IP nor accelerate transport over the backbone.
whyNots.B: CloudFront is an HTTP(S) CDN with edge caching; it is not the choice for a UDP game.
whyNots.D: Direct Connect is a dedicated link from your data center to AWS — it does not accelerate end users spread around the world.

hints: The name says it — it ACCELERATES GLOBAL traffic. It provides anycast static IPs and pulls the user into the AWS network as early as possible, including for TCP/UDP.
CloudFront is a CDN designed for cacheable HTTP(S). A UDP game is not a CloudFront case — it is a Global Accelerator case.

questions.stem:
Two scenarios: (1) a site with lots of static images and video to accelerate globally; (2) a TCP API that needs very few fixed IPs for partner firewall allowlists and deterministic regional failover.

Which combination serves each scenario?

options.text: Both with Global Accelerator, because it replaces CloudFront
Both with CloudFront, because both are HTTP

questions.explanation: CloudFront is a CDN: ideal for accelerating and caching static/dynamic HTTP(S) content globally (scenario 1). Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and fast TCP/UDP regional failover, perfect for allowlisting a few IPs in partner firewalls (scenario 2). They do not cache the same way and can even be used together.

whyNots.A: Global Accelerator does not replace CloudFront — it does not cache content at the edge.
whyNots.B: Global Accelerator is not HTTP-only nor does it cache; scenario 2 asks for fixed IP/failover, which is its specialty.
whyNots.C: Reversed: the CDN for static content is CloudFront, not Global Accelerator.

hints: Cacheable static content = CDN = CloudFront. Fixed IPs for allowlist + fast TCP failover = Global Accelerator.
CloudFront CACHES at the edge; Global Accelerator does NOT cache, it accelerates transport. They are separate and complementary services.
The clue in scenario 2 is 'very few fixed IPs for allowlist' — that screams Global Accelerator (static anycast IPs).

questions.stem:
IoT devices around the world need to talk to your application through a fixed, small set of IPs (they do not honor DNS caching well and customer firewalls only allow specific IPs).

Why does Global Accelerator fit better than relying only on DNS?

options.text: It exposes fixed static anycast IPs, independent of DNS caching
It caches the application content at the edge
It only works with DNS names, never with IP
It swaps the IPs every request to make attacks harder

questions.explanation: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs that serve as a fixed entry point — perfect when clients need to allowlist a few IPs and when devices do not honor DNS caching. The IPs do not change even if the regional endpoints behind them change.

whyNots.B: CloudFront caches content at the edge; Global Accelerator accelerates transport, it does not cache.
whyNots.C: It delivers static IPs — that is exactly the strength here.
whyNots.D: The IPs are STATIC, exactly the opposite of changing every request.

hints: The problem is 'firewall only allows fixed IP' plus 'device ignores DNS caching'. The solution must be an IP that does not change.
Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPs — you allowlist those two and you are done, valid for any region behind them.

questions.stem:
You have two independent stacks: one creates the VPC and subnet; the other creates the instances and needs to reference the subnet ID that the first created — without copying and pasting the value by hand.

Which CloudFormation mechanism shares that value between separate stacks?
questions.explanation: To share values between independent stacks, the first declares an Output with `Export` and the second uses `Fn::ImportValue` to pull that value by name — a cross-stack reference, without copying and pasting IDs. (Nested stacks use Fn::GetAtt on child Outputs; that is a different case.)

whyNots.A: Metadata holds arbitrary information about the stack — it is not used to export values to another stack.
whyNots.C: Mappings are static lookup tables inside a template (e.g., AMI per region) — they do not share values between stacks.
whyNots.D: Typing the ID by hand as a parameter is exactly the fragile copy-paste we want to avoid.

hints: One stack EXPORTS an output value; the other IMPORTS that value by name. It is the official bridge between independent stacks (cross-stack reference).
Do not confuse this with nested stacks — there, the child passes Outputs to the parent via Fn::GetAtt. Here the stacks are siblings, independent.

questions.stem:
A developer wants to store the database connection string and some application configs in a central, inexpensive place with versioning and IAM control — and the ability to encrypt sensitive values.

Which Systems Manager resource stores configuration and light secrets hierarchically?
questions.explanation: Parameter Store stores configuration and light secrets hierarchically, with versioning and IAM control. String and StringList types are plain text; SecureString encrypts the value with KMS. It is inexpensive and integrated with EC2, Lambda, ECS, and CloudFormation.

whyNots.A: Session Manager provides shell access to instances — it does not store configuration.
whyNots.B: Patch Manager applies patches to the fleet — it does not store parameters.
whyNots.D: Run Command executes commands remotely on instances — it is not a configuration vault.

hints: The name says it — it is a 'parameter store'. You store key-value data hierarchically (like folders), with versions and IAM access.
To encrypt, use the SecureString type, which uses KMS underneath. String and StringList remain in plain text.

questions.stem:
Security requires the RDS database password to be automatically rotated every 30 days without anyone touching the code. They also want to replicate the secret to another region.

Which service supports native automatic credential rotation?
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager is designed for secrets with native automatic rotation (via Lambda, at configurable intervals), database integration, and cross-region replication. Parameter Store stores light, inexpensive secrets but does not rotate them on its own. Exam rule of thumb: needs automatic rotation = Secrets Manager.

whyNots.A: Config evaluates resource compliance — it does not store or rotate passwords.
whyNots.B: Parameter Store stores the value, but does not automatically rotate credentials.
whyNots.C: Versioned S3 stores objects, it is not a credential vault with rotation.

hints: The keyword is AUTOMATIC ROTATION. Parameter Store can hold a secret, but Secrets Manager runs the swap automatically (via Lambda).
Secrets Manager also replicates secrets across regions and was built for database credentials. Parameter Store is more for simple, low-cost configuration.

questions.stem:
Audit asked to CLOSE port 22 (SSH) on all instances and stop managing SSH keys and bastion hosts. But the team still needs to open a shell on instances to investigate issues.

Which Systems Manager resource provides shell access without opening an inbound port or using an SSH key?
questions.explanation: Session Manager opens an interactive shell on instances through the SSM agent (outbound connection), with no inbound on port 22, no SSH key, and no bastion. Access is controlled by IAM and can be logged for audit — reducing the attack surface.

whyNots.B: Patch Manager applies patches — it does not open an interactive shell session.
whyNots.C: Instance Connect still involves port 22, which is exactly what audit ordered closed.
whyNots.D: Parameter Store stores configuration — it does not provide a shell.

hints: 'Session' = shell session. It connects through the SSM agent (outbound to AWS), so you do not need to open port 22 or maintain a bastion.
Access is controlled by IAM and recorded/auditable — exactly what audit wants.

questions.stem:
You have a fleet of hundreds of instances and need to apply security updates at scale, plus know WHICH ones are out of patch compliance.

Which Systems Manager resource solves this?
questions.explanation: Patch Manager applies patches at scale across the fleet and provides compliance visibility — which nodes are updated and which are not. It works with patch baselines and maintenance windows.

whyNots.A: Config evaluates general resource configuration compliance, but Patch Manager is what applies the patch.
whyNots.C: Session Manager provides a shell; it does not automate fleet patching.
whyNots.D: Parameter Store stores configuration — nothing to do with patching.

hints: 'Patch' = update/fix. It applies patches across the entire fleet and shows the compliance dashboard (who is updated and who is not).

questions.stem:
Audit asks: 'How was this security group configured three weeks ago, and how did it change over time?' You need a history of resource configurations.

Which service records and evaluates resource configuration over time?
questions.explanation: AWS Config continuously records resource configuration and maintains a timeline (resource timeline), allowing you to audit how each resource was configured and how it changed. It can also evaluate compliance through rules.

whyNots.A: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations by category — it does not maintain a configuration timeline.
whyNots.B: CloudWatch is operational metrics/logs/alarms — not configuration history.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail records API calls (who did what) — not a snapshot of configuration over time.

hints: Think of a timeline for each resource — how it was configured yesterday, last week, today. That is the focus of Config.
Config answers 'HOW the resource was/is configured'. CloudTrail answers 'WHO called which API'. They are different questions.

questions.stem:
Compliance wants to enforce, across ALL organization accounts, rules like 'every S3 bucket must be encrypted' and 'no security group may allow 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22', with remediation — in a single package.

Which AWS Config resource packages multiple rules (and remediations) for scaled deployment?
questions.explanation: A conformance pack is a collection of Config rules + remediation actions packaged as a single entity, deployable to an account/region or across the entire organization (via Organizations). It simplifies compliance and reporting at scale. A single Config rule evaluates one rule; the pack bundles many.

whyNots.A: Change sets are from CloudFormation (preview changes) — unrelated to Config compliance.
whyNots.B: A single rule covers only one criterion; the scenario asks for a set + remediation deployed at once.
whyNots.C: SCPs restrict which API actions are permitted in accounts; they do not EVALUATE existing resource configuration like Config does.

hints: 'Conformance pack' = compliance package. It bundles many Config rules + remediations into one package, deployable to account/region or the whole organization.
Do not confuse with SCP — SCP denies/permits API ACTIONS; Config rules EVALUATE whether a resource is compliant.

questions.stem:
A resource was changed and caused an incident. You need TWO answers: (1) what changed in the resource configuration; (2) who called the API that made the change and when.

Which pair of services answers, respectively, the 'what' and the 'who'?
questions.explanation: In an investigation, AWS Config shows WHAT changed in the resource configuration (and the history), while CloudTrail shows WHO called which API, when, and from where. Together they answer the complete incident: what + who + when.

whyNots.B: Neither answers 'what changed in the configuration'; Config is missing.
whyNots.C: Reverses roles — CloudTrail is the 'who', not the 'what' of configuration.
whyNots.D: CloudWatch is operational metric/log, not resource configuration detail.

hints: Config = WHAT changed in the resource configuration. CloudTrail = WHO (and when) called the API. They complement each other in an investigation.

questions.stem:
The company has 25 AWS accounts and wants to prevent, top-down, ANY child account from, for example, turning off CloudTrail or creating resources outside certain regions — regardless of what that account's IAM allows.

Which AWS Organizations resource imposes this maximum permission boundary on accounts?

options.text: IAM roles in the management account

questions.explanation: SCPs, applied through AWS Organizations to OUs/accounts, define the permission ceiling (guardrails): no identity in the account can exceed what the SCP allows, even if IAM permits it. SCPs do not grant access — they only restrict the maximum. Perfect for prohibiting turning off CloudTrail or using unauthorized regions.
