whyNots.A: Conformance packs evaluate configuration compliance (Config) — they do not block API actions.
whyNots.C: IAM roles grant permission within one account — they do not impose a ceiling over all child accounts.
whyNots.D: Security groups control network traffic — unrelated to API permissions between accounts.

hints: An SCP is a 'ceiling' of permissions for the whole account. Even if local IAM allows it, if the SCP denies it, the action does not happen.
SCP does not GRANT permission — it only limits the maximum possible (guardrail). IAM inside the account grants access.

questions.stem:
You want to AUTOMATICALLY react to events: when an EC2 instance changes state, or on a scheduled time, trigger a Lambda function — without anyone pressing a button.

Which service routes AWS events (and schedules) to targets like Lambda?
questions.explanation: EventBridge (formerly CloudWatch Events) is the event bus: rules match event patterns (e.g., EC2 state change) or schedules (cron) and route to targets like Lambda, SNS, SQS, Step Functions. It is the foundation of event-driven automation.

whyNots.A: CloudTrail records API calls; it is not the event routing/automation mechanism.
whyNots.B: Config evaluates compliance; it can emit events, but it is not the event/schedule router that triggers the flow.
whyNots.D: SQS is a message queue (pull) — it does not route AWS events by rule/pattern nor schedule cron.

hints: Think of an 'event bus' — things happen in AWS, and rules decide which target (Lambda, SNS, SQS...) to send them to. It also does cron-style scheduling.
EventBridge is the evolution of CloudWatch Events. Rule by event pattern OR schedule → target.

questions.stem:
In a governance review, four questions come up: (1) is this resource compliant with rules? (2) who called this API and when? (3) did CPU usage exceed the limit? (4) how to prevent all accounts from using a forbidden region?

Which mapping correctly answers all four?

options.text: (1) Config; (2) CloudTrail; (3) CloudWatch; (4) SCP in Organizations

questions.explanation: Each service has a role: Config evaluates resource compliance/configuration; CloudTrail records who called which API and when; CloudWatch measures metrics and alarms on limits (e.g., CPU); SCP (via Organizations) imposes the permission ceiling that blocks actions like using a forbidden region. Option D is the only one that respects all four roles.

whyNots.A: Puts CloudWatch as the compliance evaluator and SCP as API audit — scrambled.
whyNots.B: Swaps Config with CloudTrail and uses SCP for metrics, which is wrong.
whyNots.C: Uses SCP for compliance and Config to block a region — roles reversed.

hints: Separate by verb. Configuration compliance = Config. Who called API = CloudTrail. Metric/limit = CloudWatch. Cross-account permission ceiling = SCP.
The trick is mixing Config (what/compliance) with CloudTrail (who) and SCP (blocks action). Each answers a different question.

questions.stem:
A company transfers terabytes per day between its data center and AWS. The public internet is giving unstable latency and they want dedicated, predictable bandwidth.

Which service provides a private, dedicated network connection from on-premises to AWS, without crossing the public internet?
questions.explanation: Direct Connect is a dedicated, private network connection between the data center and AWS, without crossing the public internet — low latency, consistent bandwidth, and predictable throughput. It is the choice for high, steady transfer. It costs more and takes time to provision (physical link).

whyNots.B: Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted, but it traverses the public internet — latency and bandwidth vary.
whyNots.C: Global Accelerator accelerates end users through the AWS network — it is not an on-premises↔AWS hybrid link.
whyNots.D: CloudFront is a CDN for edge content — it does not connect a data center to AWS.

hints: 'Direct Connect' = direct connection. It is a dedicated physical link, outside the public internet, with predictable bandwidth and latency.
VPN also connects on-premises, but it runs OVER the internet (cheaper, less predictable). For dedicated, consistent bandwidth, use Direct Connect.

questions.stem:
A startup needs to connect its office to the VPC NOW, with encrypted traffic, low cost, and without waiting to provision a physical link. Volume is modest.

Which option fits best?

options.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec tunnel over the internet)
VPC Peering with the AWS account

questions.explanation: Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted IPsec tunnel between on-premises and the VPC over the internet — quick to set up and inexpensive, ideal for modest volume and immediate need. Direct Connect would be better for bandwidth/latency, but it costs more and takes time to provision.

whyNots.A: Direct Connect takes time to provision and costs more — does not match 'now' and 'low cost'.
whyNots.C: VPC Peering connects VPCs to each other, not an on-premises office to a VPC.
whyNots.D: An internet gateway without encryption does not meet the encrypted, secure traffic requirement.

hints: The keywords are 'now', 'encrypted', 'cheap', 'modest volume'. That is the profile of VPN, not Direct Connect.
Direct Connect is great, but it is expensive and slow (physical link). For fast, secure setup, use Site-to-Site VPN.

questions.stem:
A bank uses Direct Connect to link its data center to AWS for latency and bandwidth. But it fears that if the DX link fails, connectivity will go down. They want an automatic, cheaper backup.

Which architecture solves this with the best cost-benefit?

options.text: Direct Connect + CloudFront as backup route, since the CDN takes over hybrid traffic
Site-to-Site VPN only, dropping Direct Connect and keeping the same bandwidth
Direct Connect as primary + Site-to-Site VPN as backup (automatic failover)
Two identical Direct Connects, no VPN — full redundancy at lowest cost

questions.explanation: The classic exam pattern: Direct Connect as the primary path (latency/bandwidth) + Site-to-Site VPN as backup. If DX fails, traffic fails over to the VPN automatically (via BGP), at much lower cost than a second DX. DX is always preferred when active.

whyNots.A: CloudFront is a content CDN — it cannot serve as a backup route for hybrid connectivity.
whyNots.B: Giving up DX loses the low latency/bandwidth the bank needs daily.
whyNots.D: Two DXs provide high resilience, but it is the most expensive option — the prompt asks for a 'cheaper' backup.

hints: The exam loves this pattern — DX is expensive and great; VPN is cheap and 'good enough' for emergencies. Combine the two: DX leads, VPN covers the outage.
Failover is automatic via BGP; DX is always preferred when it is up.
Two DXs provide maximum redundancy, but the prompt asks for a 'cheaper' backup — that is where VPN comes in.

questions.stem:
The company has 40 VPCs across different accounts and needs all of them to communicate with each other and with on-premises. Building VPC peering between every pair became a mesh nightmare.

Which service centralizes this connectivity in a hub?

options.text: More VPC peerings, one per pair

questions.explanation: Transit Gateway is the central hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks (via VPN/DX) in a hub-and-spoke topology with centralized routing. It replaces the point-to-point VPC peering mesh, which is not transitive and does not scale to dozens of VPCs/accounts.

whyNots.A: Direct Connect links on-premises to AWS, but it does not solve interconnection among the 40 VPCs.
whyNots.B: Point-to-point VPC peering explodes in complexity (n² connections) and is not transitive — it is exactly the problem stated.
whyNots.C: An internet gateway provides public internet access — it does not interconnect private VPCs with each other.

hints: 'Transit' = central transit. Instead of connecting every VPC to all the others (a mesh that explodes), you connect all of them to a single hub.
VPC peering is not transitive and does not scale to dozens of VPCs. Transit Gateway is the hub-and-spoke solution.

questions.stem:
A ride-sharing app captures GPS events from drivers in real time and needs to process that stream immediately, with several different consumers and the ability to replay data.

Which service ingests and makes this stream available in real time, with replay?
questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams ingests real-time streaming data, retains the data for a period (replay), and allows multiple consumers to read the same stream (pull), ordered by shard. Ideal for real-time processing with custom logic (Lambda, KCL, EC2).

whyNots.B: Glue is ETL (batch/serverless), not real-time stream ingestion.
whyNots.C: SQS is a message queue; the message disappears once processed — there is no replay nor reading by multiple consumers of the same stream.
whyNots.D: S3 is object storage — not a real-time streaming pipeline.

hints: The clue is 'real time + multiple consumers + replay'. Kinesis Data Streams retains data and lets consumers read (PULL), reprocessing if desired.
SQS delivers and removes the message once processed — it was not built for replay or for multiple consumers reading the same ordered stream.

questions.stem:
The team just wants to dump a stream of logs straight into an S3 bucket (and later into Redshift), with buffering, compression, and without writing or maintaining pipeline code.

Which service delivers the streaming data to those destinations, fully managed and code-free?

options.text: Amazon EC2 with a custom script, no maintenance
Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose)
Amazon SNS delivering directly to S3 and Redshift
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, which delivers without code

questions.explanation: Amazon Data Firehose (renamed in 2024; formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) is fully managed and delivers streaming data directly to destinations like S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, and Splunk — with buffering by size/time, compression, transformation, and encryption, without you writing or maintaining pipeline code.

whyNots.A: An EC2 script is exactly the code/maintenance the team wants to avoid.
whyNots.C: SNS is pub/sub messaging (push to subscribers) — not a streaming delivery pipeline to S3/Redshift.
whyNots.D: Data Streams is for real-time processing with custom consumers — it requires code; it does not deliver to S3 on its own without work.

hints: The clue is 'deliver straight to S3/Redshift, no code, managed'. That is Data Firehose — it PUSHES to the destination, with buffering and compression.
Watch the name — since February 2024 it is called 'Amazon Data Firehose' (was 'Kinesis Data Firehose'). Same service, new name.

questions.stem:
Two requirements: (1) process events in real time with custom logic, multiple consumers, and replay; (2) simply unload the already-handled stream into an S3 data lake, without maintaining code.

Which combination is correct?

options.text: Both with Data Streams, because Firehose does not deliver to S3
Both with Data Firehose, because Data Streams was discontinued
(1) Kinesis Data Streams; (2) Amazon Data Firehose
(1) Amazon Data Firehose; (2) Kinesis Data Streams

questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is for real-time processing with custom consumers and replay (pull). Amazon Data Firehose is managed, code-free delivery to destinations like S3/Redshift (push with buffering). They can even work together: Streams processes, Firehose reads from the stream and unloads to the destination.

whyNots.A: Firehose DOES deliver to S3 natively — that is exactly its use case.
whyNots.B: Data Streams was not discontinued; it remains active and distinct from Firehose.
whyNots.D: Reversed: the one that processes with custom logic/replay is Data Streams, not Firehose.

hints: 'Process in real time with replay' = Data Streams (PULL, consumers). 'Just deliver to S3 without code' = Data Firehose (PUSH, managed).
You can even use both together — Data Streams processes and Firehose reads from the stream and delivers to the destination.
Streams = you write the consumer; Firehose = you just point to the destination.

questions.stem:
When an order is created, three systems need to react (inventory, email, and analytics) — each at its own pace, decoupled, so a slow one does not bring the others down.

Which pattern delivers the event to all three in a decoupled way?

options.text: Store everything in a single DynamoDB item
Call the three systems synchronously, in sequence
A single SQS queue read by all three at the same time
Fan-out: one SNS topic publishing to multiple subscribed SQS queues

questions.explanation: The fan-out pattern uses an SNS topic that publishes to multiple subscribed SQS queues (one per consumer). Each system reads from its own queue at its own pace, decoupled — if one slows or fails, the others keep going. Classic resilience and decoupling for the exam.

whyNots.A: Writing to a DynamoDB item does not distribute the event or decouple processing.
whyNots.B: Synchronous sequential calls couple the systems: one slow or down breaks the chain.
whyNots.C: A single shared queue makes consumers compete for the same messages — each does not get its own copy of the event.

hints: One event → many consumers, each at its own pace is the fan-out pattern. SNS publishes to the topic; each service has its own subscribed SQS queue.
That way each consumer processes at its own speed and a slow one does not block the others — full decoupling.

questions.stem:
A mobile app needs user sign-up and login (including Google and Apple sign-in), with user directory management and token issuance.

Which Amazon Cognito resource handles USER AUTHENTICATION?
questions.explanation: Cognito User Pool is the user directory: it handles sign-up/sign-in, attributes, MFA, and federation with IdPs (Google, Apple, OIDC, SAML), issuing JWT tokens (OAuth 2.0). It is the AUTHENTICATION layer — it answers 'who is the user'.

whyNots.B: IAM User is an identity for operating the AWS account (admin/dev), not for end users of an app.
whyNots.C: Security Group is a network firewall — nothing to do with user authentication.
whyNots.D: Identity Pool is AUTHORIZATION — it exchanges the token for temporary AWS credentials; it is not the login directory.

hints: User Pool = user directory. It handles sign-up/sign-in, federates with Google/Apple, and issues JWT tokens. It answers WHO the user is.
Do not confuse it with Identity Pool, which comes later to exchange tokens for temporary AWS credentials (authorization).

questions.stem:
After login, the app needs each authenticated user to access an S3 bucket and a DynamoDB table DIRECTLY, using temporary AWS credentials scoped via an IAM role.

Which Cognito resource provides those temporary AWS credentials?

options.text: Fixed IAM Access Key embedded in the app

questions.explanation: Cognito Identity Pool exchanges a token (from a User Pool or IdP) for temporary AWS credentials associated with IAM roles, to access services like S3 and DynamoDB directly. It even supports unauthenticated guests. It is the AUTHORIZATION layer — 'what the user can access in AWS'.

whyNots.A: KMS manages encryption keys — it does not provide access credentials for services.
whyNots.C: User Pool authenticates and issues tokens, but does not deliver AWS credentials to access S3/DynamoDB — that is Identity Pool's job.
whyNots.D: A fixed Access Key embedded in the app is a serious security flaw; never embed long-lived credentials in the client.

hints: User Pool tells WHO you are (token). Identity Pool tells WHAT you can access in AWS — it exchanges the token for temporary credentials via an IAM role.
Embedding a fixed Access Key in the app is a serious security flaw; temporary credentials via Identity Pool is the right way.

questions.stem:
In a DR meeting, someone asks: 'after a disaster, how much DATA can we lose?' and 'how much TIME does the system have to be back online?'

Which pair of metrics answers those two questions, respectively?

options.text: SLA (data you can lose) and TPS (time until back)
RTO (data you can lose) and RPO (time until back)
RPO (data you can lose) and RTO (time until back)
IOPS (data you can lose) and throughput (time)

questions.explanation: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can lose, measured in time (how far back you recover) — it depends on backup/replication frequency. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long the system can be down before coming back. Lower is better for both, but more expensive.

whyNots.A: SLA is a service-level agreement and TPS is transactions per second — not the DR metrics here.
whyNots.B: Reverses the two: RPO is about DATA/point; RTO is about TIME to recover.
whyNots.D: IOPS and throughput measure storage performance — unrelated to recovery objectives.

hints: RPO has a 'P' for Point — up to what POINT in the past do you recover (how much data is lost). RTO has a 'T' for Time — how much TIME until you are back.
RPO depends on backup/replication frequency; RTO depends on how fast you can restore/scale.

questions.stem:
The company has backups scattered around: EBS snapshots here, RDS dumps there, EFS another way. They want everything centralized under one automated policy with scheduling and retention.

Which service centralizes and automates backup across multiple AWS services?
questions.explanation: AWS Backup is the managed, policy-based, centralized service to automate backups across multiple services (EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, EKS, and more), with scheduling, retention, monitoring, and KMS encryption.

whyNots.A: Manual snapshots per service are exactly the decentralized mess the scenario wants to solve.
whyNots.B: Glacier is a low-cost archive storage class — a possible backup destination, but not central policy orchestration.
whyNots.C: Config evaluates configuration compliance — it does not back up data.

hints: The name is literal — AWS Backup. One place, policy-based, to schedule and retain backups for EC2, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, and more.
Instead of each team doing it their own way, you define a central backup plan and it applies to everything.

questions.stem:
For compliance, backups MUST NOT be deleted or altered by anyone (not even an admin or ransomware) during the retention period.

Which AWS Backup feature guarantees this WORM (write-once, read-many) model?
questions.explanation: Backup Vault Lock applies the WORM (write-once-read-many) model to the backup vault: within the retention period, backups cannot be deleted or altered — protecting against accidental deletion, malicious insiders, and ransomware. It is the immutability control for compliance.

whyNots.B: Multi-AZ is high availability, not backup immutability.
whyNots.C: S3 Versioning helps against overwrites, but it is not the WORM immutability control of a managed backup vault.
whyNots.D: Security Group is a network firewall — it does not prevent backup deletion.

hints: 'Vault' is a safe and 'Lock' is the latch. Vault Lock applies WORM — once written, no one deletes or alters it during retention.
It is the classic defense against accidental deletion and ransomware/insider threats — even root cannot bypass it in compliance mode.

questions.stem:
Compliance requires keeping a copy of backups at a minimum distance from production, to survive the loss of an entire AWS Region.

Which AWS Backup capability meets this?

options.text: Change the storage class to Glacier
Increase backup frequency in the same Region

questions.explanation: AWS Backup copies backups cross-Region (and cross-account via Organizations) by policy — taking the copy far from production so it survives the loss of the entire Region. This is the typical business-continuity and compliance requirement.

whyNots.A: Glacier reduces archive cost, but does not by itself solve geographic separation.
whyNots.C: Multi-AZ protects against AZ failure within a Region — not against losing the whole Region.
whyNots.D: More frequency improves RPO, but everything stays in the SAME Region — it does not survive a Region outage.

hints: The clue is 'minimum distance' and 'lose the entire Region'. Backups in the same Region do not help if the Region goes down — you need to copy to ANOTHER Region.
AWS Backup copies backups cross-Region (and cross-account) by policy, exactly for continuity and compliance.

questions.stem:
A nonprofit with a tight budget can tolerate being down for several hours in a disaster. It wants the cheapest and simplest DR strategy possible.

Which DR strategy fits?
questions.explanation: Backup & Restore is the simplest and cheapest strategy: you keep backups and restore in the recovery Region when needed. In exchange, it has the LARGEST RTO/RPO (hours) — acceptable for those who can tolerate downtime and prioritize cost.

whyNots.A: Warm Standby keeps a reduced environment always running — costs more than just backups.
whyNots.B: Multi-site Active/Active is the most expensive and complex (RTO/RPO near zero) — the opposite of a tight budget.
whyNots.D: Pilot Light already replicates data and keeps the core ready — more expensive than simple Backup & Restore.

hints: 'Cheapest and simplest' + 'tolerates hours down' = the bottom of the spectrum. You only keep backups and restore when needed.
The four strategies run from cheap/slow to expensive/fast: Backup & Restore → Pilot Light → Warm Standby → Active/Active.

questions.stem:
In a recovery Region, the company keeps DATA always replicated and the core infrastructure ready, but application servers are POWERED OFF — only turned on and scaled when disaster strikes.

Which DR strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Pilot Light continuously replicates data and keeps the core infrastructure provisioned in the DR Region, but with application servers powered off — they are turned on and scaled when disaster happens. RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes.

whyNots.A: In Warm Standby the application IS already running (reduced); here it is powered off.
whyNots.B: Active/Active has everything running and serving traffic in both Regions — well beyond pilot light.
whyNots.C: Backup & Restore does not keep infrastructure standing in the DR Region — you rebuild from backup (slower).

hints: Think of a gas pilot light — the core flame (replicated data) stays on, and you ignite the rest (the servers) when disaster strikes.
The difference from Warm Standby is that here the application is OFF; in Warm Standby it already runs at reduced capacity.

questions.stem:
The team wants faster recovery than pilot light: it is willing to pay to keep a REDUCED but fully functional version running in the DR Region, able to handle low traffic immediately and only needing to scale up.

Which strategy describes this?
questions.explanation: Warm Standby keeps a reduced but fully functional version already running in the DR Region — it can handle low traffic immediately, and recovery is just scaling to production capacity. That is why it has a lower RTO than pilot light, where the application is powered off.

whyNots.B: In Pilot Light the application is OFF (only data/core ready); here it already runs reduced.
whyNots.C: 'Cold standby' is not one of the four named AWS strategies; the idea of nothing running is closer to Backup & Restore.
whyNots.D: Backup & Restore does not keep anything running — it is the slowest to recover.

hints: 'Warm' means it is already running, just small. In a disaster you only scale up/out, giving a lower RTO than pilot light.
Pilot light = app is off (you turn it on). Warm standby = app is on and reduced (you scale). That is the classic trap between them.

questions.stem:
A fintech cannot afford downtime at all: it requires RPO near zero and RTO near zero, and accepts the cost of operating in more than one Region at the same time.

Which DR strategy meets this extreme requirement?

options.text: Daily snapshot in another AZ, zero RPO
Pilot Light that restarts in seconds

questions.explanation: Multi-site Active/Active keeps the workload deployed and SERVING traffic in multiple Regions simultaneously, with RPO and RTO near zero — the lowest RTO/RPO strategy, in exchange for the highest cost and complexity. Route 53 with health checks routes/redirects traffic among the Regions.

whyNots.A: A snapshot in another AZ does not protect against Region loss and does not give near-zero RTO/RPO.
whyNots.C: Backup & Restore has RTO/RPO in hours — far from 'near zero'.
whyNots.D: Pilot Light recovers in tens of minutes — it does not meet near-zero RTO.

hints: RPO~0 and RTO~0 only happen with everything already running and serving traffic in more than one Region at the same time — and accepting the cost.
Route 53 (health checks + routing) distributes and redirects traffic between the active Regions.

questions.stem:
An architect is confusing the terms. They need to understand: what protects against the failure of ONE availability zone, and what protects against the loss of an entire REGION?

Which mapping is correct?

options.text: Both only protect against a single instance failure
Multi-AZ protects against Region loss; Multi-Region protects against AZ failure
Multi-AZ protects against AZ failure; Multi-Region protects against Region loss
Neither helps in a disaster; only backup helps

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ distributes resources across multiple Availability Zones within ONE Region — it survives the failure of an AZ (local high availability). Multi-Region (cross-Region read replicas, S3 CRR, Aurora Global Database, with Route 53 failover) protects against the loss of an entire REGION — DR territory.

whyNots.A: Both go beyond a single instance — they cover AZ and Region, respectively.
whyNots.B: Reversed: Multi-AZ is inside the Region; Multi-Region covers Region loss.
whyNots.D: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region are pillars of resilience/DR, alongside backup.

hints: Count the boxes. Multi-AZ = multiple zones WITHIN one Region (survives losing one AZ). Multi-Region = different Regions (survives losing the Region).
RDS Multi-AZ is local high availability; cross-Region read replica / S3 CRR / Aurora Global = Region-level DR.

questions.stem:
Four requirements arrive: (1) lowest cost, tolerates hours down; (2) data replicated but app off; (3) reduced environment already running; (4) zero downtime, serving in two Regions.

Which strategy order maps 1→2→3→4 correctly?

options.text: Warm Standby → Active/Active → Backup & Restore → Pilot Light
Active/Active → Warm Standby → Pilot Light → Backup & Restore
Pilot Light → Backup & Restore → Active/Active → Warm Standby
Backup & Restore → Pilot Light → Warm Standby → Active/Active

questions.explanation: The four strategies in order of increasing cost/complexity and decreasing RTO/RPO: (1) Backup & Restore (cheap, hours), (2) Pilot Light (data replicated, app off), (3) Warm Standby (reduced, already running), (4) Multi-site Active/Active (zero downtime, multi-Region). Option D is the only one that respects the spectrum.

whyNots.A: Starts in the middle/top and puts the cheapest at the end — outside the cost ladder.
whyNots.B: It is the reversed order (most expensive to cheapest), not the requested mapping.
whyNots.C: Scrambles the order — Backup & Restore is the cheapest, not second, and Active/Active does not come before Warm Standby.

hints: It is the cost/RTO spectrum. Cheapest and slowest at the bottom (Backup & Restore), most expensive and instant at the top (Active/Active).
Clue 2 'app off' = Pilot Light; clue 3 'reduced and running' = Warm Standby. Only option D respects the increasing order.
Memorize the ladder — Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Active/Active, in that order of rising cost and falling RTO/RPO.

questions.stem:
The team has gigabytes of logs in an S3 bucket and wants to run a one-off SQL query to investigate an issue — without provisioning a server or loading data anywhere.

Which service queries data in S3 with SQL, serverless, paying for data scanned?
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless and queries data directly in S3 with SQL (ANSI), without provisioning infrastructure or loading/moving data. It charges by volume scanned (~$5/TB). Perfect for ad-hoc/interactive queries such as investigating logs.

whyNots.B: EMR is a Hadoop/Spark cluster for distributed processing — unnecessary weight and management here.
whyNots.C: RDS is a transactional relational database (OLTP), not analytics over files in S3.
whyNots.D: Provisioned Redshift is a data warehouse cluster — requires loading/modeling data and managing capacity; overkill for a one-off query on S3.

hints: The clue is 'one-off SQL directly on S3, no server, no loading'. That is Athena — you point it at the bucket and query.
Charged per TB scanned. The less data the query reads (e.g., columnar format, partitioning), the cheaper.

questions.stem:
The company consolidates sales, inventory, and finance data in one place to run heavy corporate reports with many JOINs on huge tables, repeatedly, for years.

Which service is best for this BI data warehouse?
questions.explanation: Redshift is the managed data warehouse (columnar, MPP) optimized for complex queries with many JOINs on very large tables and corporate BI over consolidated historical data from many sources. It is the classic warehouse use case.

whyNots.A: DynamoDB is a fast key-value NoSQL database for transactional access — it does not do complex BI JOINs.
whyNots.C: Athena shines in ad-hoc/one-off queries on S3; for heavy, recurring BI with huge joins, the warehouse (Redshift) performs better.
whyNots.D: S3 only stores; it has no analytical query engine by itself.

hints: 'Consolidate multiple sources', 'complex JOINs on big tables', 'repeated corporate report' = data warehouse = Redshift.
Athena is great for one-off/ad-hoc queries on S3; for heavy, recurring BI with huge joins, the Redshift engine is optimized for it.

questions.stem:
A data team already uses Apache Spark and Hadoop on-premises and wants to migrate heavy distributed processing to AWS with custom code and frameworks on a managed cluster.

Which service runs these distributed frameworks in a managed way?
questions.explanation: EMR (Elastic MapReduce) is the managed cluster for running distributed frameworks such as Hadoop, Spark, Presto, and Hive with custom applications and code. It is the choice for heavy distributed processing and migrating Hadoop/Spark workloads.

whyNots.A: Athena is serverless SQL on S3 — it does not run custom Spark/Hadoop code.
whyNots.B: Lambda runs short functions per event — it is not a big-data cluster for Spark/Hadoop.
whyNots.D: QuickSight is BI/dashboards — the visualization layer, not distributed processing.

hints: Hadoop, Spark, Presto, Hive on a managed cluster = EMR (Elastic MapReduce). It is the home of big-data frameworks.
EMR gives more control (compute/memory/custom code) than Athena/Glue — in exchange for more management.

questions.stem:
A data engineer needs to extract data from multiple sources, clean and transform it, and load it into a data lake — without provisioning or managing ETL servers.

Which service does serverless ETL?
questions.explanation: AWS Glue is the serverless ETL service (managed Spark): it extracts, transforms, and loads data into data lakes/warehouses without provisioning servers. It includes the Glue Data Catalog (metadata) and Crawlers (schema discovery).

whyNots.A: Config evaluates resource compliance — unrelated to data ETL.
whyNots.B: QuickSight is visualization/BI, not ETL.
whyNots.C: Redshift is the destination (warehouse), not the serverless ETL tool.

hints: 'Glue' joins the sources — extract, transform, and load (ETL) with managed Spark, without you managing servers.
Besides ETL, Glue provides the Data Catalog (metadata) and Crawlers (schema discovery).

questions.stem:
You dropped several new files into S3 and want the schema (columns/types) discovered automatically and registered in a central catalog, so Athena can query them as tables.

Which AWS Glue duo does this?

options.text: Glue Job (detects columns) + QuickSight (registers in catalog)

questions.explanation: The Glue Crawler scans data (e.g., in S3), classifies and infers the schema, automatically populating the Glue Data Catalog (central metadata repository). Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR use this catalog to query the data as tables.

whyNots.B: Lake Formation governs permissions and KMS encrypts — they do not infer or catalog schema.
whyNots.C: Redshift Spectrum queries S3 and SPICE is the QuickSight engine — they are not the discovery/catalog mechanism.
whyNots.D: Glue Job does ETL transformation; QuickSight is BI — neither is the schema discoverer + catalog.

hints: The Crawler 'crawls' the data and infers columns/types; the Data Catalog is the shelf where that schema is registered as tables.
Athena and Redshift Spectrum READ this Data Catalog to know the structure of tables in S3.

questions.stem:
The board wants interactive charts and dashboards to track sales, connecting to sources such as Athena and Redshift, with nothing to install and accessible from any device.

Which BI service delivers these dashboards?
questions.explanation: QuickSight is the AWS serverless BI service: it creates dashboards, visualizations, and ad-hoc analysis, accessible from any device, connecting to Athena, Redshift, S3, RDS, files, and SaaS. It uses the SPICE in-memory engine for acceleration. It is the visualization layer, not ETL.

whyNots.A: Glue is ETL — it prepares data, it does not visualize it.
whyNots.C: Athena queries data with SQL — it is not the visual dashboard tool.
whyNots.D: EMR is distributed processing — not panel BI.

hints: 'Interactive charts and dashboards for business' = BI = QuickSight. It connects to Athena, Redshift, S3, RDS, and more.
Serverless, with the SPICE in-memory engine for speed; it is the VISUALIZATION layer, not transformation.

questions.stem:
In the data lake, HR can only see certain COLUMNS of a table (not salary), and the regional team can only see the ROWS of its own Region. They want this controlled centrally and finely.

Which service provides fine-grained (row/column) permissions over the data lake?
questions.explanation: Lake Formation governs the data lake with a database-style permission model over the Glue Data Catalog, allowing fine-grained access at row, column, and cell level by user/role. It is the right governance layer to hide the salary column from HR and filter rows by Region.

whyNots.A: Security Group is a network firewall — it does not control access to rows/columns of data.
whyNots.B: S3 bucket policy controls access at the object/prefix level, with no row/column granularity inside the table.
whyNots.D: Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data (PII) in S3 — it does not enforce fine-grained query permissions.

hints: Database-style access control on the data lake — by row, column, and cell — is Lake Formation, on top of the Glue Data Catalog.
S3 bucket policy is coarse (object/prefix); it cannot 'hide the salary column' from a group. Lake Formation can.

questions.stem:
You want a cheap, serverless analytics pipeline: catalog raw data in S3, query it with SQL, and display it on a dashboard — without spinning up any cluster.

Which serverless combination covers the whole pipeline?
questions.explanation: Classic serverless analytics pipeline: Glue (Crawler + Data Catalog) catalogs raw data in S3 → Athena queries it in-place with SQL → QuickSight displays it on dashboards. All managed, no cluster to manage — cheap and low operations.

whyNots.A: DynamoDB/DAX/S3 is transactional/cache access — not SQL analytics or dashboards.
whyNots.B: Provisioned EMR and Redshift involve clusters to manage — not the 'serverless' path requested.
whyNots.C: RDS/Lambda/CloudFront is a web application stack, not an analytics pipeline over data in S3.

hints: The keyword is 'serverless end-to-end, no cluster'. Glue catalogs, Athena queries S3, QuickSight displays — no servers to manage.
The option with provisioned EMR and Redshift involves a cluster — it goes against the 'serverless' requirement.

questions.stem:
The Athena bill was a shock: one query read the whole bucket. You want to reduce how much each query scans (and the bill along with it).

Which practice reduces the volume scanned by Athena?

options.text: Use columnar format (Parquet/ORC), compression, and partitioning
Replace Athena with more smaller queries, each reading everything again
Turn off S3 encryption — without encrypting, scanning becomes lighter and cheaper
Increase the S3 bucket size, diluting the cost per scanned query

questions.explanation: Because Athena charges for data scanned, converting to columnar format (Parquet/ORC), compressing, and partitioning data drastically reduces the volume read per query — less scanning, lower cost, and faster performance.

whyNots.B: More queries reading everything increases cost, not reduces it.
whyNots.C: Turning off encryption does not affect scanned volume and worsens security — irrelevant to cost.
whyNots.D: Bucket size does not change how much a query scans; what matters is the data layout.

hints: Athena charges for data SCANNED. If the query reads only the columns and partitions that matter, it scans less and costs less.
Columnar format (Parquet/ORC) + compression + partitioning by date/Region is the classic cost-saving combo for Athena.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) ad-hoc SQL on S3 without servers; (2) BI data warehouse with heavy joins; (3) distributed Spark/Hadoop with custom code; (4) serverless ETL with schema catalog.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service has its specialty: Athena (serverless ad-hoc SQL on S3), Redshift (BI data warehouse with heavy joins), EMR (distributed Spark/Hadoop with custom code), Glue (serverless ETL + Data Catalog/Crawler). Option B respects all four roles.

whyNots.A: Also reverses the roles; Glue is not ad-hoc SQL and Athena is not ETL with a catalog.
whyNots.C: Swaps Athena with Redshift and Glue with EMR — outside each one's specialty.
whyNots.D: Scrambles everything: EMR is not ad-hoc SQL and Athena is not distributed Spark.

hints: Separate by function. Ad-hoc SQL on S3 = Athena. Warehouse/joins = Redshift. Spark/Hadoop = EMR. ETL+catalog = Glue.
Only option B keeps each service in its specialty; the others scramble at least one pair.

questions.stem:
A production RDS database must stay online if an Availability Zone fails. The team configures a standby that takes over automatically on failure. Then someone asks: 'can we send reads to the standby to relieve the primary?'

What is correct about RDS Multi-AZ?

options.text: Multi-AZ only works with Aurora — other RDS engines have no standby
Multi-AZ replicates asynchronously to another Region, like global DR
Multi-AZ is for high availability; the standby is synchronous and does NOT serve reads
The Multi-AZ standby serves reads and is how to scale reads in RDS

questions.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ exists for high availability/durability: it maintains a synchronous standby in another AZ and performs automatic failover. In the classic deployment (Multi-AZ DB instance with a single standby), it does NOT serve reads — it is reserved for resilience. To scale reads, use Read Replica. (Exception: the Multi-AZ DB cluster, with two readers, allows reading from readers via the reader endpoint — but that does not replace Read Replica for scaling reads outside the cluster or across Regions.)

whyNots.A: Multi-AZ exists in traditional RDS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, etc.), not only Aurora.
whyNots.B: Multi-AZ is synchronous replication inside the Region (between AZs), not asynchronous cross-Region.
whyNots.D: In the classic Multi-AZ deployment described here (single standby), it does not serve reads; Read Replica scales reads. (The Multi-AZ DB cluster, with two readers, is a more recent exception — but it is not the scenario of this question.)

hints: Multi-AZ = availability, not performance. The standby is on standby (synchronous) and takes over on failover — but it does not serve reads.
To distribute reads you use Read Replica, which is a different thing. Do not confuse the two.

questions.stem:
A news app has LOTS of reads (everyone reading articles) and few writes. The primary database is overloaded with SELECTs.

Which RDS feature distributes read load?
questions.explanation: Read Replicas are asynchronous read-only copies that distribute read traffic, increasing aggregate read throughput. Clients read from replicas (writes still go to the primary). They can be cross-Region. It is the mechanism to scale reads — complementary to Multi-AZ (availability).

whyNots.A: Backup does not distribute read load in production.
whyNots.B: Multi-AZ standby is for failover, not serving reads.
whyNots.C: Vault Lock is backup immutability (AWS Backup) — unrelated to scaling reads.

hints: 'Lots of reads' = scale reads = Read Replica. Clients read from replicas and the primary can breathe.
The replica is asynchronous (may have a small lag) and read-only; writes still happen only on the primary.

questions.stem:
A developer wants a MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible database, but managed by AWS with fault-tolerant storage and scalable reads, without them caring about disk replication.

Which service delivers this?
questions.explanation: Aurora is the AWS managed relational database, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL. The storage replicates data in 6 copies across 3 AZs (fault-tolerant, self-healing) and supports up to 15 low-latency read replicas — all managed.

whyNots.B: DynamoDB is a key-value NoSQL database, not MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible.
whyNots.C: ElastiCache is in-memory cache, not a durable relational database.
whyNots.D: Redshift is an analytical data warehouse (OLAP), not a MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible transactional database.

hints: MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible + managed + storage that takes care of itself = Aurora.
Under the hood, Aurora keeps 6 copies of data spread across 3 AZs — fault-tolerant without you touching it.

questions.stem:
A global company wants low-latency reads on several continents and fast recovery if an entire AWS Region fails, using Aurora.

Which Aurora feature meets this?

options.text: Aurora Replicas in the same Region

questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database spans multiple Regions (up to 10 secondary Regions): low-latency global reads in secondary Regions and cross-Region DR with RTO typically under 1 minute if the primary Region fails. Same-Region replicas or Multi-AZ do not protect against losing the entire Region.

whyNots.A: Multi-AZ covers AZ failure inside one Region, not loss of the whole Region.
whyNots.C: DynamoDB Streams captures DynamoDB events — unrelated to Aurora multi-Region.
whyNots.D: Aurora Replicas in the same Region scale local reads, but do not provide global presence or Region DR.

hints: 'Several continents' + 'entire Region fails' = needs MULTIPLE Regions. In Aurora, that is Global Database.
It provides global low-latency reads and cross-Region DR with RTO typically under 1 minute.

questions.stem:
An online store wants to store user sessions and cache query results to relieve the database, with microsecond reads. Eventual cache loss is not critical.

Which service delivers this in-memory cache?
questions.explanation: ElastiCache is the managed in-memory cache (Redis OSS/Valkey or Memcached engines), with microsecond latency. It sits in front of the database to store sessions and frequently read query results, relieving RDS and speeding up the application.

whyNots.A: Athena is SQL analytics on S3 — unrelated to session cache.
whyNots.B: RDS is the relational database you want to RELIEVE — not the in-memory cache.
whyNots.D: S3 is object storage, not a microsecond cache for sessions/queries.

hints: In-memory microsecond cache, for sessions and query results = ElastiCache (Redis/Valkey or Memcached).
It sits IN FRONT OF the database, keeping what is read frequently so it does not hit RDS every time.

questions.stem:
The requirement is a cache with read replicas, Multi-AZ high availability, optional persistence, and structures such as rankings (sorted sets) for a game leaderboard.

Which ElastiCache engine fits?
questions.explanation: Redis OSS (or Valkey) is the feature-rich engine: read replicas, Multi-AZ/HA, persistence (AOF), pub/sub, and structures such as sorted sets (ideal for leaderboards). Memcached is the simple one, with no persistence or replication. For the stated requirements, use Redis/Valkey.

whyNots.A: They are not identical — Memcached is simple; Redis/Valkey have the advanced features.
whyNots.B: Memcached has no replication, Multi-AZ, persistence, or sorted sets.
whyNots.C: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database, not the requested in-memory cache; ElastiCache Redis fits.

hints: Replicas, Multi-AZ, persistence, and sorted sets (ranking) are advanced features — that is Redis (or Valkey), not Memcached.
Memcached is the simple one: multi-thread, no persistence, no replication. Good for disposable cache.

questions.stem:
A real-time auction app reads the same DynamoDB items millions of times per second and wants to lower latency from milliseconds to microseconds, without rewriting logic.

Which feature accelerates DynamoDB READS?
questions.explanation: DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) is a managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB that brings read latency from milliseconds to microseconds (up to 10x), ideal for read-intensive workloads such as auctions/gaming. It does not help write-heavy workloads, and strongly consistent reads bypass the cache.

whyNots.B: Backup has no effect on production read latency.
whyNots.C: Streams captures change events — it does not accelerate reads.
whyNots.D: Global Tables replicate across Regions — it solves global presence, not local read latency.

hints: 'Accelerate DynamoDB reads to microseconds' = DAX, the native in-memory cache for DynamoDB.
Careful — DAX is for read-intensive workloads; it does not help write-heavy, and strongly consistent reads pass straight through without caching.

questions.stem:
An app needs users in Brazil and Japan to write to and read from the same DynamoDB table with low local latency, with automatic replication between the two regions (active-active).

Which DynamoDB feature meets this requirement?
questions.explanation: Global Tables replicates a DynamoDB table across regions in an active-active model: a write in one region is automatically propagated to the other replicas, providing low-latency local reads and writes in each region. It is the native multi-Region feature of DynamoDB.

whyNots.A: Streams captures changes, but alone it is not the managed multi-Region replication solution (Global Tables uses Streams under the hood, but the feature you choose is Global Tables).
whyNots.C: RDS Read Replica is for relational databases, not DynamoDB.
whyNots.D: DAX is a local read cache — it does not replicate the table across regions.

hints: Think about a single table across two regions, active-active, with automatic replication.
Remember that writes in one region are automatically replicated to the other replicas, enabling low-latency local reads and writes on both sides.

questions.stem:
Every time an item is inserted or updated in DynamoDB, you need to trigger a function that updates a search index and sends a notification — reacting to changes in real time.

Which DynamoDB feature delivers this change stream?
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams captures, in order, the change events (insert/update/delete) from the table and triggers consumers in real time, typically a Lambda function. It is the event-driven way to react to changes (update an index, notify) without periodic scans.

whyNots.A: Global Tables replicates across regions — it is not a per-change event trigger.
whyNots.B: DAX accelerates reads — it does not deliver a change stream.
whyNots.D: Periodic scans are expensive, slow, and not real time — the opposite of an event-driven solution.

hints: Think about reacting to every insert or update in real time — a change log that can trigger Lambda.
Remember that this is the foundation of CDC and event-driven architecture in DynamoDB, without scanning the whole table.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) scale READs of an RDS database; (2) high availability for RDS with failover; (3) accelerate DynamoDB reads to microseconds; (4) replicate a DynamoDB table active-active across regions.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Multi-AZ → Read Replica → Global Tables → DAX
DAX → Global Tables → Read Replica → Multi-AZ
Global Tables → DAX → Multi-AZ → Read Replica
Read Replica → Multi-AZ → DAX → Global Tables

questions.explanation: Each resource solves one thing: Read Replica scales reads on RDS; Multi-AZ provides high availability/failover on RDS; DAX accelerates DynamoDB reads to microseconds; Global Tables replicates the DynamoDB table active-active across regions. Option D respects all four roles.

whyNots.A: Swaps Read Replica with Multi-AZ and DAX with Global Tables.
whyNots.B: Scrambles everything — DAX does not scale RDS and Global Tables is not RDS HA.
whyNots.C: Also swaps the roles; none of the positions match the correct function.

hints: Separate by function: scale RDS reads = Read Replica; RDS HA = Multi-AZ; accelerate DynamoDB reads = DAX; multi-Region DynamoDB = Global Tables.
The classic trap is Read Replica (reads) versus Multi-AZ (availability). Only one option keeps each in the right place.

questions.stem:
The company wants to move an on-premises MySQL database to AWS with minimal downtime — the system must keep running during the migration.

Which service migrates databases while keeping the source operational?
questions.explanation: DMS migrates databases to AWS with minimal downtime: the source stays operational and DMS replicates ongoing changes (CDC) until cutover. It is the right tool for database migration.

whyNots.B: Snowball is offline physical transport of bulk data — it does not migrate a live database with continuous replication.
whyNots.C: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads to S3 — it is unrelated to database migration.
whyNots.D: DataSync transfers files/objects to S3/EFS/FSx — it does not migrate a live relational database.

hints: The service name gives it away — Database Migration Service. It migrates the database and also replicates ongoing changes, so downtime is minimal.
DataSync and Snowball move files/objects; for a live database, use DMS.

questions.stem:
The migration is from Oracle to PostgreSQL — DIFFERENT engines. The schema and code (procedures, types) are not directly compatible.

What is the correct path for this heterogeneous migration?

options.text: Just run DMS directly without converting anything — it translates the schema and PL/SQL code on its own
Convert schema/code with AWS SCT (or DMS Schema Conversion), then migrate data with DMS
Use DataSync to convert the schema and procedures, then copy data with SCT
Export everything to CSV and import manually — the only supported way in heterogeneous migrations

questions.explanation: Heterogeneous migration (different engines, such as Oracle→PostgreSQL) is a two-step process: (1) AWS SCT (Schema Conversion Tool) or DMS Schema Conversion converts the schema and most code to the target format, flagging what needs manual adjustment; (2) DMS migrates the data. Homogeneous (same engine) would be a single step.

whyNots.A: Without converting the schema, DMS has no compatible target for a different engine pair.
whyNots.C: DataSync transfers files — it does not convert database schema.
whyNots.D: Manual export/import is fragile and unnecessary; SCT + DMS automate most of the work.

hints: Different engines = heterogeneous migration = TWO steps. First convert the schema (SCT), then move the data (DMS).
If it were the same engine (for example, MySQL to Aurora MySQL), it would be homogeneous and DMS could do it in one step.

questions.stem:
There is good network connectivity and the team needs to copy millions of files from an on-premises NAS to Amazon S3, incrementally and on a schedule.

Which service performs this online file transfer to AWS?
questions.explanation: DataSync is the online file/object transfer service to AWS (S3, EFS, FSx): incremental (only what changed), compresses, schedules, and recovers from network drops. It is the first choice when connectivity is available.

whyNots.A: Kinesis Data Streams is real-time streaming ingestion, not copying files to S3.
whyNots.B: Snowball is offline (physical device) — indicated when bandwidth is lacking, which is not the case here.
whyNots.D: DMS migrates databases, not millions of files from a NAS.

hints: Good network + files to S3, incremental, scheduled = DataSync (online). It copies only what changed and compresses.
If there were no bandwidth, then you would think about Snowball (offline).

questions.stem:
A remote research station generated 80 TB of data and has only slow, expensive satellite internet. Uploading this online would take months.

Which service transfers this volume without depending on bandwidth?

options.text: Direct upload to S3 through the console
AWS Storage Gateway in cached mode

questions.explanation: Snowball Edge (Snow Family) performs offline transfer: you copy data to a physical device and ship it to AWS — ideal for terabytes/petabytes when bandwidth is missing or expensive. (Note: as of November 2025, Snowball is only for existing customers; new customers use DataSync, AWS Data Transfer Terminal, or partners — but the 'offline for high volume without bandwidth' concept remains exam-relevant.)

whyNots.A: Manual console upload is impractical for 80 TB over a poor connection.
whyNots.B: DataSync depends on bandwidth — over slow, expensive satellite it would take months, exactly what you want to avoid.
whyNots.C: Storage Gateway is continuous hybrid access, not offline bulk migration of a backlog.

hints: Huge volume + no decent bandwidth is the classic Snowball scenario — you copy to a physical device and ship it.
The rule: with bandwidth = DataSync (online); without bandwidth = Snowball (offline).

questions.stem:
A company wants to keep applications in the data center, but with low-latency access to data and automatic backup in the cloud — a continuous bridge between on-premises and AWS.

Which service delivers this continuous hybrid access?
questions.explanation: Storage Gateway is the hybrid appliance that connects on-premises applications to AWS storage, with a local low-latency cache, sending only changed data. It serves cloud-backed file shares, backup/archive, and low-latency access — a continuous bridge, not a one-time migration.

whyNots.B: DMS migrates databases once — it is not the daily storage bridge.
whyNots.C: Snowball is one-time offline transfer, not continuous hybrid access.
whyNots.D: CloudFront is an edge CDN — it does not integrate on-premises storage with the cloud.

hints: Continuous on-premises↔cloud bridge with local low-latency cache = Storage Gateway. It is not a one-time migration; it is daily hybrid access.
It keeps a local cache and sends only changed data to the cloud.

questions.stem:
The data center still uses a physical tape robot for backup and wants to get rid of it, keeping the same backup flow but storing the 'tapes' in the cloud (S3/Glacier) underneath.

Which Storage Gateway type replaces physical tape?
questions.explanation: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library (VTL) to your backup software: it keeps 'writing to tape', but the data goes to S3 and can archive to Glacier — eliminating the physical tape robot while preserving the backup workflow.

whyNots.A: Volume Gateway provides iSCSI block volumes with cloud backup — it does not emulate tape.
whyNots.C: S3 File Gateway exposes files via NFS/SMB to S3 — it is not a tape replacement.
whyNots.D: FSx File Gateway provides local access to FSx for Windows — it is unrelated to backup tape.

hints: Tape = Tape Gateway. It is a virtual tape library (VTL): the backup software thinks it is writing to tape, but data goes to S3/Glacier.
The other gateways are for file shares (S3/FSx) or block volumes (Volume) — they do not emulate tape.

questions.stem:
A company wants to migrate dozens of entire SERVERS (the VM as-is, with OS and application) from the data center to run natively on EC2, quickly and with little downtime — without rewriting anything (lift-and-shift).

Which service rehosts servers to EC2?

options.text: AWS DMS (migrates the whole VM with OS)

questions.explanation: Application Migration Service (MGN) performs lift-and-shift (rehost): it replicates servers at the block level and converts them to run natively on EC2, with minimal downtime at cutover. It is the successor to the legacy Server Migration Service. DMS is for databases; MGN is for entire servers.

whyNots.A: DMS migrates databases, not the complete server/VM with OS and application.
whyNots.B: DataSync transfers files/objects — it does not rehost servers on EC2.
whyNots.D: Storage Gateway is hybrid storage access, not server migration.

hints: Migrating the entire server as-is (lift-and-shift / rehost) to EC2 = Application Migration Service (MGN).
Do not confuse with DMS — DMS migrates DATABASES; MGN migrates the whole VM/server.

questions.stem:
In a large migration, two items come up: (1) move an Oracle database to Aurora PostgreSQL; (2) move an entire Windows application server to EC2.

Which pair of services is indicated, respectively?
questions.explanation: A database, especially a heterogeneous one (Oracle→Aurora PostgreSQL), is DMS with schema conversion via SCT. An entire application server to EC2 is Application Migration Service (MGN), the lift-and-shift tool. Option D matches both targets.

whyNots.A: Reversed: MGN is for servers, DMS is for databases.
whyNots.B: Storage Gateway is hybrid access; neither item fits its use case.
whyNots.C: DataSync (files) and Snowball (offline) neither migrate a live database nor rehost a server.

hints: Database = DMS (and because it is heterogeneous, SCT first). Entire server/VM = MGN. Each tool for its target.
The trap is exactly swapping DMS (database) with MGN (server).

questions.stem:
A team will migrate from on-premises MySQL to Amazon Aurora MySQL — the SAME engine on both sides.

What kind of migration is this?

options.text: Homogeneous — schema is compatible, DMS migrates in one step (no SCT needed)
Heterogeneous — schema must be converted with SCT before DMS can act
Requires rewriting the whole application, because Aurora changes MySQL syntax
Impossible without Snowball — databases only leave on-premises via offline transfer

questions.explanation: MySQL → Aurora MySQL is a homogeneous migration: because the engine is the same, the schema and code are already compatible and DMS migrates the data in one step without schema conversion (SCT). Conversion is only needed for heterogeneous migrations.

whyNots.B: Heterogeneous would be different engines; here it is the same (MySQL).
whyNots.C: There is no application rewrite in a homogeneous database migration.
whyNots.D: Snowball is offline data transfer — it is not a requirement for this database migration.

hints: Same engine on both sides (MySQL→Aurora MySQL) = homogeneous. The schema is already compatible, so no conversion step is needed.
SCT only enters when engines are different (heterogeneous).

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) migrate a live database with minimal downtime; (2) copy files to S3 with good bandwidth; (3) move 100 TB without decent connectivity; (4) give the data center continuous hybrid access with local cache.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service solves one case: DMS (live database, minimal downtime), DataSync (online files when bandwidth is available), Snowball (offline for high volume without connectivity), Storage Gateway (continuous hybrid access with local cache). Option B respects all four roles.

whyNots.A: Swaps DMS with DataSync and Snowball with Storage Gateway.
whyNots.C: Scrambles everything — Snowball does not migrate a live database and DMS is not offline bulk transfer.
whyNots.D: Also inverts the roles; no position matches the correct function.

hints: Live database = DMS. Files with bandwidth = DataSync. No bandwidth / huge volume = Snowball. Continuous hybrid = Storage Gateway.
Only one option keeps each service in its role; the others scramble at least one.

questions.stem:
The team is launching a new application version and wants to send only 10% of traffic to it at first (canary), increasing gradually while keeping 90% on the old version.

Which Route 53 routing policy splits traffic by percentage?
questions.explanation: The Weighted routing policy distributes traffic among multiple resources in the proportions you define (for example, 10% / 90%). It is ideal for canary launches, A/B tests, and simple DNS-based load balancing.

whyNots.A: Latency routes to the region with the lowest latency — it does not control percentage.
whyNots.B: Geolocation routes by the user's location — it does not perform a percentage split.
whyNots.D: Failover is active-passive (primary healthy or secondary) — it does not split by percentage.

hints: Splitting traffic by percentage = weight = Weighted. You assign a weight to each target (for example, 10 and 90).
This is the classic policy for canary releases, A/B testing, and simple DNS load balancing.

questions.stem:
The application runs in three regions (US, Europe, Brazil) and you want each user to land in the region that responds fastest for them.

Which Route 53 routing policy chooses the lowest-latency region?
questions.explanation: The Latency-based routing policy sends the user to the AWS region that offers the lowest latency for them, when you have resources in multiple regions. It optimizes perceived performance.

whyNots.A: Multivalue returns multiple healthy records at random — it does not choose by lowest latency.
whyNots.B: Weighted divides by percentage, not by latency.
whyNots.C: Simple points to a single resource, without choosing by performance.

hints: The name is literal — Latency. Resources in multiple regions, each user goes to the one with the lowest latency.
Do not confuse with geolocation, which looks at the user's country, not measured latency.

questions.stem:
You want a primary site and a standby DR site: while the primary is healthy, all traffic goes to it; if it fails (health check fails), DNS starts pointing to the secondary.

Which routing policy provides this active-passive behavior?
questions.explanation: The Failover routing policy implements the active-passive pattern: Route 53 sends traffic to the primary resource while the health check shows it is healthy; if it fails, it redirects to the secondary. This is the typical DR routing.

whyNots.B: Geoproximity routes by resource location with bias — it is not health-check failover.
whyNots.C: Weighted splits traffic by proportion — it is not primary/secondary by health.
whyNots.D: Simple has no health check and no standby secondary.

hints: Primary healthy, otherwise secondary is exactly Failover (active-passive), supported by health checks.
It pairs well with DR strategies (pilot light / warm standby) to redirect when the primary region fails.

questions.stem:
Two different requirements: (1) users in Germany must see the site in German and only access content permitted in that country; (2) you want to route by proximity of your resources and still be able to 'pull' more traffic from one region to another with an adjustment.

Which pair of policies meets the requirements, respectively?
questions.explanation: Geolocation routes by the USER's location (country/continent) — ideal for language and country compliance. Geoproximity routes by the RESOURCE's location and allows bias, which expands or shrinks the area to shift traffic between regions. These are distinct concepts that exams love to confuse.

whyNots.A: Latency is by performance and Weighted is by percentage — neither handles user/resource location as requested.
whyNots.C: Failover is active-passive and Simple is a single resource — they do not meet the geographic scenarios.
whyNots.D: Reversed: language by country is geolocation; bias is geoproximity.

hints: Geolocation looks at where the USER is (country/continent) — good for language and compliance. Geoproximity looks at where the RESOURCE is, and BIAS shifts traffic.
The word 'bias' (adjustment to pull more/less traffic) only exists in geoproximity.

questions.stem:
Instances in a PRIVATE subnet need to access Amazon S3 without going through the internet, without NAT, and without extra endpoint cost.

Which VPC endpoint type serves S3 (and DynamoDB) for free?
questions.explanation: The Gateway Endpoint provides private access to S3 and DynamoDB without internet or NAT, is free, and works via prefix list in the route table. It is the right (and cheap) choice for these two services from a private subnet.

whyNots.A: Internet Gateway exposes to the internet — the opposite of keeping it private.
whyNots.B: NAT Gateway would provide access via the internet (with cost), not private access over the AWS network.
whyNots.D: Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink) serves many services, but HAS hourly + data cost; for free S3/DynamoDB access, use Gateway.

hints: For S3 and DynamoDB there is a special, FREE endpoint that enters the route table as a prefix list: the Gateway Endpoint.
The Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink) is for many other services and HAS a cost; for free S3/DynamoDB access, use Gateway.

questions.stem:
You need PRIVATE access to an AWS service that is NOT S3/DynamoDB (for example, SQS, or your own service), including from the on-premises data center over Direct Connect.

Which resource delivers this private access?

options.text: Internet Gateway of the VPC, which also routes private traffic
Egress-only Internet Gateway — private outbound to any AWS service
Gateway Endpoint, which serves any service and on-premises too
Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) — a private ENI in the subnet

questions.explanation: The Interface Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) provisions an ENI with a private IP in the subnet to access AWS services (and third-party/own services) privately — and is accessible from on-premises (VPN/Direct Connect) and from peered VPCs. It is the path for services outside the S3/DynamoDB pair.

whyNots.A: Internet Gateway exposes to the public internet — it is not private access.
whyNots.B: Egress-only IGW is for IPv6 outbound — it does not provide private access to AWS services.
whyNots.C: Gateway Endpoint only serves S3/DynamoDB and is not accessible from on-premises.

hints: For other services (besides S3/DynamoDB) and access from on-premises, use the Interface Endpoint via PrivateLink — it creates an ENI with a private IP in your subnet.
Gateway Endpoint only serves S3/DynamoDB and is NOT accessible from on-premises.

questions.stem:
On the exam: compare the firewall at the instance level with the one at the subnet level. One is stateful (response is allowed automatically); the other is stateless (needs rules for both directions).

Which association is correct?

options.text: Both act only at the subnet, filtering traffic for the entire AZ
Both are stateful and identical — only the console name differs

questions.explanation: Security Group acts at the instance level (ENI), is stateful (response to permitted traffic is automatically allowed), and only has allow rules. NACL acts at the subnet level, is stateless (needs both inbound and outbound rules), and has allow and deny rules.

whyNots.B: Reverses the two — Security Group is stateful/instance; NACL is stateless/subnet.
whyNots.C: Security Group acts on the instance, not the subnet.
whyNots.D: They are not identical: they differ in state, level, and whether they have deny rules.

hints: Security Group sits at the INSTANCE and is stateful — if you allowed inbound, the response goes out automatically. NACL sits at the SUBNET and is stateless — you define both inbound and outbound.
Another difference: Security Group only has allow rules; NACL has allow and DENY rules (it can block an IP).

questions.stem:
A specific malicious IP is attacking your application and you need to explicitly BLOCK that address at the subnet entry.

Which resource allows a DENY rule for an IP?
questions.explanation: Only the NACL has explicit deny rules, so it is the right resource to block a specific IP/range at the subnet entry. Security Groups only have allow rules (they cannot deny an individual IP).

whyNots.A: IAM policy controls API permissions, not network traffic.
whyNots.C: Security Group has no deny rule — it cannot block a specific IP.
whyNots.D: Route table directs traffic; it does not filter or block by source IP.

hints: Security Group only has allow rules (it denies by omission, but has no deny rule). To BLOCK a specific IP, use NACL, which has deny rules.
NACL is stateless and per subnet — perfect for blocking a range/IP at the subnet edge.

questions.stem:
Instances in a private subnet need to download updates and call external APIs on the internet, but they MUST NOT be reachable from outside.

Which resource gives outbound internet access without exposing the instances?

options.text: Internet Gateway directly in the private subnet

questions.explanation: NAT Gateway allows instances in a private subnet to initiate OUTBOUND connections to the internet (updates, external APIs) without becoming reachable from outside. It is managed, scalable, sits in a public subnet, and needs a route.

whyNots.A: VPC Peering connects VPCs to each other, it does not provide internet egress.
whyNots.B: Putting instances behind an Internet Gateway would make them reachable from the internet — which you want to avoid.
whyNots.D: Gateway Endpoint gives private access to S3/DynamoDB, not general outbound internet access.

hints: NAT = outbound yes, inbound no. Private instances reach the internet (updates/APIs) through NAT, but nothing from outside initiates connections to them.
NAT Gateway sits in a public subnet and is managed/scalable (better than NAT instance).

questions.stem:
Security wants to record which IP connections were accepted or rejected in the VPC, for auditing and investigating connectivity issues — without capturing packet contents.

Which resource records this traffic metadata?
questions.explanation: VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata (source/destination, ports, accepted/rejected) from ENIs/subnets/VPCs and write to CloudWatch Logs or S3 — for auditing and troubleshooting connectivity/security. They do not capture payload.

whyNots.A: CloudTrail records API calls, not per-packet network traffic.
whyNots.B: Config evaluates resource configuration — it does not record network flow.
whyNots.C: X-Ray traces requests inside the application, not VPC IP traffic.

hints: Accepted/rejected network flow, without content = VPC Flow Logs. It records metadata (IPs, ports, action) to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
Do not confuse with CloudTrail (API calls) or X-Ray (request path inside the application).

questions.stem:
You want a service that watches the account and detects suspicious behavior — such as an instance mining cryptocurrency, access from a strange IP, or a compromised bucket — analyzing logs automatically, with no agent to install.

Which service provides intelligent threat detection?
questions.explanation: GuardDuty is the threat detection service: it analyzes VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and DNS logs with ML to identify malicious activity (reconnaissance, compromised instance/account/bucket/EKS, malware), with no agent. It focuses on behavior/threat.

whyNots.B: Macie finds sensitive data in S3 — it does not detect behavioral threats.
whyNots.C: Config evaluates configuration compliance — it is not threat detection.
whyNots.D: Inspector looks for software vulnerabilities (CVEs), not malicious behavior in real time.

hints: The 'guard' that watches BEHAVIOR — GuardDuty analyzes Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and DNS with ML to find malicious activity.
It detects THREAT/behavior, not software vulnerability (that is Inspector).

questions.stem:
The security team wants to automatically scan EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and container images for known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and network exposure.

Which service performs vulnerability management?
questions.explanation: Inspector is the vulnerability management service: it continuously scans EC2, Lambda functions, and container images (ECR) for software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintentional network exposure.

whyNots.A: Macie looks for sensitive data in S3 — it is not CVE scanning.
whyNots.C: Shield protects against DDoS — it does not scan for software vulnerabilities.
whyNots.D: GuardDuty detects threat/malicious behavior, it does not perform CVE scanning.

hints: To 'inspect' software for known holes (CVE) = Inspector. It scans EC2, Lambda, and container images.
CVE/vulnerability = Inspector; threat/behavior = GuardDuty. Do not swap the two.

questions.stem:
Compliance wants to know whether tax IDs, credit card numbers, or other personally identifiable information (PII) are unintentionally stored in S3 buckets.

Which service discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3?
questions.explanation: Macie is the sensitive data discovery service: it uses ML and pattern matching to identify and classify PII/PHI and secrets inside S3 buckets — exactly what compliance requested.

whyNots.A: KMS manages encryption keys — it does not discover PII.
whyNots.B: GuardDuty detects behavioral threats; it does not classify data content.
whyNots.D: Inspector looks for software vulnerabilities, not sensitive data.

hints: Macie is the PII finder in S3 — it uses ML and patterns to find sensitive data (tax IDs, cards, etc.).
Sensitive data in S3 = Macie. It is the only one of the four focused on DATA CONTENT.

questions.stem:
Each team looks at a different console: one sees GuardDuty, another Inspector, another Macie. A single view is missing to aggregate and prioritize all security findings and check the account against standards (CIS, PCI).

Which service centralizes and correlates these findings?
questions.explanation: Security Hub is the central security posture dashboard: it aggregates and correlates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie, and performs compliance checking (CSPM) against standards such as CIS, PCI DSS, and AWS FSBP. It is the missing single view.

whyNots.A: CloudWatch is for operational metrics/logs — it is not the security posture hub.
whyNots.B: GuardDuty is one of the SOURCES of findings, not the central aggregator.
whyNots.C: CloudTrail audits API calls — it does not correlate security findings.

hints: The 'hub' is the central point — Security Hub aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie in one dashboard and checks posture/compliance.
GuardDuty/Inspector/Macie GENERATE findings; Security Hub GATHERS and prioritizes them.

questions.stem:
Four tasks: (1) detect malicious behavior in the account; (2) find CVEs in instance software; (3) discover PII in S3 buckets; (4) gather and prioritize everything in one dashboard.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service has its role: GuardDuty (threat/behavior), Inspector (vulnerability/CVE), Macie (sensitive data in S3), and Security Hub (aggregates and prioritizes everything). Option A respects all four functions.

whyNots.B: Swaps GuardDuty with Inspector and Macie with Security Hub.
whyNots.C: Scrambles everything — Macie does not detect behavior and Security Hub does not find CVEs.
whyNots.D: Completely inverted; no position matches the correct function.

hints: Behavior = GuardDuty; CVE = Inspector; PII in S3 = Macie; central dashboard = Security Hub.
Only one option keeps each service in its function; the others scramble at least one pair.

questions.stem:
Every AWS account already comes with automatic, free protection against common network DDoS attacks (layers 3 and 4), such as SYN/UDP floods.

Which service provides this basic protection at no extra cost?
questions.explanation: Shield Standard is included automatically and at no extra cost for all AWS customers, protecting against the most common infrastructure DDoS attacks (layers 3 and 4), such as SYN/UDP floods and reflection.

whyNots.A: Shield Advanced is a paid subscription with expanded protection and SRT — it is not the free automatic protection.
whyNots.C: WAF is an application-layer (L7) firewall paid per use — it is not the automatic network DDoS protection.
whyNots.D: GuardDuty detects threats; it does not mitigate DDoS.

hints: Automatic, free, network DDoS (L3/L4) = Shield Standard, which is enabled for everyone.
Advanced is the paid version with more protection and the response team (SRT).

questions.stem:
An e-commerce company under large and frequent DDoS attacks wants advanced protection on CloudFront/ELB/Route 53, automatic layer 7 mitigation, access to a specialized response team, and protection against cost spikes caused by the attack.

Which service meets these advanced requirements?
questions.explanation: Shield Advanced is the paid subscription with expanded DDoS protection for EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator, automatic layer 7 mitigation, advanced visibility, access to the Shield Response Team (SRT), and cost protection against spikes caused by DDoS. It uses WAF for L7 protections.

whyNots.A: Inspector is for software vulnerabilities — it is not DDoS protection.
whyNots.B: Config is for configuration compliance — it has nothing to do with DDoS mitigation.
whyNots.D: Shield Standard is the free basic protection (L3/L4), without SRT or cost protection.

hints: Automatic L7 mitigation + Shield Response Team + cost protection are the trademarks of Shield Advanced (paid).
Advanced uses AWS WAF for application-layer protections and covers EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53, and Global Accelerator.

questions.stem:
The web application is suffering SQL injection and XSS attempts, and you want to block these malicious HTTP request patterns, plus limit requests per IP, on CloudFront/ALB.

Which service filters traffic at the application layer (L7)?
questions.explanation: AWS WAF is the web application firewall (layer 7): it inspects HTTP(S) requests and blocks attacks such as SQL injection and XSS, applies rate limiting, and enforces IP/geo rules. It attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and AppSync.

whyNots.A: Shield Standard protects against network DDoS (L3/L4), not SQLi/XSS at the application layer.
whyNots.B: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 — it does not filter web requests.
whyNots.C: Security Groups filter by IP/port (L3/L4); they do not understand HTTP content or block SQLi/XSS.

hints: Think layer 7: WAF = Web Application Firewall. It inspects HTTP requests and blocks SQL injection/XSS, applies rate limits, and rules by IP or geography.
It attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and AppSync. Network DDoS is Shield; HTTP exploitation is WAF.

questions.stem:
A regulatory requirement calls for a DEDICATED single-tenant HSM, under the company's exclusive control, validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3, with access via PKCS#11.

Which service meets this compliance requirement?
questions.explanation: CloudHSM provides a dedicated single-tenant HSM under exclusive customer control, validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3, with PKCS#11/JCE/KSP interfaces — exactly what the regulation demands. KMS is the general case (multi-tenant, managed, cheaper and easier).

whyNots.B: Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets — it is not an HSM.
whyNots.C: Certificate Manager manages TLS certificates — it is not a dedicated HSM.
