whyNots.D: KMS uses managed multi-tenant HSMs; it does not meet the dedicated single-tenant HSM under exclusive control requirement.

hints: A dedicated single-tenant HSM under your control with PKCS#11 points to CloudHSM. KMS is managed multi-tenant.
As a rule: use KMS for the general, easy, low-cost case; move to CloudHSM only when compliance requires a dedicated HSM or interfaces like PKCS#11/JCE.

questions.stem:
Most applications only need to encrypt data in S3, EBS, and RDS in a simple, integrated, cheap, managed way, with access control through IAM.

What is the default encryption service for this general case?
questions.explanation: KMS is AWS's default encryption service: managed, multi-tenant HSM (FIPS 140-3 Level 3), natively integrated with S3, EBS, RDS, and most services, with IAM control, low cost, and minimal management. It fits the general case.

whyNots.A: Inspector is for software vulnerabilities — it is not a key/encryption service.
whyNots.C: CloudHSM is dedicated/single-tenant, more expensive and more work — only when compliance demands it.
whyNots.D: Shield is DDoS protection — it does not encrypt data.

hints: For the general, integrated, low-cost case, choose KMS. It manages keys and integrates with S3, EBS, RDS, and more, controlled by IAM.
Only switch to CloudHSM if compliance requires a dedicated HSM — it is more expensive and more complex.

questions.stem:
A web application wants to route /api to one server group and /images to another, based on URL path, and also terminate SSL.

Which load balancer performs content-based routing at layer 7?
questions.explanation: ALB operates at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) and routes by content: path-based, host-based, headers, with SSL termination. It is the choice for web, microservices, and container workloads that need URL routing rules.

whyNots.A: GWLB is for inserting third-party virtual appliances, not for HTTP path routing.
whyNots.B: NLB is layer 4 (TCP/UDP) — it cannot see the URL path to route by content.
whyNots.D: CLB is legacy and lacks the advanced content routing of ALB.

hints: Routing by URL path or host is a layer 7 (application) decision, so use ALB. It reads HTTP and decides where to send traffic.
NLB is layer 4 and cannot see the path; GWLB is for security appliances.

questions.stem:
A trading system needs minimum latency, millions of TCP connections per second, and a fixed static IP for partner allowlists.

Which load balancer delivers this layer 4 performance?
questions.explanation: NLB operates at layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS) with ultra-high performance and low latency, scales to millions of requests per second, and provides a static IP/Elastic IP per AZ — ideal for trading, gaming, streaming, and IoT.

whyNots.A: CloudFront is an edge CDN — not a layer 4 load balancer with a static IP.
whyNots.B: GWLB is for third-party inspection appliances, not for low-latency trading traffic.
whyNots.C: ALB is layer 7 (HTTP) — it does not deliver the extreme TCP throughput or native static IP of NLB.

hints: Minimum latency, millions of TCP connections, and a static IP point to NLB at layer 4. It is the fastest and offers a fixed IP per AZ.
ALB is great for HTTP, but for extreme TCP throughput and a static IP, choose NLB.

questions.stem:
The company wants to transparently insert third-party virtual FIREWALL/IDS appliances to inspect all VPC traffic, scaling those appliances as demand changes.

Which load balancer is built for this?
questions.explanation: GWLB operates at the gateway level (layer 3) and was built to deploy and scale third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS/IPS) transparently, forwarding traffic to them for inspection. It is the only one of the three designed for this case.

whyNots.B: ALB balances HTTP application traffic; it does not transparently insert inspection appliances.
whyNots.C: NLB balances layer 4 application traffic; it is not a gateway for security appliances.
whyNots.D: CLB is legacy and lacks this appliance-gateway function.

hints: Third-party security appliances, transparent insertion, and scaling point to Gateway Load Balancer. It acts as the gateway that sends traffic to the appliances for inspection.
ALB/NLB balance your application; GWLB balances the inspection appliances.

questions.stem:
You have containers to run and do not want to manage any servers: no patching, no instance type choices, no EC2 scaling. You only want to say how much CPU/memory each task uses and pay for that.

Which option runs containers without managing servers?

options.text: Plain EC2 with Docker installed manually

questions.explanation: Fargate is the serverless compute engine for containers (works with ECS and EKS): you only specify CPU/memory per task and pay for that, without provisioning or managing servers. It exactly matches the requirement.

whyNots.A: Plain EC2 with Docker installed manually is the maximum amount of management.
whyNots.C: Batch on dedicated EC2 still involves managing the compute infrastructure.
whyNots.D: With the EC2 launch type, you manage the instance fleet (patching, type, scaling) — the opposite of the request.

hints: Not wanting to manage servers and only specifying CPU/memory per task means Fargate, the serverless container engine (works with ECS and EKS).
With the EC2 launch type you still manage the fleet; with Fargate, AWS abstracts the server.

questions.stem:
A team already uses Kubernetes on-premises, with manifests, Helm, and ecosystem tools, and wants to run that on AWS in a managed way while keeping the Kubernetes APIs.

Which service is the right choice?

options.text: Amazon ECS, which reads manifests and Helm

questions.explanation: EKS is AWS managed Kubernetes — it keeps the open-source Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem (Helm, operators), with AWS handling the control-plane heavy lifting. It is the choice for teams already living with Kubernetes.

whyNots.A: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS for web apps, not a Kubernetes cluster.
whyNots.B: ECS is AWS's own opinionated orchestrator (simpler), but it is NOT Kubernetes — it cannot run the team's manifests/Helm.
whyNots.D: Lambda is event-driven serverless functions, not Kubernetes container orchestration.

hints: Already using Kubernetes (manifests, Helm) and wanting to keep the Kubernetes APIs means EKS, AWS managed Kubernetes.
ECS is AWS's simpler orchestrator; if the requirement is Kubernetes, choose EKS.

questions.stem:
A team runs ECS and needs instances with a specific GPU and access to the host operating system for heavy customizations, accepting the need to manage the fleet.

Which ECS launch type fits?
questions.explanation: The ECS EC2 launch type gives full control of the fleet: you choose instances (including GPU), access the host, and customize the environment — in exchange for managing patching, type, and scale. Fargate abstracts the server and does not offer this level of control.

whyNots.A: Wrong — the EC2 launch type supports GPU instances.
whyNots.B: Fargate is serverless and abstracts the host — it does not allow choosing a specific GPU instance or modifying the host OS as required.
whyNots.C: Lambda is not the model for long-running GPU containers with host access.

hints: A specific GPU, host access, and willingness to manage the fleet point to the EC2 launch type, which gives full instance control.
Fargate abstracts the server (less control); to choose a GPU instance and work on the host, choose EC2.

questions.stem:
You want Auto Scaling to keep the fleet's average CPU utilization around 50%, adding or removing instances automatically as load rises or falls.

Which Auto Scaling policy does this?

options.text: None; ASG cannot scale by metric

questions.explanation: Target Tracking keeps a metric at a target value (e.g., average CPU at 50%): the Auto Scaling Group adds or removes instances automatically to stay near the target. It is the most common and recommended dynamic policy.

whyNots.B: Scheduled scaling adjusts capacity at predictable fixed times — it does not chase a real-time metric.
whyNots.C: A fixed manual policy does not react to load automatically.
whyNots.D: Wrong — ASG scales dynamically by metric via target tracking/step scaling.

hints: Keeping a metric at a TARGET (CPU at 50%) is Target Tracking. You set the target and the ASG adjusts the fleet on its own.
It works like a thermostat — you set the desired temperature and it turns on/off to maintain it.

questions.stem:
Traffic is completely predictable: it spikes every Monday morning and drops at night. You want to increase capacity BEFORE the spike at defined times and reduce it afterward to save money.

Which Auto Scaling policy fits this predictable pattern?
questions.explanation: Scheduled scaling adjusts the Auto Scaling Group's capacity at predictable times (e.g., scale up Monday 8 AM, scale down at night), anticipating known spikes and saving money outside them. It is the right policy for defined time patterns.

whyNots.A: Doing it manually every day is tedious and error-prone — scheduled scaling exists to automate this.
whyNots.C: Target Tracking reacts to a metric in real time, but it does not anticipate a predictable spike by the clock like scheduled scaling.
whyNots.D: Reserved Instances are a purchase/discount model, not a scaling policy.

hints: A predictable, defined time pattern means Scheduled scaling. You schedule capacity changes like a cron job.
Target tracking reacts to metrics; scheduled scaling acts by the CLOCK, anticipating a known spike.

questions.stem:
Comparing: (1) process a newly uploaded S3 file with a short event-driven function; (2) run a long-running containerized web API without managing servers.

Which pair of services matches, respectively?
questions.explanation: Lambda is ideal for short event-driven functions (processing the newly created S3 object), ephemeral and pay-per-invocation. Fargate runs long-running containers (web API/microservice) without managing servers. Option C pairs each case with the right service.

whyNots.A: EC2 would require managing servers; and Lambda is not ideal for a continuous containerized API.
whyNots.B: Reversed: Lambda is the event function; Fargate is the long-running container.
whyNots.D: Plain EC2 contradicts the 'without managing servers' requirement for item 2.

hints: A short function triggered by an event is Lambda. A long-running container without servers is Fargate.
Both are serverless, but Lambda is event-driven/ephemeral while Fargate is continuous containers.

questions.stem:
Three load-balancing needs: (1) HTTP path routing for microservices; (2) ultra-low-latency TCP with static IP; (3) insert a third-party virtual firewall to inspect traffic.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each load balancer has its role: ALB (L7, HTTP path/host routing for microservices), NLB (L4, low-latency TCP and static IP), and GWLB (gateway for third-party virtual appliances). Option D respects all three.

whyNots.A: It shuffles everything — GWLB does not do HTTP path routing.
whyNots.B: Swaps ALB and NLB — path routing is L7 (ALB), not NLB.
whyNots.C: Swaps NLB and GWLB; static IP/fast TCP is NLB, not GWLB.

hints: HTTP path routing = ALB (L7). Fast TCP + static IP = NLB (L4). Third-party security appliance = GWLB.
Only option D keeps each load balancer in its correct layer/function.

questions.stem:
Logs are rarely accessed, but when needed they must be available immediately (within milliseconds). You want to pay less for storage than Standard.

Which S3 storage class fits?
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA is for infrequently accessed data that still needs millisecond access when requested: cheaper storage than Standard, in exchange for a retrieval fee. Multi-AZ, 11 nines durability.

whyNots.B: Deep Archive retrieval takes 12–48 hours — it does not meet the 'immediate, in milliseconds' requirement.
whyNots.C: Intelligent-Tiering is for UNKNOWN access patterns; here the pattern (rare access) is known, so IA is more direct and cheaper.
whyNots.D: Standard does not reduce storage cost for rarely accessed data.

hints: Rarely accessed but needed in milliseconds, cheaper than Standard — that is Standard-IA (Infrequent Access).
You save on storage but pay a retrieval fee. Access is still in milliseconds (unlike Glacier).

questions.stem:
Thumbnails generated from original images: if lost, they can be easily recreated. You want the lowest possible cost and do not mind if they live in a single AZ.

Which S3 storage class is most economical for this recreatable data?
questions.explanation: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, ~20% cheaper than Standard-IA, with millisecond access. It has 11 nines durability, but the object is lost if the AZ is destroyed — ideal for infrequent, easily recreatable data such as thumbnails.

whyNots.A: Glacier Instant is archive; for data that is still read occasionally and recreatable, One Zone-IA is more suitable and cheaper in this case.
whyNots.C: Standard-IA is multi-AZ and more expensive; for recreatable data, One Zone-IA saves more.
whyNots.D: Standard is the most expensive for infrequent access.

hints: Recreatable, acceptable single AZ, and cheaper point to One Zone-IA, which stores in one AZ (cheaper than multi-AZ IA).
The risk is losing data if the AZ is destroyed — acceptable for recreatable data.

questions.stem:
A data lake has objects with UNPREDICTABLE access patterns: some become hot, others cool, with no rule. You do not want to guess the storage class or pay retrieval fees.

Which S3 storage class optimizes cost automatically?
questions.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object automatically to the most economical tier based on access, with no retrieval fees and no performance impact (only a small monitoring fee). It is the ideal class for unknown or variable access patterns.

whyNots.A: One Zone-IA has the same retrieval-fee issue as IA plus single-AZ risk.
whyNots.B: Standard-IA assumes rare access and charges retrieval fees — bad if the object becomes hot again.
whyNots.D: Glacier Flexible is archive with retrieval in minutes/hours — not suitable for data that could become hot at any time.

hints: Unpredictable pattern, do not want to guess, and no retrieval fee — that is Intelligent-Tiering, which moves objects between tiers automatically.
It charges a small monitoring fee, but saves you from choosing the wrong class.

questions.stem:
Three files: (1) a medical archive image that must open in milliseconds when the doctor requests it; (2) a backup that can wait minutes/hours to recover; (3) a compliance record kept for 10 years, where 12–48 hour recovery is fine.

Which Glacier class trio matches 1→2→3?

options.text: Glacier Deep Archive → Glacier Instant Retrieval → Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Standard → S3 Standard-IA → S3 One Zone-IA (the S3 archive classes)
Glacier Flexible Retrieval → Glacier Deep Archive → Glacier Instant Retrieval
Glacier Instant Retrieval → Glacier Flexible Retrieval → Glacier Deep Archive

questions.explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval delivers archive access in milliseconds (medical image). Glacier Flexible Retrieval recovers in minutes or free bulk in 5–12 hours (backup/DR). Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest, with 12–48 hour recovery (long-term compliance). Option D maps correctly.

whyNots.A: Reversed: Deep Archive does not open in milliseconds.
whyNots.B: These are not Glacier archive classes; the scenario asks for long-term archive.
whyNots.C: Shuffles recovery times.

hints: Immediate milliseconds = Instant; minutes/hours = Flexible; cheapest and 12–48 hours = Deep Archive.
Recovery time increases: Instant (ms) < Flexible (min–h) < Deep Archive (12–48h), and cost decreases in the same direction.

questions.stem:
You want S3 objects to move automatically to cheaper storage classes over time (e.g., to IA at 30 days, to Glacier at 90) and be deleted at 365 days — with no manual work.

Which S3 feature automates this?

options.text: Bucket policy that moves objects by age
Versioning, which expires and changes classes

questions.explanation: An S3 Lifecycle policy applies automatic rules based on object age: transitions between classes (Standard → IA → Glacier) and expiration (deletion). It optimizes cost without manual intervention.

whyNots.B: Replication copies to another region — it does not manage class transitions by age.
whyNots.C: Bucket policy controls access permissions — it does not automate lifecycle transitions.
whyNots.D: Versioning keeps old versions — it does not change class or expire by age.

hints: Moving classes over time and expiring automatically is done by a Lifecycle policy. You define rules based on object age.
It handles both transition (class change) and expiration (deletion) automatically — saving money without manual work.

questions.stem:
For a general-purpose volume on an EC2 instance, you want good performance with a guaranteed baseline and the ability to adjust IOPS and throughput separately, paying less than the previous generation.

Which EBS volume type is the recommended default choice?
questions.explanation: gp3 is the recommended general-purpose SSD: baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s independent of size, with IOPS and throughput configurable separately, and ~20% cheaper than gp2. It is the default choice for most workloads.

whyNots.A: io2 Block Express is for critical applications with extremely high IOPS — overkill and more expensive for general use.
whyNots.C: st1 is a throughput HDD for sequential big data — not a general-purpose volume (and not bootable).
whyNots.D: sc1 is a low-cost cold HDD for rarely accessed data — not general use with good IOPS.

hints: General purpose, guaranteed baseline, separately adjustable IOPS/throughput, and cheaper than gp2 — that is gp3, the current general-purpose SSD.
gp3 gives 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline regardless of volume size.

questions.stem:
A critical database needs extremely high, consistent IOPS and low latency, with enhanced durability — predictable performance is non-negotiable.

Which EBS volume type fits?

options.text: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD), the top in IOPS
gp2, which guarantees fixed IOPS for a critical database
io2 / io2 Block Express (Provisioned IOPS SSD)
sc1 (Cold HDD), ideal for minimum latency

questions.explanation: io2 (and io2 Block Express) is the Provisioned IOPS SSD: consistently high performance, low latency, and enhanced durability (up to 99.999% with Block Express) — built for critical databases that demand predictable, high IOPS.

whyNots.A: st1 is a throughput HDD — it does not deliver high low-latency IOPS for a database.
whyNots.B: gp2 is general-purpose; it does not guarantee the extremely high, consistent IOPS of io2.
whyNots.D: sc1 is a low-cost cold HDD — the opposite of high performance.

hints: Extremely high, consistent IOPS, low latency, and enhanced durability point to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2). io2 Block Express is the top tier.
You provision the IOPS you need — predictable performance, ideal for a critical database.

questions.stem:
A big data pipeline processes large sequential files (logs, MapReduce) and what matters is THROUGHPUT (MB/s) at low cost, not random-access IOPS.

Which EBS volume type is most suitable?
questions.explanation: st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) is optimized for throughput (MB/s) on frequent, large sequential workloads — big data, MapReduce, logs, and data warehouses — at a lower cost than SSD. It is the classic case described.

whyNots.A: Instance Store is ephemeral (data lost) — risky for a persistent pipeline.
whyNots.B: io2 is expensive and focused on random-access IOPS — not the best cost for sequential throughput.
whyNots.C: gp3 (SSD) works, but for large sequential reads st1 delivers throughput at lower cost.

hints: Large sequential files, throughput (MB/s), and low cost point to st1, the throughput-optimized HDD.
For sequential big data access, a throughput HDD costs less than SSD and delivers the needed MB/s.

questions.stem:
An application uses a local cache with extremely high IOPS that can be lost without issue when the instance stops (the data is reconstructable).

Which storage is most indicated for this temporary scratch?
questions.explanation: Instance Store is physical disk attached to the host: extremely high IOPS and low latency, but EPHEMERAL — data is lost when the instance stops/terminates. It is perfect for cache, scratch, and temporary buffer with reconstructable data.

whyNots.B: io2 is persistent and more expensive — unnecessary for disposable data.
whyNots.C: EFS is a shared network file system — not local scratch with extremely high IOPS.
whyNots.D: S3 is object storage, not a local low-latency disk for cache.

hints: A local cache with extremely high IOPS that can be lost on stop means Instance Store, the physical host disk, ephemeral.
If the data had to survive a stop, use EBS. Because it is disposable, Instance Store is faster and cheaper.

questions.stem:
Three file needs: (1) share files among many Linux servers via NFS; (2) SMB file share for Windows apps with Active Directory; (3) ultra-high-throughput file system for HPC/ML training.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?

options.text: EFS → FSx for Lustre → FSx for Windows
EFS → FSx for Windows File Server → FSx for Lustre
FSx for Windows → FSx for Lustre → EFS
FSx for Lustre → EFS → FSx for Windows

questions.explanation: EFS is the elastic NFS for Linux shared among many EC2 instances. FSx for Windows File Server delivers native SMB for Windows/Active Directory apps. FSx for Lustre is the ultra-high-throughput file system for HPC and ML training. Option B respects all three cases.

whyNots.A: Swaps Lustre and Windows — SMB/AD is FSx for Windows, HPC is Lustre.
whyNots.C: Shuffles everything; EFS is not for HPC nor Windows.
whyNots.D: Swaps roles — Linux NFS is EFS, not Lustre.

hints: Linux/NFS shared = EFS. Windows/SMB/AD = FSx for Windows. HPC/ML high throughput = FSx for Lustre.
Only option B keeps each case with the right file system.

questions.stem:
Three cases: (1) block storage for ONE EC2 instance (OS/database volume); (2) file system shared by MANY Linux instances at the same time; (3) object storage for files/static assets accessible over HTTP.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: EBS is block storage typically attached to one instance (OS/database volume). EFS is a file system shared by many Linux instances at the same time. S3 is object storage for files/static assets accessible over HTTP/API. Option C maps all three correctly.

whyNots.A: Starts with S3 for block storage — wrong; block is EBS.
whyNots.B: Puts EFS as block storage for a single instance — EFS is shared, not block.
whyNots.D: Swaps EFS and S3 — shared among instances is EFS, objects are S3.

hints: Block for one instance = EBS. Shared file system = EFS. Objects over HTTP = S3.
EBS = block (usually one instance); EFS = shared file; S3 = object.

questions.stem:
A startup is testing a new workload, with unpredictable and short-term use, and does not want to assume a 1- or 3-year commitment yet.

Which EC2 purchase model is most appropriate at this stage?
questions.explanation: On-Demand charges by the second with no long-term commitment — ideal for unpredictable, short-term workloads, or for benchmarking before committing to Reserved Instances/Savings Plans. It is the natural starting point.

whyNots.A: Spot can be interrupted — bad for testing a workload you still need to observe with stability.
whyNots.B: Dedicated Hosts are expensive and aimed at licensing/compliance, not an initial cheap test.
whyNots.C: A 3-year RI requires a long commitment to a specific configuration — risky before you know the pattern.

hints: Unpredictable, short-term, no commitment — that is On-Demand. Pay by the second and stop whenever you want.
Commit to 1–3 years (RI/Savings Plans) only after you know the usage pattern.

questions.stem:
A nightly batch job is stateless and can tolerate being interrupted and restarted. You want the LOWEST possible cost per instance.

Which purchase model delivers the biggest discount for this interruptible workload?
questions.explanation: Spot Instances use spare capacity with up to 90% discount vs On-Demand, and can be interrupted with a 2-minute warning. They are perfect for fault-tolerant, time-flexible workloads such as stateless nightly batch, CI/CD, and big data.

whyNots.B: RI gives a good discount but requires a 1–3 year commitment — unnecessary for an interruptible batch job.
whyNots.C: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive, aimed at licensing/compliance — the opposite of 'lowest cost'.
whyNots.D: On-Demand does not provide the aggressive discount Spot gives for a workload that accepts interruption.

hints: Stateless, tolerates interruption, lowest cost — that is Spot, spare capacity with up to 90% off.
The trade-off is that AWS can reclaim the instance with a 2-minute warning. For overnight batch, that is fine.

questions.stem:
A production application runs 24/7 with stable, predictable load for years. The company wants to reduce cost significantly and accepts a 1- to 3-year commitment, keeping the same instance type in one region.

Which purchase model gives the biggest discount for this stable, fixed usage?
questions.explanation: For stable 24/7 usage with a 1- or 3-year commitment, Reserved Instances (up to ~72% discount) or Savings Plans are the way to go. RI locks a specific configuration (and can reserve capacity); Savings Plans provide the same savings with more instance flexibility.

whyNots.A: On-Demand is the most expensive per hour — wasteful for stable long-term workloads.
whyNots.C: Data transfer is a separate cost dimension, not an instance purchase model.
whyNots.D: Spot can be interrupted — unsuitable for 24/7 production that must always be running.

hints: Stable, 24/7, accepts a 1–3 year commitment — that means Reserved Instances (or Savings Plans). Big discount in exchange for commitment.
RI can reach ~72% off vs On-Demand. If you want instance flexibility, use Savings Plans.

questions.stem:
The company wants long-term savings but changes instance families frequently (and also uses Fargate and Lambda). It can commit to a per-hour SPEND amount, but not to a fixed instance type.

Which option gives a discount while keeping this flexibility?
questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans give a discount (1 or 3 years) in exchange for a commitment to spend a certain amount in US$/hour, with full flexibility: any region/instance family and also Fargate and Lambda. It is ideal for those who change instances often and do not want to lock a configuration.

whyNots.A: On-Demand does not provide the desired long-term discount.
whyNots.B: Spot is interruptible and is not a stable long-term commitment discount plan.
whyNots.D: Standard RI locks a specific configuration — the opposite of the flexibility requested.

hints: Commit to a per-hour SPEND amount, not an instance type, and include Fargate/Lambda — that is Compute Savings Plans, the most flexible.
Reserved Instances tie you to a specific configuration; Savings Plans tie you to a US$/hour spend amount.

questions.stem:
A company needs to bring software licenses tied to physical hardware (per socket/core) and meet a compliance requirement that calls for a dedicated physical server, with host visibility.

Which EC2 model meets BYOL and dedicated hardware compliance?
questions.explanation: Dedicated Hosts provide a fully dedicated physical server, with host visibility (sockets/cores), allowing you to bring licenses tied to hardware (BYOL) and meet compliance that requires physical isolation. It is the right model for this requirement.

whyNots.A: RI is a pricing/commitment model; it does not guarantee a dedicated physical host with BYOL visibility.
whyNots.B: Shared On-Demand runs on multi-tenant hardware — it does not meet physical isolation or per-socket BYOL.
whyNots.C: Spot is interruptible spare capacity on shared hardware — it does not meet compliance or per-socket BYOL.

hints: Licenses per socket/core (BYOL), dedicated physical host, and host visibility point to Dedicated Hosts.
Dedicated Instances also use dedicated hardware, but Dedicated Hosts give the server-level control/visibility needed for BYOL.

questions.stem:
Four workloads: (1) unpredictable short-term spike; (2) stable 24/7 base for 3 years; (3) stateless queue workers that tolerate interruption; (4) an app with a per-core license that requires a physical host.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: On-Demand → Savings Plans/RI → Spot → Dedicated Hosts

questions.explanation: Each workload has its model: unpredictable spike = On-Demand; stable long-term base = Savings Plans or Reserved Instances; stateless interruptible workers = Spot; per-core license on a physical host = Dedicated Hosts. Option A respects all four.

whyNots.B: Puts RI for an unpredictable spike and Spot for a stable base — reversed.
whyNots.C: Shuffles everything; none of the positions match the right workload.
whyNots.D: Uses Spot for a spike that must run and On-Demand for a stable base — wastes savings.

hints: Unpredictable = On-Demand; stable long-term = Savings Plans/RI; interruptible cheap = Spot; physical-host license = Dedicated Hosts.
Only option A keeps each workload in the right purchase model.

questions.stem:
An HPC cluster needs node-to-node communication with the LOWEST latency and the HIGHEST possible network throughput among instances, all in the same AZ.

Which placement group delivers this network performance?

options.text: None; placement group does not affect network

questions.explanation: A Cluster placement group packs instances close together within a single AZ, delivering low latency and high network throughput among them — exactly what HPC and intense node-to-node communication require.

whyNots.A: Spread separates instances onto distinct hardware to avoid correlated failures — the opposite of packing for performance.
whyNots.C: Wrong — the placement group directly affects network topology and performance.
whyNots.D: Partition isolates by partitions for distributed big data — it does not focus on minimum node-to-node latency.

hints: Think about which placement group packs instances tightly in one AZ for the lowest latency and highest throughput.
Remember the trade-off: clustering increases rack-failure risk, but HPC workloads choose performance.

questions.stem:
You have a small number of critical instances (e.g., nodes of a quorum cluster) that CANNOT fail at the same time. You want each one on separate hardware.

Which placement group minimizes correlated failures?
questions.explanation: A Spread placement group places a small number of instances on distinct hardware (racks), reducing the risk of simultaneous failures. It is the choice for a few critical instances that must be isolated from one another.

whyNots.A: Cluster packs instances together (same rack risk) for performance — the opposite of what is wanted here.
whyNots.B: Auto Scaling group manages scale/quantity, not physical separation by hardware like spread.
whyNots.D: Partition is for large distributed workloads with partition isolation, not for a few critical instances.

hints: Think about which placement group spreads a small number of critical instances across separate hardware so they do not fail together.
Remember that spreading instances across distinct racks isolates each from the other's hardware risk.

questions.stem:
You run a large distributed cluster such as Hadoop/Cassandra/Kafka, with dozens of instances, and want to isolate the impact of a hardware failure to a subset (partition), without losing the entire cluster.

Which placement group is designed for this case?
questions.explanation: A Partition placement group divides instances into logical partitions, each with its own rack, power, and network; instances in different partitions do not share hardware. It isolates the impact of a failure to a partition — ideal for Hadoop, Cassandra, and Kafka at scale.

whyNots.A: Cluster packs everything together — a rack failure can hit many instances.
whyNots.B: Without a placement group, you do not have the partition isolation that protects the distributed cluster.
whyNots.C: Spread is for a SMALL number of critical instances, not for dozens of big data nodes.

hints: Think about which placement group isolates large distributed big-data clusters into partitions.
Remember that each partition has its own rack, power, and network, so one failure does not take down the rest.

questions.stem:
Three placement objectives: (1) minimum latency between HPC nodes; (2) a few critical instances that cannot fail together; (3) large Cassandra cluster with failure isolation by block.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Cluster delivers minimum node-to-node latency (HPC); Spread separates a few critical instances onto distinct hardware; Partition isolates failures by partition in large distributed clusters (Cassandra, Hadoop, Kafka). Option A maps all three correctly.

whyNots.B: Reverses Cluster and Partition.
whyNots.C: Swaps Cluster and Spread — minimum latency is Cluster, not Spread.
whyNots.D: Swaps Spread and Partition — a few critical instances is Spread; big data is Partition.

hints: Think about the three placements: Cluster for minimum latency, Spread for separated critical instances, Partition for isolated big data.
Remember: Cluster keeps instances together, Spread keeps a few apart, Partition uses blocks. Only option A matches.

questions.stem:
An application on an EC2 instance needs to read from an S3 bucket. A developer suggested pasting the access key inside the code to authenticate.

What is the SAFE and recommended way to grant this access?

options.text: Attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance (instance profile)
Save the secret key in a .txt file on the instance
Embed the access key in the code

questions.explanation: The secure way is to attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance (via instance profile): the application receives temporary credentials automatically, with no long-term key embedded. This eliminates the risk of leaking an access key in the code.

whyNots.A: Using the root account is forbidden for day-to-day operation — it is the most dangerous credential of all.
whyNots.C: Storing the secret key in a file on the instance is equally insecure.
whyNots.D: Embedding the access key in the code is the classic anti-pattern — it leaks easily (git, logs) and does not rotate.

hints: Think about attaching an IAM Role to EC2 so the application gets temporary credentials automatically, instead of embedding keys.
Remember that a role rotates credentials on its own and never leaks into code.

questions.stem:
On the exam: distinguish a PERMANENT identity with a long-term credential from an ASSUMABLE identity with a temporary credential.

Which association is correct?

options.text: Both are the same; only the name differs — the type of credential issued is the same for both
IAM User = temporary credential (rotated); IAM Role = long-term credential
IAM User = long-term credential; IAM Role = temporary credential (assumed)
Both use only temporary credentials — AWS has retired long-term keys

questions.explanation: An IAM User is a permanent identity with long-term credentials (password, access keys). An IAM Role is an assumable identity that delivers temporary credentials via STS, used by AWS services, external accounts, and federated users. Preferring roles is a best practice.

whyNots.A: They differ in nature (permanent vs assumable) and credential type.
whyNots.B: Reverses — user is long-term; role is temporary.
whyNots.D: User uses long-term credentials, not temporary.

hints: Think about which identity is permanent with long-term credentials and which is assumed for temporary credentials.
Remember that services and cross-account access use roles, not users.

questions.stem:
A user in account A needs to access resources in account B temporarily, without creating a new user in account B.

Which mechanism delivers this cross-account access with temporary credentials?

options.text: Create an IAM User in account B and share the password
Use the root account of account B
STS AssumeRole (assume a role in account B)

questions.explanation: STS AssumeRole is the path for cross-account access: account B creates a role with a trust policy that trusts account A; the user in account A calls AssumeRole and receives temporary credentials (access key + secret + session token) to act in account B — without creating a new user.

whyNots.A: Creating a user and sharing a password is insecure and contrary to temporary credentials best practice.
whyNots.B: Using account B's root is forbidden for this type of access.
whyNots.C: Security Group filters network — it does not grant identity access between accounts.

hints: Think about STS AssumeRole for temporary cross-account access, where account B trusts account A.
Remember that the role's trust policy in account B defines who can assume it, and the caller receives temporary credentials.

questions.stem:
You want to allow a principal from ANOTHER account to access a specific S3 bucket, defining the permission on the bucket itself.

What type of policy do you use?

options.text: Identity-based policy only on the user

questions.explanation: A resource-based policy (such as an S3 bucket policy) is attached to the resource and specifies WHO (which principal, including from another account) can access it. It is the way to grant cross-account access directly on the bucket.

whyNots.B: Permissions boundary limits the maximum of a principal — it does not grant access to a bucket.
whyNots.C: Identity-based policy states what the identity can do, but for cross-account the resource must also allow the external principal (resource-based).
whyNots.D: SCP is a ceiling for the account in Organizations — it is not what grants access to a specific bucket.

hints: Think about the policy attached to the resource that says WHO can access it — for S3, that is the bucket policy.
Remember that a resource-based policy can list a principal from another account, making it ideal for cross-account S3 access.

questions.stem:
The central security team wants to let developers CREATE their own roles and policies, while ensuring none of them can grant themselves permissions beyond a defined ceiling.

Which IAM feature imposes this ceiling per identity?
questions.explanation: A permissions boundary is a managed policy that defines the MAXIMUM permissions an identity policy can grant to a user/role. The effective permissions are the intersection (boundary ∩ identity policy), which lets you delegate role creation to developers without risk of escalation beyond the ceiling.

whyNots.A: Resource-based policy controls access to a resource, not the permission ceiling of an identity.
whyNots.C: Key rotation is credential hygiene — it does not impose a permission ceiling.
whyNots.D: MFA adds an authentication factor — it does not limit the scope of permissions.

hints: Think about the feature that sets the maximum permissions a user or role can have, even if its identity policy grants more.
Remember that effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and the identity policy.

questions.stem:
In an account within an Organization, an action is permitted by the user's identity policy, but an SCP and a permissions boundary also apply.

When is the action effectively permitted (ignoring explicit deny)?

options.text: When only the identity policy allows — SCP and boundary are just informational
When at least one of the three allows — IAM sums permissions (union)
Only when the identity policy, the SCP, AND the permissions boundary all allow
When the SCP allows, ignoring the rest — it is the final layer and decides

questions.explanation: When identity policy + SCP + permissions boundary all apply, an action is permitted only if ALL of them allow it (intersection). Each is an independent ceiling; if any one does not allow (or an explicit deny exists anywhere), it is blocked.

whyNots.A: SCP and boundary cannot be ignored; they limit the effective permissions.
whyNots.B: One allowing is not enough — it is an intersection; all must allow.
whyNots.D: The SCP alone is not enough; the identity policy and boundary must also allow.

hints: Think of permission layers as ceilings: identity policy, SCP, and permissions boundary must all allow the action.
Remember that an explicit deny in any layer overrides any allow.

questions.stem:
A company with 30 AWS accounts wants to give employees a single SSO experience, with MFA, and centrally manage who accesses which accounts and with what permissions.

Which service delivers this centralized workforce access?
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO) centrally manages access to multiple AWS accounts, with SSO protected by MFA and permission sets, connecting to an external IdP (SAML 2.0/SCIM) or its own directory. It is the recommended service for workforce access.

whyNots.A: A shared access key is insecure and does not provide managed SSO/MFA.
whyNots.B: IAM Users per account multiplies management and does not provide central SSO — the opposite of the request.
whyNots.C: Security Group is a network firewall — it has nothing to do with identity SSO.

hints: Think about the service that provides central SSO, MFA, and permission sets across many AWS accounts.
Remember that it connects to an external IdP via SAML/SCIM or uses its own directory.

questions.stem:
A company already has a corporate directory (Active Directory) with SAML 2.0 and wants employees to access AWS using those existing identities, without creating IAM Users.

Which approach enables this federated access?

options.text: SAML 2.0 identity federation (users assume a role via AssumeRoleWithSAML)
S3 bucket policy allowing the corporate domain of the identity provider
Share the root account with the team, protected by MFA and a rotated password
Create an IAM User for each employee, syncing passwords manually

questions.explanation: SAML 2.0 identity federation establishes trust between the corporate IdP (e.g., AD) and AWS: the IdP authenticates the user, who assumes a role via AssumeRoleWithSAML and receives temporary credentials — without creating IAM Users. (For many accounts with central SSO, IAM Identity Center is even more recommended.)

whyNots.B: Bucket policy controls access to a bucket, not employee federated authentication.
whyNots.C: Sharing root is forbidden and extremely dangerous.
whyNots.D: Creating an IAM User per employee is exactly what federation avoids — it duplicates identities.

hints: Think about SAML 2.0 federation when you already have a corporate directory and do not want IAM Users.
Remember that users assume a role with AssumeRoleWithSAML and receive temporary credentials.

questions.stem:
An audit recommends reducing the risk of the account's most powerful credential: the root account.

What is the AWS-recommended best practice for the root account?

options.text: Share the root password with the team so no one gets stuck waiting for access
Enable MFA on root, do not use it for day-to-day work, and operate with IAM/lower-privilege identities
Use root for all daily administrative tasks, since it never hits a permission boundary
Create multiple root access keys for automation, with a separate key for each script

questions.explanation: The best practice is to protect the root account with MFA, avoid using it for day-to-day work, and operate with lower-privilege IAM identities (roles/users with only what is needed). You should not create root access keys or share its credentials.

whyNots.A: Sharing the root password is a serious security failure.
whyNots.C: Using root for daily tasks increases risk — it has unrestricted power.
whyNots.D: Creating root access keys for automation is discouraged — use roles instead.

hints: Think of the root account as the master key: enable MFA, lock it away, and use lower-privilege identities daily.
Remember that AWS recommends not creating root access keys and not using root for routine tasks.

questions.stem:
Four mechanisms: (1) what the identity CAN do; (2) WHO can access a resource; (3) maximum ceiling of a user/role; (4) permission ceiling for the entire account in the Organization.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Identity-based policy → Resource-based policy → Permissions boundary → SCP

questions.explanation: An identity-based policy states what the identity can do; a resource-based policy states who can access the resource; a permissions boundary is the ceiling for a user/role; an SCP is the ceiling for the entire account in the Organization. Option C respects all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps identity with resource-based and SCP with boundary.
whyNots.B: Jumbles everything; no position matches the correct function.
whyNots.D: Reverses the order — SCP is account ceiling, not 'what the identity can do'.

hints: Think about the four IAM controls: identity-based permissions, resource-based access, per-principal ceiling, and account ceiling.
Remember that only option C keeps each mechanism in its proper role.

questions.stem:
A front-end receives order spikes and the back-end cannot process everything immediately. You want to decouple the two so the spike does not bring down processing.

Which service places a queue between producer and consumer to absorb the spike?
questions.explanation: SQS places a queue between producer and consumer: the front-end enqueues orders and the back-end pulls them at its own pace. It absorbs spikes and decouples components, without losing messages if the consumer is slow.

whyNots.A: CloudFront is a content CDN — it does not queue orders for asynchronous processing.
whyNots.B: RDS is a relational database — it is not a decoupling queue.
whyNots.C: Config evaluates compliance — nothing to do with message queues.

hints: Think about the service that places a queue between producer and consumer so the back-end consumes at its own pace.
Remember that a queue decouples the two sides and holds orders when the back-end slows down.

questions.stem:
A financial system requires messages to be processed EXACTLY once and in the ORDER they were sent — duplicating or swapping the order would cause an accounting error.

Which SQS queue type meets the requirement?

options.text: Any of them; it makes no difference

questions.explanation: The FIFO queue preserves strict sending order and guarantees exactly-once processing (no duplicates) via MessageGroupId and MessageDeduplicationId. It is the right type for financial scenarios where order and non-duplication are critical. Standard is at-least-once and best-effort order.

whyNots.B: Standard is at-least-once (may duplicate) and only best-effort order — unacceptable for the requirement.
whyNots.C: They are not equivalent — only FIFO guarantees strict order and exactly-once.
whyNots.D: More consumers on Standard does not solve duplication or guarantee order.

hints: Think about which queue type gives strict ordering and exactly-once processing.
Remember that FIFO uses MessageGroupId for ordering and MessageDeduplicationId to prevent duplicates.

questions.stem:
When a consumer takes a message from the queue to process, you do not want another consumer to get the SAME message at the same time. But if processing fails, it must become available again.

Which SQS feature controls this behavior?
questions.explanation: Visibility timeout makes the message invisible to other consumers as soon as one receives it, preventing simultaneous duplicate processing. If the consumer processes and deletes it within the timeout, great; if it fails (does not delete), the message becomes visible again for a new attempt.

whyNots.A: Long polling reduces empty calls when fetching messages — it does not control invisibility during processing.
whyNots.C: DLQ is where a message that has failed repeatedly goes — it is not what temporarily hides during processing.
whyNots.D: Message group ID orders messages in FIFO — it does not handle visibility during processing.

hints: Think about the timeout that hides a message from other consumers while it is being processed.
Remember that if the consumer fails to delete the message in time, it reappears for another attempt.

questions.stem:
Some messages are 'poison': they fail processing every time and keep returning to the queue indefinitely, blocking the flow and hiding the problem.

Which feature isolates these problematic messages for analysis?
questions.explanation: The Dead-Letter Queue receives messages that exceed maxReceiveCount (fail repeatedly), removing them from the main queue for analysis. It avoids the infinite reprocessing loop and flow stalling. The DLQ is the same type as the source queue.

whyNots.A: FIFO handles order/duplication, not isolating messages that always fail.
whyNots.B: Increasing visibility timeout only delays reprocessing — it does not isolate the problematic message.
whyNots.D: More consumers does not solve a message that fails by nature — it only spreads the problem.

hints: Think about the queue that receives messages after they fail too many times, so the main queue keeps flowing.
Remember that the DLQ must be the same type as the source queue.

questions.stem:
A single 'order created' event must reach, at the same time, several independent systems (inventory, email, BI), each with its own queue to process at its own pace.

Which combination implements this fan-out?

options.text: Step Functions with no queue — the state machine already delivers decoupled
API Gateway calling each system in sequence, delivering simultaneously to all
A single SQS queue read by all, where each system receives its copy of the event
SNS publishing to multiple SQS queues (pub/sub + queue per consumer)

questions.explanation: The fan-out pattern uses an SNS topic (pub/sub, push) publishing to multiple subscribed SQS queues, one per consumer. Each system processes at its own pace, decoupled — if one is slow, the others continue. SNS distributes; SQS decouples.

whyNots.A: Step Functions orchestrates steps, but the scenario calls for simultaneous decoupled delivery (fan-out), which is SNS+SQS.
whyNots.B: Sequential calls via API Gateway couple the systems — a slow one breaks the chain.
whyNots.C: A single queue makes consumers compete for the same messages — each does not receive its own copy of the event.

hints: Think about using SNS to fan out one event to multiple SQS queues, one per consumer.
Remember that SNS pushes to subscribers while each SQS queue decouples its consumer.

questions.stem:
A workflow has several steps with dependencies, conditional branches, and error/retry handling across multiple Lambda functions. You do not want to hand-code this 'glue' and state control.

Which service orchestrates this workflow?

options.text: One giant Lambda calling another Lambda

questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates workflows as a serverless state machine: sequential/parallel steps, branching, retry and error catch, timeouts — without you writing glue logic or managing state. It coordinates Lambda, ECS, SNS, SQS, and more.

whyNots.B: Chaining Lambda functions manually is fragile, hard to handle error/retry, and hard to visualize state.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a CDN — nothing to do with workflow orchestration.
whyNots.D: SQS is a message queue, not a step orchestrator with branching and retry.

hints: Think about the serverless state machine that coordinates steps, branches, retries, and errors.
Remember that Step Functions controls flow, errors, and state instead of manually chaining Lambda functions.

questions.stem:
You need an API that keeps a BIDIRECTIONAL persistent connection to send real-time updates to the client (a live chat).

Which API Gateway type meets the requirement?

options.text: None; API Gateway does not support real-time

questions.explanation: API Gateway WebSocket API maintains a persistent bidirectional connection, ideal for real-time use: live chat, push notifications, self-updating dashboards. REST and HTTP APIs are request/response and do not keep the channel open to push data.

whyNots.A: HTTP API is simple, cheap request/response — it is also not persistent bidirectional.
whyNots.C: Wrong — API Gateway supports real-time via WebSocket API.
whyNots.D: REST API is request/response with many features (API keys, usage plans), but it does not maintain a persistent bidirectional channel.

hints: Think about which API Gateway type keeps a persistent bidirectional connection for real-time updates.
Remember that REST and HTTP APIs are request/response; WebSocket is for continuously pushing data to clients.

questions.stem:
You want a simple, inexpensive, low-latency API, basically a proxy for Lambda functions, WITHOUT needing API keys, usage plans, or advanced request validation.

Which API Gateway type is most appropriate?

options.text: There is no cost difference between the types

questions.explanation: HTTP API is simpler, cheaper, and lower latency, ideal as a proxy for Lambda/HTTP when you do not need the advanced features (API keys, usage plans, request validation, cache) of REST API. For this lean case, it is the best choice.

whyNots.A: REST API has more features (and cost) — overkill when you just want a simple, cheap proxy.
whyNots.B: There is a difference — HTTP API is usually cheaper and lower latency than REST API.
whyNots.D: WebSocket is for persistent bidirectional connection, not for a simple request/response proxy.

hints: Think about the API Gateway type that is simple, cheap, and low-latency for a Lambda proxy.
Remember that if you needed API keys, usage plans, or rich validation, REST API would be the choice.

questions.stem:
A company is migrating to AWS an on-premises application that already uses a traditional message broker with JMS/AMQP protocols, and does NOT want to rewrite the messaging code.

Which service eases this migration while maintaining protocol compatibility?
questions.explanation: Amazon MQ is the managed message broker (Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ) compatible with standard protocols (JMS, AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, OpenWire). It is the choice for migrating existing applications that depend on these protocols without rewriting messaging code. New cloud-native applications benefit more from SQS/SNS.

whyNots.A: Kinesis is data streaming — it is not a message broker compatible with JMS/AMQP.
whyNots.B: SQS is great for new apps, but has its own API — it would require rewriting code that uses JMS/AMQP.
whyNots.C: SNS is pub/sub with its own API — it also does not maintain compatibility with the legacy broker protocols.

hints: Think about the managed broker that supports JMS/AMQP so legacy messaging code does not need rewriting.
Remember: SQS/SNS for new cloud-native apps, Amazon MQ for migrating legacy protocol compatibility.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) decouple with a queue and process at the consumer's pace; (2) one event to many subscribers (fan-out); (3) orchestrate a multi-step workflow with retry; (4) migrate a legacy AMQP broker without rewriting.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: SQS → SNS → Step Functions → Amazon MQ
SNS → SQS → Amazon MQ → Step Functions
Amazon MQ → Step Functions → SNS → SQS
Step Functions → Amazon MQ → SQS → SNS

questions.explanation: Each service has its role: SQS (queue/decoupling, pull), SNS (pub/sub, fan-out), Step Functions (step orchestration with retry/error), and Amazon MQ (managed broker for migrating apps with AMQP/JMS). Option A respects all four.

whyNots.B: Swaps SQS with SNS and Amazon MQ with Step Functions.
whyNots.C: Reverses everything; no position matches the correct function.
whyNots.D: Jumbles everything — Step Functions is not a queue and Amazon MQ is not fan-out.

hints: Think about which service handles queues, fan-out, step orchestration, and legacy broker migration.
Remember that only option A keeps each service in its proper role.

questions.stem:
A website serves files from an S3 bucket through CloudFront. You want no one to download directly via the S3 URL — only through CloudFront.

Which feature restricts access to the origin bucket in this way (current recommended mode)?
questions.explanation: OAC (Origin Access Control) is the current way to allow an S3 bucket to be accessed only by the CloudFront distribution, blocking direct access via the S3 URL. It supports all regions, SSE-KMS, and uses short-term credentials — it replaces the legacy OAI.

whyNots.A: Signed cookies control who accesses the distributed content, they do not restrict the S3 ORIGIN to CloudFront.
whyNots.C: Security Group is an instance/ENI firewall — it does not apply to an S3 bucket.
whyNots.D: A public bucket is the opposite of what you want — it exposes files directly.

hints: Think about Origin Access Control when CloudFront should access an S3 bucket but direct S3 access must be blocked.
Remember that you grant the CloudFront OAC read access to the bucket and remove public/direct S3 access.

questions.stem:
You sell a specific file (an e-book) and want to give each buyer a temporary link, valid only for 24 hours, to download THAT file.

Which CloudFront feature delivers access to an individual file?
questions.explanation: Signed URL controls access to an individual file: you generate a signed URL with expiration (and optionally IP), perfect for releasing a specific download (the e-book) for a limited time to each buyer.

whyNots.A: Signed cookies are for releasing MULTIPLE files at once without changing URLs — overkill for a single item.
whyNots.B: Geo restriction blocks by country — it does not control temporary access to a specific file.
whyNots.D: OAC restricts the S3 origin to CloudFront — it does not issue a per-file temporary link to the user.

hints: Think about signed URLs when you need a temporary link for one specific file.
Remember that signed cookies are for granting access to many files without changing each URL.

questions.stem:
A streaming platform wants to release the entire catalog (many files) to an authenticated subscriber, without having to sign a URL for each video.

Which CloudFront feature is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Signed cookies grant access to multiple restricted files without needing to change/sign each URL — ideal for streaming, where the authenticated subscriber receives a signed cookie (with expiration) that grants access to the entire catalog.

whyNots.A: OAC protects the S3 origin — it is not the mechanism for releasing content to the end user.
whyNots.B: Cache TTL affects caching, not access control for private content.
whyNots.C: A signed URL per video would require generating and managing a signed URL for each file — cumbersome for a large catalog.

hints: Think about signed cookies when you want to release many files without signing each URL.
Remember: signed URL is per file; signed cookie is for many files or a restricted area.

questions.stem:
Due to licensing, content can only be displayed in certain countries and must be blocked in the others.

Which CloudFront feature applies this country-level blocking?

options.text: Signed URL with the country embedded in the token
OAC, which validates the country of each request
Cache policy with country rule in the TTL

questions.explanation: CloudFront geographic restriction (geo restriction) allows blocking or allowing access by country (allowlist/blocklist), applied to the entire distribution. It is the right feature for regional licensing/compliance requirements.

whyNots.B: Signed URL controls temporary access to a file — it does not filter by country.
whyNots.C: OAC protects the S3 origin — it does not block by country.
whyNots.D: Cache policy defines cache key/TTL — it does not restrict geography.

hints: Think about geo restriction when content must be allowed or blocked by country.
Remember that geo restriction applies to the whole distribution, not individual paths.

questions.stem:
You want to control how long objects stay cached at the edge before CloudFront checks the origin for an updated version.

Which setting controls this?
questions.explanation: TTLs (minimum, default, and maximum) control how long CloudFront keeps an object in cache before checking the origin for updates. The default Default TTL is 86400s (1 day). Adjusting TTL balances content freshness vs. origin load/cost.

whyNots.A: Visibility timeout is for SQS — nothing to do with CloudFront cache.
whyNots.C: Permissions boundary is IAM — it does not control cache.
whyNots.D: Multi-AZ is database/infrastructure resilience — not CDN TTL.

hints: Think about TTL settings to control how long objects stay cached at the edge.
Remember: a shorter TTL means fresher content but more origin requests; a longer TTL means more caching and lower origin load.

questions.stem:
You need lightweight, extremely cheap edge logic to rewrite URLs and adjust headers on EACH viewer request, with minimal latency and huge scale — without any external network call.

Which edge feature is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: CloudFront Functions runs lightweight JavaScript on viewer events (request/response), with sub-ms startup, scales to millions of req/s, and costs about 1/6 of Lambda@Edge. It is ideal for manipulating headers, rewriting/redirecting URLs, and normalizing cache key — but it cannot make external network calls.

whyNots.A: Lambda@Edge has more power and allows external network, but it is more expensive/slower — overkill for a simple URL/header rewrite.
whyNots.B: There is no 'EC2 at the edge' as this feature — CloudFront's edge uses edge functions.
whyNots.D: Step Functions orchestrates workflows — it does not run at CloudFront's edge per request.

hints: Think about CloudFront Functions for lightweight, sub-ms viewer request/response logic that scales massively.
Remember that if you need more power or external calls, Lambda@Edge is the alternative.

questions.stem:
You need to generate dynamic content at the edge and make a CALL to an external service (for example, fetch data from an API) before the response is cached, while also being able to act on the origin event.

Which edge resource handles this heavier logic?
questions.explanation: Lambda@Edge runs Node.js/Python at the edge, on viewer AND origin events, with more compute power and the ability to make external network calls — ideal for generating/manipulating content (including before caching). CloudFront Functions is lightweight and cannot make external network calls or run on origin events.

whyNots.A: Geo restriction blocks by country — it does not execute logic or external calls.
whyNots.B: Signed cookies control access — they do not generate dynamic content at the edge.
whyNots.C: CloudFront Functions are lightweight, viewer-only, and cannot make external network calls — they do not meet the requirement.

hints: Think about: external network call + origin event + heavier logic = Lambda@Edge. CloudFront Functions cannot make external network calls.
Remember that Lambda@Edge runs on viewer and origin events; CloudFront Functions only on viewer events.

questions.stem:
You will host a static website with low global latency and protection against SQLi/XSS, while keeping the origin bucket private.

Which architecture meets these requirements?

options.text: Private S3 + CloudFront with OAC + WAF on the distribution
Single EC2 in one region serving the site
S3 + direct access via the bucket URL

questions.explanation: The classic pattern for a secure, global static site: private S3 as the origin, CloudFront in front with OAC (so the bucket is only reachable via CloudFront), and AWS WAF attached to the distribution to filter SQLi/XSS at layer 7. This accelerates, protects, and keeps the origin private.

whyNots.B: A single EC2 in one region does not deliver low global latency nor the scale/caching of CloudFront.
whyNots.C: Direct access via the bucket URL exposes the origin and provides neither a CDN nor WAF.
whyNots.D: Public S3 without CloudFront lacks global low latency and WAF filtering, and exposes the bucket.

hints: Think about: global static site + private origin + layer-7 filtering = private S3 + CloudFront (OAC) + WAF attached to the distribution.
Remember that OAC keeps the bucket private; CloudFront accelerates delivery; WAF blocks SQLi/XSS at the edge.

questions.stem:
A site has many users worldwide downloading the same static images and videos from the origin server, overloading it and causing high latency for users far away.

Which service caches this content at the edge, close to users?
questions.explanation: CloudFront is the AWS CDN: it caches content (static and dynamic) at edge locations near users, reducing global latency and offloading the origin server. This is the classic use case for images/videos accessed worldwide.

whyNots.A: SQS is a message queue — it is not a CDN and does not cache content.
whyNots.C: Direct Connect is a hybrid on-premises↔AWS link — it does not distribute content to global users.
whyNots.D: EBS is block storage for an instance — it is not edge content delivery.

hints: Think about: repeated static content + global users + offloading the origin = CDN = CloudFront, which caches at edge locations.
Remember that the user fetches from the nearest point of presence, so the origin stops getting hammered.

questions.stem:
Four needs in CloudFront: (1) keep the S3 bucket accessible only through CloudFront; (2) give temporary access to ONE file; (3) unlock MANY files for a subscriber without changing URLs; (4) block access by country.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Geo restriction → Signed cookies → OAC → Signed URL
OAC → Signed cookies → Signed URL → Geo restriction
OAC → Signed URL → Signed cookies → Geo restriction
Signed URL → OAC → Geo restriction → Signed cookies

questions.explanation: Each feature has its role: OAC restricts the S3 origin to CloudFront; Signed URL releases an individual file for a limited time; Signed cookies release many files without changing URLs; Geo restriction blocks/allows by country. Option C respects all four.

whyNots.A: Reverses the order — geo restriction is not for keeping the origin private.
whyNots.B: Swaps Signed URL and Signed cookies — one file is Signed URL; many files is Signed cookies.
whyNots.D: Swaps OAC with Signed URL and Geo restriction with Signed cookies.

hints: Think about: private origin = OAC; one file = Signed URL; many files = Signed cookies; by country = Geo restriction.
Remember that only option C keeps each feature in its proper role.

questions.stem:
You want to track CPU, network, and status of EC2 instances, store application logs, and trigger alerts when something crosses a threshold.

Which service handles metrics, logs, and alarms?
questions.explanation: CloudWatch is the AWS monitoring/observability service: it collects metrics, centralizes logs, and fires alarms (with actions), giving real-time visibility into the health and performance of resources and applications.

whyNots.A: CloudTrail audits API calls (who did what) — it is not the metrics/alarms dashboard.
whyNots.B: Config evaluates configuration compliance — it does not collect operational metrics.
whyNots.C: X-Ray performs distributed request tracing — it is not the metrics/logs/alarms service.

hints: Think about: metrics + logs + real-time alarms = CloudWatch, the AWS observability service.
Remember that CloudTrail is API audit; X-Ray is request tracing. CloudWatch is the health/performance dashboard.

questions.stem:
By default, EC2 metrics are delivered every 5 minutes, but you need 1-minute granularity so Auto Scaling can react faster to spikes.

What do you enable?
questions.explanation: Detailed monitoring publishes EC2 metrics every 1 minute (vs. 5 minutes for basic), at additional cost. The finer granularity lets Auto Scaling and alarms react faster to load changes.

whyNots.B: VPC Flow Logs capture network metadata — they do not change EC2 metric frequency.
whyNots.C: CloudTrail data events record API calls on resources — they are not EC2 performance metrics.
whyNots.D: Basic monitoring is the 5-minute default — it does not provide the requested 1-minute granularity.

hints: Think about: 5 minutes is basic (free). For 1 minute you enable detailed monitoring (paid).
Remember that finer granularity lets Auto Scaling react sooner to spikes.

questions.stem:
You want to monitor MEMORY (RAM) and DISK usage of an EC2 instance in CloudWatch, but these metrics do not appear by default.

What is required to collect them?

options.text: Just enable detailed monitoring, which already brings memory and disk
Install the unified CloudWatch agent (send as custom metrics)
They already come by default; just open the console on the metrics tab
Enable CloudTrail, which collects operating-system metrics

questions.explanation: EC2 does not publish memory (RAM) or disk metrics by default — these are OS/in-guest metrics. To get them in CloudWatch, install the unified CloudWatch agent, which collects and sends them as custom metrics.

whyNots.A: Detailed monitoring only changes the frequency (1 min) of existing metrics — it does not add memory/disk.
whyNots.C: Wrong — memory and disk do NOT come by default; the agent is required.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail audits APIs — it does not collect OS metrics.

hints: Think about: classic trap — EC2 does NOT publish memory or disk by default (they are OS-level metrics). Install the CloudWatch agent.
Remember that the agent sends mem_used_percent, disk_used_percent, etc. as custom metrics.

questions.stem:
When average CPU exceeds 80% for 5 minutes, the team needs to receive an email/SMS alert.

How do you configure this in CloudWatch?

options.text: A NACL rule that sends email when CPU rises
A VPC Flow Log with built-in CPU alert in the logs
A CloudWatch alarm with an SNS notification action
An S3 bucket policy configured to send the SMS

questions.explanation: You create a CloudWatch alarm on the CPU metric (threshold of 80% for N periods) with an SNS notification action. When the alarm enters ALARM state, it publishes to the SNS topic, which sends email/SMS to subscribers.

whyNots.A: A NACL is a subnet firewall — it does not trigger notifications based on metrics.
whyNots.B: Flow Logs capture network traffic — they do not alert on CPU.
whyNots.D: A bucket policy is S3 access permissions — it has nothing to do with CPU alerts.

hints: Think about: alarm on the CPU metric + SNS action (which sends email/SMS to subscribers).
Remember that the alarm fires, triggers the SNS topic, and SNS notifies the team.

questions.stem:
An application has dozens of individual alarms and the team is being bombarded with notifications. You want to alert ONCE, at an aggregated level, only when the set indicates a real problem.

Which CloudWatch feature reduces this noise by combining alarms?
questions.explanation: A composite alarm combines multiple alarms using boolean logic (AND/OR) into a single aggregated health indicator. It notifies at the set level, reducing noise (alarm fatigue) instead of firing a notification for every individual alarm.

whyNots.A: Detailed monitoring changes metric frequency — it does not aggregate alarms.
whyNots.B: Logs Insights queries logs — it does not combine alarms.
whyNots.C: More individual alarms increase noise — the opposite of what is requested.

hints: Think about: combining several alarms with AND/OR logic into a single indicator = composite alarm. It notifies on the aggregate, not per alarm.
Remember that this reduces alarm fatigue — the team gets one alert for the health of the set.

questions.stem:
After an incident, you need to interactively query and filter gigabytes of logs (by error pattern, by field) to find the cause, without building your own analytics stack.

Which CloudWatch feature performs this interactive log analysis?
questions.explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights is the interactive service for querying, filtering, analyzing, and visualizing logs (with a query language) directly in CloudWatch log groups — ideal for incident investigation without building your own analytics infrastructure.

whyNots.B: Athena queries data in S3; the native, direct path for CloudWatch logs is Logs Insights.
whyNots.C: Alarms fire on metrics — they do not perform interactive log queries.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail records API calls — it is not the query tool for application logs.

hints: Think about: interactively querying and filtering logs with a query language inside CloudWatch = Logs Insights.
Remember that it is pay-as-you-go and integrated — you run queries directly on log groups.

questions.stem:
When the fleet's average CPU exceeds 70%, you want Auto Scaling to add instances automatically.

What connects the metric to the scaling action?

options.text: A signed URL that authorizes the ASG to scale
A CloudWatch alarm with an Auto Scaling action
A permissions boundary with a CPU trigger
A Gateway Endpoint linking the metric to the ASG

questions.explanation: A CloudWatch alarm monitors the metric (CPU > 70%) and, when triggered, executes an Auto Scaling action that adds instances. It is the bridge between the metric and dynamic fleet scaling.

whyNots.A: A Signed URL is for accessing CloudFront content — it has nothing to do with scaling a fleet.
whyNots.C: A permissions boundary is an IAM ceiling — it does not trigger scaling by metric.
whyNots.D: A Gateway Endpoint is private access to S3/DynamoDB — it does not scale instances.

hints: Think about: alarm on the CPU metric + Auto Scaling action = the fleet grows when the threshold is crossed.
Remember that this is how the dynamic scaling policy connects to the CloudWatch metric.

questions.stem:
When a CloudWatch alarm changes state, you want to automatically trigger remediation (for example, a Lambda function or a Systems Manager automation) without human intervention.

Which service routes the alarm state change to those actions?

options.text: Amazon Route 53, using health checks to trigger Lambda
AWS Direct Connect, which delivers the event over the dedicated network
Amazon S3, with event notifications of the alarm state change

questions.explanation: CloudWatch sends events to EventBridge when an alarm changes state. You create EventBridge rules to trigger targets such as Lambda, SSM Automation, SQS, or Step Functions — implementing event-driven auto-remediation without human intervention.

whyNots.A: Route 53 is DNS — it does not orchestrate actions from alarm state changes.
whyNots.B: Direct Connect is hybrid connectivity — it has nothing to do with alarm-driven automation.
whyNots.D: S3 is object storage — it does not route alarm events to actions.

hints: Think about: the alarm emits a state-change event to EventBridge, which has rules to trigger Lambda, SSM Automation, SQS, Step Functions...
Remember that this is the event-driven auto-remediation path: alarm → EventBridge → action.

questions.stem:
You need to collect in-guest logs and metrics from both EC2 instances and ON-PREMISES servers, sending everything to a centralized observability place.

Which tool collects this from both?
questions.explanation: The unified CloudWatch agent collects in-guest logs and metrics (CPU, memory, disk, etc.) from EC2 instances AND on-premises servers, sending everything to CloudWatch — centralizing observability for hybrid environments.

whyNots.A: Flow Logs capture VPC network metadata — not in-guest logs/metrics from on-premises servers.
whyNots.B: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities — it is not a logs/metrics collector for the OS.
whyNots.C: Config evaluates AWS resource configuration — it does not collect in-guest logs.

hints: Think about: the same agent that collects memory/disk also runs on-premises — the unified CloudWatch agent.
Remember that it sends in-guest logs and metrics to CloudWatch, from EC2 and from servers outside AWS.

questions.stem:
Three operational questions: (1) what is the CPU usage and how long have 5xx errors been rising? (2) who called the API that deleted the resource? (3) in which microservice is the request spending time?

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: CloudWatch answers metrics/logs/errors (CPU, 5xx over time); CloudTrail answers who called which API and when; X-Ray shows where the request spends time among microservices. Option A respects all three.

whyNots.B: Swaps X-Ray and CloudTrail — who called the API is CloudTrail, not X-Ray.
whyNots.C: Puts X-Ray for metrics and CloudWatch for API audit — mixed up.
whyNots.D: Starts with CloudTrail for metrics — wrong; metrics/errors are CloudWatch.

hints: Think about: metric/log/error = CloudWatch; who called the API = CloudTrail; time per microservice = X-Ray.
Remember that only option A keeps each service in its proper role.

questions.stem:
A 3-tier web application needs to: distribute HTTP traffic across instances; scale the fleet with load; survive the loss of an AZ in the database; and offload the database on repeated reads.

Which combination of services meets all requirements?

options.text: NLB + a single EC2 instance + RDS Single-AZ
ALB + Auto Scaling (multi-AZ) + RDS Multi-AZ + ElastiCache

questions.explanation: ALB distributes HTTP traffic (layer 7); Auto Scaling across multiple AZs adjusts the fleet and provides resilience; RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby for automatic failover if an AZ fails; ElastiCache caches repeated reads, offloading the database. This is the classic resilient 3-tier design.

whyNots.A: A single instance and RDS Single-AZ do not survive AZ loss or scale.
whyNots.C: A single Spot instance is interruptible and not resilient; the scenario describes a relational 3-tier app.
whyNots.D: Instance Store is ephemeral and the stack does not cover the requested resilient relational database.

hints: Break it down: distribute HTTP = ALB; scale = Auto Scaling across AZs; survive AZ loss in the DB = RDS Multi-AZ; offload reads = ElastiCache.
Remember that each requirement points to a service; only option B assembles the four correctly.

questions.stem:
An endpoint receives unpredictable bursts of requests that trigger processing. The team wants to absorb the peak without losing requests and process in a serverless, decoupled way.

Which serverless, decoupled architecture meets this?

options.text: CloudFront → static S3 processing the requests
API Gateway → synchronous Lambda directly, with no queue or limit
API Gateway → SQS → Lambda (consuming the queue) → DynamoDB
A single EC2 processing everything immediately, serverless and elastic

questions.explanation: Placing an SQS queue between the entry point (API Gateway) and the processing (Lambda) absorbs bursts without losing requests and decouples the components. Lambda consumes at its own pace and writes to DynamoDB — all serverless and resilient, with a DLQ for problematic messages.

whyNots.A: CloudFront + S3 serves static content — it does not process dynamic requests.
whyNots.B: Synchronous Lambda directly without a queue can hit concurrency limits during the burst and lose requests — it lacks the buffer.
whyNots.D: A single EC2 does not absorb bursts and is not serverless/resilient.

hints: Think about: 'absorb peak without losing + serverless + decoupled' calls for a QUEUE in the middle. API Gateway puts messages in SQS, Lambda consumes at its pace, writes to DynamoDB.
Remember that SQS dampens the burst; if processing fails, the message returns (visibility timeout) or goes to a DLQ.

questions.stem:
You will publish a global static site, with a private origin bucket, protection against SQLi/XSS at the edge, and a custom domain.

Which combination delivers this?
