options.text: S3 + direct access via the bucket URL, which already includes built-in SQLi/XSS filtering
Public S3 + Route 53, without CloudFront — S3 already does global edge caching
EC2 with Nginx in a single region, without CDN or WAF
Private S3 + CloudFront with OAC + WAF on the distribution + Route 53 for the domain

questions.explanation: Private S3 as the origin, CloudFront in front with OAC (bucket only reachable via CloudFront), AWS WAF attached to the distribution to filter SQLi/XSS at layer 7, and Route 53 pointing the domain to the distribution. This is the secure, global static-site pattern.

whyNots.A: Direct access via the bucket URL exposes the origin and has no edge protection.
whyNots.B: Public S3 without CloudFront exposes the origin and has neither CDN nor WAF.
whyNots.C: A single-region EC2 does not deliver global low latency nor the scale/cache of CloudFront.

hints: Think about: global static = CloudFront; private origin = OAC; SQLi/XSS at the edge = WAF; domain = Route 53. Stack all four.
Remember that OAC ensures S3 only responds via CloudFront; WAF attaches to the distribution.

questions.stem:
A global fintech requires RPO and RTO near zero, with low-latency reads on multiple continents and recovery if an entire AWS region fails, using a PostgreSQL-compatible relational database.

Which combination meets the extreme requirement?

options.text: Aurora Global Database (multi-Region) + Route 53 with health checks/failover
Aurora in a single region with Multi-AZ — the synchronous replica covers regional failure
Local DynamoDB with continuous backup — it speaks PostgreSQL natively via PartiQL
RDS Single-AZ + daily snapshots replicated, guaranteeing near-zero RPO

questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database spans multiple Regions with low-latency global reads and cross-region DR (RTO in minutes, fast replication), PostgreSQL-compatible. Route 53 with health checks performs DNS failover between Regions. This is the design for minimum RPO/RTO at global scale.

whyNots.B: Multi-AZ covers AZ failure within one Region, not loss of the entire Region.
whyNots.C: DynamoDB is not PostgreSQL-compatible (it is NoSQL) — it does not meet the relational requirement.
whyNots.D: Single-AZ + daily snapshots has RPO/RTO in hours and does not protect the Region — far from near-zero.

hints: Think about: 'near-zero RPO/RTO + multi-continent + lose the Region + PostgreSQL' = Aurora Global Database, with Route 53 routing between Regions.
Remember that Multi-AZ in a single Region does not protect against losing the whole Region.

questions.stem:
A stateless, interruption-tolerant batch pipeline runs at night over data in S3 and later needs to query the results with ad-hoc SQL, all at the LOWEST cost.

Which combination minimizes cost?

options.text: 3-year Reserved Instances for the nightly batch — RI is the cheapest
Spot Instances for processing + data in S3 + Athena for querying
Dedicated Hosts + always-on EMR — dedicated hardware is more cost-effective
On-Demand instances 24/7 + always-on provisioned Redshift that is cheap

questions.explanation: Spot delivers up to 90% discount for a stateless, interruptible nightly batch; data lives in S3; Athena queries with ad-hoc SQL in a serverless way (pay only for data scanned). Nothing stays provisioned idle — minimum end-to-end cost.

whyNots.A: 3-year RI assumes constant usage; an interruptible nightly batch benefits more from Spot.
whyNots.C: Dedicated Hosts and always-on EMR are the opposite of lowest cost here.
whyNots.D: On-Demand 24/7 and always-on Redshift are expensive for nightly/point usage.

hints: Think about: interruptible batch = Spot (up to 90% off); data in S3; ad-hoc serverless SQL = Athena (pay per data scanned).
Remember that nothing stays idle — Spot only runs when needed, Athena only when queried.

questions.stem:
A company wants to connect its data center to multiple VPCs in AWS with low latency and dedicated bandwidth, have a cheaper automatic backup if the dedicated link fails, and centralize connectivity in a hub.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: CloudFront + Global Accelerator, which already deliver a dedicated link to the data center
Site-to-Site VPN only, without a hub — the VPN over the internet already guarantees dedicated bandwidth
Direct Connect (primary) + Site-to-Site VPN (backup) + Transit Gateway (hub)
VPC Peering between every pair + Internet Gateway closing the link with the data center

questions.explanation: Direct Connect provides the low-latency dedicated link; Site-to-Site VPN serves as a cheaper automatic backup (failover via BGP); Transit Gateway centralizes connectivity between the multiple VPCs and on-premises in a hub. This is the typical resilient hybrid architecture.

whyNots.A: CloudFront and Global Accelerator are for end-users/content, not hybrid data-center connectivity.
whyNots.B: VPN-only does not provide the dedicated bandwidth/low latency of Direct Connect nor a central hub.
whyNots.D: Point-to-point VPC Peering does not scale (mesh) and an Internet Gateway exposes traffic to the internet — it does not privately connect the data center.

hints: Think about: dedicated bandwidth = Direct Connect; cheap automatic backup = VPN; hub for multiple VPCs/on-prem = Transit Gateway.
Remember that this is the classic hybrid pattern — Direct Connect leads, VPN secures the outage, Transit Gateway centralizes.

questions.stem:
Every time an image is uploaded to S3, you need to generate a thumbnail, write metadata to a NoSQL database, and notify several systems — in an event-driven, serverless way.

Which combination implements this event-driven flow?

options.text: API Gateway WebSocket + RDS, with the app notifying the server for every generated thumbnail
Kinesis Data Streams + Redshift, processing uploads as an analytics stream
A cron on an EC2 that scans the bucket every hour looking for new images to process
S3 event → Lambda (generates thumbnail) → writes to DynamoDB → publishes to SNS (fan-out)

questions.explanation: The S3 object-creation event triggers a Lambda function that generates the thumbnail, writes metadata to DynamoDB, and publishes to an SNS topic to notify several systems (fan-out). This is event-driven, serverless, and decoupled — with no periodic scanning.

whyNots.A: WebSocket + RDS is not the pattern for processing S3 uploads in an event-driven way.
whyNots.B: Kinesis/Redshift is for streaming/analytics, not reacting to each upload with thumbnail generation.
whyNots.C: A cron scanning the bucket is inefficient, delayed, costly, and not event-driven.

hints: Think about: 'on every S3 upload' = S3 event triggering Lambda. NoSQL metadata = DynamoDB. Notify many = SNS fan-out.
Remember that everything is serverless and event-driven — no scanning the bucket.

questions.stem:
EC2 instances in a private subnet need to read data from an encrypted S3 bucket, without traffic over the internet, without embedded access keys, and with data encrypted by a managed key.

Which combination meets security and private access?

options.text: IAM Role on the EC2 + SSE-KMS on S3 + Gateway Endpoint for S3

questions.explanation: An IAM Role on the instance delivers temporary credentials (no embedded access key); SSE-KMS encrypts objects with a managed key; the VPC Gateway Endpoint gives private access to S3 without traversing the internet or NAT. This covers secure, private end-to-end access.

whyNots.B: Embedded access keys and public buckets are serious security flaws.
whyNots.C: NAT Gateway sends traffic over the internet (with cost) and an unencrypted bucket fails the requirement.
whyNots.D: A shared user and Internet Gateway violate least privilege and private access.

hints: Think about: no embedded key = IAM Role on EC2; managed encryption = SSE-KMS; no internet = Gateway Endpoint for S3.
Remember that the Gateway Endpoint keeps traffic to S3 private (on the AWS network), without NAT/internet.

questions.stem:
Clickstream events arrive in real time. You want to process some of them immediately with custom logic and also dump the raw stream into an S3 data lake, without managing servers, to query later with SQL.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: CloudFront + S3 static site, which already deliver real-time streaming analytics
Kinesis Data Streams (real-time processing) + Data Firehose (delivery to S3) + Athena (query)
SNS to ingest the stream + continuous delivery Lambda + EBS as the SQL query layer
SQS to ingest the stream + a single EC2 consumer + MySQL for ad-hoc queries

questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams processes the clickstream in real time with custom consumers; Amazon Data Firehose delivers the raw stream to S3 (managed, no code), forming the data lake; Athena queries that data with ad-hoc SQL. This is the classic serverless streaming/analytics pipeline.

whyNots.A: CloudFront + static S3 serves content — it does not process clickstreams in real time.
whyNots.C: SNS + Lambda + EBS does not form the requested streaming + data lake + SQL query pipeline.
whyNots.D: SQS + EC2 + MySQL is not scalable real-time streaming nor a serverless SQL-queryable data lake.

hints: Think about: real-time with custom logic = Kinesis Data Streams; dump raw to S3 without code = Data Firehose; SQL on the data lake = Athena.
Remember that Streams and Firehose can work together — Streams processes, Firehose unloads to S3.

questions.stem:
A news portal has extremely high read traffic: many people reading the same articles and downloading the same images. The relational database is overloaded with SELECTs and distant users complain about slow images.

Which combination improves performance and offloads the database?

options.text: Increase the RDS backup window and size, which speeds up read queries
RDS Multi-AZ with the synchronous standby serving heavy report reads
RDS Read Replicas + ElastiCache (query cache) + CloudFront for statics on S3
Move the database and application to a single larger EC2 instance, eliminating network latency

questions.explanation: Read Replicas distribute RDS read load; ElastiCache caches the most repeated queries, further offloading the database; CloudFront caches static images (on S3) near users, reducing global latency. Each piece attacks a different bottleneck.

whyNots.A: Backup has no effect on production read load.
whyNots.B: The Multi-AZ standby is only for failover — it does NOT serve read traffic.
whyNots.D: A bigger EC2 (scale up) does not solve distributed reads nor global image latency.

hints: Think about: scale database reads = Read Replicas; cache repeated queries = ElastiCache; accelerate global images = CloudFront (over S3).
Watch out — the Multi-AZ standby does NOT serve reads; Read Replica is what scales reads.

questions.stem:
A team accidentally deletes and overwrites objects in S3 and loses data. You want to keep old versions so you can restore them.

Which S3 feature protects against accidental deletion/overwriting?
questions.explanation: Versioning keeps multiple versions of the same object: overwriting creates a new version and deleting creates a delete marker, so you can restore the previous state. It protects against accidental mistakes and is a prerequisite for Replication and Object Lock.

whyNots.A: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance uploads — it does not preserve versions.
whyNots.B: One Zone-IA is a storage class (cost optimization) — it does not keep old versions.
whyNots.C: A Presigned URL grants temporary access to an object — it does not version objects.

hints: Think about: keeping OLD versions of an object = versioning. Overwriting creates a new version; deleting creates a delete marker (you can revert).
Remember that versioning is still a prerequisite for replication and Object Lock.

questions.stem:
Due to DR and compliance requirements, a copy of objects must exist in ANOTHER AWS Region, updated automatically.

Which S3 feature meets this?
questions.explanation: CRR automatically replicates objects to a bucket in another Region — ideal for DR, geographic compliance, and lower-latency access in another Region. It requires versioning on source and destination, and incurs cross-Region transfer cost.

whyNots.B: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads — it does not create a replicated copy in another Region.
whyNots.C: A lifecycle policy changes class/expires objects — it does not replicate across Regions.
whyNots.D: SRR replicates in the SAME Region — it does not meet the other-Region requirement.

hints: Think about: 'automatic copy in ANOTHER Region' = CRR (Cross-Region Replication).
Remember that it requires versioning on source and destination; CRR has cross-Region transfer cost.

questions.stem:
Several application buckets in the SAME Region generate logs, and you want to aggregate them automatically into a central bucket, without cross-Region transfer cost.

Which S3 feature is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: SRR replicates objects to a bucket in the same Region, with no cross-Region transfer cost — perfect for aggregating logs from several buckets into a central one, replicating prod→test, or meeting same-Region data residency.

whyNots.A: Object Lock is WORM/immutability — it does not aggregate/replicate logs.
whyNots.C: CRR is cross-Region and would incur unnecessary cross-Region transfer cost here.
whyNots.D: A Presigned URL is temporary object access — it does not replicate buckets.

hints: Think about: same Region + aggregate logs + no cross-Region cost = SRR (Same-Region Replication).
Remember that CRR would also work, but would pay cross-Region transfer unnecessarily — everything here is in the same Region.

questions.stem:
You tried to enable S3 replication and it does not work. A basic prerequisite is missing on the buckets.

What is REQUIRED for replication (CRR or SRR) to work?

options.text: Versioning enabled on source AND destination
Using the Glacier Deep Archive storage class

questions.explanation: S3 replication (CRR or SRR) requires versioning enabled on both the source and the destination. It is the basic prerequisite — without it, replication cannot be configured.

whyNots.A: Public buckets are not a replication requirement (and would be a security risk).
whyNots.B: Transfer Acceleration is independent — it does not enable replication.
whyNots.D: Storage class is not a prerequisite for replication.

hints: Think about: replication only works with VERSIONING enabled on both buckets (source and destination).
Remember that without versioning, S3 cannot track/replicate object versions.

questions.stem:
A regulation requires that certain records CANNOT be altered or deleted by ANYONE (not even the root account) during a defined period.

Which S3 feature guarantees this immutability?
questions.explanation: Object Lock applies the WORM model. In Compliance mode, no identity — not even the root account — can alter or delete the object version until the retention period expires. This is the immutability control for regulatory compliance. (Requires versioning.)

whyNots.A: A read bucket policy controls access, but does not prevent an admin with permission from deleting the object.
whyNots.B: Standard-IA is a cost class — it does not guarantee immutability.
whyNots.C: Versioning helps revert, but does not prevent permanent deletion by someone with permission — it is not WORM.

hints: Think about: 'no one, not even root, can delete during the period' = Object Lock in Compliance mode (WORM).
Remember that in Governance mode, users with special permission could bypass; in Compliance mode, they cannot.

questions.stem:
In Object Lock, distinguish: (1) lock the object for a FIXED period of time; (2) lock the object WITHOUT a defined deadline, until someone manually removes the lock (for example, during legal proceedings).

Which pair of mechanisms corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: In Object Lock, the retention period locks the version for a fixed period of time; the legal hold locks it without a defined deadline, lasting until manually removed (useful in litigation/investigations). An object can have one, the other, or both.

whyNots.B: Versioning and lifecycle are not Object Lock locking mechanisms.
whyNots.C: Governance/Compliance are retention MODES (who can bypass), not the fixed-period vs. indefinite mechanisms.
whyNots.D: Reversed: fixed period is retention period; no deadline is legal hold.

hints: Think about: fixed deadline = retention period; NO deadline, until manually removed = legal hold (like 'frozen by court order').
Remember that an object can have retention, legal hold, or both at the same time.

questions.stem:
Users around the world upload large files to an S3 bucket in a distant region, and uploads are slow and variable over the public internet.

Which S3 feature accelerates these long-distance uploads?
questions.explanation: S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest edge location and the AWS backbone network (instead of the variable public internet), accelerating long-distance transfers of large objects by 50–500%. It is the solution for global users uploading to a distant bucket.

whyNots.A: Versioning preserves versions — it does not speed up transfers.
whyNots.C: Standard-IA is a cost storage class — it does not speed up uploads.
whyNots.D: Object Lock is WORM immutability — it has no effect on upload speed.

hints: A slow global upload to a distant bucket points to Transfer Acceleration, which uses AWS edge locations and the AWS backbone network.
It logically shortens the distance to S3 and works well with multipart upload for large files.

questions.stem:
You want to allow an external user to upload ONE specific file to your bucket for a limited time, WITHOUT giving them AWS credentials or permissions.

Which S3 feature provides this temporary access?

options.text: Create an IAM user for them

questions.explanation: A presigned URL grants temporary permission to download or upload a specific object without the third party having AWS credentials or permissions. The generator signs it with their own credentials; the URL expires (1 minute–12 hours in the console, up to 7 days via SDK/CLI).

whyNots.A: Creating an IAM user for a one-off upload is excessive and goes against the practice of temporary credentials.
whyNots.B: Making the bucket public is a security risk and does not limit access to the specific file or time window.
whyNots.D: Object Lock is immutability — it does not grant temporary upload access.

hints: Uploading one file for a limited time without handing out credentials means a presigned URL.
You sign the URL with your own credentials; the third party just uses the link, which expires (up to 7 days via SDK/CLI).

questions.stem:
You configured S3 event notifications to send to an SQS queue, but you chose a FIFO queue and the configuration fails.

What is the correct explanation?

options.text: You forgot to enable Transfer Acceleration on the bucket, a prerequisite for event notifications
S3 cannot send events to SQS at all — notifications only work with SNS and Lambda
S3 events only go to EC2 instances registered as consumers in the bucket
S3 event notifications do NOT support SQS FIFO as a direct destination (SQS standard, SNS, Lambda, or EventBridge)

questions.explanation: S3 event notifications publish to Lambda, SNS, SQS, and Amazon EventBridge — but SQS FIFO queues are NOT supported as a direct destination, only SQS standard. That is why the FIFO configuration fails; use a standard queue, or route via EventBridge if you truly need a FIFO queue at the end of the path.

whyNots.A: Transfer Acceleration is about upload speed — unrelated to event-notification destination.
whyNots.B: S3 does send events to SQS — as long as it is a standard queue.
whyNots.C: S3 events go to Lambda/SNS/SQS/EventBridge, not 'only to EC2'.

hints: Destinations for event notifications can be SQS standard, SNS, Lambda, or EventBridge; SQS FIFO directly is NOT supported.
Switch the queue to standard and it works (or route through EventBridge if you truly need a FIFO queue at the end).

questions.stem:
Four S3 needs: (1) restore an object deleted by mistake; (2) automatic copy to another region for DR; (3) records that must be immutable by law; (4) fast global upload to a distant bucket.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Versioning → CRR → Object Lock → Transfer Acceleration
Object Lock → Transfer Acceleration → Versioning → CRR
CRR → Versioning → Transfer Acceleration → Object Lock
Transfer Acceleration → Object Lock → CRR → Versioning

questions.explanation: Each feature solves one case: versioning (restore deleted objects), Cross-Region Replication (automatic copy to another region for DR), Object Lock (WORM immutability required by law), and Transfer Acceleration (fast global uploads to a distant bucket). Option A matches all four.

whyNots.B: It shuffles everything — Object Lock does not restore deleted objects.
whyNots.C: It swaps versioning with CRR and Object Lock with Transfer Acceleration.
whyNots.D: It completely reverses the order; no position matches the correct role.

hints: Restore = versioning; cross-region copy for DR = CRR; legally immutable = Object Lock; fast global upload = Transfer Acceleration.
Only option A keeps each feature in its correct role.

questions.stem:
A team has an application that uses MongoDB and stores flexible JSON documents (user profiles and preferences). They want to migrate to a compatible managed service without administering the infrastructure.

Which AWS database is recommended?

options.text: Amazon Neptune, the AWS JSON database
Amazon RDS for MySQL storing the JSON

questions.explanation: DocumentDB is AWS's managed document database, compatible with MongoDB (JSON/BSON). It is the choice for migrating MongoDB workloads and storing flexible documents (profiles, preferences, catalogs) without managing the infrastructure.

whyNots.A: Neptune is a graph database (relationships), not a document store.
whyNots.C: Redshift is an analytical data warehouse — not a transactional document database.
whyNots.D: RDS for MySQL is relational — it is not MongoDB-compatible nor suited to flexible documents.

hints: JSON documents + MongoDB-compatible + managed = DocumentDB.
'Document' is in the name. It is AWS's document database.

questions.stem:
A social network needs to query complex relationships ('friends of friends', who knows whom) and feed a recommendation engine over highly connected data.

Which database is ideal for this graph data?
questions.explanation: Neptune is the managed graph database: it models entities as nodes and relationships as edges, querying highly connected relationships within seconds. It is ideal for social networks, recommendation engines, fraud detection, and knowledge graphs.

whyNots.A: Timestream is for time-series data — it does not model relationships.
whyNots.B: DocumentDB is a document database — it is not optimized for traversing graph relationships.
whyNots.D: A relational RDS would require expensive JOINs for deep graph queries; the native graph database is Neptune.

hints: Complex relationships, friends of friends, recommendations = graph = Neptune (nodes + edges).
Graph databases also excel at fraud detection and knowledge graphs.

questions.stem:
A company wants to migrate Apache Cassandra (CQL) workloads to the cloud in a managed, serverless way, with automatic scaling and extremely high read/write throughput.

Which service fits?
questions.explanation: Amazon Keyspaces is the managed, serverless Apache Cassandra-compatible service (CQL), with automatic scaling and virtually unlimited throughput. It is the choice for migrating Cassandra workloads without managing clusters.

whyNots.A: Neptune is a graph database — not Cassandra/wide-column.
whyNots.B: Aurora is relational (MySQL/PostgreSQL) — not compatible with CQL/Cassandra.
whyNots.C: DocumentDB is a document database (MongoDB), not Cassandra.

hints: Managed, serverless Cassandra/CQL = Amazon Keyspaces.
'for Apache Cassandra' is in the name — wide-column store at massive scale.

questions.stem:
Millions of IoT sensors send time-stamped readings (temperature, vibration) continuously, and you need to store and analyze this telemetry efficiently over time intervals.

Which database is optimized for this time-series data?
questions.explanation: Timestream is AWS's serverless time-series database, optimized to store and analyze time-indexed data (IoT sensors, telemetry, application metrics, monitoring) — up to ~1,000x faster than a relational database for this pattern.

whyNots.B: Neptune is a graph database — not a time-series store.
whyNots.C: RDS PostgreSQL, as a relational database, does not match Timestream's efficiency for trillions of time-indexed events.
whyNots.D: DocumentDB is a document database — not optimized for large-scale interval-based queries.

hints: Time-stamped data (IoT, telemetry, metrics) = time series = Timestream.
It is optimized for interval-based queries, much faster than a relational database for this pattern.

questions.stem:
Microservices need microsecond reads and sub-millisecond writes AS A PRIMARY DATABASE, with durability (they cannot lose data), Redis-compatible — without having to maintain a separate cache and database.

Which service fits?
questions.explanation: MemoryDB is a durable, Redis-compatible in-memory database, with microsecond reads, sub-millisecond writes, and Multi-AZ durability. It can act as a PRIMARY DATABASE, eliminating the need to maintain a separate cache and durable database.

whyNots.A: S3 is object storage, not a low-latency in-memory database.
whyNots.C: RDS is a disk-based relational database — it does not deliver microsecond in-memory performance.
whyNots.D: ElastiCache is a cache — data can be lost; it cannot serve as a durable primary database.

hints: In-memory + durable + Redis-compatible + PRIMARY DATABASE = MemoryDB.
ElastiCache is a cache (data can be lost); MemoryDB is durable (Multi-AZ) and can serve as the primary store.

questions.stem:
Two situations: (1) speed up reads in front of an RDS, accepting that the cache can be lost on failure; (2) have an in-memory database that is the primary source of data and cannot lose it.

Which pair matches (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: ElastiCache is the in-memory cache (data can be lost, sits in front of a database to speed up reads). MemoryDB is the DURABLE in-memory database (Multi-AZ), used as a primary source that cannot lose data. The distinction 'cache vs durable' is the key.

whyNots.A: DynamoDB is not in-memory; case (2) asks for a durable in-memory database (MemoryDB).
whyNots.B: Reversed: the durable primary is MemoryDB, not ElastiCache.
whyNots.D: RDS is disk-based, not the durable in-memory database requested in (2).

hints: A disposable cache in front of a database = ElastiCache; a durable, primary in-memory database = MemoryDB.
The clue is 'accepts losing it' (cache = ElastiCache) vs 'cannot lose it' (durable = MemoryDB).

questions.stem:
A bank wants to detect fraud by analyzing, in near real time, connection patterns among accounts, devices, and transactions (fraud rings).

Which database is most suitable for modeling and querying these connections?
questions.explanation: Fraud detection based on relationships (fraud rings among accounts, devices, and transactions) is a classic graph database use case. Neptune models these connections as nodes and edges and traverses them quickly.

whyNots.A: Keyspaces is a wide-column (Cassandra) store — not a graph database.
whyNots.B: Redshift is an analytical data warehouse — it does not traverse graph relationships in near real time.
whyNots.C: Timestream is a time-series database — it does not model graph relationships.

hints: Connection patterns / fraud rings = relationships = graph = Neptune.
Fraud detection is a classic graph database use case.

questions.stem:
When choosing a managed NoSQL database, the team is weighing a general-purpose serverless key-value/document store with massive scale against a document database compatible with the MongoDB API.

Which association is correct?

options.text: General-purpose serverless key-value/document = DynamoDB; MongoDB-compatible = DocumentDB
DynamoDB and DocumentDB are both MongoDB API-compatible; only the price differs
DynamoDB and DocumentDB are both managed relational databases, with SQL and full ACID transactions
MongoDB-compatible = DynamoDB; general-purpose serverless key-value = DocumentDB

questions.explanation: DynamoDB is AWS's general-purpose serverless key-value/document NoSQL database (with its own API and massive scale). DocumentDB is the MongoDB API-compatible document database. The choice depends on whether MongoDB compatibility is required.

whyNots.B: DynamoDB is not MongoDB-compatible; it has its own API.
whyNots.C: Both are NoSQL databases, not relational.
whyNots.D: Reversed — the MongoDB-compatible one is DocumentDB, not DynamoDB.

hints: DynamoDB = AWS's serverless key-value/document NoSQL database (own API). DocumentDB = MongoDB API-compatible.
If the requirement is 'MongoDB-compatible', it is DocumentDB; if it is a general-purpose managed NoSQL database with massive scale, it is DynamoDB.

questions.stem:
A monitoring platform collects usage and application health metrics over time (latency per minute, errors per hour) for dashboards and temporal analysis.

Which purpose-built database fits?
questions.explanation: Metrics indexed by time (latency per minute, errors per hour) are time-series data. Timestream is the purpose-built database for this, with efficient storage and interval-based querying — ideal for application monitoring and temporal dashboards.

whyNots.A: Keyspaces is a more general-purpose wide-column store; the purpose-built choice for time data is Timestream.
whyNots.C: DocumentDB is a document database — not optimized for time series.
whyNots.D: Neptune is a graph database — not a time-series store.

hints: Metrics 'over time' (per minute/hour) = time series = Timestream.
Application/usage monitoring and telemetry are direct use cases for Timestream.

questions.stem:
Four workloads: (1) MongoDB-style JSON documents; (2) recommendation/graph relationships; (3) IoT telemetry over time; (4) durable Redis-compatible in-memory database.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each database serves a model: DocumentDB (JSON/MongoDB documents), Neptune (graph/relationships), Timestream (time-series/IoT), and MemoryDB (durable Redis-compatible in-memory). Option C matches all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps DocumentDB with Neptune and Timestream with MemoryDB.
whyNots.B: Completely reverses the order; no position matches the correct model.
whyNots.D: Shuffles everything — Timestream is not a document database.

hints: Documents = DocumentDB; graph = Neptune; time series = Timestream; durable in-memory = MemoryDB.
Only option C keeps each database matched to its data model.

questions.stem:
On the exam, you must distinguish the isolated geographic area (for example, an AWS Region) from the isolated data centers within it.

Which association is correct?

options.text: Region and AZ are practically the same thing: two names for the same physical set of data centers
Region = a single specific data center; AZ = an entire continent with several regions inside
AZ = the broad geographic area; Region = an isolated rack of servers inside the data center
Region = geographic area; Availability Zone (AZ) = one or more isolated data centers within the region

questions.explanation: A Region is an isolated geographic area (for example, sa-east-1). Each Region has multiple Availability Zones (AZs), which are one or more isolated data centers (with independent power/network). Distributing across AZs provides resiliency within the region.

whyNots.A: They are different concepts — a region contains multiple AZs.
whyNots.B: A region is not a single data center, and an AZ is not a continent.
whyNots.C: It reverses everything — the geographic area is the region, not the AZ.

hints: A Region is the 'place on the map' (for example, us-east-1); an AZ is one or more isolated data centers within that region.
A region has multiple AZs — that is what enables high availability within it.

questions.stem:
You want an application to survive the failure of a data center, staying online within the same region and with low latency between components.

What is the recommended practice?

options.text: Distribute resources across multiple Availability Zones in the same region
Put everything in an edge location — they host the app close to the end user
Put everything in a single AZ — the AZ already replicates everything internally
Use a region with a single large instance — AWS handles its failover

questions.explanation: Distributing resources across multiple AZs (multi-AZ) in the same region is the high-availability practice: if one AZ (data center) fails, the others keep serving, and latency between AZs is low. It underpins resilient designs such as RDS Multi-AZ and ASG multi-AZ.

whyNots.B: Edge locations are CDN/cache points, not where you host a resilient application.
whyNots.C: Everything in a single AZ creates a single point of failure — if it fails, the app fails.
whyNots.D: A single instance in a region has no redundancy.

hints: Surviving the loss of a data center within the region means spreading across multiple AZs (multi-AZ).
AZs are isolated but close together — high availability with low latency.

questions.stem:
An application needs single-digit millisecond latency for users in a large city, closer than the nearest AWS Region can deliver.

Which resource extends AWS infrastructure close to those users?

options.text: A second region on the other side of the world
More Availability Zones in the same distant region

questions.explanation: AWS Local Zones extend an AWS Region close to large metropolitan areas, delivering compute and storage with single-digit-millisecond latency for local users — useful for gaming, streaming, and latency-sensitive workloads.

whyNots.A: A bucket policy is an S3 permission — unrelated to geographic latency.
whyNots.C: A distant region would increase latency, not reduce it.
whyNots.D: More AZs in a distant region do not move infrastructure closer to local users.

hints: Extending AWS close to a large city with single-digit-ms latency means Local Zones.
They bring compute and storage closer to users than the region would.

questions.stem:
In the shared responsibility model, you must know what is AWS's responsibility and what is the customer's.

What is AWS's responsibility ('security OF the cloud')?

options.text: Configuring the customer's IAM permissions — AWS defines who accesses what
Applying patches to the guest operating system of the customer's EC2 every month
Protecting the physical infrastructure: hardware, underlying software, network, and facilities
Encrypting the customer's application data automatically and by default

questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for 'security OF the cloud': the physical infrastructure that runs services — hardware, underlying software, network, and facilities (data centers). The customer handles 'security IN the cloud' (data, IAM, encryption, and, for IaaS, the guest OS).

whyNots.A: Configuring IAM is the CUSTOMER's responsibility.
whyNots.B: Patching the guest OS of EC2 is the CUSTOMER's responsibility (IaaS).
whyNots.D: Encrypting application data is the CUSTOMER's responsibility.

hints: AWS handles security OF the cloud (the physical base: hardware, facilities, network). The customer handles security IN the cloud.
IAM, data encryption, and guest OS patching are the CUSTOMER's responsibility.

questions.stem:
An EC2 instance is running an outdated operating system with vulnerabilities. Who is responsible for patching the guest OS?

Whose responsibility is this?

options.text: The customer (security IN the cloud, for IaaS)

questions.explanation: For IaaS services such as EC2, patching the guest operating system is the CUSTOMER's responsibility (security IN the cloud), along with the application, data, and security group configuration. AWS manages the physical/hypervisor layer below it.

whyNots.A: EC2 does not update the guest OS by itself.
whyNots.B: The internet service provider has nothing to do with OS patching.
whyNots.C: AWS does not patch the guest OS of a customer's EC2 instance — that is the customer's responsibility.

hints: For IaaS (EC2), the guest OS is the CUSTOMER's responsibility — patching, hardening, and security group configuration are yours.
AWS handles the hardware/hypervisor; the guest OS and above (on EC2) is the customer's.

questions.stem:
For a managed/abstracted service such as S3, the responsibility split differs from EC2.

In S3, what remains the CUSTOMER's responsibility?

options.text: Managing the data: classifying it, defining encryption, and controlling access via IAM/policies
Operating the physical network between AWS data centers, including the links between AZs
Maintaining and replacing the physical storage hardware in the data centers where S3 runs
Applying security patches to the operating system of the servers that run S3

questions.explanation: For abstracted services such as S3, AWS operates the infrastructure and the operating system. The customer remains responsible for managing their DATA: classifying it, choosing encryption options, and controlling access with IAM and bucket policies. The responsibility split varies by service type.

whyNots.B: The physical network is AWS's responsibility.
whyNots.C: Data-center hardware is AWS's responsibility.
whyNots.D: For S3, patching the server OS is AWS's responsibility — not the customer's.

hints: For an abstracted service (S3, DynamoDB), AWS operates the infrastructure AND the OS. The customer handles the DATA: classification, encryption, and permissions.
Responsibility varies by service type — with IaaS the customer manages more; with abstracted services, only data/access.

questions.stem:
The AWS Well-Architected Framework organizes best practices into pillars. A team is confused about what they are.

Which of these is one of the six pillars?
questions.explanation: The six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework are: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability. Sustainability is the sixth, added in 2021.

whyNots.A: Marketing is not a pillar of the framework.
whyNots.C: Accounting is not a pillar; the finance-related pillar is 'cost optimization'.
whyNots.D: Gamification is not a pillar (it is just this game's theme!).

hints: The six pillars are operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability.
Sustainability was the sixth pillar, added in 2021.

questions.stem:
A company has several AWS accounts in an Organization and wants a single bill, plus the ability to share volume discounts, Reserved Instances, and Savings Plans across accounts.

Which feature delivers this at no additional cost?

options.text: Trusted Advisor, which unifies the Organization accounts' bill
Cost Explorer alone, which already allocates discounts across accounts
Create one giant single account and migrate everything, as AWS recommends

questions.explanation: AWS Organizations consolidated billing provides a single bill (the management account pays) and combines usage from all accounts, sharing volume discounts, Reserved Instances, and Savings Plans — usually lowering the total cost. It is offered at no additional cost.

whyNots.A: Trusted Advisor provides recommendations — it does not consolidate billing or share discounts.
whyNots.B: Cost Explorer analyzes/visualizes costs — it is not the consolidated billing mechanism that shares discounts.
whyNots.D: Migrating everything to one giant account is risky and loses account isolation — it is not the solution.

hints: Single bill + sharing volume/RI/Savings Plan discounts across accounts = consolidated billing (Organizations).
It is offered at no additional cost, and the management account pays the bill for all accounts.

questions.stem:
A user asks what AWS 'edge locations' (points of presence) are.

What are edge locations?

options.text: EC2 instance types optimized for delivering content near end users
Regional data centers where you host your primary relational databases and critical workloads
Private subnets inside a VPC, replicated by AWS at each global point of presence
AWS network points close to users, used by services such as CloudFront and Global Accelerator

questions.explanation: Edge locations (points of presence/PoPs) are sites in the global AWS network, close to users, used by edge services such as CloudFront (content caching) and Global Accelerator (traffic ingress). They are far more numerous than Regions.

whyNots.A: Edge locations are not EC2 instance types.
whyNots.B: You do not host primary databases in edge locations — that happens in Regions/AZs.
whyNots.C: Subnets live inside a VPC in a Region — they are not edge locations.

hints: Edge location = point of presence (PoP) close to the user, used by CDN (CloudFront) and Global Accelerator.
It is not where you host the app — it is the 'edge' that accelerates traffic delivery/ingress.

questions.stem:
Four items: (1) isolated geographic area; (2) isolated data center(s) within it; (3) point of presence near the user; (4) AWS responsibility in the shared model.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Region → Availability Zone → Edge location → Security OF the cloud (physical infrastructure)
Edge location → Region → Availability Zone → Security IN the cloud
Region → Edge location → Availability Zone → Security IN the cloud
Availability Zone → Region → Security OF the cloud → Edge location

questions.explanation: A Region is the geographic area; an Availability Zone is the isolated data center(s) within it; an Edge location is the point of presence near the user; and 'security OF the cloud' (physical infrastructure) is AWS's responsibility in the shared model. Option A matches all four.

whyNots.B: Starts with edge location as the geographic area — wrong.
whyNots.C: Swaps AZ with edge location and assigns AWS's responsibility to the customer.
whyNots.D: Swaps Region with AZ and scrambles the rest.

hints: Geographic area = Region; isolated data centers = AZ; near the user = Edge location; AWS responsibility = security OF the cloud (infrastructure).
Only option A keeps each concept in place.

questions.stem:
A process needs to run for about 40 minutes nonstop. The team considered using a Lambda function.

What is the limitation and the correct alternative?

options.text: Just increase the function memory: above 10 GB the timeout limit disappears
Lambda has a maximum timeout of 15 minutes; for 40 minutes use Fargate/ECS, Step Functions, or Batch
Lambda only runs for 1 minute at most, so even 5-minute tasks are impossible
Lambda runs indefinitely as long as reserved concurrency is configured

questions.explanation: A Lambda invocation's maximum timeout is 15 minutes (900 s). A 40-minute process does not fit — the alternative is a long-running container (Fargate/ECS), AWS Batch, or breaking the work into steps with Step Functions.

whyNots.A: Increasing memory improves CPU but does not remove the 15-minute limit.
whyNots.C: It is not 1 minute — the maximum is 15 minutes.
whyNots.D: Lambda does NOT run indefinitely — the ceiling is 15 minutes.

hints: Lambda has a 15-minute ceiling per invocation. 40 minutes does not fit — use a container (Fargate/ECS) or orchestration (Step Functions).
Lambda is for short, event-driven tasks, not long-running processes.

questions.stem:
A latency-sensitive web API suffers from the delay of the FIRST invocation (cold start) when the function was idle, hurting the user experience.

What eliminates the cold start while keeping environments ready?
questions.explanation: Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a defined number of execution environments, keeping them ready before invocation — eliminating the cold start and delivering responses in tens of ms. It is ideal for latency-sensitive interactive workloads (web/mobile APIs).

whyNots.A: Reducing memory can even hurt performance; it does not solve cold start.
whyNots.B: Reserved concurrency reserves/limits concurrent capacity but does not pre-warm environments — the cold start remains.
whyNots.D: Timeout is the maximum execution time — it has nothing to do with cold start.

hints: 'Eliminate cold start, pre-initialized environments' = provisioned concurrency (responses in tens of ms).
Reserved concurrency reserves capacity but does NOT pre-warm environments (it does not remove the cold start).

questions.stem:
A critical function must ALWAYS have guaranteed concurrent capacity, without being 'starved' by other functions in the account that fire at the same time.

Which resource guarantees this exclusive concurrency pool?
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency reserves an exclusive pool of concurrent executions for a function — ensuring it always has capacity and that other functions cannot consume that pool. It can also be used to throttle (limit) a function and protect the account quota.

whyNots.A: /tmp is ephemeral storage — unrelated to guaranteed concurrency.
whyNots.B: Provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments (latency), but what GUARANTEES/isolates the concurrency pool is reserved concurrency (they can be combined).
whyNots.C: Layers package dependencies — they do not manage concurrency.

hints: Reserving a concurrency ceiling just for that function (so no one else uses it) = reserved concurrency.
It can also LIMIT a function and protect the rest of the account from exhausting concurrency.

questions.stem:
A function is invoked asynchronously by S3 events. Sometimes it fails during processing, and you do not want to lose those events — you want to capture them for investigation/reprocessing.

Which resource captures failed asynchronous invocation events?
questions.explanation: For asynchronous invocations (S3, SNS, EventBridge), Lambda performs automatic retries and, if it still fails, can send the event to a Dead-Letter Queue (SQS or SNS) — capturing failures for analysis/reprocessing without losing the event. (Lambda Destinations also route success/failure.)

whyNots.B: Increasing timeout does not prevent losing events that failed.
whyNots.C: Multi-AZ is infrastructure resilience — it does not capture failed Lambda events.
whyNots.D: Provisioned concurrency reduces cold start — it does not capture failures.

hints: A failed asynchronous invocation (after retries) goes to a DLQ (SQS or SNS) so it is not lost.
S3/SNS/EventBridge invoke Lambda asynchronously — that is why a DLQ makes sense here.

questions.stem:
You want a Lambda function to process messages from an SQS queue in batches, with Lambda polling the queue automatically.

Which mechanism connects the SQS queue to Lambda this way?

options.text: A signed URL pointing the SQS queue directly at the function
Event source mapping (Lambda polls the queue in batches)
Provisioned concurrency, which already includes queue polling
A synchronous invocation via API Gateway reading the queue in batches

questions.explanation: For poll-based sources (SQS, Kinesis Data Streams, DynamoDB Streams), Lambda uses an event source mapping: it polls the source automatically and invokes the function with batches of records. This is the poll-based integration model.

whyNots.A: A signed URL is for accessing an object in S3/CloudFront — unrelated to consuming a queue.
whyNots.C: Provisioned concurrency handles latency/cold start — it does not connect the queue to Lambda.
whyNots.D: API Gateway is synchronous (request/response) invocation — not polling an SQS queue.

hints: For SQS, Kinesis, and DynamoDB Streams, Lambda uses event source mapping — it POLLs and invokes in batches.
Unlike S3/SNS (asynchronous push), here Lambda PULLs from the source.

questions.stem:
Several Lambda functions share the same heavy libraries, and each function's deployment package is becoming large and repetitive.

Which resource lets you share dependencies across functions and reduce package size?
questions.explanation: Lambda Layers package libraries, dependencies, or custom runtimes separately from the function code and can be shared across multiple functions. They reduce the deployment package size and centralize common dependencies.

whyNots.A: Reserved concurrency manages concurrency — it does not share dependencies.
whyNots.B: Transfer Acceleration speeds up upload to S3 — it is not a Lambda feature.
whyNots.D: DLQ captures failures — unrelated to package size/dependencies.

hints: Packaging libraries/dependencies separately and sharing them across functions = Lambda Layers.
It reduces the deployment package size of each function and centralizes common dependencies.

questions.stem:
A Lambda function has insufficient CPU and is slow. You notice that in Lambda CPU is allocated proportionally to another parameter.

How do you increase the CPU available to the function?

options.text: Reduce the number of layers — each layer reserves a slice of CPU
Add a DLQ, which frees CPU by removing failures from the path
Increase the timeout — CPU is allocated proportionally to the time limit
Increase the configured memory (CPU scales along with memory)

questions.explanation: In Lambda, CPU and network bandwidth are allocated proportionally to the configured memory (up to 10,240 MB). To get more CPU, increase the memory — which often reduces execution time and even total cost.

whyNots.A: Reducing layers does not increase the available CPU.
whyNots.B: A DLQ handles failures — it does not affect CPU.
whyNots.C: Timeout is the maximum allowed time — it does not change the allocated CPU.

hints: Remember that in Lambda you do not choose vCPU directly — CPU (and network) grows proportionally to the MEMORY you configure.
Sometimes increasing memory makes the function faster AND cheaper (it runs for less time).

questions.stem:
A Lambda function needs to access an RDS database that is in a PRIVATE subnet of the VPC, without exposing the database to the internet.

How do you enable this access?

options.text: Configure the Lambda function in the VPC (subnets/security group) to reach the private RDS
Generate a signed URL from CloudFront pointing directly to the private RDS endpoint
Make the RDS public on the internet, allowing 0.0.0.0/0 in the database security group
It is not possible for a Lambda function to access resources inside a VPC; use EC2 instead

questions.explanation: To access private resources such as RDS in a private subnet, configure the Lambda function in the VPC (providing subnets and security group). The function gets ENIs in those subnets and reaches the database over the private network, without exposing RDS to the internet.

whyNots.B: Signed URLs are for S3/CloudFront — they do not apply to RDS access.
whyNots.C: Making RDS public is a security risk and unnecessary.
whyNots.D: It is indeed possible — just configure the function in the VPC.

hints: To reach a private resource (RDS) in the VPC, configure the Lambda function INSIDE the VPC (subnets + security group).
That way the function gets network interfaces in those subnets and talks to the database without exposing it to the internet.

questions.stem:
A function has stable load during the week and predictable spikes on weekends. The team wants low latency on the weekly baseline and still absorb the spikes without 'stealing' concurrency from other functions.

Which combination makes sense?

options.text: Only increase the function timeout, which already eliminates cold starts and absorbs any spike
Provisioned concurrency for the weekly baseline + reserved concurrency to isolate/absorb the spike
Only add Lambda Layers, which speed up initialization and control concurrency
Turn the function off on weekends and back on Monday, avoiding the cost of the spike

questions.explanation: The two combine: provisioned concurrency keeps pre-warmed environments for the weekly baseline (no cold start, low latency), and reserved concurrency guarantees/isolates a concurrency pool to absorb weekend spikes without competing with other functions in the account.

whyNots.A: Timeout does not address cold-start latency or concurrency.
whyNots.C: Layers handle dependencies — not latency or concurrency.
whyNots.D: Turning off on weekends is exactly when the spike occurs — the opposite of what is needed.

hints: You can use both together — provisioned (no cold start on the baseline) + reserved (guarantees/isolates the pool for the spike).
Provisioned handles latency; reserved handles guaranteeing/limiting concurrency.

questions.stem:
Four Lambda needs: (1) eliminate cold start for an interactive API; (2) guarantee/limit the concurrency pool of a function; (3) share libraries across functions; (4) capture asynchronous events that failed.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Reserved concurrency → Provisioned concurrency → DLQ → Layers
DLQ → Layers → Reserved concurrency → Provisioned concurrency
Provisioned concurrency → Reserved concurrency → Layers → DLQ
Layers → DLQ → Provisioned concurrency → Reserved concurrency

questions.explanation: Each resource solves one problem: provisioned concurrency (eliminates cold start), reserved concurrency (guarantees/limits the concurrency pool), Layers (share libraries), and DLQ (captures asynchronous events that failed). Option C respects all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps provisioned with reserved and DLQ with Layers.
whyNots.B: Completely reverses; no position matches the right function.
whyNots.D: Shuffles everything — Layers do not eliminate cold starts.

hints: Cold start = provisioned; guarantee/limit concurrency = reserved; share libraries = layers; capture async failure = DLQ.
Only option C keeps each resource in its correct role.

questions.stem:
On the exam: what exactly makes a subnet 'public'?

Which statement is correct?

options.text: The subnet has a 'public' attribute set in the console, independent of routes
The subnet is in a region, not an AZ — and that is what makes it public
It is enough for the instance to have a public IP — with it traffic already reaches the internet
The subnet's route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 route pointing to an Internet Gateway

questions.explanation: A subnet is public when its route table contains a route (0.0.0.0/0) pointing to an Internet Gateway. It is the route to the IGW that defines the subnet as public — not an isolated attribute nor just the instance's public IP.

whyNots.A: There is no 'public' attribute that ignores routes — the route to the IGW is what counts.
whyNots.B: A subnet is in an AZ; that has nothing to do with being public or private.
whyNots.C: Without a route to the IGW, even with a public IP the instance cannot reach the internet.

hints: What makes a subnet public is the ROUTE to the Internet Gateway in the route table — not a magic button.
Without the route to the IGW, not even a public IP helps — the subnet is private.

questions.stem:
You want a database in a subnet to NOT be reachable from the internet at all.

How do you ensure the subnet is private?

options.text: Do not have a route to the Internet Gateway in the subnet's route table
Add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the IGW, which isolates the subnet
Place the subnet in another region, far from the internet
Give each instance a public IP, just for internal use

questions.explanation: A subnet is private when its route table does NOT have a route to the Internet Gateway. Without that path, instances do not communicate directly with the internet (even with a public IP). For controlled outbound access, use a NAT Gateway.

whyNots.B: Adding a route to the IGW would make the subnet public — the opposite of the request.
whyNots.C: Changing regions does not make a subnet private; what matters is the absence of a route to the IGW.
whyNots.D: A public IP without a route to the IGW does not provide internet access — and the goal is precisely NOT to expose.

hints: Private = NO route to the IGW. Without that route, there is no path to/from the internet.
If outbound access is needed for updates, use NAT (outbound yes, inbound no).

questions.stem:
Instances in a public subnet need a component that gives them the path to the internet and performs public IPv4 translation.

Which VPC component is this?
questions.explanation: The Internet Gateway (IGW) gives public subnets the path to the internet and performs address translation (NAT) for the public IPv4 of instances. It is the target of the 0.0.0.0/0 route in a public route table. There is one IGW per VPC.

whyNots.A: Security Group is an instance firewall — not the internet gateway.
whyNots.C: VPC Peering connects two VPCs to each other — it does not provide internet access.
whyNots.D: NAT Gateway gives outbound access to PRIVATE instances; it itself depends on an IGW in the public subnet.

hints: The gateway to the internet for the VPC is the Internet Gateway. It is the target of the 0.0.0.0/0 route in public subnets.
One IGW per VPC; it performs NAT for the public IPv4 of instances.

questions.stem:
A route table has several routes that match a packet's destination. You need to know which one the VPC router uses.

How does the VPC decide which route to apply?

options.text: The first route in the list wins (creation order)
The least specific route wins (shortest prefix)
The most specific route (longest prefix match) wins

questions.explanation: The VPC routes by destination using longest prefix match: among the matching routes, the most specific (longest prefix) is chosen. That is why a /24 route beats 0.0.0.0/0 for a destination that fits in the /24. The VPC's 'local' route always exists for internal traffic.

whyNots.A: It is not by order in the list — it is by prefix specificity.
whyNots.B: It is the opposite — the MOST specific wins, not the least.
whyNots.D: It is not random; it follows the deterministic longest prefix match rule.

hints: Routing uses 'longest prefix match' — the route with the most specific (longest) prefix wins.
Example: 10.0.1.0/24 wins over 0.0.0.0/0 for a destination within 10.0.1.0/24.

questions.stem:
Administrators need to access instances in a PRIVATE subnet via SSH, without exposing those instances directly to the internet.

Which traditional pattern solves this access?

options.text: Move the instances to a public subnet, protected only by the security group
Give public IPs to the private instances — SSH with a key protects everything
Open port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 on the private instances; the key is enough
A bastion host (jump server) in a public subnet, used as a bridge

questions.explanation: A bastion host (jump server) is an instance in a public subnet that acts as a secure bridge: the administrator connects to it (SSH/RDP) and from it reaches the instances in the private subnet — without exposing those instances directly to the internet. A modern alternative without opening a port is SSM Session Manager.

whyNots.A: Moving to a public subnet exposes the instances — it contradicts the goal.
whyNots.B: Giving public IPs to the private instances and exposing them is exactly what you want to avoid.
whyNots.C: Opening port 22 to everyone on private instances is a serious security flaw.

hints: A bastion host is an instance in the public subnet that acts as a BRIDGE; the admin logs into it and from there reaches the private ones.
This way the private instances are never exposed directly to the internet. (A modern alternative is SSM Session Manager.)

questions.stem:
Two VPCs need to communicate using private IP, as if they were on the same network.

Which resource connects two VPCs directly?
questions.explanation: VPC Peering connects two VPCs so they communicate using private IP, as if they were a single network (including cross-account and cross-region). For many VPCs, a hub (Transit Gateway) scales better.

whyNots.B: Internet Gateway gives internet access — it does not connect two VPCs privately.
whyNots.C: Bastion host is an administration bridge for SSH/RDP — it does not link VPCs.
whyNots.D: NAT Gateway gives internet outbound access for a private subnet — it does not connect VPCs.

hints: Connecting TWO VPCs with private IP = VPC Peering.
It works across accounts and regions; for MANY VPCs, a hub (Transit Gateway) is better.

questions.stem:
There is peering between VPC A↔B and between VPC A↔C. The team expects that, because of this, VPC B can talk to VPC C through A.

What is correct about this expectation?

options.text: Correct, as long as VPC A has a NAT Gateway routing transitive traffic between B and C
Wrong: VPC Peering is NOT transitive; B needs direct peering with C (or use Transit Gateway)
Wrong, because peering does not exist between VPCs; the only possible connection is site-to-site VPN
Correct: traffic from B reaches C automatically via A, because peering is transitive by default

questions.explanation: VPC Peering is not transitive: having A↔B and A↔C does not let B talk to C through A. For B to reach C, a direct B↔C peering is needed. When there are many VPCs, Transit Gateway (hub) avoids a full mesh of peerings.

whyNots.A: NAT Gateway does not enable peering transitivity; it gives internet outbound access.
whyNots.C: Peering does exist between VPCs; the point is that it is not transitive.
whyNots.D: There is no transitivity — traffic from B does not automatically reach C via A.

hints: Peering is NOT transitive — A↔B and A↔C do not make B talk to C. It needs B↔C directly.
To avoid a mesh of peerings, Transit Gateway centralizes everything in a hub.

questions.stem:
You try to create a VPC peering between two VPCs, but both use the same CIDR block 10.0.0.0/16, and creation fails.

What is the cause?

options.text: Peering requires the VPCs to be in the same AZ
VPC Peering does not allow overlapping CIDR blocks

questions.explanation: VPC Peering cannot be created between VPCs whose CIDR blocks overlap — it is a strict requirement. With both using 10.0.0.0/16, there is total overlap and the connection fails. Planning distinct IP ranges avoids the problem.

whyNots.A: Peering does not depend on an Internet Gateway.
whyNots.B: Peering does not require the same AZ (or even the same region/account) — the issue is the CIDR.
whyNots.D: Peering works with IPv4; the impediment here is the overlapping CIDR.

hints: Overlapping CIDR = peering impossible. The VPCs need IP ranges that do not overlap.
Plan distinct CIDRs from the start (for example, 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/16).

questions.stem:
Instances in a private subnet need to download updates from the internet, but cannot receive inbound connections. How should the private subnet's route look?

Which route configuration is correct?

options.text: No outbound route; it is impossible to update without making the subnet public
0.0.0.0/0 pointing to the Internet Gateway, which only lets outbound traffic pass
0.0.0.0/0 pointing to a bastion host, which proxies the updates
0.0.0.0/0 pointing to a NAT Gateway (which sits in a public subnet)

questions.explanation: To provide outbound access without exposing inbound access, the private subnet's route table should send 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT Gateway (located in a public subnet). The NAT allows outbound connections (updates) and blocks connections initiated from outside.

whyNots.A: It is indeed possible to provide outbound access via NAT — updating is not impossible.
whyNots.B: Pointing the private subnet directly to the IGW would make it public and expose instances to inbound traffic.
whyNots.C: A bastion host is for administrative SSH/RDP access — it is not an internet outbound route.

hints: Outbound yes, inbound no = NAT. The private subnet's route sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway.
If it pointed directly to the IGW, the subnet would become public (inbound possible).

questions.stem:
Four network components: (1) gives internet access to a public subnet; (2) gives internet outbound access to a private subnet without exposing inbound; (3) administration SSH bridge to private instances; (4) connects two VPCs with private IP.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Internet Gateway → NAT Gateway → Bastion host → VPC Peering
Internet Gateway → Bastion host → NAT Gateway → VPC Peering
Bastion host → VPC Peering → Internet Gateway → NAT Gateway
NAT Gateway → Internet Gateway → VPC Peering → Bastion host

questions.explanation: Each component has its role: Internet Gateway (internet access for the public subnet), NAT Gateway (outbound from the private subnet without exposing inbound), Bastion host (administration SSH/RDP bridge to private instances), and VPC Peering (connect two VPCs with private IP). Option A respects all four.

whyNots.B: Swaps NAT and bastion; private subnet outbound is NAT, not bastion.
whyNots.C: Shuffles everything — bastion does not give internet access to a public subnet.
whyNots.D: Swaps IGW with NAT and bastion with peering.

hints: Internet to public = IGW; private subnet outbound = NAT; SSH bridge = bastion; link VPCs = peering.
Only option A keeps each component in its correct role.

questions.stem:
An app receives photos uploaded by users and needs to automatically detect inappropriate content and identify objects/faces in the images.

Which AI service is indicated?
questions.explanation: Rekognition analyzes images and videos: object/scene detection, faces, content moderation, and more. It is the right service for processing user-uploaded photos.

whyNots.A: Comprehend is TEXT NLP — it does not analyze images.
whyNots.C: Textract is OCR/extraction for scanned documents (forms, tables) — not generic photo analysis.
whyNots.D: Polly converts text to speech — nothing to do with images.

hints: Image and video analysis (objects, faces, moderation) = Rekognition.
'Recognition' = visual recognition. Textract is for documents, not user photos.

questions.stem:
A company wants to digitize scanned invoices and forms (PDF/image), automatically extracting the text and the DATA from fields and tables.

Which service performs this document extraction?
questions.explanation: Textract uses OCR and ML to extract text, handwriting, and especially structured data from form fields and tables in scanned documents/PDFs. It is the service for digitizing invoices, forms, and contracts.

whyNots.A: Translate translates languages — it does not extract document data.
whyNots.B: Lex is a chatbot service — it does not perform document OCR.
whyNots.D: Rekognition analyzes generic images/videos; for documents with forms/tables, Textract is the specialized one.

hints: OCR + extracting FORM and TABLE fields from documents = Textract (goes beyond simple OCR).
'Extract' from 'text' is in the name — documents, not photos.

questions.stem:
You want to analyze thousands of customer reviews (text) to discover sentiment (positive/negative) and extract entities and key phrases.

Which NLP service does this?
questions.explanation: Comprehend is the NLP service: it analyzes sentiment, entities, key phrases, language, and topics from unstructured text. It is ideal for mining insights from customer reviews at scale.

whyNots.A: Polly converts text to speech — it does not perform sentiment analysis.
whyNots.B: Rekognition is computer vision — it does not analyze text.
whyNots.C: Transcribe converts speech to text — it does not analyze text sentiment.

hints: Sentiment, entities, and key phrases from TEXT = NLP = Comprehend.
'Comprehend' = understand the text.

questions.stem:
A call center wants to automatically transcribe call audio recordings into text for later analysis.

Which service converts speech to text?
questions.explanation: Transcribe is the speech-to-text (ASR) service: it converts spoken audio into text, supporting files and streaming. It is ideal for transcribing call-center calls, captioning audio, and indexing spoken content.

whyNots.B: Polly does the reverse: text → speech.
whyNots.C: Comprehend analyzes text (NLP) — it does not transcribe audio.
whyNots.D: Translate translates languages — it does not transcribe speech.

hints: Speech → text = Transcribe.
Do not confuse it with Polly (text → speech).

questions.stem:
An accessibility app wants to read article text aloud to users using realistic voices.

Which service converts text to speech?
questions.explanation: Polly converts text into realistic speech (text-to-speech), with dozens of voices and languages. It is ideal for content readers, accessibility, and voice applications.

whyNots.A: Transcribe is the reverse: speech → text.
whyNots.C: Lex is a chatbot (conversation) — although it can use Polly to speak, the TTS service itself is Polly.
whyNots.D: Textract extracts text from documents — it does not generate speech.

hints: Text → speech (text-to-speech) with realistic voices = Polly.
Polly speaks; Transcribe listens. Do not swap the two.

questions.stem:
A company wants to build a customer-service chatbot that understands natural language (voice and text) and responds to customers, using the same engine as Alexa.

Which service is indicated?
questions.explanation: Lex builds conversational interfaces (chatbots) by voice and text, with speech recognition and natural-language understanding — the same engine as Alexa. It is often combined with Polly to speak responses.

whyNots.A: Comprehend analyzes text (sentiment/entities) — it does not build the chatbot conversation flow.
whyNots.B: SageMaker is for building your own models — overkill when Lex already delivers a ready chatbot.
whyNots.D: Polly only converts text to speech — it does not understand user intent.

hints: Building a CHATBOT / conversational interface (voice and text) = Lex (Alexa engine).
Lex understands intent; to speak the response, it usually uses Polly together.

questions.stem:
A data science team needs to BUILD, TRAIN, and DEPLOY a custom machine learning model tailored to the company's problem, because the ready-made services do not meet the need.

Which AWS service is indicated?
questions.explanation: SageMaker is the platform for building, training, and deploying custom ML models. It is the choice when ready-made AI services (Rekognition, Comprehend, etc.) do not meet the need and a tailored model is required.

whyNots.A: Lex is a ready chatbot — it does not train arbitrary models.
whyNots.B: Comprehend is ready NLP — not a custom ML platform.
whyNots.C: Rekognition is ready vision — not for training a generic custom model.

hints: Build/train/deploy your OWN model = SageMaker (the ML platform).
The others are ready-made services (vision, NLP, chatbot); SageMaker is when you need a tailored model.

questions.stem:
You want to take spoken audio in one language, turn it into text, translate it into another language, and generate narration in that language — a voice translation pipeline.

Which service sequence implements this?
questions.explanation: The voice translation pipeline combines three services: Transcribe converts speech to text, Translate translates the text into the target language, and Polly generates narration in the new language. It is the speech→text→translation→speech sequence.

whyNots.B: Comprehend/Lex/Rekognition do not form a voice translation pipeline.
whyNots.C: Reverses the order — starting with Polly (text→speech) makes no sense for an audio input.
whyNots.D: Textract is for documents; the starting point here is audio (Transcribe).

hints: Speech becomes text (Transcribe), the text is translated (Translate), and the translated text becomes speech (Polly).
It is the classic 'break the language barrier by voice' combo.

questions.stem:
You have scanned contracts (PDF) and want to (1) extract the text and fields, and then (2) detect entities and sentiment in that text.

Which pair of services handles (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: First Textract extracts the text and fields from the scanned document; then Comprehend performs NLP analysis (entities, sentiment, key phrases) on that text. It is the classic document → insight pipeline.

whyNots.A: Rekognition/Polly are vision/voice — they do not extract document fields or perform NLP.
whyNots.C: Transcribe/Translate are speech/language — not the case for scanned documents.
whyNots.D: Reversed — Textract extracts from the PDF; Comprehend analyzes the text.

hints: Extracting text/fields from a PDF = Textract; analyzing entities/sentiment of the text = Comprehend.
Textract pulls the text out of the document; Comprehend understands the text.

questions.stem:
Four tasks: (1) moderate image content; (2) extract fields from a scanned form; (3) detect sentiment of reviews; (4) read text aloud.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service has its domain: Rekognition (image/moderation), Textract (OCR/forms), Comprehend (NLP/sentiment), and Polly (text→speech). Option C respects all four.

whyNots.A: Completely reversed; no position matches the right function.
whyNots.B: Shuffles everything — Comprehend does not moderate images.
whyNots.D: Swaps Rekognition with Textract and Comprehend with Polly.

hints: Image = Rekognition; document/form = Textract; text sentiment = Comprehend; text to voice = Polly.
Only option C keeps each service in its correct role.

questions.stem:
A company has dozens of AWS accounts and wants to group them into logical units (Production, Development, Sandbox) to apply different policies to each group.

Which AWS Organizations resource allows this grouping?
questions.explanation: Organizational Units (OUs) group AWS Organizations accounts into logical units (Prod, Dev, Sandbox). You apply SCPs per OU, giving each group of accounts the appropriate policies and guardrails.

whyNots.A: Security Groups are instance firewalls — they do not group accounts.
whyNots.B: Route tables route network traffic — they do not group accounts.
whyNots.C: Availability Zones are data centers in a region — they do not organize accounts.

hints: Grouping ACCOUNTS into logical units = Organizational Units (OUs).
You apply SCPs per OU, so each group can have different policies.

questions.stem:
A company wants to set up a well-architected multi-account environment from scratch, with governance and security best practices already applied automatically (landing zone), instead of configuring everything manually.

Which service automates this?
questions.explanation: Control Tower creates and governs a landing zone (well-architected multi-account environment) automatically, orchestrating Organizations, Service Catalog, and IAM Identity Center. It is the automation/governance layer on top of Organizations.

whyNots.B: CloudFront is a CDN — unrelated to multi-account governance.
whyNots.C: RAM shares resources across accounts — it does not build the landing zone.
whyNots.D: Organizations is the foundation (accounts/OUs/SCPs), but building the automated landing zone with best practices is Control Tower's role.

hints: Building a multi-account 'landing zone' with automatic governance = Control Tower (the automation layer on top of Organizations).
Organizations is the foundation; Control Tower is the automation that applies best practices.

questions.stem:
In Control Tower, distinguish: (1) a guardrail that PROHIBITS an action that violates policy (e.g., blocking unauthorized regions); (2) a guardrail that DETECTS and reports non-compliance (e.g., public S3 bucket), without blocking.

Which pair of types corresponds to (1) and (2)?

options.text: Both use only SCPs, including detection

questions.explanation: Preventive guardrails use SCPs to prohibit actions that violate policy (and inherit through the OU hierarchy). Detective guardrails use AWS Config rules to detect and report non-compliance without blocking. Option B makes the correct association.

whyNots.A: The correct names are preventive and detective, not 'reactive/proactive'.
whyNots.C: Detective guardrails use Config rules, not SCPs.
whyNots.D: Reversed — prohibit is preventive (SCP); detect is detective (Config).

hints: Preventive PROHIBITS (uses SCP, inherited through the OU); detective only REPORTS (uses Config rules).
'Block' = preventive; 'detect/report' = detective.

questions.stem:
The company wants several accounts to use the SAME subnets from a central VPC, without having to recreate the network in each account.

Which service shares this resource across accounts?
questions.explanation: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) shares resources securely across accounts (and OUs), such as VPC subnets, Transit Gateway, and Route 53 Resolver rules. The resource is created once and shared, avoiding duplication in each account.

whyNots.A: VPC Peering connects two VPCs so they can communicate — it does not share the SAME subnet across accounts.
whyNots.B: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not share resources across accounts.
whyNots.D: Service Catalog curates products for self-service — it does not share an existing resource across accounts.

hints: SHARING a resource (VPC subnet, Transit Gateway...) across accounts without duplicating it = RAM.
You create the subnet once and share it; the other accounts see it as their own.

questions.stem:
A company wants teams to launch only APPROVED infrastructure configurations (e.g., a standardized EC2, a baseline VPC) in self-service, without departing from security standards.

Which service delivers this curated catalog of approved products?
questions.explanation: AWS Service Catalog creates a curated catalog of approved products (IaC templates, usually CloudFormation) that end users can deploy in self-service within defined permissions. It standardizes environments and ensures governance/compliance.

whyNots.A: RAM shares resources across accounts — it is not a catalog of products to launch.
whyNots.B: Config evaluates compliance — it is not a self-service catalog.
whyNots.C: Inspector scans vulnerabilities — it does not curate infrastructure products.

hints: A catalog of APPROVED products (IaC templates) for self-service = Service Catalog.
Users only launch what has been approved — standardization and governance.

questions.stem:
An architect confuses the two: what is the FOUNDATION of multi-account management and what is the AUTOMATION/GOVERNANCE layer with landing zone?

Which association is correct?

options.text: Foundation = AWS Organizations; automation/landing zone = AWS Control Tower
They are the same service — Control Tower is the new name for Organizations
Foundation = AWS Control Tower; automation/landing zone = AWS Organizations
Foundation = AWS RAM; automation/landing zone = AWS Service Catalog

questions.explanation: AWS Organizations is the foundation of multi-account management (accounts, OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing). Control Tower is the automation/governance layer on top that builds the landing zone and applies guardrails using Organizations underneath.

whyNots.B: They are distinct services (related, but not the same).
whyNots.C: Reversed — the foundation is Organizations; the automation is Control Tower.
whyNots.D: RAM and Service Catalog are not the foundation/automation of multi-account management.

hints: Organizations is the base (accounts, OUs, SCPs); Control Tower automates and governs on top (landing zone, guardrails).
Control Tower USES Organizations underneath.

questions.stem:
To reduce cost and overhead, the company wants to avoid provisioning the same Transit Gateway separately in each account.

How do you share a single Transit Gateway across accounts?

options.text: Use signed URLs to grant temporary access to the gateway
Share it through AWS RAM (create once and share)
Recreate the Transit Gateway in every account, for security
