Use a bucket policy to release the gateway to the accounts

questions.explanation: With AWS RAM, you create the Transit Gateway once and share it with the other accounts (or OUs), avoiding the need to provision and pay for duplicated resources in each account. It reduces cost and operational overhead while maintaining consistency.

whyNots.A: Signed URLs belong to S3/CloudFront — they do not share a Transit Gateway.
whyNots.C: Recreating it in every account is exactly the duplication you want to avoid.
whyNots.D: A bucket policy is an S3 permission — it does not share network resources across accounts.

hints: Think: create a resource ONCE and share it across accounts = RAM. Avoid duplicating (and paying for) the same resource multiple times.
Remember: Transit Gateway is one of the classic resources shareable through RAM.

questions.stem:
You need a guardrail that PREVENTS resource creation in a prohibited region across all accounts in an OU — actually blocking the action.

Which Control Tower guardrail type does this, and with what mechanism?
questions.explanation: To actually block the action (creating resources in a prohibited region) across the entire OU, you use a PREVENTIVE guardrail from Control Tower, implemented via SCP — it prohibits the action and is inherited through the OU hierarchy. A detective guardrail would only report it.

whyNots.A: A NACL filters network traffic — it does not block API actions by region.
whyNots.B: A CloudWatch alarm notifies about metrics — it does not prevent resource creation.
whyNots.D: A detective guardrail (Config) only detects/reports — it does not block the action.

hints: Think: PREVENT/block the action means a preventive guardrail, which uses an SCP underneath and is inherited through the OU.
Remember: if it were only 'detect and report', it would be detective (Config).

questions.stem:
Reinforcement: which Organizations feature imposes the permissions CEILING (guardrail) on accounts, regardless of what local IAM allows?

Which one?
questions.explanation: SCPs (Service Control Policies) in AWS Organizations define the permissions ceiling for accounts/OUs: no identity can exceed what an SCP permits, even if local IAM grants it. SCPs do not grant access — they only restrict the maximum.

whyNots.A: A Security Group is a network firewall — it does not limit API permissions across accounts.
whyNots.B: RAM shares resources across accounts — it does not impose a permissions ceiling.
whyNots.C: Service Catalog curates self-service products — it is not the permissions guardrail.

hints: Think: the account permissions ceiling (guardrail), even if IAM allows it = SCP.
Remember: SCPs do not grant access — they only limit the maximum possible.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) group accounts and apply policy by group; (2) set up an automatically governed multi-account environment (landing zone); (3) share a subnet across accounts without duplicating it; (4) offer an approved self-service product catalog.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Organizations (OUs) → Control Tower → RAM → Service Catalog
Control Tower → Organizations → Service Catalog → RAM
Service Catalog → RAM → Control Tower → Organizations
RAM → Service Catalog → Organizations → Control Tower

questions.explanation: Each service has its role: Organizations/OUs (group accounts + policies by group), Control Tower (automatically governed landing zone), RAM (share resources across accounts), and Service Catalog (approved self-service product catalog). Option A matches all four.

whyNots.B: Swaps Organizations with Control Tower and RAM with Service Catalog.
whyNots.C: Completely reversed; none of the positions match the correct role.
whyNots.D: Jumbles everything — RAM does not group accounts.

hints: Think: grouping accounts = Organizations/OUs; automated landing zone = Control Tower; sharing resources = RAM; product catalog = Service Catalog.
Remember: only option A keeps each service in its correct role.

questions.stem:
The company wants to be automatically alerted about unexpected SPIKES in spending (for example, a forgotten resource left running), without having to set a fixed threshold, by learning from historical patterns.

Which tool detects anomalous spending using ML?

options.text: AWS Budgets with a fixed threshold

questions.explanation: Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn your historical spending pattern and detect anomalies (spikes outside the expected range), with root-cause analysis and alerts — without requiring you to define a fixed threshold.

whyNots.A: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations by category — it is not ML-based spending anomaly detection.
whyNots.C: Budgets triggers against a limit that YOU define — it does not learn the pattern or detect anomalies automatically.
whyNots.D: Pricing Calculator estimates costs for something you plan to create — it does not monitor actual spending.

hints: Think: anomalous spike, no fixed threshold, based on history = Cost Anomaly Detection (uses ML).
Remember: Budgets requires a defined threshold; Anomaly Detection learns what is normal and alerts on the abnormal.

questions.stem:
Management wants to know how much each TEAM and each ENVIRONMENT (prod/dev) spends on AWS, breaking the bill down by these criteria.

Which feature enables this cost breakdown?

options.text: Placement Groups organized by team, project, and environment
Route 53 health checks named by team and project
Cost Allocation Tags (activated and analyzed in Cost Explorer/CUR)
Security Groups named by project, read in Cost Explorer

questions.explanation: Cost Allocation Tags are key-value tags applied to resources and activated in the Billing console. Once active, they appear in Cost Explorer and CUR, letting you break down cost by team, project, or environment.

whyNots.A: Placement Groups control instance placement — not cost by tag.
whyNots.B: Route 53 health checks monitor endpoint health — not cost.
whyNots.D: Security Groups are firewalls — they do not track cost.

hints: Think: tag resources (for example, team=marketing, environment=prod) and ACTIVATE the tags to see cost by them = Cost Allocation Tags.
Remember: once activated in Billing, they appear in Cost Explorer and CUR to filter/group.

questions.stem:
When a development environment's budget exceeds a limit, you want the system to automatically STOP that environment's EC2 instances, with no manual intervention.

Which feature performs this automatic action when the budget is exceeded?

options.text: Pricing Calculator — estimates and automatically turns off anything that exceeds
Cost Explorer — has an automatic spending action button
Cost Anomaly Detection (stops instances when detected)
AWS Budgets Actions (stop EC2/RDS, apply IAM/SCP)

questions.explanation: AWS Budgets Actions execute an automatic (or approval-required) response when a budget exceeds its limit: apply an IAM policy, apply an SCP, or stop specific EC2/RDS instances. It is active cost control beyond simple alerting.

whyNots.A: Pricing Calculator estimates costs — it does not take action.
whyNots.B: Cost Explorer analyzes/visualizes costs — it does not execute actions when a budget is exceeded.
whyNots.C: Cost Anomaly Detection alerts on anomalies — it does not stop instances based on budget.

hints: Think: budget exceeded → automatic ACTION (stop EC2/RDS, apply IAM policy or SCP) = Budget Actions.
Remember: Budgets only alerts; Budget Actions actually takes the action.

questions.stem:
You suspect many EC2 instances and EBS volumes are over-provisioned (paying for capacity they do not use) and want right-sizing recommendations based on actual usage.

Which service provides right-sizing recommendations?
questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer analyzes actual usage (ML) and recommends right-sizing configurations for EC2, Auto Scaling, EBS, ECS/Fargate, Lambda, and RDS — identifying over-provisioned resources (savings), under-provisioned resources (performance), and idle resources.

whyNots.B: Config evaluates compliance — it does not recommend sizing.
whyNots.C: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities — it does not right-size.
whyNots.D: Budgets controls budgets/limits — it does not recommend resource sizes.

hints: Think: ideal resource size, based on actual usage = Compute Optimizer (ML-based right-sizing).
Remember: it covers EC2, ASG, EBS, ECS/Fargate, Lambda, and RDS, and detects over-provisioned, under-provisioned, and idle resources.

questions.stem:
A company with hundreds of S3 buckets across multiple accounts wants a single view of usage, trends, and recommendations to optimize storage cost across the whole organization.

Which tool delivers this organization-wide S3 visibility?
questions.explanation: S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide visibility into S3 storage (usage, activity trends) with actionable recommendations to optimize cost, performance, and protection. It presents everything in a dashboard, with free and advanced metrics.

whyNots.A: Config evaluates configuration compliance — it is not the S3 usage/optimization dashboard.
whyNots.C: CloudWatch Logs stores logs — it does not provide the aggregated S3 usage/cost view.
whyNots.D: Athena queries data — it is not the ready-made organization-wide S3 visibility dashboard.

hints: Think: organization-wide view of S3 USAGE + cost recommendations = S3 Storage Lens (dashboard).
Remember: it has free and advanced metrics; integrates with Organizations to see all accounts.

questions.stem:
Two use cases: (1) quick visual analysis of spending trends with forecasting; (2) raw, line-by-line data to process with Athena/Redshift for deep analysis.

Which pair serves (1) and (2)?

options.text: (1) Cost Explorer; (2) Cost and Usage Report (CUR)

questions.explanation: Cost Explorer is the visual tool for analyzing and forecasting costs (charts, history, forecast). The Cost and Usage Report (CUR) is the most detailed raw data, delivered to S3, ideal for deep analysis and integration with Athena/Redshift/QuickSight.

whyNots.A: Budgets/Pricing Calculator are neither visual analysis of actual spending nor raw data.
whyNots.B: Reversed — visual analysis is Cost Explorer; granular raw data is CUR.
whyNots.D: Storage Lens/Compute Optimizer are neither general cost visual analysis nor billing raw data.

hints: Think: quick visual analysis + forecast = Cost Explorer; detailed raw data in S3 for Athena = CUR.
Remember: Cost Explorer is the dashboard; CUR is the granular raw material.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) alert when spending EXCEEDS a target value you defined; (2) alert when spending deviates from learned historical patterns, with no fixed target.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets alerts when spending exceeds a limit that YOU define (fixed target). Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to alert when spending deviates from the learned historical pattern, with no fixed target needed. They are complementary.

whyNots.A: Compute Optimizer/Storage Lens are not spending alerts by threshold/anomaly.
whyNots.B: Cost Explorer/CUR are analysis/raw data — not alerts by limit vs anomaly.
whyNots.C: Reversed — the defined limit is Budgets; the learned pattern is Anomaly Detection.

hints: Think: a limit that YOU define = Budgets; ML-learned pattern, no fixed target = Cost Anomaly Detection.
Remember: Budgets = you set the ceiling; Anomaly = the AI flags what is abnormal.

questions.stem:
Some instances are practically IDLE (very low usage) and wasting money. You want to identify them and get recommendations on what to do.

Which service identifies idle resources and recommends action?

options.text: AWS WAF (inspects traffic and points out stopped instances)
AWS Shield (Advanced includes an idle-resource report)
Amazon Macie (scans the account and recommends shutting down idle resources)

questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer, in addition to right-sizing, performs idle resource detection — it identifies instances with very low usage and recommends action, helping cut waste.

whyNots.B: WAF is an application firewall — it does not analyze resource usage/cost.
whyNots.C: Shield is DDoS protection — it has nothing to do with idle resources.
whyNots.D: Macie finds sensitive data in S3 — it does not detect idle resources.

hints: Think: identify IDLE resources + recommend action = Compute Optimizer (has idle detection).
Remember: it looks at actual usage and suggests reducing or shutting down what is excess.

questions.stem:
A manager wants to open a dashboard and see, in charts, how much was spent by service over the last few months and a forecast for the coming months.

Which tool delivers this visual view and forecast?
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer is the visual tool for analyzing cost and usage: charts by service/account/tag, up to 13 months of history, and forecasts for upcoming months. It is perfect for the dashboard the manager wants.

whyNots.A: CloudTrail audits API calls — it does not show spending.
whyNots.C: CUR is raw line-by-line data in S3 — not a ready-made visual view.
whyNots.D: Inspector is for vulnerabilities — not costs.

hints: Think: visual spending dashboard by service + forecast = Cost Explorer.
Remember: CUR is the raw data; for ready-made charts, use Cost Explorer.

questions.stem:
Four objectives: (1) detect anomalous spending spikes using ML; (2) break down cost by team/environment; (3) find the ideal instance size; (4) organization-wide S3 visibility and optimization.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Cost Allocation Tags → Cost Anomaly Detection → Storage Lens → Compute Optimizer
S3 Storage Lens → Compute Optimizer → Cost Allocation Tags → Cost Anomaly Detection
Cost Anomaly Detection → Cost Allocation Tags → Compute Optimizer → S3 Storage Lens
Compute Optimizer → Storage Lens → Cost Anomaly Detection → Cost Allocation Tags

questions.explanation: Each tool has its role: Cost Anomaly Detection (anomalous spikes by ML), Cost Allocation Tags (cost by team/environment), Compute Optimizer (right-sizing/idle), and S3 Storage Lens (organization-wide S3 visibility/optimization). Option C matches all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps the first two and the last two.
whyNots.B: Completely reversed; none of the positions match the correct role.
whyNots.D: Jumbles everything — Compute Optimizer does not detect spending anomalies.

hints: Think: ML anomaly = Cost Anomaly Detection; cost by team = Cost Allocation Tags; ideal size = Compute Optimizer; org-wide S3 = Storage Lens.
Remember: only option C keeps each tool in its role.

questions.stem:
A team wants to automate the entire release flow — from code commit to production deploy — modeling stages for source, build, test, and deploy.

Which service ORCHESTRATES this end-to-end CI/CD pipeline?
questions.explanation: CodePipeline models and orchestrates the end-to-end CI/CD flow in stages (source, build, test, deploy), each with actions. It invokes the other services (CodeBuild to build, CodeDeploy to deploy) as part of the flow.

whyNots.A: CodeCommit is the code repository — the source, not the orchestrator.
whyNots.B: CodeBuild performs build/test — it is a stage, not the orchestrator.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a CDN — it has nothing to do with CI/CD pipelines.

hints: Think: 'pipeline' is in the name — CodePipeline orchestrates the stages (source → build → test → deploy).
Remember: the other Code* services are pieces INSIDE the pipeline; the conductor is CodePipeline.

questions.stem:
You want to compile, test, and package code on every change, without maintaining your own build servers, with automatic scaling.

Which service provides managed build?
questions.explanation: CodeBuild is a fully managed build service: it compiles, tests, and packages code without you maintaining build servers, scaling capacity automatically with demand.

whyNots.B: Jenkins on EC2 self-managed is exactly the build server that CodeBuild avoids.
whyNots.C: CodePipeline orchestrates; the build itself is CodeBuild.
whyNots.D: CodeDeploy handles deployment, not build.

hints: Think: build without your own server, scales by itself = CodeBuild.
Remember: it compiles/tests/packages; deployment is CodeDeploy's job.

questions.stem:
You want to automate application deployment to EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and ECS services, with the option to use blue/green to switch traffic with easy rollback.

Which service automates this deployment?
questions.explanation: CodeDeploy automates deployment to EC2, on-premises, Lambda, and ECS, with strategies such as in-place (updates existing instances) and blue/green (creates a new environment and switches traffic, making rollback easy).

whyNots.A: CodeBuild performs build/test — it does not deploy.
whyNots.C: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities — it does not deploy applications.
whyNots.D: CodeCommit stores code — it does not deploy.

hints: Think: automate DEPLOYMENT (EC2/Lambda/ECS) with in-place or blue/green = CodeDeploy.
Remember: blue/green spins up a new environment and switches traffic — rollback is just pointing back to the old one.

questions.stem:
The company wants to host its private Git repositories in a managed AWS service, integrated with the account and IAM.

Which service is the managed Git repository?
questions.explanation: CodeCommit is AWS's private, managed Git repository service, integrated with IAM. (Status: it was closed to new customers in July 2024, but returned to general availability in November 2025.) It is the source of code in the pipeline.

whyNots.A: CodeDeploy deploys — it does not store source code.
whyNots.B: CodePipeline orchestrates the flow — it is not a code repository.
whyNots.D: S3 is object storage — it is not a Git repository.

hints: Think: the managed AWS Git repository = CodeCommit (the name says 'commit').
Remember: it returned to general availability in November 2025 after a period closed to new customers.

questions.stem:
In a CI/CD pipeline: (1) store the code; (2) orchestrate the stages; (3) compile and test; (4) deploy to instances.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service has its role: CodeCommit (repository/code), CodePipeline (orchestrates stages), CodeBuild (compiles and tests), and CodeDeploy (deploys). Option D matches all four in the natural pipeline order.

whyNots.A: Completely reversed; none of the positions match the correct role.
whyNots.B: Swaps CodeCommit with CodePipeline and CodeBuild with CodeDeploy.
whyNots.C: Jumbles everything — CodeBuild does not store code.

hints: Think: code = CodeCommit; orchestrate = CodePipeline; build/test = CodeBuild; deploy = CodeDeploy.
Remember: only option D keeps each piece in its role.

questions.stem:
A developer team wants to define infrastructure using a familiar programming language (TypeScript/Python) instead of writing YAML, and have it turn into CloudFormation underneath.

Which IaC tool fits?
questions.explanation: AWS CDK lets you define infrastructure in programming languages (TypeScript, Python, Java, C#); when run, CDK compiles everything into CloudFormation templates. It is the choice for those who prefer code over YAML.

whyNots.B: CodeBuild performs builds — it is not an IaC tool.
whyNots.C: CloudFormation in plain YAML is the opposite of the request (programming language).
whyNots.D: QuickSight is BI — it has nothing to do with IaC.

hints: Think: infrastructure in a PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE (TS/Python/Java) that compiles to CloudFormation = CDK.
Remember: if you preferred declarative YAML, you would use CloudFormation directly.

questions.stem:
A serverless team wants a lean, declarative IaC framework specific to Lambda/API Gateway/DynamoDB, with a CLI to test functions locally before deploying.

Which tool is recommended?
questions.explanation: AWS SAM is the IaC framework focused on serverless: compact declarative syntax (a CloudFormation shortcut) for Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB, with the SAM CLI to test and debug functions locally before deploying.

whyNots.A: Athena is SQL querying — it is not IaC.
whyNots.C: CodeDeploy is for deployment — it is not a serverless declarative IaC framework.
whyNots.D: CDK uses a programming language and is generic; the request is for a declarative framework focused on serverless (SAM).

hints: Think: lean declarative IaC FOCUSED on serverless + CLI for local testing = SAM.
Remember: SAM is a CloudFormation shortcut for serverless; CDK is a generic programming language.

questions.stem:
Three IaC preferences: (1) generic declarative YAML/JSON templates; (2) declarative framework focused on serverless; (3) infrastructure defined in a programming language.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: CloudFormation is the generic declarative IaC (YAML/JSON); SAM is the declarative framework focused on serverless; CDK defines infrastructure in a programming language. Both SAM and CDK compile/expand into CloudFormation underneath. Option C matches all three.

whyNots.A: Starts with SAM as generic — wrong; the generic one is CloudFormation.
whyNots.B: Puts CDK as generic and SAM as programming language — jumbled.
whyNots.D: Swaps CDK with SAM — serverless is SAM, programming language is CDK.

hints: Think: generic YAML = CloudFormation; declarative serverless = SAM; programming language = CDK.
Remember: SAM and CDK generate CloudFormation underneath; only option C keeps each in place.

questions.stem:
Distinguish two CodeDeploy strategies: (1) update the application ON the existing instances; (2) spin up a NEW environment in parallel and switch traffic to it, with easy rollback.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: In-place updates the application on the existing instances; blue/green creates a new environment in parallel and switches traffic to it, allowing fast rollback (return to the old environment). These are the two classic CodeDeploy strategies.

whyNots.A: 'Rolling/Spot' is not the right pair here (Spot is an EC2 purchase model).
whyNots.B: Canary/all-at-once are traffic-shift modes, not the requested distinction between existing and new environments.
whyNots.C: Reversed — updating on existing instances is in-place; new environment is blue/green.

hints: Think: updating on existing instances = in-place; new environment + traffic switch = blue/green.
Remember: blue/green makes rollback easy — just point back to the old environment.

questions.stem:
You want the pipeline to run automatically on every push to the repository. The source can be CodeCommit, GitHub, S3, or ECR.

Which service triggers and drives this flow from the source?

options.text: AWS CodePipeline (source stage triggered by change)
AWS Config, which listens to the repo push and triggers the flow
AWS CodeDeploy alone, which already listens to the source and drives everything
Amazon Route 53, which routes the repo push to the pipeline

questions.explanation: CodePipeline has a source stage that monitors the source (CodeCommit, GitHub, S3, or ECR) and, on every change, triggers the pipeline — automatically chaining build (CodeBuild) and deploy (CodeDeploy).

whyNots.B: Config evaluates compliance — it does not drive CI/CD.
whyNots.C: CodeDeploy is only the deploy stage — it does not orchestrate the flow from the source.
whyNots.D: Route 53 is DNS — it does not trigger pipelines.

hints: Think: CodePipeline's SOURCE stage detects the change (CodeCommit/GitHub/S3/ECR) and triggers the flow.
Remember: from there it chains build (CodeBuild) and deploy (CodeDeploy).

questions.stem:
A small business wants to host a simple website (WordPress) with quick setup and a fixed, predictable monthly price, without needing EC2 scale and complexity.

Which service is the best fit?
questions.explanation: Amazon Lightsail offers pre-configured VPS bundles with a fixed, predictable monthly price, ideal for simple sites and apps (WordPress, blogs) and for those who prefer simplicity — without EC2 complexity/scale.

whyNots.A: Batch is for large-scale batch jobs — not for hosting a simple website.
whyNots.C: EKS (Kubernetes) is the opposite of simple for a small WordPress site.
whyNots.D: Outposts is AWS hardware in your data center — overkill for a simple website.

hints: Think: simple site + quick setup + fixed monthly price = Lightsail (pre-configured VPS).
Remember: when you do NOT need EC2 scale/complexity, Lightsail is simpler and cheaper.

questions.stem:
A team has a container image for a web API and wants to publish it in a fully managed way — with automatic build, deploy, load balancing, and auto scaling — without configuring ECS, ALB, or a cluster.

Which service delivers this?
questions.explanation: AWS App Runner is fully managed for web apps and APIs in containers: you provide the image (or source code), and it builds, deploys, balances, and scales automatically — without you configuring ECS, a cluster, or a load balancer.

whyNots.A: Batch is for batch jobs — not a request-response web API.
whyNots.B: Plain EC2 would require configuring everything manually — the opposite of 'fully managed'.
whyNots.D: Lightsail is a simple VPS — it is not the managed container API service with automatic auto scaling in this model.

hints: Think: fully managed web/API app container (automatic build/deploy/scale/load balancing) = App Runner.
Remember: you just provide the image; it handles the rest — simpler than building ECS/Fargate + ALB by hand.

questions.stem:
A genomics company needs to run hundreds of thousands of batch processing jobs, with the infrastructure automatically provisioning the ideal compute type/quantity based on the job queue.

Which service manages batch compute at scale?
questions.explanation: AWS Batch is the managed service for large-scale batch computing: it dynamically provisions the ideal type and quantity of compute (CPU/memory) based on submitted jobs. It is ideal for genomics, simulations, and heavy ETL.

whyNots.A: App Runner is for web/API request-response apps — not batch jobs.
whyNots.B: API Gateway is an API gateway — it does not run batch.
whyNots.C: Lightsail is a simple VPS — it does not orchestrate batch jobs at scale.

hints: Think: hundreds of thousands of BATCH jobs, provisions ideal compute on its own = AWS Batch.
Remember: it scales the instance type/quantity based on job load.

questions.stem:
Due to data-residency requirements and local latency needs, an industrial company must run AWS compute/storage services INSIDE its own data center, but integrated with the AWS cloud.

Which service brings AWS hardware on-premises?
questions.explanation: AWS Outposts are racks of AWS hardware installed in your own data center (or colocation), running AWS compute/storage on-premises and connected transparently to cloud services. It is the choice for data residency/local latency with AWS integration.

whyNots.B: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not run compute on-premises.
whyNots.C: Local Zones is AWS infrastructure near the city — it does not sit inside your data center.
whyNots.D: Wavelength sits inside the carrier's 5G network — not in your data center.

hints: Think: AWS hardware installed IN YOUR data center (on-premises) = Outposts.
Remember: Local Zones and Wavelength are AWS infrastructure (outside your DC); Outposts sits in your DC.

questions.stem:
A mobile game streaming service needs single-digit millisecond latency for users connected via 5G, with processing as close as possible inside the carrier's network.

Which service serves this 5G ultra-low-latency case?
questions.explanation: AWS Wavelength embeds AWS compute/storage inside carriers' 5G networks, delivering single-digit millisecond latency for 5G users — ideal for game streaming, AR/VR, and autonomous vehicles. Access is through the partner carrier's 5G network.

whyNots.A: Lightsail is a simple VPS — it is not a 5G ultra-low-latency edge.
whyNots.C: Batch is for batch jobs — it does not serve interactive 5G latency.
whyNots.D: Outposts sits in the customer's data center — not inside the 5G network.

hints: Think: processing INSIDE the carrier's 5G network, single-digit ms latency for 5G users = Wavelength.
Remember: it is accessible only through the partner carrier's 5G network.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) low latency near a major city, accessible over ANY network (5G or Wi-Fi); (2) ultra-low latency accessible ONLY through the carrier's 5G network.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Local Zones extend AWS near major cities with multi-network access (5G or Wi-Fi, any carrier). Wavelength sits inside the carrier's 5G network and is accessible only via that 5G network. The difference lies in the access pattern.

whyNots.A: Outposts sits in the customer's data center — it is not 'near the city, multi-access'.
whyNots.B: Swaps the roles and includes Outposts inappropriately.
whyNots.D: Reversed — multi-access is Local Zones; 5G-only is Wavelength.

hints: Think: near the city, multi-access (5G/Wi-Fi) = Local Zones; carrier 5G only = Wavelength.
Remember: the clue is 'any network' (Local Zones) vs '5G only' (Wavelength).

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) infrastructure installed in YOUR own data center (on-premises); (2) AWS infrastructure near a major city, operated by AWS itself.

Which pair matches (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: AWS Outposts is AWS hardware installed in YOUR data center (on-premises), managed by AWS. AWS Local Zones is AWS infrastructure near major urban centers, operated by AWS itself. The difference is the LOCATION and who hosts it.

whyNots.A: Wavelength is not 'near the city, multi-access' — that is Local Zones.
whyNots.B: Wavelength is inside the 5G network — not 'in your data center'.
whyNots.C: Reverses them — your DC is Outposts; near the city (AWS) is Local Zones.

hints: Think about where the hardware lives: your own data center points to Outposts, while AWS-operated infrastructure near a city points to Local Zones.
Remember that Outposts is installed on your premises, and Local Zones are operated by AWS.

questions.stem:
A developer is weighing a simple fixed-price VPS against EC2 with the full ecosystem. The project is a small app that may eventually need scale and deep AWS service integration.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: Lightsail is great for starting simple and cheap; if scale and deep integration are needed, EC2 (and the broader ecosystem) is the path
EC2 is only for hosting simple static websites; apps that need scale and deep integrations require Lightsail
Lightsail scales better than EC2 for any workload, including unpredictable spikes with advanced Auto Scaling
Lightsail and EC2 are exactly the same service underneath, with the same price, limits, and integration

questions.explanation: Amazon Lightsail is ideal for starting simple and cheap (fixed price). When the project needs scale, varied instances, and deep integration with the AWS ecosystem, EC2 (and other services) is the choice. You can start on Lightsail and migrate later.

whyNots.B: EC2 runs any workload, not just static websites.
whyNots.C: Lightsail is intentionally the simpler, more limited option; for high scale, EC2 is better.
whyNots.D: They are not the same — Lightsail is simplified; EC2 is full and flexible.

hints: Think about the trade-off: Lightsail offers simplicity and predictable pricing to start, while EC2 offers flexibility, scale, and the full AWS ecosystem.
Remember that you can start on Lightsail and move to EC2 as the project grows.

questions.stem:
One team wants to publish a containerized API with the MINIMUM possible infrastructure configuration. Another team needs fine-grained control over tasks, networking, and container integration in an orchestrator.

Which pairing makes the most sense?

options.text: App Runner is for batch jobs; otherwise the two are identical, only pricing differs
Minimum config = App Runner; fine-grained container control = ECS/Fargate
Minimum config = ECS/Fargate; fine-grained tasks and networking = App Runner
Both only run on Outposts, the hardware requirement for containers

questions.explanation: AWS App Runner is the minimum-configuration path to publish a containerized web app/API (automated build, deploy, and scale). Amazon ECS/Fargate provides more control over tasks, networking, and container orchestration, at the cost of more configuration.

whyNots.A: App Runner is for web apps/APIs (not batch jobs, which is Batch), and the two are NOT identical — they differ in control versus simplicity.
whyNots.C: Reverses them — App Runner abstracts configuration, while ECS/Fargate provides control.
whyNots.D: Neither requires Outposts.

hints: Think about abstraction: App Runner hides almost everything for minimal configuration, while ECS/Fargate gives more control over tasks and networking.
Remember that App Runner is for simple web apps, and ECS/Fargate is for orchestration with more control.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) simple website with fixed pricing; (2) fully managed containerized API; (3) hundreds of thousands of batch jobs; (4) AWS compute inside your own data center.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service has its role: Lightsail (simple website, fixed price), App Runner (fully managed containerized API), AWS Batch (batch jobs at scale), and Outposts (AWS compute on-premises). Option C matches all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps Lightsail with App Runner and Batch with Outposts.
whyNots.B: Completely reversed; none of the positions match the right role.
whyNots.D: Shuffles everything — Batch is not a simple website.

hints: Match each service to its common use: a simple website is Lightsail, a managed container API is App Runner, batch jobs are Batch, and AWS in your data center is Outposts.
The correct mapping keeps each service in its usual role.

questions.stem:
A site behind an Application Load Balancer needs HTTPS with a TLS certificate, and the team does not want to pay for the certificate or worry about manually renewing it every year.

Which service provisions and renews the certificate automatically?
questions.explanation: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions free public SSL/TLS certificates and renews them automatically (DNS validation, ~45 days before expiry, keeping the same ARN), deploying them to ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway. It eliminates manual certificate management.

whyNots.A: CloudHSM is a dedicated HSM for keys — it does not issue or renew public TLS certificates.
whyNots.B: KMS manages encryption KEYS — it does not issue TLS certificates.
whyNots.C: Secrets Manager stores secrets (passwords/keys) — it is not a TLS certificate.

hints: Remember that a free public SSL/TLS certificate with automatic renewal for ELB/CloudFront is ACM.
ACM handles certificates; KMS and CloudHSM handle encryption keys — these are different things.

questions.stem:
The company wants to inspect and filter ALL traffic entering and leaving the VPC (including via Internet Gateway, NAT, VPN), with managed IDS/IPS capability.

Which service is a network firewall at the VPC perimeter?
questions.explanation: AWS Network Firewall is a managed, stateful network firewall (with IDS/IPS) for the VPC, filtering traffic at the perimeter — to/from Internet Gateway, NAT, VPN, or Direct Connect. It goes beyond IP/port (can filter domain/protocol/payload).

whyNots.B: Detective investigates incidents — it is not a firewall.
whyNots.C: WAF is a web application firewall (HTTP/S), attached to CloudFront/ALB — not the VPC network perimeter.
whyNots.D: Security Group is an instance-level firewall (L3/L4) — it does not inspect the VPC perimeter with IDS/IPS.

hints: Remember that a managed, stateful network firewall at the VPC perimeter with IDS/IPS is Network Firewall.
WAF is for web applications (HTTP); security groups and NACLs are L3/L4 per instance/subnet. For the whole VPC perimeter, use Network Firewall.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) block SQL injection and XSS in HTTP requests to a web application on CloudFront/ALB; (2) filter all network traffic entering/leaving the VPC with IDS/IPS.

Which pair matches (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: AWS WAF is the web application firewall (layer 7) that blocks SQLi/XSS in HTTP requests to CloudFront/ALB. AWS Network Firewall is the network firewall that filters all traffic at the VPC perimeter with IDS/IPS. Option B makes the right association.

whyNots.A: Reverses them — SQLi/XSS in a web app is WAF; VPC network traffic is Network Firewall.
whyNots.C: Security Group does not inspect HTTP content (SQLi/XSS) — that is WAF.
whyNots.D: NACL is L3/L4 per subnet — it is not the web application firewall asked for in (1).

hints: Think about the layer: SQLi/XSS in a web app is WAF (layer 7); VPC network traffic is Network Firewall.
Remember that WAF protects the application, while Network Firewall protects the VPC network.

questions.stem:
A company with many accounts in an Organization wants to apply and MAINTAIN a consistent WAF policy (and firewall rules) across all accounts and VPCs, with new accounts automatically inheriting it.

Which service manages firewalls centrally across accounts?

options.text: AWS WAF configured account by account

questions.explanation: AWS Firewall Manager centrally manages firewall policies (WAF rules, Shield Advanced, Network Firewall, and security groups) across multiple accounts and VPCs via Organizations — new accounts inherit the policy automatically. It ensures consistency at scale.

whyNots.A: ACM is for TLS certificates — it does not manage firewall policies.
whyNots.B: Configuring WAF account by account is neither central nor automatically consistent — the opposite of what is asked.
whyNots.D: Detective investigates incidents — it does not apply firewall policies.

hints: Remember that applying firewall policies (WAF/Shield/Network Firewall/security groups) centrally across many accounts is Firewall Manager (via Organizations).
New accounts inherit the policy automatically.

questions.stem:
After a security alert, the team needs to INVESTIGATE thoroughly: correlate logs, review related historical activity, and discover the root cause and scope of the incident.

Which service is built for this investigation?
questions.explanation: Amazon Detective automatically collects logs and uses ML, statistical analysis, and graph theory to build a linked view of data, helping investigate incidents, review related historical activity, and determine root cause and scope. It ingests findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and others.

whyNots.A: ACM is for TLS certificates — it does not investigate incidents.
whyNots.B: Lightsail is a simple VPS — unrelated to investigation.
whyNots.C: Budgets is for cost — not security investigation.

hints: Remember that investigating root cause by correlating logs with graphs and ML is Amazon Detective.
GuardDuty DETECTS the threat; Detective helps INVESTIGATE it in depth.

questions.stem:
Distinguish three roles: (1) DETECT malicious activity; (2) AGGREGATE and prioritize findings in a dashboard; (3) INVESTIGATE root cause in depth.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: The three complement each other: Amazon GuardDuty detects malicious activity, AWS Security Hub aggregates and prioritizes findings in a dashboard, and Amazon Detective investigates deeply to find root cause. Option A matches all three roles.

whyNots.B: Starts with Detective as the detector — wrong; GuardDuty does the detection.
whyNots.C: Reverses aggregation and detection roles.
whyNots.D: Swaps Detective and Security Hub — aggregation is Security Hub; investigation is Detective.

hints: Match each role to the service: detect is GuardDuty, aggregate/prioritize is Security Hub, investigate is Detective.
The correct mapping keeps each service in its usual role.

questions.stem:
Reinforcement: you need to store an RDS password and ROTATE it automatically every 30 days without touching code.

Which service provides native automatic rotation?
questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets (such as the RDS password) with native automatic rotation (via Lambda), at configurable intervals, without touching code — plus cross-region replication. It is the choice when the requirement is automatic rotation.

whyNots.A: Parameter Store stores the value but does not automatically rotate credentials.
whyNots.C: ACM manages TLS certificates — not database passwords.
whyNots.D: Detective investigates incidents — it does not store or rotate secrets.

hints: Remember that a secret with native automatic rotation is Secrets Manager.
Parameter Store can hold a secret but does not rotate it on its own; ACM is for certificates, not passwords.

questions.stem:
An architect confuses the roles: what manages TLS CERTIFICATES (identity/encryption in transit) and what manages ENCRYPTION KEYS (data at rest)?

Which association is correct?

options.text: They both do the same thing
TLS certificates = ACM; encryption keys = KMS

questions.explanation: AWS Certificate Manager manages SSL/TLS certificates (site identity and encryption in transit, HTTPS). AWS KMS manages encryption keys (data at rest in S3, EBS, RDS, etc.). They are distinct and complementary responsibilities.

whyNots.A: They do not do the same thing — TLS certificate vs encryption key.
whyNots.B: TLS certificates are ACM, not Secrets Manager.
whyNots.D: Reverses them — certificate is ACM; key is KMS.

hints: Remember that ACM is for TLS certificates (HTTPS) and KMS is for encryption keys (S3/EBS/RDS).
A certificate proves identity and encrypts data in transit; a key encrypts data at rest.

questions.stem:
You want to serve a site over HTTPS via CloudFront, with the TLS certificate managed by AWS and renewed automatically.

Where do you provision that certificate?

options.text: Generate a certificate manually and upload it by FTP to the distribution
In Amazon S3 as an object, which CloudFront reads and renews automatically
In AWS Budgets, which manages certificates along with costs
In AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and associate it with the CloudFront distribution

questions.explanation: You provision the TLS certificate in ACM (free, with automatic renewal) and associate it with the CloudFront distribution to serve the site over HTTPS — without having to generate and renew the certificate manually.

whyNots.A: A manual certificate via FTP is exactly the work/risk that ACM eliminates.
whyNots.B: S3 stores objects — it is not where you manage the CloudFront TLS certificate.
whyNots.C: Budgets is for cost — unrelated to certificates.

hints: Remember that you provision the certificate in ACM and associate it with CloudFront — automatic renewal, no headache.
ACM integrates natively with CloudFront, ELB, and API Gateway.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) free TLS certificate with auto-renewal; (2) network firewall at the VPC perimeter; (3) central firewall policy across accounts; (4) investigate the root cause of an incident.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: ACM → Network Firewall → Firewall Manager → Detective
Detective → Firewall Manager → ACM → Network Firewall
Firewall Manager → Detective → Network Firewall → ACM
Network Firewall → ACM → Detective → Firewall Manager

questions.explanation: Each service has its role: ACM (TLS certificate with auto-renewal), Network Firewall (network firewall at the VPC perimeter), Firewall Manager (central firewall policy across accounts), and Detective (investigation/root cause). Option A matches all four.

whyNots.B: Shuffles everything — Detective is not a certificate.
whyNots.C: Completely reversed; none of the positions match the right role.
whyNots.D: Swaps ACM with Network Firewall and Detective with Firewall Manager.

hints: Map each need to its service: TLS certificate is ACM, VPC network firewall is Network Firewall, central policy is Firewall Manager, investigation is Detective.
The correct mapping keeps each service in its usual role.

questions.stem:
A company with more than 5,000 users needs a REAL Microsoft Active Directory managed in AWS, with a trust relationship with the on-premises AD and support for Windows workloads (RDS for SQL Server, FSx for Windows).

Which Directory Service option fits?
questions.explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a real Microsoft Active Directory managed by AWS (two DCs in distinct AZs), with support for trusts with on-premises AD and Windows workloads (RDS SQL Server, FSx for Windows, EC2 domain join). It is the choice for a complete AD at scale.

whyNots.A: Cognito is for app user authentication (web/mobile) — not a corporate Active Directory.
whyNots.C: Simple AD is low cost/scale (≤5,000) and does NOT support trusts.
whyNots.D: AD Connector is a proxy to an existing on-premises AD — it is not a complete managed AD in AWS.

hints: Think about the requirements: real Microsoft AD, trust, more than 5,000 users, Windows workloads — that points to AWS Managed Microsoft AD.
Remember that Simple AD does not support trusts, and AD Connector only proxies to an existing on-premises AD.

questions.stem:
The company already has an on-premises Active Directory and wants AWS services to authenticate against that EXISTING directory, forwarding requests WITHOUT storing or caching directory data in the cloud.

Which Directory Service option is indicated?
questions.explanation: AD Connector is a directory gateway that forwards (proxies) AWS service authentication requests to your existing on-premises Active Directory, without caching information in the cloud. It is ideal for reusing an on-premises directory with AWS services.

whyNots.A: IAM Identity Center is workforce SSO — it is not the gateway to on-premises AD in this sense.
whyNots.B: Managed Microsoft AD creates a new managed AD in AWS — the scenario asks to use the existing on-premises AD.
whyNots.D: Simple AD is its own directory (Samba) in AWS — it does not proxy to on-premises AD.

hints: Think about using the EXISTING on-premises AD as a proxy without caching in the cloud — that is AD Connector (a gateway).
If you wanted a new AD in the cloud, you would choose Managed Microsoft AD.

questions.stem:
A small company (fewer than 5,000 users) wants a low-cost AD-compatible directory with accounts/groups, EC2 domain join, and Kerberos SSO — and does NOT need a trust relationship with another AD.

Which Directory Service option is the most economical and adequate?
questions.explanation: Simple AD is a managed directory based on Samba 4, low cost and scale (≤5,000 users), with a subset of AD (accounts, groups, EC2 domain join, Kerberos SSO, Group Policies). It does not support trust relationships — suitable when trust is not needed.

whyNots.A: CloudHSM is an HSM for keys — not a directory.
whyNots.B: AD Connector is a proxy to on-premises AD — the scenario wants a simple own directory in AWS.
whyNots.C: Managed Microsoft AD is more robust/expensive — overkill for this small case without trust.

hints: Think about a small, low-cost, AD-compatible directory without trust — that is Simple AD (based on Samba 4).
If trust or more than 5,000 users were needed, Managed Microsoft AD would be the choice.

questions.stem:
Three scenarios: (1) real managed AD with trust and Windows workloads; (2) proxy to existing on-premises AD without caching; (3) small, low-cost directory without trust.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?

options.text: Managed Microsoft AD → AD Connector → Simple AD
Managed Microsoft AD → Simple AD → AD Connector
Simple AD → Managed Microsoft AD → AD Connector
AD Connector → Simple AD → Managed Microsoft AD

questions.explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD (real AD with trust and Windows workloads); AD Connector (proxy to existing on-premises AD, no cache); Simple AD (small, low-cost directory without trust). Option A matches all three.

whyNots.B: Swaps Simple AD and AD Connector in the last two positions.
whyNots.C: Starts with Simple AD for the trust case — wrong; trust requires Managed Microsoft AD.
whyNots.D: Reverses the order — AD Connector is not the real AD with trust.

hints: Match each scenario: real AD with trust is Managed Microsoft AD; proxy to on-premises is AD Connector; small/low-cost without trust is Simple AD.
The correct mapping keeps each option in its usual role.

questions.stem:
A company wants to give remote employees a complete virtual desktop (Windows or Linux), persistent and managed in the cloud, accessible from anywhere.

Which service delivers this virtual desktop (VDI)?
questions.explanation: Amazon WorkSpaces provides persistent, managed virtual desktops (VDI) in the cloud — Windows or Linux — accessible from anywhere. It is ideal for remote workers who need a complete, always-available desktop.

whyNots.A: Lightsail is a VPS — not an end-user desktop (VDI).
whyNots.C: AppStream 2.0 streams individual applications, not the whole persistent desktop.
whyNots.D: Lambda is serverless functions — not a virtual desktop.

hints: Remember that a complete, persistent virtual desktop in the cloud (VDI) is Amazon WorkSpaces.
If the need were only to stream a single application, AppStream would be the choice.

questions.stem:
A university wants to give each student access to ONE specific piece of software (for example, a CAD app) via browser, on any computer, without installing anything locally, delivered by streaming.

Which service streams the application to users?
questions.explanation: Amazon AppStream 2.0 is application streaming: it delivers individual applications to users via browser with no local installation, typically non-persistent. It is perfect for giving students access to software on any computer, demos, and training. (It has been regrouped as WorkSpaces Applications.)

whyNots.A: Batch runs batch jobs — it does not stream interactive apps.
whyNots.B: WorkSpaces delivers the whole persistent desktop — overkill when only one app is needed.
whyNots.D: S3 is object storage — it does not stream applications.

hints: Think about streaming a single application via browser with no installation — that is AppStream 2.0 (application streaming).
WorkSpaces delivers the whole desktop; AppStream delivers only the app.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) deliver a complete, persistent virtual desktop; (2) stream only a specific application, without persistence.

Which pair matches (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Amazon WorkSpaces delivers the complete, persistent virtual desktop (VDI); AppStream 2.0 streams only a specific application, usually without persistence. Option D makes the right association.

whyNots.A: Swaps the roles and includes Lightsail inappropriately.
whyNots.B: Lightsail is a VPS, not an end-user virtual desktop.
whyNots.C: Reverses them — the full desktop is WorkSpaces; the streamed app is AppStream.

hints: Remember: a complete persistent desktop is WorkSpaces; a streamed non-persistent app is AppStream 2.0.
WorkSpaces equals desktop; AppStream equals application.

questions.stem:
You want to domain-join Windows EC2 instances to a managed Active Directory in AWS, with centralized authentication and Group Policies.

Which service provides this managed AD?

options.text: Amazon Inspector, which manages the AD domain
Amazon Cognito, performing EC2 domain join
AWS WAF, applying Group Policies on EC2

questions.explanation: AWS Directory Service (Managed Microsoft AD) provides a managed Active Directory for domain-joining Windows EC2 instances, with centralized authentication, Group Policies, and integration with Windows workloads. It is the foundation of corporate identity in AWS.

whyNots.B: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities — it is not a directory.
whyNots.C: Cognito authenticates web/mobile application users — it is not AD for Windows EC2 domain join.
whyNots.D: WAF is a web application firewall — unrelated to Active Directory.

hints: Think about domain-joining EC2 Windows + Group Policies + centralized auth — that is a managed AD, AWS Directory Service (Managed Microsoft AD).
Remember that Cognito is for app users, not corporate Active Directory.

questions.stem:
A software vendor wants to offer DEMOS and TRIALS of its desktop application without the customer needing to download or install anything.

Which service delivers the app via streaming for this case?
questions.explanation: Amazon AppStream 2.0 lets you stream applications via browser without download or installation — perfect for vendors offering demos, trials, and training of their software, and for giving users access to apps on any computer.

whyNots.A: Polly is text-to-speech — unrelated to application streaming.
whyNots.C: CodeDeploy automates software deployment — it does not stream apps to end users.
whyNots.D: WorkSpaces delivers the complete desktop — unnecessary for demonstrating a single app.

hints: Think about demos or trials of an app without any installation — that is AppStream 2.0 (application streaming).
The customer runs the app in the browser; nothing is downloaded or installed.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) real managed AD with trust; (2) proxy to existing on-premises AD; (3) persistent virtual desktop; (4) application streaming.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: WorkSpaces → AppStream 2.0 → Managed Microsoft AD → AD Connector
AD Connector → Managed Microsoft AD → AppStream 2.0 → WorkSpaces
Managed Microsoft AD → AD Connector → WorkSpaces → AppStream 2.0
Managed Microsoft AD → WorkSpaces → AD Connector → AppStream 2.0

questions.explanation: Each service has its role: Managed Microsoft AD (real AD with trust), AD Connector (proxy to on-premises AD), WorkSpaces (persistent virtual desktop), and AppStream 2.0 (application streaming). Option C matches all four.

whyNots.A: Shuffles everything — WorkSpaces is not AD with trust.
whyNots.B: Swaps Managed Microsoft AD with AD Connector and WorkSpaces with AppStream.
whyNots.D: Swaps AD Connector with WorkSpaces in position.

hints: Map each need to its service: AD with trust is Managed Microsoft AD; on-premises proxy is AD Connector; desktop is WorkSpaces; app streaming is AppStream.
The correct mapping keeps each service in its usual role.

questions.stem:
An application needs to send transactional emails (order confirmation, password reset) at scale, via API or SMTP.

Which service is dedicated to sending email?
questions.explanation: Amazon SES (Simple Email Service) is the dedicated email service, with API and SMTP interface, ideal for sending transactional (confirmations, resets) and mass email at scale, also handling deliverability.

whyNots.A: SQS is a message queue between systems — it does not send email to users.
whyNots.B: SNS sends pub/sub notifications (SMS, push, simple email) — it is not the dedicated rich/transactional email service.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not send email.

hints: Remember that 'Email Service' is in the name — SES is the dedicated email service (API and SMTP).
SNS sends multi-channel notifications (SMS/push), but rich/mass application email is SES.

questions.stem:
An alerting system needs to send TEXT messages (SMS) to users' phones when a critical event occurs.

Which service sends SMS to users?
questions.explanation: Amazon SNS can send SMS messages directly to users' phones (plus mobile push, email, and HTTP). It is the choice for SMS alerts.

whyNots.B: Lambda executes code — it would need a messaging service (SNS) to send the SMS.
whyNots.C: SES sends email — not SMS.
whyNots.D: SQS is a queue between systems — it does not send SMS to users.

hints: Remember that SMS (and mobile push) to users is SNS, which has SMS and push notification channels.
SES is email only; for text to a phone, use SNS.

questions.stem:
A mobile app (iOS/Android) needs to receive PUSH notifications (via APNs/FCM) when there are updates.

Which service delivers push notifications to mobile apps?
questions.explanation: Amazon SNS supports mobile push, integrating with APNs (Apple) and FCM (Google) to deliver push notifications to iOS/Android apps. It is the right channel for push notifications.

whyNots.A: Athena is SQL query — it does not send push.
whyNots.C: SES is email — not mobile push.
whyNots.D: EBS is block storage — unrelated to push.

hints: Think about push to iOS/Android (APNs/FCM) — that is SNS mobile push.
SNS talks to APNs (Apple) and FCM (Google) to deliver the notification.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) send rich/mass emails from an application (with SMTP and deliverability); (2) send SMS, mobile push, or notify multiple subscribers.

Which pair matches (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Amazon SES is the dedicated email service (transactional/marketing, SMTP, deliverability). Amazon SNS is multi-channel pub/sub notifications (SMS, push, simple email, HTTP, fan-out). Option C makes the right association.

whyNots.A: Reverses them — rich email is SES; SMS/push is SNS.
whyNots.B: SQS does not send SMS/push to users; that is SNS.
whyNots.D: SQS is a queue between systems — it is not the email service.

hints: Match the channel to the service: rich/mass email is SES; SMS/push/notifying subscribers is SNS.
Remember: SES = email service; SNS = notification service.

questions.stem:
Reinforcement: an event must be delivered simultaneously to multiple SQS queues (each belonging to a different system), in a fan-out pattern.

Which service publishes the event to all subscribers?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch, the native pub/sub for queues
AWS Config, which publishes to subscribers
Amazon SES, which fan-outs to SQS queues
Amazon SNS (topic with fan-out to SQS queues)

questions.explanation: Amazon SNS is pub/sub: a topic publishes the event and each subscriber (multiple SQS queues, Lambda, etc.) receives its own copy — the fan-out pattern. It decouples one producer from many consumers.

whyNots.A: CloudWatch is for metrics/logs — it is not the event pub/sub for queues.
whyNots.B: Config evaluates compliance — it does not publish events to subscribers.
whyNots.C: SES is email — it does not fan out to SQS queues.

hints: Think about one event to many subscribers (SQS queues) — that is SNS in a fan-out pattern (pub/sub).
SNS publishes; each subscribed SQS queue receives its own copy.

questions.stem:
A company wants to monitor the SENDING REPUTATION of its emails — bounce and complaint rates — so it does not end up on blacklists.

Which service handles email sending with this deliverability control?
questions.explanation: Amazon SES is the email service that monitors deliverability — bounce and complaint rates — helping maintain sending reputation and avoid blacklists. It is the right service for email with this control.

whyNots.B: SNS is multi-channel notification — it is not the email service with deliverability management.
whyNots.C: SQS is a queue between systems — it does not send email.
whyNots.D: Pinpoint used SES under the hood, but it is reaching END OF SUPPORT (Oct 30, 2026) — it is not the current choice.

hints: Think about email sending plus bounce/complaint metrics (deliverability) — that is SES.
Managing sending reputation is a core part of SES.

questions.stem:
A company wants to RECEIVE inbound emails on its own domain and, upon receipt, save the content to S3 and trigger a Lambda to process it.

Which service can receive the email and trigger those actions?

options.text: Amazon SNS (subscribes the domain via SMTP)
Amazon Route 53 (the MX record already receives everything)

questions.explanation: Amazon SES also receives emails (inbound): when a message arrives at the configured domain, it can save to S3, trigger a Lambda function, or publish to an SNS topic for processing. It is email in both directions.

whyNots.A: SNS is pub/sub notification — it does not receive inbound SMTP email.
whyNots.C: EBS is disk — it does not receive email.
whyNots.D: Route 53 is DNS (although it points the MX record) — SES receives and processes the email.

hints: SES does not only SEND — it also RECEIVES email (inbound) and can trigger S3/Lambda/SNS upon receipt.
It is the email service on both sides: sending and receiving.

questions.stem:
A notification flow requires messages to reach subscribers in EXACT order and without duplication (e.g., synchronizing ordered events with SQS FIFO queues).

Which SNS resource provides order and no duplication?
questions.explanation: SNS has FIFO topics that preserve order and avoid duplication, ideal for ordered fan-out to SQS FIFO queues. Standard topics prioritize throughput with best-effort ordering.

whyNots.A: Standard is best-effort on order and may duplicate — it does not guarantee ordering.
whyNots.B: SES is email — not a notification ordering mechanism.
whyNots.D: S3 is storage — not an ordered notification topic.

hints: Strict order + no duplicates in SNS = FIFO topic (combines with SQS FIFO queues).
Standard is high throughput, but best-effort order.

questions.stem:
You want administrators to receive a simple email whenever a CloudWatch alarm fires, without building a full email service.

Which service delivers this simple email/SMS notification to subscribers?

options.text: AWS Batch, which sends the email in batch
Amazon SES with a campaign directly tied to the alarm
Amazon SNS (email/SMS subscription to the topic)

questions.explanation: Amazon SNS lets subscribers (email, SMS) receive simple notifications from a topic — the standard pattern for operational alerts, such as a CloudWatch alarm publishing to an SNS topic that notifies administrators.

whyNots.A: Batch runs batch jobs — it does not notify subscribers.
whyNots.B: SES with a campaign is overkill for a simple operational alert; the direct path is SNS.
whyNots.C: QuickSight is BI/dashboards — it does not send alarm notifications.

hints: alarm → SNS topic → subscribers receive simple email/SMS. This is the classic operational notification path.
For simple alerts to subscribers, SNS is enough; SES is for rich/mass application email.

questions.stem:
Three needs: (1) send a rich transactional email from an application; (2) send an SMS alert to a phone; (3) send a push notification to a mobile app.

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Rich transactional application email is SES; SMS to a phone is SNS; push to a mobile app is also SNS (via APNs/FCM). Option A respects all three channels.

whyNots.B: Puts SES in the middle and swaps the SNS channels in a way that does not match the statement.
whyNots.C: SQS is a queue between systems — it does not send email/SMS/push to users.
whyNots.D: Starts with SNS for rich email — application email is SES; and SQS does not notify users.

hints: Rich email = SES; SMS = SNS; mobile push = SNS.
SES covers email; SNS covers SMS and push.

questions.stem:
A team needs to store, version, and scan the application's Docker images, and have ECS/EKS pull them to run.

Which service is the managed container image registry?

options.text: Amazon ECS, which embeds the registry
Amazon S3, with native image scanning

questions.explanation: Amazon ECR is the managed container image registry (Docker/OCI): it stores, versions, scans for vulnerabilities, and distributes images, integrating with ECS, EKS, and CI/CD. It is where orchestrators pull the image to run.

whyNots.A: ECS runs containers — it is not the image registry (that is ECR).
whyNots.C: CodeCommit is a Git source-code repository — not for container images.
whyNots.D: S3 stores generic objects — it is not a container image registry with scanning/versioning.

hints: 'Registry' of container images = ECR (Elastic Container Registry).
ECR stores/scans images; ECS/EKS run them.

questions.stem:
In ECS, you need to define WHICH image to use, how much CPU/memory, which ports and volumes — the application blueprint in JSON.

Which ECS element is this blueprint?
questions.explanation: The task definition is the blueprint (JSON) of the application in ECS: it specifies the image, CPU/memory, ports, volumes, and variables. It is the mold from which running tasks (instances) are created.

whyNots.A: Capacity provider manages capacity (Fargate/EC2) — not the blueprint.
whyNots.B: Cluster is the infrastructure/grouping — not the application blueprint.
whyNots.D: Service keeps N tasks running — not the blueprint itself.

hints: The blueprint (image, CPU/memory, ports) = task definition.
The task definition is the mold; the task is the running instance of it.

questions.stem:
You want to ensure there are ALWAYS, for example, 4 copies of the task running; if one fails, another must automatically start to maintain that number.

Which ECS element maintains the desired number of tasks?
questions.explanation: The ECS Service maintains the desired number of tasks running simultaneously: if a task fails or stops, the service scheduler starts another from the task definition to maintain the desired count. It also integrates with ELB and supports auto scaling.

whyNots.A: Cluster is the infrastructure/grouping — it does not manage the desired number of tasks.
whyNots.B: Task definition is the blueprint — it does not keep tasks running.
whyNots.C: ECR is the image registry — it does not orchestrate execution.

hints: Keeping N tasks running and replacing failed ones = ECS Service (the scheduler handles it).
The service also integrates with ELB and supports auto scaling.

questions.stem:
Four ECS concepts: (1) the application JSON blueprint; (2) a running instance; (3) what keeps N copies running; (4) the grouping that provides infrastructure capacity.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: The ECS hierarchy: task definition (blueprint) → task (running instance) → service (keeps N tasks and replaces failures) → cluster (infrastructure that hosts everything). Option A respects all four.

whyNots.B: Inverts task with task definition and scrambles service/cluster.
whyNots.C: Starts with service and puts cluster before task — out of order.
whyNots.D: Puts cluster as the blueprint — wrong; the blueprint is the task definition.

hints: Blueprint = task definition; instance = task; keeps N = service; infrastructure = cluster.
Only option A follows the natural ECS order.

questions.stem:
A batch processing job runs in Fargate containers, is interruption-tolerant, and the team wants to greatly reduce cost, accepting that tasks may be interrupted with a 2-minute warning.

Which option delivers up to 70% discount for this workload?
questions.explanation: Fargate Spot runs tasks on spare capacity with up to 70% discount over Fargate on-demand, but tasks are interruptible (2-minute warning). It is ideal for interruption-tolerant workloads such as batch and dev/staging.

whyNots.A: EC2 RIs are a long-term instance commitment — not the case for interruptible Fargate batch.
whyNots.C: Fargate on-demand is reliable but does not give the aggressive Spot discount for a workload that accepts interruption.
whyNots.D: Dedicated Hosts are for licensing/compliance on EC2 — not the cheap interruptible container model.

hints: Interruption-tolerant container + up to 70% off + 2-minute warning = Fargate Spot (spare capacity).
It is the 'Spot' of the Fargate world — cheap, but interruptible.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) reliable on-demand capacity for the production base that cannot be interrupted; (2) cheap, interruptible capacity to absorb spikes/batch.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Fargate on-demand provides reliable capacity for the production base; Fargate Spot provides cheap, interruptible capacity for spikes/batch. They can be combined (stable on-demand base + Spot burst at lower cost). Option C is correct.

whyNots.A: Reversed — reliable is on-demand; cheap interruptible is Spot.
whyNots.B: Mixes EC2 Spot inappropriately; the context is Fargate.
whyNots.D: Reserved Instances are an EC2 commitment, not Fargate interruptible burst capacity.

hints: Reliable base = Fargate on-demand; cheap interruptible spikes/batch = Fargate Spot.
You can mix the two (on-demand base + Spot burst).

questions.stem:
You want the service task count to automatically increase and decrease to keep average CPU utilization around 60%.

Which resource does this most simply?

options.text: Use ECR, which scales tasks according to image pulls
Manually edit the task definition every time CPU varies
Increase the cluster size manually whenever CPU rises
ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking (e.g., target average CPU)

questions.explanation: ECS Service Auto Scaling with target tracking keeps a metric at a target value (e.g., average CPU at 60%, or ALBRequestCountPerTarget) by automatically adjusting the number of service tasks — without manually defining alarms.

whyNots.A: ECR is an image registry — it does not scale the service.
whyNots.B: Editing the task definition manually does not automatically scale the number of tasks.
whyNots.C: Manually tweaking the cluster is the opposite of automatic.

hints: Keeping a metric at a target (CPU 60%) by adjusting the number of tasks = ECS Service Auto Scaling, target tracking.
Target tracking avoids creating alarms manually — you just set the target.

questions.stem:
The ideal scale trigger is not CPU or memory, but the number of MESSAGES waiting in an SQS queue that the tasks process.

How do you scale the ECS service by this metric?

options.text: ECS Service Auto Scaling with custom metric (e.g., SQS queue size in CloudWatch)
Replace ECS with Lightsail, which already auto-scales containers by queue
It is not possible to scale an ECS service by queue; only CPU and memory can be metrics
Use CloudFront signed URLs to control queue message throughput

questions.explanation: ECS Service Auto Scaling accepts custom metrics (via Application Auto Scaling/CloudWatch), such as the number of messages in an SQS queue. When CPU/memory do not reflect real load, scaling by queue depth is more appropriate.

whyNots.B: Lightsail is a simple VPS — it does not solve ECS queue-based scaling.
whyNots.C: It is possible — custom metrics (queue size) are a classic case.
whyNots.D: Signed URLs are for S3/CloudFront — nothing to do with scaling.

hints: CPU/memory are not always the best signal; you can scale by a CUSTOM metric, such as the SQS queue size.
ECS Application Auto Scaling accepts custom CloudWatch metrics.

questions.stem:
In a pipeline: you package the image, store it in a registry, and run it in containers without managing servers.

Which combination represents this flow?

options.text: Image in ECS → run in ECR
Image in ECR → run in ECS/Fargate
Image in Lightsail → run in Athena
Image in S3 → run in CloudFront

questions.explanation: The typical flow: the image is packaged and stored in ECR (registry), then run in containers by ECS with Fargate (serverless, no server management). ECR stores; ECS/Fargate runs.

whyNots.A: Reversed — the image lives in ECR (registry), not ECS; ECS executes.
whyNots.C: Lightsail/Athena are not registry or container orchestrator in this flow.
whyNots.D: S3/CloudFront are storage/CDN — they do not run containers.

hints: ECR stores the image; ECS/Fargate runs it (serverless).
Registry = ECR; orchestrator/execution = ECS (with Fargate).

questions.stem:
Four roles: (1) image registry; (2) application blueprint; (3) keeps N tasks running; (4) serverless on-demand container capacity.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each element has its role: ECR (image registry), task definition (application blueprint), service (keeps N tasks), and Fargate (serverless on-demand container capacity). Option C respects all four.

whyNots.A: Scrambles everything — service is not an image registry.
whyNots.B: Swaps ECR with task definition and service with Fargate.
whyNots.D: Completely reversed; no position matches the right role.

hints: Registry = ECR; blueprint = task definition; keeps N = service; serverless on-demand = Fargate.
Only option C keeps each piece in its role.

questions.stem:
You need to point the ROOT domain (apex, e.g., example.com, without www) to an Application Load Balancer. A CNAME at the apex is not allowed.

Which Route 53 record type solves this?
questions.explanation: The Alias record is specific to Route 53 and works at the zone apex (root domain), pointing to AWS resources such as ELB, CloudFront, and S3. CNAME is not allowed at the apex. Also, alias queries to AWS resources are free.

whyNots.A: TXT holds text (e.g., domain verification) — it does not route to the ALB.
whyNots.B: CNAME does not work at the zone apex — only for subdomains.
whyNots.C: MX is for mail servers — it does not point the apex to the ALB.

hints: Pointing the APEX (root domain) to an AWS resource (ELB/CloudFront/S3) = Alias record (CNAME does not work at the apex).
Alias to an AWS resource is also free for queries.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) points the apex to AWS resources and is free for queries to those resources; (2) points a name to any domain, but not at the apex, and is charged.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Alias is the Route 53 record that works at the apex, points to AWS resources, and is free for those queries. CNAME points to any domain, does not work at the apex, and is charged. Option A is correct.

whyNots.B: MX/TXT are for mail/text — not the requested distinction.
whyNots.C: Reversed — apex/free/AWS is Alias; the standard charged one is CNAME.
whyNots.D: A/NS are other types — they do not match the statement.

hints: Apex + AWS resources + free = Alias; any domain, not at apex, charged = CNAME.
Alias is exclusive to Route 53; CNAME is standard DNS.

questions.stem:
An internal application needs DNS names (e.g., db.internal.local) that only resolve INSIDE the VPCs, without exposing the records (names/IPs) to the internet.

Which Route 53 resource meets this?
questions.explanation: A Route 53 private hosted zone provides authoritative DNS only inside the associated VPCs, without exposing the records (names and IPs) to the internet. It is ideal for internal application names.

whyNots.A: Public hosted zone exposes records on the internet — the opposite of the request.
whyNots.C: Public domain registration is for an internet domain — not VPC internal DNS.
whyNots.D: Health check monitors endpoint health — not an internal DNS zone.

hints: Internal DNS, only inside the VPC, without exposing to the internet = private hosted zone.
The private hosted zone is associated with VPCs and only answers from inside them.

questions.stem:
ON-PREMISES servers need to resolve DNS names hosted in AWS (e.g., a private hosted zone), sending queries FROM OUTSIDE into the VPC, over Direct Connect.

Which Route 53 Resolver resource meets this?
questions.explanation: The Route 53 Resolver Inbound endpoint lets on-premises resources (or another VPC) send DNS queries INTO the VPC, resolving names hosted in AWS (such as a private hosted zone), typically over VPN/Direct Connect.

whyNots.A: Outbound endpoint is the opposite: VPC querying on-premises DNS.
whyNots.B: Alias record is a record type — not the hybrid DNS endpoint.
whyNots.D: Health check monitors health — it does not resolve hybrid DNS.

hints: Queries ENTERING (on-premises → AWS DNS) = Inbound endpoint.
'Inbound' = into the VPC. The on-prem sends the query to the Resolver.

questions.stem:
Distinguish in Route 53 Resolver: (1) on-premises queries resolving AWS DNS; (2) VPC queries resolving on-premises DNS.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Inbound endpoint = queries entering the VPC (on-premises resolves AWS DNS). Outbound endpoint = queries leaving the VPC (the VPC resolves on-premises DNS via forwarding rules). Option D makes the correct association.

whyNots.A: Public/private hosted zone are zone types, not the hybrid endpoints.
whyNots.B: Alias/CNAME are record types, not Resolver endpoints.
whyNots.C: Reversed — on-prem→AWS is inbound; VPC→on-prem is outbound.

hints: On-prem → AWS = inbound (entering); VPC → on-prem = outbound (leaving).
Think by the direction of the query relative to the VPC.

questions.stem:
You have two servers that perform the same function and want Route 53 to stop sending traffic to a server that goes down, sending everything to the healthy one.

Which resource enables this health-based redirection?

options.text: Private hosted zone with internal failover
CNAME at the apex swapping to the healthy one

questions.explanation: Route 53 health checks monitor endpoint health and, combined with failover routing, redirect traffic from an unhealthy resource to a healthy one. They can also trigger CloudWatch alarms.

whyNots.B: Private hosted zone is internal DNS — it does not do health-based failover.
whyNots.C: Outbound endpoint is hybrid DNS — not the health failover mechanism.
whyNots.D: CNAME at the apex is not even allowed — and does not do health failover.

hints: Monitor health and redirect from the unhealthy to the healthy = health check + failover routing.
The health check can even follow a CloudWatch alarm.

questions.stem:
A company wants to buy and manage the domain 'mycompany.com' and use Route 53 as authoritative DNS.

Route 53 can act as?
questions.explanation: Route 53 is an authoritative DNS service and also a domain registrar — you can buy/manage the domain and host its DNS zone in the same place. It supports DNSSEC to sign the zone.

whyNots.A: Route 53 is not a load balancer (that is ELB), although it routes by DNS.
whyNots.C: Application firewall is WAF, not Route 53.
whyNots.D: CDN cache is CloudFront, not Route 53.

hints: Route 53 is a DNS service — and also a DOMAIN REGISTRAR (buy/manage the domain).
You can register the domain and host the DNS zone in the same service.

questions.stem:
You host a static website on S3 + CloudFront and want the root domain (apex) to point to the CloudFront distribution, with no extra DNS query cost.

Which record to use?

options.text: CNAME at the apex pointing to CloudFront

questions.explanation: An Alias record points the root domain (apex) to the CloudFront distribution, works at the apex (where CNAME does not work), and does not charge for queries to AWS resources. It is the right path for the S3+CloudFront static site.

whyNots.A: MX is for email — it does not point the site to CloudFront.
whyNots.B: Outbound endpoint is hybrid DNS — not related to pointing the apex.
whyNots.D: CNAME is not allowed at the apex — and would be charged.

hints: Apex → CloudFront, no query cost = Alias record.
CNAME at the apex is not even allowed.

questions.stem:
To protect the DNS zone against spoofing and cache poisoning, the company wants to cryptographically sign DNS responses.

Which Route 53 feature offers this?
questions.explanation: DNSSEC cryptographically signs zone DNS responses, protecting against spoofing and cache poisoning (forged DNS responses). Route 53 supports DNSSEC signing for hosted zones.

whyNots.A: Private hosted zone is limited to the VPC — not cryptographic signing.
whyNots.B: Alias is a routing record type — it does not sign the zone.
whyNots.C: Health check monitors health — it does not protect against DNS spoofing.

hints: Cryptographically signing DNS against spoofing/cache poisoning = DNSSEC.
Route 53 supports DNSSEC signing for hosted zones.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) point the apex to an ELB; (2) internal DNS only in the VPC; (3) on-premises resolve AWS DNS; (4) redirect from the unhealthy resource to the healthy one.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Alias → Private hosted zone → Resolver inbound endpoint → Health check failover
CNAME → Public hosted zone → Resolver outbound endpoint → Alias record
Private hosted zone → Alias → Health check failover → Resolver inbound endpoint
Health check failover → Resolver inbound endpoint → Alias → Private hosted zone
