questions.explanation: Each resource has its role: Alias (apex → AWS resource), private hosted zone (internal DNS in the VPC), Resolver inbound endpoint (on-premises resolves AWS DNS), and health check with failover (redirects from unhealthy to healthy). Option A respects all four.

whyNots.B: CNAME does not work at the apex and the rest is scrambled.
whyNots.C: Swaps roles — private hosted zone is not the apex record.
whyNots.D: Completely reversed; no position matches the right role.

hints: Apex→ELB = Alias; internal DNS = private hosted zone; on-prem resolves AWS = inbound endpoint; unhealthy→healthy = health check failover.
Only option A keeps each resource in its role.

questions.stem:
A site needs to serve STATIC content globally with low latency AND have a serverless DYNAMIC API behind it, all without servers to manage.

Which architecture meets this?

options.text: A single EC2 serving static and dynamic — with an Elastic IP it becomes serverless
CloudFront + S3 (static) and API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB (dynamic)
Only S3 with static website, no API — S3 executes the dynamic logic
Only RDS exposed to the internet — the database serves pages and API directly to the client

questions.explanation: CloudFront in front of S3 delivers static content with global low latency; API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB provide the serverless dynamic part. It is the modern serverless site pattern, with no servers to manage.

whyNots.A: A single EC2 does not give global low latency nor is it serverless, and becomes a single point of failure.
whyNots.C: Static S3 alone does not meet the dynamic API requirement.
whyNots.D: Exposing RDS to the internet is insecure and does not solve global static content.

hints: Global static = CloudFront+S3; serverless dynamic API = API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB.
No servers to manage = serverless end to end.

questions.stem:
When a business event happens (e.g., an order status changes), multiple services need to react with different rules, in a decoupled, event-driven way, with routing by event pattern.

Which service routes events to the right actions?

options.text: A cron on EC2 checking orders — frequent polling becomes event
A single SQS queue read by everyone — each consumer filters its own rule
Amazon EventBridge (rules by event pattern → Lambda/SNS/etc.)
Chained synchronous calls — simpler and equally decoupled

questions.explanation: EventBridge is the event bus: rules match event patterns and route to targets (Lambda, SNS, SQS, Step Functions). It is the foundation of event-driven architectures, decoupling the producer from many consumers with different logics.

whyNots.A: Cron on EC2 is not event-driven (and has a server to manage).
whyNots.B: A single queue does not route by pattern/rule to distinct targets.
whyNots.D: Chained synchronous calls couple services — a slow one brings down the chain.

hints: 'Route events by RULE/pattern to different targets' = EventBridge (event bus).
Each rule sends the event to the right target (Lambda, SNS, Step Functions...).

questions.stem:
The company wants to migrate an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime; the schema/code needs to be converted because they are different engines.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: Only an offline Snowball, which converts the database schema during transport
Recreate tables and data manually without a tool, the only way between engines
Copy database files with DataSync, which adjusts the SQL dialect on its own
AWS SCT (converts schema) + AWS DMS (migrates data with continuous replication)

questions.explanation: Heterogeneous migration (Oracle → Aurora PostgreSQL): first AWS SCT converts the schema and code; then DMS migrates the data with continuous replication (CDC), minimizing downtime at cutover.

whyNots.A: Snowball is offline mass data transport — it does not convert schema nor migrate a live database.
whyNots.B: Recreating manually is fragile and slow; SCT+DMS automate.
whyNots.C: DataSync transfers files — it does not migrate a live relational database with conversion.

hints: Different engines = heterogeneous = SCT to convert schema + DMS to migrate data (minimal downtime).
DMS replicates changes until cutover, reducing downtime.

questions.stem:
An application on EC2 needs to access an RDS database without embedded credentials, and the database password must be automatically ROTATED.

Which combination meets security and rotation?

options.text: IAM Role on EC2 + Secrets Manager storing and rotating the RDS password
Public S3 bucket with the password in a file — versioning already does rotation
Fixed password embedded in code, protected by EBS volume encryption
Shared root account among instances — it already comes with native rotation

questions.explanation: An IAM Role on EC2 gives temporary credentials (no embedded key) for the application to read the secret, and Secrets Manager stores and automatically rotates the RDS password (via Lambda). Covers secure access and rotation.

whyNots.B: A public bucket with the password is a serious security flaw.
whyNots.C: Password embedded in code is the classic anti-pattern — it leaks and does not rotate.
whyNots.D: Sharing the root account is forbidden and dangerous.

hints: No embedded credential = IAM Role on EC2; automatically rotated password = Secrets Manager.
The app gets the password from Secrets Manager via the role, and Secrets Manager rotates it automatically.

questions.stem:
Logs go to S3: they are accessed a lot in the first 30 days, rarely until 90 days, and then only need to be archived for 7 years for compliance, with recovery taking hours being acceptable.

Which cost strategy is ideal?

options.text: Delete logs after 30 days to save money, since the retention requirement does not apply to old logs
Lifecycle policy: Standard → Standard-IA (30d) → Glacier Deep Archive (90d), expiring at 7 years
Keep everything in S3 Standard forever, because infrequent access classes do not accept log objects
Move everything to dedicated EBS volumes, which are cheaper than S3 for rarely read files

questions.explanation: A lifecycle policy automates savings: Standard for the hot 30 days, transition to Standard-IA at 30 days, to Glacier Deep Archive at 90 days (7-year archive, acceptable hours-long recovery), and expiration at the end of retention. Minimum cost without manual work.

whyNots.A: Deleting at 30 days violates the required 7-year retention.
whyNots.C: Standard forever is the most expensive — wasteful for cooling data.
whyNots.D: EBS is instance disk — expensive and unsuitable for archiving logs for years.

hints: Access decays over time = lifecycle. Hot (Standard) → warm (IA) → cheap archive (Deep Archive) → expire.
'Hours' recovery accepts Deep Archive, the cheapest for long-term archive.

questions.stem:
An on-premises office wants to access files via NFS/SMB with local low-latency cache, while data is stored durably in S3.

Which solution meets this hybrid file access?

options.text: Copy everything to S3 with presigned URLs

questions.explanation: S3 File Gateway (Storage Gateway) exposes a local NFS/SMB file share with low-latency cache, while persisting files as objects in S3. It is the classic hybrid file access solution.

whyNots.A: CloudFront is an edge CDN for content — not a hybrid file share.
whyNots.B: EBS is block disk for an EC2 instance — not mounted on-premises this way.
whyNots.D: Presigned URLs give temporary access to objects — not a local cached file share.

hints: Local NFS/SMB file share + cache + data in S3 = S3 File Gateway (a type of Storage Gateway).
The local app sees files; underneath, they become objects in S3.

questions.stem:
Telemetry events arrive at a high rate and must be processed in real time by a function that writes results to a low-latency NoSQL database.

Which combination meets this requirement?

options.text: S3 → Athena → QuickSight, all in real time
SQS FIFO → SES, processing the stream by email

questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams ingests telemetry in real time; a Lambda function consumes the stream (event source mapping) and processes it; results go to DynamoDB (low-latency NoSQL). This is the classic real-time processing pipeline.

whyNots.A: S3→Athena→QuickSight is batch analytics/visualization — not real-time processing.
whyNots.B: RDS→CloudFront is not a real-time telemetry ingestion pipeline.
whyNots.C: SQS FIFO→SES is queue + email — not real-time stream ingestion.

hints: Real-time ingestion points to Kinesis Data Streams; processing points to Lambda; fast NoSQL writes point to DynamoDB.
Lambda consumes the stream in batches through an event source mapping.

questions.stem:
A company wants to standardize dozens of AWS accounts with automatic governance: security baseline, guardrails that block prohibited actions, and detection of non-compliance.

Which foundation meets this with the least manual effort?

options.text: AWS Control Tower (landing zone) over Organizations, with preventive (SCP) and detective (Config) guardrails
Configure each account manually, one by one, repeating the security and network baseline for every new account
Enable CloudFront in all accounts; it automatically delivers a landing zone with guardrails
A single Security Group shared across all accounts, centralizing preventive and detective governance

questions.explanation: Control Tower builds a governed landing zone automatically over AWS Organizations, applying preventive guardrails (SCPs that block prohibited actions, inherited by the OU) and detective guardrails (Config rules that report non-compliance). It minimizes manual effort at scale.

whyNots.B: Configuring accounts one by one is exactly the manual work Control Tower avoids.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a CDN — unrelated to account governance.
whyNots.D: A Security Group is an instance firewall — not multi-account governance.

hints: Automated multi-account governance with a landing zone and guardrails means Control Tower on top of Organizations.
Preventive guardrails use SCPs to block actions; detective guardrails use Config to report issues.

questions.stem:
A global application has (1) cacheable static content and (2) a TCP API that needs a static IP and fast regional failover, and wants to route users to the lowest-latency region.

Which combination meets this requirement?

options.text: Route 53 with latency routing alone, without CloudFront or Global Accelerator, solves caching and static IP
CloudFront (static) + Global Accelerator (TCP API, static IP/failover) + Route 53 latency routing
CloudFront for everything, including the TCP API with a fixed static IP, which it provides natively
Just one ELB in a single region, which already delivers global failover and low latency for both sides

questions.explanation: CloudFront caches static content at the edge; Global Accelerator provides an anycast static IP and fast regional failover for the TCP API; Route 53 with latency routing sends users to the lowest-latency region. Each piece solves one part.

whyNots.A: Route 53 alone routes DNS but does not cache (CloudFront) nor accelerate transport (Global Accelerator).
whyNots.C: CloudFront is for cacheable HTTP; the TCP API with static IP is a Global Accelerator use case.
whyNots.D: An ELB in one region does not provide global presence or static IP/multi-region failover.

hints: Cacheable static content points to CloudFront; TCP with static IP and failover points to Global Accelerator; lowest latency points to Route 53 latency routing.
CloudFront caches at the edge; Global Accelerator accelerates transport but does not cache.

questions.stem:
A web tier on EC2 needs to self-heal (replace unhealthy instances) and scale with load, distributing traffic across healthy instances.

Which combination delivers self-healing, scaling, and distribution?

options.text: A larger EC2 instance (scale up) only — vertical scaling handles and recovers by itself
A single Spot instance without a load balancer — AWS replaces the Spot immediately at no extra cost
Auto Scaling group (multi-AZ, health checks) + ELB + CloudWatch alarms
Lambda behind CloudFront for everything — runs the EC2 tier without changing it

questions.explanation: The Auto Scaling group (across multiple Availability Zones, with health checks) replaces unhealthy instances and adjusts capacity; the ELB distributes traffic across healthy instances; CloudWatch alarms trigger scaling actions. This is the classic trio for elasticity and self-healing.

whyNots.A: Scaling up a single instance does not provide self-healing or distribution — it is a single point of failure.
whyNots.B: A single Spot instance without a load balancer is fragile and interruptible.
whyNots.D: Lambda+CloudFront is serverless; the scenario is an EC2 web tier with ASG/ELB.

hints: Replacing unhealthy instances and scaling calls for an Auto Scaling group; distributing traffic calls for an ELB; triggering scaling calls for CloudWatch alarms.
The ASG uses health checks to swap unhealthy instances automatically.

questions.stem:
A company wants to centralize logs from several applications and perform real-time analysis and troubleshooting, with indexing and interactive dashboards (Kibana-style).

Which service is indicated for log analysis with search and dashboards?
questions.explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Service is the managed search and analytics engine, widely used for real-time log analytics: it indexes logs from multiple sources and provides OpenSearch Dashboards (formerly Kibana) to monitor, visualize, and troubleshoot.

whyNots.A: RDS is a transactional relational database — not a log search/analytics engine with dashboards.
whyNots.B: Budgets is for cost — unrelated to log analysis.
whyNots.C: Glacier is cheap archiving — it does not index or analyze logs in real time.

hints: Real-time log analysis with indexing and dashboards (Kibana-style) points to OpenSearch Service.
The service used to be called Amazon Elasticsearch Service before it was renamed to OpenSearch.

questions.stem:
An e-commerce site needs fast, relevant full-text search across its product catalog (matching by words, relevance, filters).

Which service provides this text search?
questions.explanation: OpenSearch Service is optimized for full-text search: it indexes the catalog and responds to word queries with relevance, suggestions, and filters — the classic e-commerce and content/document search use case.

whyNots.B: DynamoDB is a low-latency key-value NoSQL database — it does not do text search by relevance.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not index or search catalogs.
whyNots.D: Athena is ad-hoc SQL over S3 (batch) — not an interactive full-text search engine.

hints: Full-text search with relevance for a catalog or documents points to OpenSearch.
DynamoDB is a fast key-value store, but it does not perform text search with relevance scoring.

questions.stem:
You want to ingest a near-real-time log stream directly into an OpenSearch cluster, in a managed way and without writing pipeline code.

Which service delivers streaming into OpenSearch?

options.text: Amazon SQS (queue that dumps into the cluster)

questions.explanation: Amazon Data Firehose delivers streaming data in a managed, code-free way to destinations such as S3, Redshift, and OpenSearch. It is the common way to ingest near-real-time logs into an OpenSearch cluster.

whyNots.A: Lightsail is a VPS — not an ingestion pipeline.
whyNots.C: SQS is a message queue between systems — not the delivery pipeline to OpenSearch.
whyNots.D: Budgets is for cost — it does not ingest data.

hints: Delivering managed streaming without code to a destination such as S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch points to Data Firehose.
OpenSearch is one of Firehose's native destinations.

questions.stem:
Three ways to handle logs: (1) index and search/visualize logs in real time with dashboards; (2) interactively query CloudWatch logs on demand; (3) run ad-hoc SQL over logs already in S3 (data lake).

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: OpenSearch indexes and visualizes logs in real time with dashboards; CloudWatch Logs Insights interactively queries CloudWatch logs; Athena runs ad-hoc SQL over logs in S3 (data lake). Option C matches all three.

whyNots.A: Starts with Athena for real-time dashboards — wrong; that is OpenSearch.
whyNots.B: Swaps Athena and Logs Insights in the last two positions.
whyNots.D: Puts Logs Insights for text-search dashboards — not its focus.

hints: Indexing, searching, and dashboarding logs points to OpenSearch; investigating CloudWatch logs points to Logs Insights; SQL on S3 points to Athena.
Only option C keeps each tool in its proper role.

questions.stem:
A company wants to transfer data from Salesforce to S3 (and Redshift) securely, without writing code, in a few clicks, with scheduling.

Which service does this SaaS↔AWS integration without code?

options.text: Amazon EC2 with a custom script

questions.explanation: Amazon AppFlow is the managed no-code service to securely transfer data between SaaS apps (Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow...) and AWS services (S3, Redshift), with scheduling, transformation, and encryption in transit — all in a few clicks.

whyNots.A: Glue is a general serverless ETL (with scripts) — the request is no-code SaaS integration, which is AppFlow.
whyNots.B: A script on EC2 is exactly the code and maintenance AppFlow avoids.
whyNots.C: SQS is a message queue — not a SaaS connector.

hints: Moving data from a SaaS such as Salesforce to AWS with no code and a few clicks points to Amazon AppFlow.
AppFlow has native connectors for Salesforce, SAP, Google Analytics, ServiceNow, and others.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) pull data from a SaaS (Salesforce) to AWS without code, with a native connector; (2) general serverless ETL (Spark) with Data Catalog to transform data from many sources.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: AppFlow is specialized for no-code SaaS integration (Salesforce → AWS). Glue is the general serverless ETL (Apache Spark) with Data Catalog, used to transform data from many sources. Option A makes the correct association.

whyNots.B: Athena is SQL query — not the SaaS connector nor the general ETL.
whyNots.C: Reversed — the SaaS no-code connector is AppFlow; the general ETL is Glue.
whyNots.D: Puts Athena as the general ETL — ETL is Glue.

hints: A SaaS no-code connector points to AppFlow; general serverless ETL with a Data Catalog points to Glue.
AppFlow is specialized for SaaS; Glue is general-purpose ETL.

questions.stem:
An app uses DynamoDB for its data but needs advanced text search (by words, relevance) that DynamoDB does not provide.

Which service complements DynamoDB for full-text search?

options.text: Amazon RDS — SQL LIKE already delivers relevance search
Amazon OpenSearch Service (indexing the data for search)
Amazon CloudFront — its cache also indexes content
Amazon SQS — the queue scans messages textually

questions.explanation: DynamoDB is excellent at key-value access but does not do full-text relevance search. The pattern is to index the data in OpenSearch Service (for example, via streams) to provide the advanced text search the app needs.

whyNots.A: RDS is relational — not an optimized full-text search engine.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not index or search.
whyNots.D: SQS is a queue — it does not search.

hints: DynamoDB is fast by key, but it does not perform text search — for that, index the data in OpenSearch.
A common pattern stores data in DynamoDB and keeps a search index in OpenSearch.

questions.stem:
DevOps engineers want interactive dashboards (charts, filters) to monitor and explore logs indexed in OpenSearch.

Which feature provides this visualization?
questions.explanation: OpenSearch Dashboards (formerly Kibana) is the visualization layer for OpenSearch Service: charts, filters, and interactive dashboards to monitor and explore indexed data/logs.

whyNots.A: Lightsail is a VPS — not the dashboard layer.
whyNots.B: Polly is text-to-speech — not log visualization.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail audits API calls — not an OpenSearch logs dashboard.

hints: Dashboards and visualizations on top of OpenSearch come from OpenSearch Dashboards, formerly Kibana.
This is where teams create charts and explore indexed logs.

questions.stem:
When moving data from a SaaS to AWS, the company requires that traffic NOT traverse the public internet and that data be encrypted in transit.

Which Amazon AppFlow capability meets this?

options.text: Expose the flow in a public S3 bucket with HTTPS enabled
Use the root account for the flow, which is already the most secure
Turn off encryption to go faster over the private network
Integration via AWS PrivateLink + encryption in transit

questions.explanation: AppFlow encrypts data in transit and, for SaaS apps integrated with AWS PrivateLink, allows traffic to avoid the public internet — reducing exposure. It meets the security requirement.

whyNots.A: A public bucket is the opposite of private/secure.
whyNots.B: Using root is forbidden and dangerous.
whyNots.C: Disabling encryption violates the security requirement.

hints: Traffic that stays off the public internet points to PrivateLink; AppFlow encrypts data in transit by default.
For SaaS integrations that support PrivateLink, AppFlow can avoid the public internet.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) full-text search and log dashboards; (2) move Salesforce data to AWS without code; (3) ad-hoc SQL over data in S3; (4) deliver managed streaming to a destination, without code.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each service has its role: OpenSearch (full-text search and log dashboards), AppFlow (no-code SaaS integration), Athena (ad-hoc SQL on S3), and Data Firehose (managed streaming delivery). Option A matches all four.

whyNots.B: Swaps OpenSearch with AppFlow and Athena with Data Firehose.
whyNots.C: Scrambles everything — Athena is not full-text log search.
whyNots.D: Swaps Athena with AppFlow in position.

hints: Search and logs point to OpenSearch; SaaS no-code points to AppFlow; SQL on S3 points to Athena; streaming delivery points to Data Firehose.
Only option A keeps each service in its proper role.

questions.stem:
A company exchanges files with partners over SFTP and wants to migrate this to a fully managed SFTP endpoint, delivering directly to S3, without operating its own SFTP servers.

Which service meets this?
questions.explanation: AWS Transfer Family offers fully managed transfer over SFTP, FTPS, FTP, and AS2, directly to/from S3 or EFS. It is ideal for exchanging files with partners via SFTP without maintaining your own SFTP servers.

whyNots.A: CloudFront is a CDN — not SFTP transfer.
whyNots.C: Snowball is offline physical transport — not a managed SFTP endpoint.
whyNots.D: DataSync is for bulk migration/copy between storages — not an SFTP endpoint for partners.

hints: A managed SFTP/FTPS endpoint that delivers to S3 or EFS for partner exchange points to AWS Transfer Family.
You keep client configurations; AWS operates the SFTP server underneath.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) expose an SFTP endpoint for partners to send files to S3; (2) bulk migrate terabytes from an on-premises NAS (NFS/SMB) to AWS, with integrity verification.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: Transfer Family exposes the standard protocol endpoint (SFTP) for partners to send files to S3. DataSync performs bulk migration/copy between storage systems (NFS/SMB → S3/EFS/FSx) with integrity verification. Option C is correct.

whyNots.A: Storage Gateway is continuous hybrid access — not the bulk migration requested in (2).
whyNots.B: Snowball is offline; scenario 1 is online SFTP (Transfer Family).
whyNots.D: Reversed — partner SFTP is Transfer Family; bulk migration is DataSync.

hints: SFTP for partners points to Transfer Family; bulk NFS/SMB migration points to DataSync.
Standard protocol exchange points to Transfer Family; copying large volumes between storages points to DataSync.

questions.stem:
You need to copy, automatically and repeatedly, large volumes of data from an on-premises SMB file share to Amazon FSx, with retry and bandwidth control.

Which service is indicated?
questions.explanation: DataSync automates bulk transfer between storage systems (including SMB → FSx), with integrity verification, retry, and bandwidth control. It is the choice for recurring copies of large volumes.

whyNots.A: SES is email — unrelated to file transfer.
whyNots.B: Budgets is for cost — it does not transfer data.
whyNots.C: Transfer Family is an SFTP/FTPS endpoint for file exchange — not bulk SMB→FSx migration.

hints: Automated bulk migration or copy between storages such as SMB to FSx, with retry and bandwidth control, points to DataSync.
DataSync supports NFS, SMB, S3, EFS, and FSx; Transfer Family is a protocol endpoint for SFTP.

questions.stem:
A company wants DR for on-premises servers with RPO in seconds and RTO in minutes: continuously replicate servers to AWS and, in a disaster, launch fully provisioned machines in minutes.

Which service meets this?

options.text: AWS Backup alone, with RPO of seconds

questions.explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) continuously replicates (block-level) on-premises/cloud servers to a low-cost staging area in AWS, allowing fully provisioned machines to launch in minutes during a disaster — with RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes. It supports failback.

whyNots.B: Lightsail is a VPS — not a DR service.
whyNots.C: Transfer Family is SFTP file transfer — not server DR.
whyNots.D: AWS Backup backs up/restores data (larger RPO/RTO, redeploy infra) — not continuous server replication with fast failover.

hints: Continuous server replication with RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes, and ready-to-launch machines points to Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS).
DRS replicates at the block level to a low-cost staging area and converts servers to run on AWS during a disaster.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) migrate on-premises servers to EC2 permanently (lift-and-shift, one-time); (2) keep servers continuously replicated for fast failover in case of disaster.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?

options.text: (1) Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS); (2) Application Migration Service (MGN)
(1) Application Migration Service (MGN); (2) Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
(1) AWS DataSync (copy between storages); (2) Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
(1) AWS Backup (centralized backups); (2) Application Migration Service (MGN)

questions.explanation: MGN (Application Migration Service) performs lift-and-shift migration of servers to EC2 (one-time, at cutover). DRS (Elastic Disaster Recovery) keeps servers continuously replicated for fast failover during a disaster. Option B makes the correct association.

whyNots.A: Reversed — one-time migration is MGN; continuous DR is DRS.
whyNots.C: DataSync is file copy — it does not migrate whole servers.
whyNots.D: Backup is data copies for restore — not the lift-and-shift migration in (1).

hints: Migrate once and for all points to MGN; continuous replication for failover points to DRS.
MGN is lift-and-shift; DRS is continuous replication for recovery.

questions.stem:
An architect weighs between only periodic data backups or continuous server replication. The requirement is RPO in seconds and recovery in minutes, without manually redeploying infrastructure.

Which approach meets this requirement?

options.text: Weekly volume snapshots, restored when disaster strikes
AWS Backup with manual infrastructure restore, guaranteeing RPO of a few seconds
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (continuous replication + automatically ready infrastructure)
It is impossible to achieve RPO of seconds in AWS; the minimum is several hours

questions.explanation: For RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes without manually redeploying infrastructure, DRS is the choice: it replicates servers continuously and leaves infrastructure ready to launch automatically. Backup/restore has larger RPO/RTO and requires manual redeployment.

whyNots.A: Weekly snapshots have RPO of days — far from seconds.
whyNots.B: Backup with manual restore does not achieve RPO of seconds nor avoid redeploying infrastructure.
whyNots.D: It is indeed possible — with DRS (continuous replication).

hints: RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes, and ready infrastructure without redeploying points to DRS continuous replication.
Backup/restore typically has larger RPO/RTO and requires redeploying infrastructure.

questions.stem:
A bank needs to receive files from partners using the AS2 protocol (common in B2B/EDI exchange), delivering them to S3, in a managed way.

Which service supports this file exchange protocol?

options.text: Amazon Athena, which receives files via SQL
AWS DataSync, which exposes a native AS2 endpoint
Amazon SNS, sending files as notifications
AWS Transfer Family (supports SFTP, FTPS, FTP, and AS2)

questions.explanation: AWS Transfer Family supports standard protocols SFTP, FTPS, FTP, and also AS2 (used in B2B/EDI exchange), delivering files to S3/EFS in a managed way. It is the right service for this case.

whyNots.A: Athena is SQL query — unrelated to AS2.
whyNots.B: DataSync is migration/copy between storages — not an AS2 protocol endpoint.
whyNots.C: SNS is pub/sub notification — it does not transfer files over AS2.

hints: Besides SFTP/FTPS/FTP, Transfer Family also supports AS2 for B2B/EDI exchange into S3.
Transfer Family is the managed standard transfer protocols service.

questions.stem:
After the primary on-premises environment returned to normal, the company wants to return workloads that were running in AWS back to the source.

Which AWS DRS feature helps with this return?

options.text: Failback (replicate back to the source servers)
Transfer Family, which replicates servers via SFTP
Glacier Deep Archive, which restores workloads at the source
CloudFront, which redirects workloads back to the source

questions.explanation: AWS DRS supports failback: it replicates data from the recovery instances back to the source servers, allowing workloads to return when the primary environment recovers. (Traffic redirection/failover itself is done by you.)

whyNots.B: Transfer Family is SFTP file transfer — not DR failback.
whyNots.C: Glacier is archiving — unrelated to server failback.
whyNots.D: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not fail back.

hints: Moving workloads from AWS back to the source is called failback; DRS replicates the data back.
DRS handles recovery (launch) and failback (return); traffic failover itself is your responsibility.

questions.stem:
A legacy partner application uploads files over SFTP that need to land in a shared Linux file system (NFS) used by several instances.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: AWS Transfer Family delivering to Amazon EFS

questions.explanation: AWS Transfer Family delivers files received over SFTP directly to Amazon EFS, which is the NFS file system shared among several Linux instances — supporting the legacy partner flow.

whyNots.A: DataSync is not an SFTP endpoint, and DynamoDB is not a shared file system.
whyNots.C: SNS is notification — it does not receive SFTP or write to EFS.
whyNots.D: Glacier is archiving, not an active shared NFS file system.

hints: Managed SFTP through Transfer Family can deliver to S3 or EFS, the shared Linux file system.
EFS is the NFS shared among several instances.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) managed SFTP endpoint for partners; (2) bulk migration from NAS to AWS; (3) continuous DR of servers with fast failover; (4) lift-and-shift migration of servers to EC2.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: DRS → MGN → Transfer Family → DataSync, matching each service with the current requirement
DataSync → Transfer Family → MGN → DRS, in the order the scenarios appear
Transfer Family → DataSync → Elastic Disaster Recovery → Application Migration Service
Transfer Family → DataSync → MGN → DRS, ending with continuous server migration

questions.explanation: Each service has its role: Transfer Family (managed SFTP endpoint), DataSync (bulk migration between storages), Elastic Disaster Recovery/DRS (continuous server DR), and Application Migration Service/MGN (lift-and-shift). Option C matches all four.

whyNots.A: Completely reversed; no position matches the right function.
whyNots.B: Swaps Transfer Family with DataSync and MGN with DRS.
whyNots.D: Swaps DRS with MGN in the last two positions (continuous DR is DRS; lift-and-shift is MGN).

hints: Partner SFTP points to Transfer Family; bulk migration points to DataSync; continuous DR points to DRS; lift-and-shift points to MGN.
Only option C keeps each service in its proper role.

questions.stem:
An auditor asks for the SOC 2 and PCI DSS reports that prove AWS infrastructure is compliant with these standards. The company needs to download them.

Where can you obtain these AWS compliance reports?
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal to download AWS compliance reports (SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO) and legal agreements. It proves that AWS infrastructure meets the standards — to hand to auditors or customers.

whyNots.A: Inspector scans vulnerabilities — it does not provide AWS compliance reports.
whyNots.B: CloudTrail audits API calls — it is not the repository of AWS reports.
whyNots.C: Audit Manager audits your environment — it does not provide AWS reports.

hints: Downloading AWS compliance reports such as SOC, PCI, and ISO points to AWS Artifact, the self-service portal.
Artifact is about AWS compliance; Audit Manager is about your own compliance.

questions.stem:
A company needs to continuously audit its own AWS usage and automate evidence collection against frameworks (SOC 2, PCI, GDPR) to prove its controls work.

Which service automates this audit evidence collection?
questions.explanation: AWS Audit Manager continuously audits your AWS usage and automates evidence collection against frameworks (SOC 2, PCI DSS, GDPR, HIPAA), evaluating whether your controls are effective. It is about compliance of your workload on AWS.

whyNots.B: Athena is SQL query — not audit evidence management.
whyNots.C: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 — it does not automate framework audit evidence.
whyNots.D: Artifact provides AWS's own reports — it does not collect evidence from your environment.

hints: Auditing your own usage and automating evidence collection against frameworks points to AWS Audit Manager.
Artifact downloads AWS reports; Audit Manager collects evidence from your environment.

questions.stem:
Distinguish: (1) prove AWS infrastructure is compliant (download SOC/PCI); (2) prove your workload on AWS is compliant, collecting evidence automatically.

Which pair corresponds to (1) and (2)?
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact provides AWS compliance reports (proves AWS infrastructure is compliant). AWS Audit Manager automatically collects evidence about your environment (proves your compliance). Option B is correct.

whyNots.A: Inspector is for vulnerabilities — not the AWS report.
whyNots.C: Reversed — AWS's reports are in Artifact; your environment evidence is in Audit Manager.
whyNots.D: CloudTrail/Config are API/configuration auditing — not AWS reports or framework evidence collection.

hints: AWS compliance reports point to Artifact; automatic evidence about your environment points to Audit Manager.
Artifact downloads; Audit Manager collects.

questions.stem:
Security wants to discover whether any S3 bucket, IAM role, or KMS key is accessible by an external account unintentionally (unintended sharing).

Which service identifies this external access?
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to analyze resource-based policies and identify S3 buckets, roles, KMS keys, and others shared with external entities, generating findings of unintended access for review.

whyNots.A: Artifact downloads AWS reports — it does not analyze access to your resources.
whyNots.B: Budgets is for cost — unrelated to access analysis.
whyNots.D: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not analyze access/policies.

hints: Finding resources shared with an external entity unintentionally points to IAM Access Analyzer.
It analyzes resource-based policies and generates external-access findings.

questions.stem:
Before applying a new policy, the team wants to preview how it would affect public and cross-account access to the resource, to avoid accidental exposure.

Which IAM Access Analyzer feature helps with this?

options.text: Download SOC report directly in Analyzer
Create an SQS queue to receive findings

questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer offers policy validation and preview: you see how a policy would affect public and cross-account access to the resource before applying it, preventing accidental exposure. It also performs internal access analysis (least privilege).

whyNots.A: Framework evidence collection is Audit Manager.
whyNots.B: SOC download is Artifact — not Access Analyzer.
whyNots.C: Creating an SQS queue is unrelated to policy validation.

hints: Previewing a policy's effect on public or cross-account access before applying it points to policy validation/preview in Access Analyzer.
This helps avoid accidental exposure before deployment.

questions.stem:
Three questions: (1) is this resource shared with an external account unintentionally? (2) is the resource configuration compliant with rules? (3) who called the API that changed the resource?

Which 1→2→3 mapping is correct?

options.text: IAM Access Analyzer → AWS Config → AWS CloudTrail
AWS Config → IAM Access Analyzer → CloudTrail

questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer identifies external/unintended access; AWS Config evaluates whether configuration is compliant; CloudTrail records who called the API. Option A respects all three roles.

whyNots.B: Swaps CloudTrail and Config in the last two positions.
whyNots.C: Puts CloudTrail for external access — scrambled.
whyNots.D: Starts with Config for external access — that is Access Analyzer.

hints: External access points to Access Analyzer; configuration compliance points to Config; API caller history points to CloudTrail.
Only option A keeps each service in its proper role.

questions.stem:
A healthcare company needs to accept and download the BAA (Business Associate Agreement) with AWS to process data under HIPAA.

Where can it manage and accept this type of legal agreement?

options.text: AWS WAF (legal agreements and BAA tab)
AWS Artifact (reports and agreements, such as BAA)
AWS Audit Manager (signs the BAA with AWS)

questions.explanation: AWS Artifact, in addition to compliance reports, lets you review, accept, and manage legal agreements with AWS, such as the BAA (for HIPAA) and NDA. It is the central portal for these documents.

whyNots.A: WAF is an application firewall — nothing to do with legal agreements.
whyNots.C: Audit Manager collects evidence from your environment — it does not manage the BAA with AWS.
whyNots.D: GuardDuty detects threats — it is not the agreements portal.

hints: In addition to reports (SOC/PCI), Artifact manages LEGAL agreements with AWS, such as the BAA.
It is the central portal for compliance documents.

questions.stem:
The company wants to enforce least privilege on critical resources by identifying WHICH internal principals have access to them.

Which IAM Access Analyzer feature helps with this internal analysis?

options.text: Create a CloudFront distribution to list accesses
Secret rotation, which reveals who uses each resource
Download a PCI report with the list of principals

questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer also performs internal access analysis: it identifies which principals within your organization or account have access to critical resources, supporting the principle of least privilege.

whyNots.A: CloudFront is a CDN — it does not analyze internal access.
whyNots.B: Secret rotation is Secrets Manager — not access analysis.
whyNots.D: The PCI report is Artifact — not Access Analyzer.

hints: In addition to external access, Access Analyzer performs INTERNAL analysis — which principals in your organization access critical resources.
It supports least privilege by showing who can access what.

questions.stem:
To speed up a PCI DSS audit, the team wants a pre-built framework that maps controls and automatically collects evidence from the AWS environment.

Which service offers these audit frameworks?
questions.explanation: AWS Audit Manager offers pre-built frameworks (PCI DSS, SOC 2, GDPR, etc.) that map controls and automate evidence collection from your AWS environment, speeding up audits.

whyNots.A: Artifact provides AWS reports — not evidence-collection frameworks for your environment.
whyNots.B: Lambda is serverless compute — not an audit framework service.
whyNots.C: QuickSight is BI — not compliance auditing.

hints: Pre-built frameworks (PCI, SOC 2...) plus automatic evidence collection equals Audit Manager.
It maps controls and gathers evidence from your environment for you.

questions.stem:
Four needs: (1) download the AWS SOC 2 report; (2) automate audit evidence from your environment; (3) find a bucket shared with an external account; (4) know who called the API that changed a resource.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: Artifact → Audit Manager → IAM Access Analyzer → CloudTrail
IAM Access Analyzer → CloudTrail → Artifact → Audit Manager
Artifact → IAM Access Analyzer → Audit Manager → CloudTrail
Audit Manager → Artifact → CloudTrail → IAM Access Analyzer

questions.explanation: Each service has its role: Artifact (AWS compliance reports), Audit Manager (audit evidence from your environment), IAM Access Analyzer (external or unintended access), and CloudTrail (who called the API). Option A respects all four.

whyNots.B: It shuffles everything — Access Analyzer does not download the AWS SOC report.
whyNots.C: Swaps Audit Manager and Access Analyzer positions.
whyNots.D: Swaps Artifact and Audit Manager, and CloudTrail and Access Analyzer.

hints: AWS SOC report = Artifact; environment evidence = Audit Manager; external access = Access Analyzer; who called the API = CloudTrail.
Only option A keeps each service in its role.

questions.stem:
A team wants to launch dozens of identical EC2 instances quickly, with the OS, patches, and application already installed, without repeating the configuration every time.

Which resource is the 'golden image' for launching pre-configured instances?

options.text: An Elastic IP with the OS pre-installed
An EBS snapshot alone, already bootable
A bucket policy storing the image

questions.explanation: An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is the template that contains the OS, software, and configuration for launching EC2 instances. Creating a custom AMI (golden image) lets you launch dozens of identical instances quickly without repeating configuration.

whyNots.A: Elastic IP is a static IP — not a launch image.
whyNots.C: An EBS snapshot is a backup of a volume — not the complete instance launch template (the AMI references snapshots, but the template is the AMI).
whyNots.D: Bucket policy is an S3 permission — nothing to do with launching instances.

hints: A template for launching instances with OS and software ready equals an AMI (golden image).
You create the AMI once and launch N identical instances from it.

questions.stem:
You have a custom AMI in one region and need to launch instances with the SAME configuration in another AWS region.

What is required?

options.text: Enable Transfer Acceleration, which replicates AMIs between regions
The AMI already works in any region automatically because it is global
Copy the AMI to the other region (AMIs are region-specific)
Create an Elastic IP in the other region to pull the image

questions.explanation: AMIs are specific to the region in which they were created. To launch instances with the same configuration in another region, you must copy the AMI to that region. Common in multi-region and DR strategies.

whyNots.A: Transfer Acceleration is for S3 upload — it does not copy AMIs between regions.
whyNots.B: Wrong — the AMI is not global; it must be copied to the other region.
whyNots.D: Elastic IP is a static IP — it does not replicate the AMI.

hints: An AMI is REGION-specific — to use it in another region, copy the AMI there.
This is a common step in DR and multi-region expansion.

questions.stem:
You take daily backups of an EBS volume. You want to know why the second backup onward is fast and cheap.

Which EBS snapshot characteristic explains this?

options.text: Snapshots do not store data, only metadata
Snapshots stay on the volume itself
Each snapshot copies the entire volume every time
They are incremental (only changed blocks are saved)

questions.explanation: EBS snapshots are incremental: the first captures everything, and subsequent ones save only the blocks changed since the last one — saving time and space. They are stored in S3 (managed by AWS).

whyNots.A: Snapshots store block data, not just metadata.
whyNots.B: Snapshots are stored in S3, not on the volume itself.
whyNots.C: It does not copy the entire volume every time — only the delta (incremental).

hints: EBS snapshots are INCREMENTAL — after the first, only what CHANGED is saved.
That is why subsequent backups are fast and cheap; they are stored in managed S3.

questions.stem:
For DR, the company wants to keep copies of EBS backups in ANOTHER region and in an isolated account, encrypted with its own key.

Which snapshot feature meets this?

options.text: Cross-Region and cross-account snapshot copy (with KMS encryption)
User data with embedded backup — the boot script restores everything by itself
Snapshots only exist in the same AZ — they are tied to the EBS volume hardware
Elastic IP replicated to another region — the static IP carries the data with it

questions.explanation: EBS snapshots can be copied cross-Region and cross-account, encrypted via KMS — letting you keep backups in a separate region and account for DR and protection against account compromise. Data Lifecycle Manager automates this.

whyNots.B: User data is a boot script — it does not replicate backups.
whyNots.C: Wrong — snapshots (in S3) can be copied across regions and accounts.
whyNots.D: Elastic IP is a static IP — not a replicated backup.

hints: Copying a snapshot to another REGION and another ACCOUNT, re-encrypting, is the EBS DR pattern.
You can automate this with Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM).

questions.stem:
An IN-MEMORY database processes huge datasets in RAM and needs A LOT of memory per instance.

Which EC2 instance family is recommended?
questions.explanation: Memory optimized instances (R, X families) deliver a lot of RAM per instance, ideal for in-memory databases, large in-memory dataset analysis, and enterprise apps (SAP). Choose the family by the dimension the workload consumes most.

whyNots.A: Compute optimized is for high CPU (batch, transcoding) — not the memory focus.
whyNots.C: General purpose is balanced — it does not maximize memory like Memory optimized.
whyNots.D: Storage optimized is for high local I/O — not RAM.

hints: 'In-memory plus lots of RAM' means the Memory optimized family (R, X).
Choose the family by the dominant dimension — here it is memory.

questions.stem:
A media transcoding and batch processing workload is CPU-bound and benefits from high-performance processors.

Which instance family is recommended?
questions.explanation: Compute optimized (C family) offers high-performance processors for compute-bound loads — batch, media transcoding, game servers, and HPC. It is the right family when the bottleneck is CPU.

whyNots.A: Storage optimized focuses on local I/O — not CPU.
whyNots.B: Memory optimized focuses on RAM — not the bottleneck here.
whyNots.D: Accelerated is GPU/FPGA (ML/graphics) — not the case for generic CPU-bound transcoding (although GPU helps in some cases, the request is 'compute-bound plus high-performance CPU').

hints: Compute-bound (transcoding, batch) means Compute optimized (C), high-performance CPU.
If GPU were needed (ML/graphics), then Accelerated would be the choice.

questions.stem:
Four workloads: (1) lots of RAM for an in-memory database; (2) high CPU for batch; (3) GPU for ML training; (4) high local I/O for big data.

Which 1→2→3→4 family mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: Each family targets one dimension: Memory optimized (RAM/in-memory), Compute optimized (CPU/batch), Accelerated (GPU/ML), and Storage optimized (local I/O/big data). Option D respects all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps Memory with Compute and Storage with Accelerated.
whyNots.B: Shuffles everything — Storage is not for RAM.
whyNots.C: Swaps Compute and Storage positions.

hints: RAM = Memory optimized; CPU = Compute optimized; GPU = Accelerated; local I/O = Storage optimized.
Map each workload to its dominant resource to find the matching option.

questions.stem:
An application needs a FIXED public IP address that can be quickly remapped to a standby instance if the current instance fails.

Which resource provides this remappable static IP?
questions.explanation: An Elastic IP is a static IPv4 public address allocated to your account that can be quickly remapped to another instance — masking the original instance's failure. The default public IP, by contrast, changes when the instance stops or starts.

whyNots.B: The default dynamic public IP changes on stop or start — it is not fixed or remappable in the same way.
whyNots.C: AMI is a launch image — not an IP.
whyNots.D: Snapshot is a volume backup — not an IP.

hints: A static public IP that remaps to another instance on failure equals an Elastic IP.
The default public IP changes when the instance stops; the EIP stays fixed until you release it.

questions.stem:
You want an EC2 instance to automatically run a script at launch to install packages and configure the application (bootstrap).

Which EC2 feature runs this script at launch?
questions.explanation: User data is the script or commands the instance runs at launch for bootstrap (install packages, configure the app). It is limited to 16 KB (raw). Instance metadata (IMDS) only provides information about the instance itself.

whyNots.A: Placement group controls physical placement — it does not run bootstrap.
whyNots.C: Elastic IP is a static IP — it does not run scripts.
whyNots.D: Instance metadata exposes instance data (ID, IP, role) — it does not run the bootstrap script.

hints: A bootstrap script run at instance boot equals user data (16 KB limit).
Do not confuse it with instance metadata, which only EXPOSES data about the instance.

questions.stem:
Four concepts: (1) template for launching an instance; (2) incremental volume backup; (3) remappable static public IP; (4) bootstrap script at boot.

Which 1→2→3→4 mapping is correct?

options.text: AMI → Elastic IP → EBS snapshot → user data
Elastic IP → user data → AMI → EBS snapshot
AMI → EBS snapshot → Elastic IP → user data
EBS snapshot → AMI → user data → Elastic IP

questions.explanation: Each resource has its role: AMI (launch template), EBS snapshot (incremental volume backup), Elastic IP (remappable static public IP), and user data (bootstrap script at boot). Option C respects all four.

whyNots.A: Swaps Elastic IP and EBS snapshot positions.
whyNots.B: Shuffles everything — Elastic IP is not the template.
whyNots.D: Swaps AMI with snapshot and user data with Elastic IP.

hints: Template = AMI; incremental backup = snapshot; remappable fixed IP = Elastic IP; bootstrap = user data.
Only one option keeps each concept in place.

questions.stem:
Images uploaded to an S3 bucket need to be processed asynchronously, absorbing spikes and without losing any, using serverless processing.

Which architecture is the most resilient?

options.text: Cron on EC2 scanning the bucket, reacting to the event
S3 event → synchronous Lambda without a queue, holding the spike
Write the images to RDS, which processes and absorbs the spike
S3 event → SQS → Lambda consuming the queue (with DLQ)

questions.explanation: The S3 event publishes to an SQS queue that buffers spikes; Lambda consumes at its own pace (event source mapping), with a DLQ for problematic messages. No image is lost and processing is serverless and decoupled.

whyNots.A: A cron scanning the bucket is inefficient and not event-driven.
whyNots.B: Synchronous Lambda without a queue can exhaust concurrency during a spike and lose events.
whyNots.C: Writing images to RDS does not process them or absorb spikes.

hints: Absorbing a spike without losing messages means a queue (SQS) between the event and Lambda; DLQ for failures.
S3 can notify an SQS standard queue that Lambda consumes at its own pace.

questions.stem:
A global HTTPS static site, with the bucket private, custom domain at the apex, and managed TLS certificate with auto-renewal.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: Private S3 + CloudFront (OAC) + ACM (certificate) + Route 53 Alias at the apex
S3 with website endpoint + Route 53, no CloudFront or certificate
Public S3 bucket + a CNAME record pointed directly at the zone apex
An EC2 instance with a TLS certificate installed and renewed manually

questions.explanation: Private S3 with OAC (CloudFront-only access), CloudFront for global low latency and HTTPS, ACM for the TLS certificate with auto-renewal, and Route 53 with Alias pointing the apex to the distribution. This is the secure static site pattern.

whyNots.B: Without CloudFront there is no CDN or managed HTTPS edge as requested.
whyNots.C: Public S3 exposes the origin and CNAME does not work at the apex.
whyNots.D: EC2 with manual certificate does not provide global low latency or managed auto-renewal.

hints: Global plus private means CloudFront (OAC); managed TLS means ACM; apex means Route 53 Alias.
CNAME does not work at the apex; Alias does.

questions.stem:
A read-heavy portal overloads the relational database with the same repeated SELECTs.

Which combination relieves the database while keeping relational consistency?

options.text: Replace RDS with S3, which handles relational SELECTs at scale
RDS Read Replicas + ElastiCache to cache hot queries
Multi-AZ standby serving reads, splitting the SELECTs
Increase only the backup, which relieves read load

questions.explanation: Read Replicas distribute read load and ElastiCache caches the most repeated queries, relieving RDS. The Multi-AZ standby is only for failover, not read serving.

whyNots.A: S3 is object storage — it does not replace a relational database.
whyNots.C: The Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads — a classic trap.
whyNots.D: Backup does not reduce production read load.

hints: Scaling reads = Read Replica; caching repeated queries = ElastiCache.
Remember — Multi-AZ standby does NOT serve reads.

questions.stem:
A containerized batch processing workload is interruption-tolerant and the team wants the lowest possible cost.

Which option reduces cost by accepting interruption?
questions.explanation: Fargate Spot runs interruptible tasks on spare capacity with up to 70% discount — ideal for interruption-tolerant batch. On-demand would be more expensive for this workload.

whyNots.A: Dedicated Hosts is for licensing and compliance — not the cheapest here.
whyNots.B: On-demand 24/7 does not give the Spot discount for a workload that accepts interruption.
whyNots.D: Lightsail is a simple VPS — not the interruptible container batch model.

hints: Interruptible container batch means Fargate Spot (spare capacity, cheap).
You get a 2-minute interruption notice — fine for batch.

questions.stem:
Every change to a DynamoDB table needs to trigger, in real time, a function that updates a search index and notifies systems.

Which resource delivers the change stream?
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams captures insert, update, and delete events in order and triggers a Lambda in real time — the basis of event-driven and CDC architectures. DAX (cache) and Global Tables (multi-region) solve different problems.

whyNots.A: Global Tables replicate across regions — it is not a per-change trigger.
whyNots.B: DAX accelerates reads — it does not deliver a change stream.
whyNots.C: Periodic scan is expensive, slow, and not real time.

hints: Reacting to every table change means DynamoDB Streams plus Lambda.
DAX is a read cache; Global Tables is multi-region — neither is the change log.

questions.stem:
Instances in a private subnet must access S3 without internet, without NAT, and without embedded access keys.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: IAM Role on EC2 + Gateway Endpoint for S3
VPC Peering with the AWS account

questions.explanation: An IAM Role gives temporary credentials (no embedded key) and the Gateway Endpoint provides private S3 access without internet or NAT. Covers secure and private access.

whyNots.B: NAT goes through the internet (with cost) and embedded access keys are insecure.
whyNots.C: Internet Gateway plus public bucket exposes everything.
whyNots.D: VPC Peering connects VPCs — it does not provide private S3 access this way.

hints: No internet or NAT to S3 means Gateway Endpoint (free); no keys means IAM Role.
The Gateway Endpoint routes traffic to S3 through the AWS network.

questions.stem:
A global application requires near-zero RPO/RTO and low-latency reads across multiple continents, on a MySQL-compatible database.

Which solution meets this?

options.text: Aurora in one region with Multi-AZ only

questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database spans multiple regions with global low-latency reads and cross-region DR (RTO in minutes), compatible with MySQL/PostgreSQL. Route 53 routes between regions.

whyNots.A: Multi-AZ does not cover region loss or provide global presence.
whyNots.C: Single-AZ plus snapshots has RPO/RTO in hours.
whyNots.D: DynamoDB is not MySQL-compatible (it is NoSQL).

hints: Multi-continent plus near-zero RPO/RTO plus MySQL-compatible equals Aurora Global Database.
Multi-AZ only covers AZs within one region.

questions.stem:
You want to unload an event stream into S3 without code, query with SQL, and build dashboards, all serverless.

Which pipeline meets this?
questions.explanation: Amazon Data Firehose delivers the stream to S3 without code; Athena queries with SQL; QuickSight builds the dashboards. End-to-end serverless pipeline.

whyNots.A: EC2 plus MySQL is not serverless nor the requested pipeline.
whyNots.B: CloudFront plus S3 serves static content — not an analytics pipeline.
whyNots.D: SQS/Lambda/EBS does not form a data lake plus SQL plus dashboard.

hints: Deliver stream to S3 without code = Firehose; SQL on S3 = Athena; dashboard = QuickSight.
All serverless, no cluster.

questions.stem:
Connect the data center to multiple VPCs with low latency and dedicated bandwidth, with cheap automatic backup if the link fails, all centralized in a hub.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: Point-to-point VPC Peering between all VPCs, routing transitively
CloudFront + Global Accelerator, acting as a hub between networks
Only independent VPN tunnels, with no central hub to concentrate routing
Direct Connect (primary) + Site-to-Site VPN (backup) + Transit Gateway (hub)

questions.explanation: Direct Connect provides the dedicated link; Site-to-Site VPN is the cheaper automatic backup (BGP failover); Transit Gateway centralizes the VPCs and on-premises in a hub.

whyNots.A: Point-to-point VPC Peering does not scale and does not connect the data center.
whyNots.B: CloudFront/Global Accelerator are for end users, not hybrid connectivity.
whyNots.C: VPN only does not provide dedicated bandwidth or a central hub.

hints: Dedicated bandwidth = Direct Connect; cheap backup = VPN; multi-VPC hub = Transit Gateway.
Classic resilient hybrid pattern.

questions.stem:
Govern dozens of accounts with automatic baseline, guardrails that block prohibited actions, and detection of non-compliance.

Which foundation meets this?

options.text: Control Tower (landing zone) on Organizations, with preventive guardrails (SCP) and detective guardrails (Config)
A single global Security Group applied to all accounts, controlling the organization's guardrails
Configure each account manually, repeating the security and network baseline one by one as they appear
Enable CloudFront in all new accounts, which applies governance and guardrails automatically

questions.explanation: Control Tower builds the governed landing zone on Organizations, with preventive guardrails (SCP) and detective guardrails (Config). Multi-account governance with minimal manual effort.

whyNots.B: Security Group is an instance firewall — not governance.
whyNots.C: Configuring account by account is the work Control Tower avoids.
whyNots.D: CloudFront is a CDN — irrelevant here.

hints: Automatic landing zone plus guardrails equals Control Tower on Organizations.
Preventive (SCP) blocks; detective (Config) reports.

questions.stem:
A serverless REST API needs to authenticate end users and persist NoSQL data, with no server to manage.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: SQS + SES + EBS — queue, email, and disk cover the authenticated API
API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB, with Cognito authenticating users
CloudFront + S3 + KMS, with KMS handling user login
EC2 + MySQL + IAM Users for each end user (the serverless combo)

questions.explanation: API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB deliver the serverless API; Cognito (User Pool) authenticates end users and can issue tokens. No servers to manage.

whyNots.A: SQS/SES/EBS is not the authenticated REST API stack.
whyNots.C: CloudFront/S3/KMS does not form a dynamic API with user auth.
whyNots.D: EC2/MySQL is not serverless, and one IAM User per end user is an anti-pattern.

hints: Serverless API = API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB; end-user login = Cognito.
IAM Users are for operating the account, not app users.

questions.stem:
A web app on EC2 needs to distribute traffic, scale with demand, replace unhealthy instances, and point the root domain to the load balancer.

Which combination meets this?

options.text: A single instance with Elastic IP — the fixed IP already provides failover and points to the apex
CNAME at the apex pointing to the ELB — Route 53 accepts CNAME for any record
ELB + Auto Scaling (multi-AZ, health checks) + Route 53 Alias for the apex → ELB
CloudFront only, no ELB or ASG — the CDN scales and replaces unhealthy instances by itself

questions.explanation: ELB distributes traffic, the Auto Scaling group (multi-AZ, health checks) scales and replaces unhealthy instances, and Route 53 with Alias points the apex to the ELB. Elasticity plus self-recovery plus correct DNS.

whyNots.A: A single instance is a single point of failure with no scaling.
whyNots.B: CNAME is not allowed at the apex — Alias is correct.
whyNots.D: Without ELB/ASG there is no distribution or self-recovery at the EC2 layer.

hints: Distribute = ELB; scale and heal = ASG; apex → ELB = Route 53 Alias.
CNAME does not work at the apex — use Alias.

questions.stem:
Trap #1: what is the difference between RDS Multi-AZ and Read Replica?

Which statement is correct?

options.text: Read Replica replicates synchronously and serves automatic failover; Multi-AZ exists only for read reports
Multi-AZ serves to scale reads by distributing queries; Read Replica serves only automatic failover of the primary
Multi-AZ and Read Replica are the same thing: both maintain synchronous copies that serve reads and failover equally
Multi-AZ = high availability (synchronous standby, does not serve reads); Read Replica = scale reads (asynchronous, read-only)

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby for automatic failover (does not serve reads); Read Replica is asynchronous and read-only, for scaling read throughput. They are complementary.

whyNots.A: Read Replica is asynchronous and is not the automatic failover mechanism.
whyNots.B: Reverses the roles.
whyNots.C: They differ in objective and mechanism.

hints: Multi-AZ = availability (standby does not read); Read Replica = scale reads.

questions.stem:
Trap: Security Group vs NACL.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: SG is stateful (instance-level, allow only); NACL is stateless (subnet-level, allow and deny)
Both only have deny rules — in AWS allow is always implicit by default
SG is stateless and has deny rules, requiring you to allow each response back
NACL is stateful and acts at the instance, remembering connections it opened

questions.explanation: Security Group is stateful, acts at the instance, and only has allow rules (response is allowed automatically). NACL is stateless, acts at the subnet, and has allow and deny (needs rules for both directions). To block a specific IP, use NACL.

whyNots.B: SG only has allow; only NACL has deny.
whyNots.C: SG has no deny rule and is stateful.
whyNots.D: NACL is stateless and acts at the subnet.

hints: SG: stateful/instance/allow only; NACL: stateless/subnet/allow+deny.

questions.stem:
Trap: SQS vs SNS.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: SQS is the push pub/sub with fan-out; SNS is the pull queue with consumer group
SQS = queue (pull, one consumer group); SNS = pub/sub (push, fan-out to many)
SQS sends push notifications directly to mobile apps, like SNS's mobile feature
SQS and SNS are for sending rich marketing email, competing with Amazon SES

questions.explanation: SQS is a queue (consumers pull messages, decoupling). SNS is pub/sub (pushes the event to many subscribers — fan-out). Combined they form the fan-out pattern (SNS → multiple SQS).

whyNots.A: Reverses them — queue is SQS; pub/sub is SNS.
whyNots.C: Mobile push is an SNS channel, but the SQS queue does not send push.
whyNots.D: Rich marketing email is SES.

hints: SQS = queue (pull); SNS = pub/sub (push, fan-out).

questions.stem:
Trap: Alias vs CNAME in Route 53.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: Alias and CNAME only point to AWS resources; external domains require a manual A record
Alias points to any external domain and is charged; CNAME is the free one for AWS resources
Alias works at the apex and is free for AWS resources; CNAME does not work at the apex and is charged
CNAME works normally at the zone apex; Alias cannot be used at the apex

questions.explanation: Alias works at the zone apex, points to AWS resources, and is free for those queries; CNAME does not work at the apex, points to any domain, and is charged.

whyNots.A: CNAME points to any domain, not only AWS.
whyNots.B: The one that points to any domain is CNAME.
whyNots.D: Reverses — CNAME does NOT work at the apex; Alias does.

hints: Alias = apex + AWS resources + free; CNAME = non-apex + charged + any domain.

questions.stem:
Trick question: ACM vs KMS.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: ACM and KMS do exactly the same thing; choosing between them is just console preference
ACM is for automatically rotating database passwords, like Secrets Manager
ACM manages encryption keys at rest; KMS issues in-transit TLS certificates
ACM manages TLS certificates (in transit); KMS manages encryption keys (at rest)

questions.explanation: ACM manages SSL/TLS certificates (identity + in-transit encryption). KMS manages encryption keys (data at rest in S3/EBS/RDS). They have distinct roles.

whyNots.A: They do different things.
whyNots.B: Rotating database passwords is Secrets Manager.
whyNots.C: Reversed — certificates are ACM; keys are KMS.

hints: Remember: ACM handles certificates for TLS/HTTPS, while KMS handles encryption keys for data at rest.

questions.stem:
Trick question: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: CloudWatch = metrics/logs/alarms (performance); CloudTrail = audit of API calls (who did what)
CloudWatch audits API calls (who did what); CloudTrail collects performance metrics and logs
CloudWatch and CloudTrail are the same thing: both store metrics and API audit indistinctly
CloudTrail is for measuring CPU and memory usage of instances, with built-in performance alarms

questions.explanation: CloudWatch handles metrics, logs, and alarms (health/performance). CloudTrail records API calls (who did what, when). X-Ray, in turn, traces request paths.

whyNots.B: Reverses the roles.
whyNots.C: They are different.
whyNots.D: CPU is a CloudWatch metric, not CloudTrail.

hints: Think of CloudWatch as watching metrics and CloudTrail as tracking API calls.

questions.stem:
Trick question: Kinesis Data Streams vs Amazon Data Firehose.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: Data Firehose is for replay with multiple real-time consumers; Data Streams delivers to S3/Redshift without code
Data Streams = process in real time with consumers/replay; Data Firehose = deliver to S3/Redshift without code
Data Streams and Data Firehose only send email notifications; data streaming is SNS
Data Firehose has been discontinued by AWS; today all delivery to S3/Redshift is done only with manual consumers

questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is for real-time processing with your own consumers and replay; Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) delivers the stream to destinations like S3/Redshift, managed and code-free.

whyNots.A: Reversed — replay/consumers is Streams; codeless delivery is Firehose.
whyNots.C: Neither is an email service.
whyNots.D: Firehose was not discontinued; it was renamed Amazon Data Firehose.

hints: Remember: Data Streams is for processing, while Data Firehose is for delivery.

questions.stem:
Trick question: Global Accelerator vs CloudFront.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: CloudFront and Global Accelerator are distributed databases, replicated across all AWS edge locations
CloudFront only serves real-time UDP game traffic; HTTP cached content goes in Global Accelerator
CloudFront = CDN that caches HTTP content at the edge; Global Accelerator = anycast static IP, accelerates TCP/UDP (no cache)
Global Accelerator caches HTTP content at the edge; CloudFront provides anycast static IP for TCP/UDP

questions.explanation: CloudFront is a CDN and caches HTTP(S) content at the edge. Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and accelerates TCP/UDP transport over the AWS network, with fast regional failover — it does not cache.

whyNots.A: They are not databases.
whyNots.B: CloudFront is for cacheable HTTP; UDP for games is Global Accelerator.
whyNots.D: Reversed — caching is CloudFront; static IP/anycast is Global Accelerator.

hints: Remember: CloudFront caches HTTP content, while Global Accelerator speeds up TCP/UDP transport without caching.

questions.stem:
Trick question: ElastiCache vs MemoryDB.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: MemoryDB is low-latency object storage, a direct S3 competitor for hot data
ElastiCache and MemoryDB are columnar data warehouses, aimed at in-memory analytics and BI
ElastiCache is the durable database to use as primary; MemoryDB is just a cache that can lose data
ElastiCache = in-memory cache (data can be lost); MemoryDB = DURABLE in-memory database (primary)

questions.explanation: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache (data can be lost, sits in front of the database). MemoryDB is a durable in-memory database (Multi-AZ) that can be the primary source. Both are Redis-compatible.

whyNots.A: MemoryDB is in-memory, not object storage.
whyNots.B: They are not data warehouses (that is Redshift).
whyNots.C: Reversed — the durable/primary one is MemoryDB.

hints: Think of ElastiCache as a disposable cache and MemoryDB as a durable primary database.

questions.stem:
Trick question: KMS vs CloudHSM.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: KMS = managed multi-tenant (general case); CloudHSM = dedicated single-tenant HSM (compliance/PKCS#11)
CloudHSM is a key CDN, distributing cryptographic material at edge locations
KMS and CloudHSM are used to issue and renew public TLS certificates, like ACM
KMS is the dedicated single-tenant HSM for compliance; CloudHSM is the managed multi-tenant general one

questions.explanation: KMS uses a managed multi-tenant HSM — easy, inexpensive, general case. CloudHSM is a dedicated single-tenant HSM under your control, for compliance that requires it or PKCS#11/JCE interfaces.

whyNots.B: CloudHSM is not a CDN.
whyNots.C: TLS certificates are ACM.
whyNots.D: Reversed — dedicated/single-tenant is CloudHSM.

hints: Remember: KMS is managed and multi-tenant; CloudHSM is dedicated and single-tenant.

questions.stem:
Trick question: Application Migration Service (MGN) vs Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS).

Which statement is correct?

options.text: MGN is the continuous DR service with fast failover; DRS does the one-time lift-and-shift migration
MGN = lift-and-shift migration (one time); DRS = continuous server DR (fast failover)
MGN and DRS are transactional email services, one for bulk sending and the other for failover
DRS is for transferring files over managed SFTP, like Transfer Family

questions.explanation: MGN performs lift-and-shift server migration to EC2 (one time). DRS replicates servers continuously for fast failover in a disaster (RPO seconds/RTO minutes).

whyNots.A: Reverses the roles.
whyNots.C: They are not email services.
whyNots.D: SFTP is Transfer Family, not DRS.

hints: Remember: MGN migrates servers once; DRS replicates continuously for fast failover.

questions.stem:
Trick question: AWS Artifact vs Audit Manager.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: Audit Manager is a CDN that distributes AWS compliance reports at edge locations
Artifact collects audit evidence from YOUR environment; Audit Manager is where you download AWS SOC/ISO
Artifact = download AWS compliance reports; Audit Manager = collect evidence of YOUR compliance
Artifact and Audit Manager are managed firewalls, one for edge and one for VPC internal traffic

questions.explanation: Artifact is the portal to download AWS's own compliance reports (SOC/PCI/ISO). Audit Manager automates evidence collection about your environment to demonstrate your compliance.

whyNots.A: Audit Manager is not a CDN.
whyNots.B: Reversed — downloading AWS SOC reports is Artifact; auditing your environment is Audit Manager.
whyNots.D: They are not firewalls.

hints: Remember: Artifact is for AWS compliance reports; Audit Manager collects evidence for your compliance.

questions.stem:
Trick question: Transfer Family vs DataSync.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: Transfer Family and DataSync are managed databases, one for partner data and one for internal data
Transfer Family is the bulk migration/copy service between storages; DataSync is the SFTP/FTPS endpoint for partners
DataSync is for issuing and renewing TLS certificates used in file transfers with external partners
Transfer Family = managed SFTP/FTPS endpoint (exchange with partners); DataSync = bulk migration/copy between storages

questions.explanation: Transfer Family is a standard protocol endpoint (SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2) → S3/EFS for partner exchange. DataSync automates bulk migration/copy between storage systems (NFS/SMB/S3/EFS/FSx).

whyNots.A: They are not databases.
whyNots.B: Reversed — SFTP is Transfer Family; bulk migration is DataSync.
whyNots.C: Certificates are ACM.

hints: Remember: Transfer Family is for partner SFTP/FTPS; DataSync is for bulk data movement.

questions.stem:
Query data in S3 with SQL, serverless, paying per data scanned.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Athena runs ad-hoc SQL directly on data in S3, serverless, charging by volume scanned.

whyNots.B: EMR is a Hadoop/Spark cluster.
whyNots.C: RDS is a transactional database, not for querying S3.
whyNots.D: Provisioned Redshift is a data warehouse cluster.

hints: Think about a serverless SQL query service for data in S3.

questions.stem:
Intelligent threat detection analyzing logs (Flow Logs, CloudTrail, DNS).

Which service?
questions.explanation: GuardDuty detects malicious activity by analyzing Flow Logs, CloudTrail, and DNS with ML.

whyNots.A: Config is configuration compliance.
whyNots.C: Inspector is vulnerability/CVE.
whyNots.D: Macie is sensitive data in S3.

hints: Think about a service that detects threats by analyzing logs.

questions.stem:
Extract text, form fields, and tables from scanned documents (OCR).

Which service?
questions.explanation: Textract uses OCR + ML to extract text, fields, and tables from scanned documents.

whyNots.A: Polly is text-to-speech.
whyNots.B: Comprehend is NLP for text.
whyNots.D: Rekognition is general image/video.

hints: Remember: Textract extracts text and structured data from scanned documents.

questions.stem:
Rightsizing recommendations (overprovisioned/idle) for EC2, EBS, Lambda, RDS.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer recommends ideal sizing and detects idle resources.

whyNots.A: Inspector is vulnerability.
whyNots.B: Budgets manages budget/alerts.
whyNots.C: Pricing Calculator estimates future cost.

hints: Think about a service that recommends optimal resource sizing.

questions.stem:
Orchestrate a multi-step flow with branching and retry, without coding the glue.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates workflows as state machines, with branching, retry, and error handling.

whyNots.B: Lambda calling Lambda manually is fragile.
whyNots.C: SQS is a queue.
whyNots.D: SNS is pub/sub.

hints: Remember: Step Functions orchestrates workflows with branching and retry.

questions.stem:
Discover whether an S3 bucket or role is unintentionally shared with an external account.

Which service?
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer identifies resources shared with external entities, generating findings.

whyNots.A: Artifact downloads AWS reports.
whyNots.C: Budgets is cost.
whyNots.D: Macie finds sensitive data in S3.

hints: Think about a service that flags unintentional external access to resources.

questions.stem:
Centralize and automate backup of EC2, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS by policy, with Vault Lock (WORM).

Which service?
questions.explanation: AWS Backup centralizes and automates backups across services, with Vault Lock (WORM) and cross-Region copy.

whyNots.A: Config is compliance.
whyNots.B: DataSync is transfer between storages.
whyNots.D: Glacier is an archive storage class (destination), not orchestration.

hints: Remember: AWS Backup centralizes policy-based backups with Vault Lock.

questions.stem:
Extremely high-throughput file system for HPC and ML training.

Which service?
questions.explanation: FSx for Lustre is the high-throughput file system for HPC and ML; EFS is general-purpose Linux NFS; FSx for Windows is SMB.

whyNots.A: sc1 is cold, low-cost HDD.
whyNots.B: Glacier is archive.
whyNots.C: EFS is general-purpose NFS, not HPC.

hints: Think about a high-throughput file system for HPC and ML.

questions.stem:
Block SQL injection and XSS in HTTP requests of a web app on CloudFront/ALB.

Which service?
questions.explanation: WAF filters HTTP(S) requests and blocks SQLi/XSS, attached to CloudFront/ALB/API Gateway.

whyNots.B: GuardDuty detects threats; it does not filter HTTP.
whyNots.C: Shield is network DDoS (L3/L4).
whyNots.D: Security Group is L3/L4; it does not understand HTTP.

hints: Remember: WAF blocks SQL injection and XSS at layer 7.

questions.stem:
Graph database for recommendation relationships and fraud detection.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Neptune is the managed graph database, ideal for highly connected data (recommendations, fraud, social networks).

whyNots.A: Timestream is time series.
whyNots.C: DocumentDB is document (MongoDB).
whyNots.D: Redshift is data warehouse.

hints: Think about a managed graph database for connected data.

questions.stem:
