A web app needs to stay online if an AZ fails, distribute HTTP traffic, and scale on demand; the relational database cannot have downtime during an AZ failure.

Which design meets the requirements?

options.text: ALB + Auto Scaling across multiple AZs + RDS Multi-AZ

questions.explanation: ALB distributes traffic, Auto Scaling across multiple AZs scales and replaces unhealthy instances, and RDS Multi-AZ automatically fails over if an AZ fails. Classic resilient design.

whyNots.A: Single Spot is interruptible and fragile.
whyNots.B: Instance Store is ephemeral; a resilient database is missing.
whyNots.D: Single instance and Single-AZ do not survive an AZ outage.

hints: Think about distributing HTTP traffic, scaling across AZs, and a resilient database.

questions.stem:
An application on EC2 needs to read from an S3 bucket without embedded credentials in the code.

What is the secure way?

options.text: Embed the access key in the code, but in a separate file
Make the bucket public — read-only poses no risk
Use the root account, which does not need permission configuration
Attach an IAM Role to the instance (temporary credentials)

questions.explanation: The IAM Role delivers temporary credentials to the instance via an instance profile, without long-term keys in the code. It is the number-one best practice.

whyNots.A: Embedded access keys leak easily.
whyNots.B: A public bucket is a serious flaw.
whyNots.C: Root is forbidden for daily use.

hints: Remember: attach an IAM Role to EC2 for temporary credentials.

questions.stem:
A stateless, interruption-tolerant nightly batch processes data in S3; afterwards it must be queried with SQL. Lowest possible cost.

Which combination?

options.text: Spot Instances + data in S3 + Athena

questions.explanation: Spot (up to 90% off) runs the interruptible batch; Athena queries S3 serverless (pay per data scanned). Nothing stays running unnecessarily.

whyNots.B: RI assumes constant use.
whyNots.C: Dedicated/always-on EMR is the opposite of cheap.
whyNots.D: On-Demand 24/7 + always-on Redshift is expensive.

hints: Think about low-cost compute for interruptible batch plus serverless SQL on S3.

questions.stem:
Global users download the same static images from an overloaded origin server, with high latency for those far away.

Which service solves this?

options.text: Amazon EBS, caching near the user
Amazon CloudFront (CDN caching at the edge)
AWS Direct Connect to each user

questions.explanation: CloudFront caches content at edge locations near users, reducing latency and offloading the origin.

whyNots.A: EBS is instance disk.
whyNots.C: SQS is a queue.
whyNots.D: Direct Connect is a hybrid link.

hints: Remember: a CDN caches static content at the edge near users.

questions.stem:
An endpoint receives unpredictable bursts that trigger processing. Absorb the peak without losing requests, serverless and decoupled.

Which architecture?

options.text: API Gateway -> synchronous Lambda, no queue
API Gateway -> SQS -> Lambda consuming the queue

questions.explanation: SQS cushions the burst; Lambda consumes at its own pace (with DLQ). Serverless, decoupled, without losing requests.

whyNots.A: Synchronous without a queue can exceed concurrency.
whyNots.B: Static cannot process dynamic requests.
whyNots.D: A single EC2 cannot absorb a burst.

hints: Think about placing a queue between the API and processing to absorb bursts.

questions.stem:
Prevent, from the top down, any child account from turning off CloudTrail or creating resources outside certain regions, regardless of local IAM.

Which resource imposes this guardrail?

options.text: Security Groups applied across the Organization
IAM roles in the management account valid in every account
Bucket policies, the global ceiling for child accounts

questions.explanation: SCPs define the maximum permission ceiling for OUs/accounts: even if IAM allows, if an SCP denies, the action does not happen. They do not grant access, only limit.

whyNots.A: SG is networking.
whyNots.B: IAM grants within an account, not a global ceiling.
whyNots.C: Bucket policy is S3 access.

hints: Remember: Service Control Policies set the maximum permissions across accounts.

questions.stem:
Repeated reads of the same data are overloading RDS. Reduce latency and relieve the database.

Which service to place in front?

options.text: Amazon S3 (read cache for the database)

questions.explanation: ElastiCache keeps hot results in memory (microseconds), offloading RDS from repeated SELECTs.

whyNots.B: Athena is SQL on S3.
whyNots.C: S3 is object storage.
whyNots.D: Glue is ETL.

hints: Think about an in-memory cache for repeated reads.

questions.stem:
Logs go to S3: hot for 30 days, rare until 90, then archive for 7 years (retrieval in hours is OK).

Ideal cost strategy?

options.text: Expire and delete all logs at 30 days, since old retention is not required
Lifecycle: Standard -> Standard-IA (30d) -> Glacier Deep Archive (90d), expire at 7 years
Move logs to provisioned EBS volumes, which cost less than S3
Keep everything in S3 Standard forever, because archiving does not accept logs

questions.explanation: A lifecycle policy transitions by age (Standard -> IA -> Deep Archive) and expires at the end of retention — minimum cost without manual work.

whyNots.A: Deleting violates retention.
whyNots.C: EBS is expensive for archiving.
whyNots.D: Standard forever is expensive.

hints: Remember: match S3 lifecycle transitions to declining access patterns.

questions.stem:
A web application suffers SQL injection and XSS attempts on CloudFront/ALB.

Which service filters this at layer 7?
questions.explanation: WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks SQLi/XSS, attached to CloudFront/ALB/API Gateway.

whyNots.A: SG is L3/L4.
whyNots.B: Shield is network DDoS.
whyNots.D: Macie is sensitive data in S3.

hints: Remember: WAF filters SQL injection and XSS at layer 7.

questions.stem:
Global app requires near-zero RPO/RTO, low-latency reads on multiple continents, PostgreSQL-compatible database.

Which solution?

options.text: Aurora in one Region with Multi-AZ, covering the globe
RDS Single-AZ + snapshots with zero RPO

questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database spans multiple Regions (global reads + cross-region DR, RTO in minutes), PostgreSQL-compatible. Route 53 routes between regions.

whyNots.A: Multi-AZ does not cover region loss.
whyNots.B: DynamoDB is not PostgreSQL-compatible.
whyNots.C: RPO/RTO in hours.

hints: Think about a multi-Region, PostgreSQL-compatible database for global reads and disaster recovery.

questions.stem:
An in-memory database processes huge datasets in RAM and needs a lot of memory per instance.

Which EC2 instance family?
questions.explanation: Memory optimized (R, X) delivers a lot of RAM per instance — ideal for in-memory databases and analysis of large in-memory datasets.

whyNots.B: Compute is CPU.
whyNots.C: Storage is local I/O.
whyNots.D: General is balanced.

hints: Remember: choose Memory optimized instances for high memory requirements.

questions.stem:
The RDS password must be rotated automatically every 30 days without touching the code.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager stores the secret and rotates it automatically (via Lambda) without changing the code.

whyNots.A: KMS is for keys, not passwords.
whyNots.C: ACM is for certificates.
whyNots.D: Parameter Store does not rotate on its own.

hints: Think about automatic credential rotation.

questions.stem:
A financial system requires messages to be processed in exact order and exactly once.

Which SQS queue type?
questions.explanation: The FIFO queue preserves ordering and guarantees exactly-once processing (no duplicates). Standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort ordering.

whyNots.A: More consumers do not fix ordering or duplication.
whyNots.B: Standard queues can duplicate or reorder messages.
whyNots.D: Only FIFO guarantees the requirement.

hints: Remember that strict order plus exactly-once processing means FIFO.

questions.stem:
A UDP game has lag by country; the team wants to enter the AWS network at the closest edge and have a static entry IP.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and moves traffic onto the AWS network at the closest edge, supporting both TCP and UDP — ideal for UDP games.

whyNots.A: Direct Connect is a link from your data center.
whyNots.B: Route 53 depends on DNS caching.
whyNots.C: CloudFront is a cacheable HTTP CDN.

hints: Think about UDP, static IPs, and accelerating transport through the AWS edge.

questions.stem:
Administrators need SSH access to instances in a private subnet without exposing them to the internet.

Which pattern?

options.text: Bastion host in a public subnet (or SSM Session Manager)
Open port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 — the security group already filters who gets in
Move to a public subnet while keeping everything equally protected
Public IP on the private instances, only for the admin team

questions.explanation: A bastion host in the public subnet acts as an SSH bridge to private instances without exposing them. A modern alternative is SSM Session Manager, which requires no open port.

whyNots.B: Open port 22 is a serious security flaw.
whyNots.C: Moving to a public subnet exposes the instances.
whyNots.D: Exposing a public IP is exactly what you want to avoid.

hints: Think about an administration bridge that keeps private instances off the internet.

questions.stem:
When a dev environment budget is exceeded, EC2 instances must stop automatically without manual intervention.

Which feature?
questions.explanation: Budget Actions execute an automatic response when the budget crosses a threshold: stopping EC2/RDS instances, applying IAM policies, or applying SCPs.

whyNots.A: Pricing Calculator only estimates costs.
whyNots.C: Trusted Advisor only recommends.
whyNots.D: Cost Explorer only analyzes.

hints: Remember that automatic responses to budget overruns are called Budget Actions.

questions.stem:
A critical database requires extremely high, consistent IOPS and low latency.

Which EBS volume type?

options.text: gp2, which guarantees constant maximum IOPS
io2 / io2 Block Express (Provisioned IOPS SSD)

questions.explanation: io2 (and Block Express) deliver high, consistent provisioned IOPS, low latency, and enhanced durability — ideal for critical databases.

whyNots.A: gp2 does not guarantee consistently very high IOPS.
whyNots.B: st1 is for sequential throughput.
whyNots.D: sc1 is a cold HDD.

hints: Think about Provisioned IOPS SSD for the highest consistent IOPS.

questions.stem:
For disaster recovery, a copy of objects must automatically exist in ANOTHER AWS region.

Which S3 feature?

options.text: Transfer Acceleration, which copies to another region
Same-Region Replication, the multi-region S3 option
Lifecycle policy moving objects to another region

questions.explanation: CRR replicates objects automatically to a bucket in another region (requires versioning on source and destination) — useful for DR and geographic compliance.

whyNots.A: Transfer Acceleration is for uploads.
whyNots.B: SRR is same-region only.
whyNots.C: Lifecycle policies change storage class or expire objects.

hints: Remember that automatic copies across regions use Cross-Region Replication with versioning enabled.

questions.stem:
A site behind an ALB needs HTTPS with a free TLS certificate that renews automatically.

Which service?
questions.explanation: ACM provisions free public TLS certificates and renews them automatically, integrating with ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway.

whyNots.B: CloudHSM is a dedicated HSM.
whyNots.C: Secrets Manager is for secrets.
whyNots.D: KMS is for keys.

hints: Remember that free TLS certificates with automatic renewal come from ACM.

questions.stem:
A real-time auction reads the same DynamoDB items millions of times per second and wants microsecond latency.

Which feature?
questions.explanation: DAX is the in-memory cache for DynamoDB, reducing read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for read-intensive workloads.

whyNots.A: Global Tables are for multi-region replication.
whyNots.C: Streams capture changes.
whyNots.D: Backup does not accelerate reads.

hints: Think about the in-memory cache that accelerates DynamoDB reads to microseconds.

questions.stem:
A bank uses Direct Connect and fears going offline if the link fails; it wants a cheaper automatic backup.

Which architecture?

options.text: Only a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet, which gives the same bandwidth guarantee
Two Direct Connect links at the same location, with no backup VPN
Primary Direct Connect + backup Site-to-Site VPN (automatic failover)
Primary Direct Connect + CloudFront as a fallback path to the data center

questions.explanation: Direct Connect as the primary path and Site-to-Site VPN as the backup (failover via BGP) combines low latency with a cheaper standby option.

whyNots.A: VPN-only loses Direct Connect's low latency.
whyNots.B: Two Direct Connect links is the most expensive option.
whyNots.D: CloudFront is not a hybrid connectivity path.

hints: Think about the classic pattern of a primary Direct Connect with a cheaper VPN backup.

questions.stem:
Compliance wants to know whether personally identifiable information and credit card numbers are stored unintentionally in S3 buckets.

Which service?
questions.explanation: Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and classify sensitive data (PII) in S3 buckets.

whyNots.A: GuardDuty is for threat detection.
whyNots.B: Config is for configuration compliance.
whyNots.C: Inspector is for vulnerability assessment.

hints: Remember that discovering sensitive data (PII) in S3 is Macie's job.

questions.stem:
A steady 24/7 workload runs for 3 years; the company changes instance families frequently and also uses Fargate and Lambda. They want a discount without tying the commitment to a specific instance.

Which purchasing model?
questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans provide a discount for a committed USD/hour spend that is flexible across instance families, regions, and includes Fargate and Lambda.

whyNots.B: Standard Reserved Instances lock you to a specific configuration.
whyNots.C: On-Demand does not provide the discount.
whyNots.D: Spot Instances are interruptible.

hints: Think about a flexible spending commitment that includes Fargate and Lambda.

questions.stem:
A developer wants to run containers without managing servers: just specify CPU and memory per task and pay for that.

Which option?
questions.explanation: Fargate is the serverless container engine (works with ECS and EKS): you specify CPU and memory per task and pay for that, with no servers to manage.

whyNots.A: EC2 launch type requires managing the fleet.
whyNots.C: AWS Batch on dedicated EC2 still manages infrastructure.
whyNots.D: Plain EC2 involves the most management.

hints: Remember that running containers without managing servers means Fargate.

questions.stem:
For every image uploaded to S3, generate a thumbnail, write NoSQL metadata, and notify several systems — event-driven and serverless.

Which combination?

options.text: Cron on EC2 scanning the bucket every minute (pure event)
API Gateway WebSocket + RDS notifying the systems

questions.explanation: The S3 event triggers Lambda (to generate the thumbnail), writes metadata to DynamoDB, and publishes to SNS for fan-out to multiple systems — serverless and event-driven.

whyNots.A: A cron scanning the bucket is inefficient and not event-driven.
whyNots.B: Kinesis and Redshift are for streaming and analytics.
whyNots.D: WebSocket plus RDS is not the standard pattern for processing uploads.

hints: Think about S3 events triggering Lambda, DynamoDB for NoSQL metadata, and SNS to fan out notifications.
